scenes.synopsis: dawn at the finished Park — the whole, complete; the walk, the accounting. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dawn, and the Park whole. Rose walks the west gallery before the household is up, and the portraits hang straight in the morning light — the Ravencrofts, the Hartwells, the whole long argument of her blood, framed and dusted and exactly where they belong. Ten seasons of scaffolding, and now: the plaster dry, the floors waxed, the windows washed. It smells of beeswax and cut grass and nothing else. Nothing unfinished.)*
> *(She counts the way Augusta taught her — once for the sum, once for the nerve. The west gallery: confronted and hung. The servants' hall: governed. The stables: running. The library: ordered. The cottages: lived in. The lake pavilion: gleaming. The walled garden: open. The grounds: dressed. The state rooms: ready. She has said these words before, as promises. This morning they are inventory.)*
> *(At the gallery's end the window gives onto the drive, and the drive is empty, and the empty is a question she has not yet asked: now that the house is finished, what is it for? The question sits in her the way the dawn sits on the lawn — early, and not to be hurried. She turns back toward the stairs. The household will be stirring. The day — the first day of the finished house — is about to begin.)*

scenes.synopsis: the announcement — the housewarming ball, declared at breakfast; Letitia's arithmetic of joy. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Breakfast, and Letitia reads the Gazette with the air of a woman checking the weather for a voyage she has already decided to take.)*
> "Say it again, darling." Letitia does not look up. "Slowly. I want to hear whether it sounds mad in daylight."
> "A housewarming ball." Rose butters her toast with undue care. "The Park is finished. The ton is invited to see what we built. Music, supper, the ballroom lit the way it was meant to be lit."
> "In daylight," Letitia says, "it sounds madder. Which is how I know it's right." She folds the paper. "When?"
> "Three weeks. The full moon — the drive will light itself."
> "The full moon." Letitia reaches for the household book. "Darling, the moon is a guest too, and she'll want the good candles. Write to Élise today. And Rose —" the hawk's eyes, suddenly grave — "do it properly. A finished house deserves a finished party. No economies where the ton can see them."
> *(Rose writes it down: Élise, today. The household book gains its first line of the finished era, and the ink is barely dry before Letitia has filled half a page with candles.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Dowager's verdict — what was built, and what it cost; Augusta at seventy-two, exact. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta's morning room. The Dowager sits with the Park's completion laid out before her like a hand of cards — the mason's final account, the gardeners' roster, the inventory of the state rooms — and regards it all with the particular stillness of a woman who has waited a very long time to be unsurprised.)*
> "Well." The spectacles lower. "It is done."
> "It is done, Grandmama."
> "I watched your grandfather break the entail to save this house." A tap on the papers. "I watched your father let it rot to punish it. I watched Rackham sell it stone by stone to pay for his ruin." The spectacles rise. "And now I am watching you finish it. Child —" the rarest pause — "this is the first time in my life the house has looked the way it was meant to look."
> *(Rose finds, to her annoyance, that her eyes are wet. Augusta pretends not to see, which is the Dowager's entire philosophy of tenderness.)*
> "The ball," Augusta says. "You will invite the dragon, of course."
> "Of course."
> "Good. A victory no one witnesses is a rumor. A victory the dragon attends is history." She returns to her letters. "Invite her first, child. Let the town watch her decide."

scenes.synopsis: the settlement's last paper — Quill closes the file; the house, hers beyond challenge. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Mr. Quill's chambers, by post and by visit both — the solicitor has come down to the Park himself, which he does for exactly two kinds of business: funerals and finalities.)*
> "The settlement is enrolled, Miss Hartwell." Quill lays the last paper on the library desk with something like ceremony. "The entail's true history is found, recorded, and beyond dispute. Mr. Hugh Hartwell's father's name stands cleared in the record —" he nods toward the window, toward the stone where the name is cut — "and in the stone. The mortgages are discharged. The title is —" the professional's pause — "unassailable."
> "Say it plainly, Mr. Quill."
> "The house is yours, miss. Beyond challenge. Forever is a word solicitors are not paid to use, so I will use it once and charge you nothing for it: forever."
> *(He stays for luncheon, which he never does, and eats Letitia's chicken pie with the air of a man who has closed a very long book. On the step he turns.)*
> "Miss Hartwell. In fifty-eight years of practice I have never seen a client finish what you have finished. Build something worthy of the paper it's written on." He bows. "That is my whole advice, and it is free."

scenes.synopsis: the atelier's commission — the housewarming gown; the finest thing the atelier has ever made. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The atelier, and Élise at twenty-two with chalk on her fingers and the whole of her future in her eyes. The commission is laid out like a treaty: the housewarming ball, the series' grandest occasion, and the gown that must answer it.)*
> "The finest thing we have ever made." Élise says it flatly, the way other people say the weather. "Not the finest of the season. The finest of the atelier. Ten seasons of everything I have learned, in one gown."
> "Can you?" Rose asks. "In three weeks?"
> "I can." The chalk turns in her fingers. "The modiste's girl is the ton's dressmaker now, Miss Hartwell. It is time the ton knew it." A smile, sudden and young. "Ivory. Not white — ivory, the color of the Park's stone at noon. And the embroidery —" she unrolls the sketch — "the Hartwell rose. Not yet blooming in the garden. Blooming on you first."
> *(Rose looks at the sketch for a long time. The gown is not armor and not apology. It is a house, rendered in silk.)*
> "Begin," Rose says.

scenes.synopsis: the west gallery, hung — the portraits, the argument of blood, at rest. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The west gallery at noon. Rose walks it again — she has walked it three times today, and means to walk it a fourth — and the portraits hang in their restored order: the Ravencrofts who built, the Hartwells who kept and broke and sold, and the empty frame at the end that is not empty anymore.)*
> *(The frame holds Harrow's gift: not a portrait but a plan — the Park drawn as it is now, whole, every zone inked in the historian's careful hand, with the date written underneath in Quill's clerkly script. A house, documented. She stands before it longer than the ancestors.)*
> *(A housemaid passes with a duster and bobs, unselfconscious, the way servants bob in a house that is loved. The gallery holds its beeswax smell. The light does what light does in a finished room: it stays.)*

scenes.synopsis: the servants' hall, governed — the household's pride in the finished house. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Below stairs, and the servants' hall at dinner — the long table, the good joints, the particular noise of a household that has won.)*
> "To the house!" The footmen drink it standing, which is against Mrs. Quick's rules and therefore permitted once. Mrs. Quick herself, forty-four and immovable, permits it with a nod that is almost a smile.
> "Miss Hartwell." The housekeeper finds Rose by the dresser afterward. "Ten years I've kept this house through —" she stops, because housekeepers do not name ruins. "The ball. The staff are —" another stop — "we mean to show them, miss. The silver the way it should be. The linen pressed twice."
> "Twice, Mrs. Quick?"
> "For the ton, miss." The immovable mouth does something extraordinary. "They'll see what a house looks like when it's kept."
> *(Rose goes upstairs with the noise of the hall in her ears, and understands that the housewarming has two hosts: herself, and everyone below stairs who kept the place while she was earning it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the stables, running — the courier lines, the horses; the house, in motion. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The stables at exercise hour: the strings going out in the morning mist, the yard swept, the tack room smelling of leather and order.)*
> "All sound, Miss Hartwell." The head groom walks her down the boxes. "The courier lines run clean to London and back. The carriage horses are fit for the moonlight drive —" he grins — "and the greys have been washed twice already, miss, in anticipation."
> "Twice?"
> "The lads are keen, miss. It's the ball." He lowers his voice. "Begging your pardon, but the yard means to turn out the carriages the way the hall means to turn out the silver. There is —" he searches — "professional feeling involved."
> *(Rose lays a hand on the nearest grey's neck, and the horse blows warm into her palm. The Park is not only stone and paper. It is this: the warm breath, the swept yard, the professional feeling. She walks back to the house through the mist, and the mist is burning off, and the day is going to be fine.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE INVITATION (the ball's character: triumph, gratitude, or challenge). The guest list waits; decide what the night is for. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library, afternoon: the guest list spread across the desk like a battlefield map, and Letitia with her pen poised. The first invitations go out tomorrow. The question is not who. The question is what the night is for — and the wording of the first cards will tell the ton before the ball does.)*
> "Triumph," Letitia says, "says: look what I built. Gratitude says: look what we built together. Challenge says: come and see if you can deny it." She taps the list. "The town will read the invitation the way Bell reads a leader — for the thesis. Decide, darling, before the ink does it for you."
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — The invitation:*
- **Triumph, openly declared** — *look what I built.* The cards announce a celebration of the Park's completion, plainly and proudly. (Consequence: the bold come curious and the timid come wary — the night has a spine, but spines invite breaking.)
- **Gratitude, widely shared** — *look what we built together.* The cards honor everyone who kept the house — servants named, tenants named, the town named. (Consequence: the household weeps and the ton is disarmed — but gratitude gives the dragon room to call it sentiment.)
- **Challenge, politely issued** — *come and see.* The cards are simple, confident, and impossible to refuse without admitting fear. (Consequence: the brave come and the cowards show themselves by staying — but a challenge is a dare, and dares get answered.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: triumph, gratitude, or challenge. The ball was always going to happen. The thesis is hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry rides over with the morning post; the gift of attention, on purpose. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He rides over most mornings now — not every morning; most. Today the post bag is the excuse, and they both know it is an excuse, and neither of them minds.)*
> "The London letters." Henry hands them over on the terrace steps, and his hand is careful with hers in the way it has been careful for years. "I took the liberty of sorting. The bills at the bottom. The interesting at the top."
> "You sorted my post, Major?"
> "I did." Unmoved. "You have a ball to plan. The bills can wait at the bottom, where they belong. It is —" he considers — "a small thing. I am practicing small things."
> *(She reads the top letter standing on the steps, and he holds the horses, and the morning does what mornings do at the Park now: it behaves. When she looks up he is watching the drive, not her — the gift of attention, given the way he gives everything: sideways, and on purpose.)*
> "Stay for breakfast, Henry."
> "I had planned to." The smallest smile. "It was in the post bag too."

scenes.synopsis: the library, ordered — the house's paper memory, reclaimed and shelved. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library at three: the shelves ordered, the catalogues fair-copied, the paper memory of the house reclaimed from ten seasons of strongboxes and hiding places.)*
> *(She runs a finger along the spines — the estate books, the letter files, the bound Gazettes, Harrow's histories — and stops at the shelf where the Network's paper used to live. It is empty now. The last of it went to the S9 settlement, spent and exhausted. The empty shelf is the truest thing in the room.)*
> *(Quill's final paper lies on the desk, sealed and enrolled. She does not need to read it again. The library holds the afternoon the way it holds everything: patiently, and as a promise kept. She takes down a novel instead — something frivolous, something French — and reads for an hour, which is the most radical thing she has done in weeks.)*

scenes.synopsis: the walled garden — the Hartwell rose, not yet blooming; the legacy, literal and living. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The walled garden, late afternoon: the reclaimed beds in their restored order, the roses bred across the seasons standing in their rows — and at the row's end, the Hartwell rose, budded but not yet open.)*
> "Not yet, Miss Hartwell." The gardener touches the bud the way other men touch money. "Another week. Perhaps two. It'll open when it's ready, and not a day before — roses are like the ton, miss. They bloom on their own terms."
> "And the housewarming's flowers?"
> "All Hartwell-grown, miss. Every stem from this garden. The ton'll walk through flowers we grew ourselves —" he straightens, pride and soil in equal measure — "and they'll know it."
> *(She bends to the bud. It is green and tight and absolutely certain of itself. Somewhere in the next fortnight, the first bloom of the Hartwell rose will open — her legacy, literal and living — and she means to be there when it does.)*

scenes.synopsis: the portrait, nearly finished — Octavia's studio at the Park; devotion, witnessed. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia has taken the old still-room for her studio — the north light, the quiet — and the picnic portrait stands on the easel nearly finished: Rose, laughing, the Park behind her, the paint still wet at the edges.)*
> "Another week." Octavia wipes her brush. "The laugh is the hard part. I have painted you angry, afraid, triumphant, exhausted —" a look — "but laughing, from the picnic, with the light doing what it did — that I have had to earn."
> "And have you?"
> "Nearly." She steps back. "When it's done, it hangs in the Park. Not in London. Here." The precise voice, precise as ever. "Two houses, one shared life, Rose. That was the arrangement. The portrait is my half of it."
> *(Rose looks at the almost-laugh — her own face, caught mid-joy — and feels the peculiar vertigo of being seen accurately. Octavia cleans her brushes. The north light holds. The devotion in the room is the quietest thing in the finished house.)*

scenes.synopsis: the canal — Julian's mended gloves; the debts, nearly paid; the terrace, in view. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The canal walk at dusk. Julian falls into step beside her the way he has fallen into step for years — a little behind, then alongside, then exactly where he means to be.)*
> "The last of the brother's debts." He says it the way other men say the weather. "Paid Tuesday. With money I earned. Your money never touched it —" a quick look — "you'll have Quill check, I know. Have him check."
> "I won't."
> "You will." The ghost of the old smile. "It's your nature, Rose. It's why the house is finished." He turns the mended gloves in his hands — the gloves, mended years ago, kept ever since. "I keep these. Not as penance. As —" he searches — "evidence. That a man can be mended too."
> *(They walk to the terrace and stand at its edge, and the Park lies below them in the dusk, whole. He does not offer his arm. He offers his company, which is rarer.)*
> "Free," he says quietly. "The terrace. The gloves. All of it. Nearly."

scenes.synopsis: the woman the house chose — dress the finished era's first morning; direction + twenty 5-coin pins, story morsels between, reveal coda. (Turns: 21)
scenes.prose:
> **Occasion brief — The finished house, announced:** "Three weeks to the housewarming. The ton has heard. Dress for the woman the Park chose — not the girl who was ruined, not the warrior who fought, but the mistress of the finished whole. **Editorial criterion: completion.**"
>
> **A. The Heir** — the Ravencroft line, stated; deep claret, the archive's color, re-cut for the finished era. Motif: the Hartwell oak at the hem, restrained — the line, embroidered. Thread: **gold** (the landed, stated) / **claret silk** (the archive, matched) / **ivory whitework** (the finished, lit). Colorway: claret + gold + ivory. Accessories: the grandmother's pearls; pearl drop earrings; claret kid gloves.
> **B. The Mistress** — the house's own colors; dove grey, the Park's stone at noon, severe and exact. Motif: feather-stitch, grey on grey — quietness with a spine. Thread: **silver** (the exact, edged) / **dove silk** (the stone, matched) / **pearl** (the finished, lit). Colorway: dove grey + silver + pearl. Accessories: a silver ribbon at the throat; no pendant — the throat, plain and unowned; grey kid gloves, immaculate.
> **C. The Builder** — work-dress honored; deep green, the garden's color, practical silk that moves. Motif: the rosebud, small at cuff and hem — the growing, embroidered. Thread: **bronze** (the earned, stated) / **green silk** (the garden, matched) / **cream** (the honest, lit). Colorway: deep green + bronze + cream. Accessories: a bronze hair comb; the mended gloves, carried; green kid gloves.
>
> *(The dressing room, the finished house's first morning: the season's opening gown. She dresses the way the house has taught her: completion, not display.)*
> (T1 · choice — the direction) *She commits: the heir, the mistress, or the builder — the finished era's thesis, remembered. The hair, composed. The accessories, exact. The mirror, to be consulted briefly. **Direction.** Three weeks to the housewarming — dress for the woman the Park chose. **Editorial criterion.** Completion — every choice must answer the finished house, not the ballroom.*
> *(System: commit to a direction — remembered for the finished era. Then the pins begin. Each pin costs 5 coins; no Crown SKUs; jewels from owned pieces only, never a ritual step.)*
> **Pin 1 (T2 · micro-decision) — Gown, chosen:** the morning's face — the claret stated, or the grey exact, or the green honored — whichever the day chose, the completion worn. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 2 (T3 · micro-decision) — Fit, exact:** the composed — no rustle for the stairs, no train for the morning's business. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 3 (T4 · micro-decision) — Sleeves, long:** the day's — composed, unhurried, giving nothing away. *5 coins.*
> *(The pins accumulate — the gown's line set, the morning's sleeves — and the dressing room holds its candlelight the way the gallery holds the dawn: patiently.)*
> **Pin 4 (T5 · micro-decision) — Neckline, modest:** the mistress's — the finished house asks for the serious. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 5 (T6 · micro-decision) — Hair, coiled:** the braided — the composed, the kept; the ornament's none. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 6 (T7 · micro-decision) — Ribbon, throat's:** the direction's punctuation — gold, silver, or bronze — the completion, tied. *5 coins.*
> *(The throat's ribbon tied — the completion's knot — and the morning leans in, the finished house waiting.)*
> **Pin 7 (T8 · micro-decision) — Gloves, immaculate:** the mistress's gauntlets — expected, and without a mark. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 8 (T9 · micro-decision) — Slippers, quiet:** the stairs' — the gallery floor's, the unheard. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 9 (T10 · micro-decision) — Fan, carried:** the reticule's companion — the day's punctuation, the wrist's. *5 coins.*
> *(Quiet slippers, the fan's weight — the morning asks for the unheard, and she gives it.)*
> **Pin 10 (T11 · micro-decision) — Brooch, small:** the oak's — the line's, the unshowy; the heir's, not the mourner's. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 11 (T12 · micro-decision) — Scent, none:** the morning's — the house smells of beeswax; the lady adds nothing. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 12 (T13 · micro-decision) — Posture, straight:** the builder's — the earned, the stood; the spine's. *5 coins.*
> *(The spine straightens — the earned, stood — and the mirror is consulted briefly from the corner of her eye.)*
> **Pin 13 (T14 · micro-decision) — Gaze, level:** the mistress's — met eye to eye, the day's. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 14 (T15 · micro-decision) — Voice, even:** the completion's — the finished, the unhurried. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 15 (T16 · micro-decision) — Hands, still:** the fan's — the held, the composed. *5 coins.*
> *(Level gaze, even voice, still hands — the completion's instruments, tuned for the finished house.)*
> **Pin 16 (T17 · micro-decision) — Step, measured:** the stairs' — the gallery's, the entered. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 17 (T18 · micro-decision) — Smile, rare:** the heir's — the finished, the priced. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 18 (T19 · micro-decision) — Nod, once:** the morning's answer — the household's, the returned. *5 coins.*
> *(The step measured, the smile rare, the nod once — the finished house's own grammar, spoken fluently.)*
> **Pin 19 (T20 · micro-decision) — Turn, away:** the gallery's — the entered, the owned. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 20 (T21 · micro-decision) — Door, held:** the morning's — passed, standing straighter, the completion's. *5 coins.*
> *(System: 20 pins × 5 coins = 100 coins. The completed direction is remembered. Owned jewels may be added freely from the open shelf, never as a step. No Crown SKU touches the ritual.)*
> *(Story morsel: Letitia's voice through the bedroom door: "A finished house, darling, is like a finished sentence — it wants a full stop, not an exclamation. Dress the period.")*
> *(Story morsel: a card slipped under the door, Augusta's hand — "Completion, child. Not display." She pins it inside the wardrobe door, where she will see it last.)*
> *(Reveal coda: the mirror, consulted briefly — and the woman in it is not the girl who was ruined and not the warrior who fought. She is the mistress of the finished whole, and the gown knows it before she does.)*

scenes.synopsis: a letter from Paris — Laurent's news; England, the subject. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The letter comes with the afternoon post, the seal French, the hand unmistakable. Rose reads it on the terrace, where the light is honest.)*
> *"My dear Rose — Paris writes to me daily, and daily I do not answer. The family has opinions about England. The family has always had opinions about everything; it is their chief manufacture. I find I have opinions of my own now, which surprises us both..."*
> *(She reads it twice. The charm is all there — the polish, the lightness — and underneath it, for the first time in ten seasons, something unpolished: a man deciding. He does not say what he has decided. Laurent never says. He arrives, or he does not, and the arriving is the sentence.)*
> *(She folds the letter and keeps it. The terrace holds the afternoon. Somewhere across the Channel, a Frenchman is being un-French about making up his mind, and the comedy of it steadies her more than the sentiment.)*

scenes.synopsis: a glittering letter — Lavinia writes from London; loyal, hers, sharpening. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Lavinia's letter arrives on scented paper, the handwriting all angles and velocity.)*
> *"Darling — a housewarming! At last, something worth dressing for. London is already at war over the invitations, which is exactly as it should be. I have told everyone who matters that I am coming, which means everyone who matters is coming, because no one can bear to be where I am not. You may thank me in pearls..."*
> *(Rose laughs aloud, alone in the morning room, which is the correct response to Lavinia and has been for years. The letter goes on — gossip, alliances, a list of who has asked after the ball with what expression — and underneath the glitter, the intelligence is exact. Lavinia has always been the best scout in London. She is simply, these days, Rose's scout.)*
> *(She writes back: come early, stay late, bring the pearls yourself. Some alliances are load-bearing, and this one is holding up the whole season.)*

scenes.synopsis: the tenant cottages — power measured by whose lives it touches. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The cottages at tea-time: smoke from the chimneys, washing on the lines, children on the lane who stare and then wave, having decided she is safe.)*
> *(She walks the row with the agent's book in her head — roofs sound, rents fair, the schoolroom's new slates ordered — and stops at the end cottage, where the widow keeps the garden that won the parish prize. The widow bobs and offers tea, and Rose takes it standing at the gate, because sitting would make it a visit and standing keeps it a call.)*
> "The ball, Miss Hartwell." The widow's eyes shine. "Our lads are polishing the carriages. Our girls are pressing the linen. It's our house too, miss —" she stops, embarrassed.
> "It is," Rose says. "That's why the invitations went to the cottages first."
> *(She walks back up the lane with the tea warm in her, and the Park behind her, and the arithmetic of the whole thing suddenly simple: a house is not finished when the plaster dries. It is finished when the people in it stand straighter.)*

scenes.synopsis: the lake pavilion, gleaming — beauty, bought with clean money, kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The lake pavilion at sunset: the glass gleaming, the water flat, the whole small building lit from inside like a lantern.)*
> *(She stands on the jetty and remembers what this cost — not the money, the money was clean, but the nerve: the season she bought beauty back with new money and the ton watched to see if it would vulgarize her. It did not. The pavilion gleams, and the gleam is hers.)*
> *(A moorhen crosses the water, leaving its exact line. The sun goes down behind the Park, and the windows catch it one by one, and the house — her house, beyond challenge, forever, Quill's word charged at nothing — lights up like something that intends to be seen. She stands on the jetty until the light goes. Then she goes in to dress for dinner, because even finished houses keep dinner hours.)*

scenes.synopsis: the historian's record — Harrow documents the completion; the past, filed. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Harrow has set up his table in the library's bay window — the pensioner-historian, sixty-one, scarred and exact, with his papers in their archival order.)*
> "The completion, Miss Hartwell." He shows her the page: the Park drawn whole, every zone dated, every restoration entered. "Ten seasons. I have written it the way it happened — the scaffolding and the scandal both. History doesn't flinch, miss. That's its job."
> "And the verdict, Mr. Harrow? In your history — what was it all for?"
> He considers. "For this." He taps the drawing — the whole, the complete. "Ruin proved engineered. Debts followed up the chain. The libel war won in the open. The confrontation faced. The price paid. The paper trail run down. The sin answered. The war survived. The claim settled." A pause. "A woman built a house out of all of that, miss. That's the history. The rest is footnotes."
> *(She leaves him to his papers. In the hall, she stops — a woman built a house out of all of that — and lets the sentence stand. It is the truest thing anyone has said about the decade, and it came from the scarred gentleman with the archival boxes.)*

scenes.synopsis: the grounds, dressed — the Park's face, presented to the coming weeks. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The grounds at morning: the dressed lawns, the swept drives, the ornamental water bright, the whole estate presenting its face to the three weeks ahead.)*
> *(She walks the carriage sweep with the head gardener's list in her hand — the moonlight drive's lanterns, the terrace's urns, the ball's outdoor stations — and checks each against the ground itself. The lanterns will hang from the limes. The urns are already planted with Hartwell-grown flowers. The stations are marked with pegs and string, like a campaign.)*
> *(It is a campaign. She has run enough of them to know the signs: the pegs, the lists, the particular alertness of a household about to be looked at. The difference is the objective. Not survival. Not vindication. Celebration — which is, she is discovering, the hardest campaign of all, because it has to be deserved.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE DRAGON (how to handle Drummond: invite first, invite last, or let the town tell her). The invitation waits; decide the dragon's order. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room, evening: the invitation to Lady Agatha Drummond lies written but unsealed on the desk, and Augusta sits opposite with the particular expression she wears when she is about to be right.)*
> "First," Augusta says, "says: I am not afraid of you. Last says: I have not forgotten you. Never sent — let the town tell her — says: you are not worth the postage." The spectacles lower. "All three are true, child. All three are weapons. Choose the one the season needs."
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The dragon:*
- **Invite her first** — *I am not afraid.* Drummond's card goes out with the first post, ahead of everyone. (Consequence: the town watches her decide under maximum light — but first invitation is first honor, and honor is a currency dragons spend.)
- **Invite her last** — *I have not forgotten.* Her card goes out with the final post, deliberate and pointed. (Consequence: the slight is exquisite and everyone will savor it — but a dragon slighted early has three weeks to sharpen her claws.)
- **Let the town tell her** — *not worth the postage.* No card is sent; London's talk carries the news. (Consequence: the insult is absolute — but an uninvited Drummond is a free agent, and free dragons are the dangerous kind.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: first, last, or never. The dragon will answer. Dragons always answer.)*

scenes.synopsis: Honoria — Drummond's daughter, sponsored, grown; the price, long paid. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Honoria calls in the afternoon — forty-eight, composed, the sponsorship's long debt paid in full years ago — and walks the gallery with Rose like a woman visiting a museum she helped fund.)*
> "Mother will come." Honoria says it without being asked. "Whatever the card says — first, last, or never. She will come, because not coming would be the concession, and Mother has never conceded anything in her life."
> "And you, Honoria? Will you come?"
> "I am already here." A smile, dry as dust. "Rose —" the name, used rarely, used now — "what she does at your ball, she does as herself. Not as my mother. I have spent twenty years learning the difference. You might —" a pause — "you might learn it in an evening. You're quicker than I am."
> *(They walk the gallery to its end. The empty frame that is not empty anymore — the Park drawn whole — holds them both for a moment. Two women, two mothers, one house. Honoria touches the frame's edge lightly, and goes.)*

scenes.synopsis: the paper's season — Bell on the housewarming; the Gazette's last Book One word, begun. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Bell comes herself, which she does perhaps twice a year, and stands in the library with her notebook shut — the proprietor, mid-forties, soft-voiced and sharp-eyed as ever.)*
> "The final issue." She says it plainly. "Book One closes with your ball, Miss Hartwell. The Gazette will print its last word on the woman who changed the Season —" a look — "on the paper's own terms. You know that."
> "I know it."
> "Unsparing and just." The notebook stays shut. "That's the verdict I'm writing toward. Not kind. Not cruel. True." She moves to the window. "Ten seasons I've judged you in print. This is the last judgment, and I mean it to be the one they quote."
> *(Rose pours the tea herself, which is the library's whole protocol for important visitors.)*
> "Then judge truly, Mrs. Bell. It's all I've ever asked of you."
> "It is all I have ever done." Bell takes the cup. "Whether you asked or not."

scenes.synopsis: the state rooms, ready — the seat, prepared for its first great occasion. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The state rooms at dusk: the great hall, the saloon, the drawing rooms in their restored order — the seat, ready.)*
> *(She walks them with the housekeeper's keys in her hand, though she needs no keys; the doors stand open. The saloon's chandeliers are dressed. The drawing room's hangings are brushed. The great hall's floor gleams with a decade of wax. These rooms have waited — through ruin, through war, through claim and counterclaim — for a night that is simply a celebration. They are about to get it.)*
> *(In the great hall she stops beneath the chandelier and looks up. Ten seasons ago she stood in a ruined house and priced what it would cost to save. Tonight she stands in a finished one and prices nothing. The arithmetic is done. What remains is the lighting of the candles — and that, she thinks, is somebody else's department now. Mrs. Quick's, specifically. She goes to tell her so.)*

scenes.synopsis: the ballroom, empty — the great room, waiting; the verdict's stage, set. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The ballroom, empty. She stands in its center at midnight — she has dismissed the maid, kept the candle — and the room holds her the way a held breath holds.)*
> *(It is the largest room she owns and the emptiest, and in three weeks it will hold the ton. Or it will not. Drummond is already writing letters somewhere in London — Augusta is sure of it, Honoria is sure of it, and Rose, standing in the candlelight, is sure of it too. The guest-list war has begun, whether she has declared it or not.)*
> *(She sets the candle down and walks the floor's length, counting her steps the way she counts everything. Forty paces. The room is forty paces of polished possibility. An empty ballroom is public humiliation. A full one is the verdict. She knows the stakes the way she knows the floor: exactly.)*

scenes.synopsis: the war-room — the guest list as campaign; Letitia's intelligence network, deployed. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library after midnight: the guest list spread, the candles low, Letitia with three address books and the particular expression of a quartermaster who has just been given a war.)*
> "We fight for attendance person by person." Letitia's pen moves. "The Almerias are wobbling — Drummond's been writing. The Trelawneys owe her a debt from '09. The Craykes will follow whoever looks like winning." She looks up, hawk-bright. "Calls, letters, debts of gratitude called in. Each recovered guest is a small social battle won in daylight."
> "And Drummond's weapons?"
> "Letters. Old debts called in. Blackballing by absence — she doesn't forbid, darling, she just makes coming feel unwise." The pen taps. "Within the rules. Perfectly within the rules. That's what makes her good."
> *(Rose takes a pen. The war-room holds its candlelight. The guest list is a battlefield map, and they are going to win it the way they have won everything: person by person, in daylight, with better arithmetic.)*
> "Then we begin tomorrow. First light."
> "First light, darling. The dragon writes at night. We write at dawn."

scenes.synopsis: the first replies — acceptances arrive; the ballroom, beginning to fill. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Morning post, and the first replies: the Almerias accept — "delighted" — the Craykes accept with a speed that suggests they have decided Rose looks like winning, and Lavinia's card arrives accepting for a party of six she has not been asked to bring but will be forgiven.)*
> "Six!" Letitia waves the card. "She's bringing six! Darling, I love her, but six is a delegation."
> "Six is six chairs filled." Rose sorts the pile. "Count them, Aunt. Don't curate them."
> *(The acceptances go onto the list in Letitia's best hand, and the list — which yesterday was a battlefield map — begins to look like a guest list. Thirty names by noon. The ballroom, in three weeks, will need four hundred. But thirty is a beginning, and beginnings are Letitia's favorite arithmetic.)*
> "The Trelawneys wobble still," Letitia says. "And the —" she stops.
> "Say it."
> "Nothing yet from —" another stop. "No. Nothing. The dragon's post hasn't answered."

scenes.synopsis: Cecilia, unmentioned — the war ended; the coda, waiting; the door, open. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She does not write to Cecilia. She has not written since the assembly where the war ended — the defeat or the redemption, the player's texture, the door left open on purpose.)*
> *(In the library she pauses at the desk where the S8 letters lie filed — the last intelligence, the last terms — and does not open the drawer. Some codas cannot be hurried. The woman who was once the dearest friend is gone or reconciled; either way, the reckoning waits for its chapter, and the chapter is not this one.)*
> *(She closes the drawer without opening it. The Park is finished. The ball is announced. The past has its own rooms in this house — the gallery, the archive, the filed drawers — and they are kept, dusted, and not lived in. That is the whole of her philosophy on the subject, and it has served her for ten seasons.)*

scenes.synopsis: the kitchens — the ball's logistics; supper, planned like a campaign. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The kitchens at full council: the cook, the confectioner brought down from London, Mrs. Quick with her lists, and the ball's supper spread across the table in diagrams.)*
> "Four hundred covers, Miss Hartwell." The cook taps the diagram. "The ices in the new flavors — the Hartwell rose ice, if the garden obliges — the savories at midnight, the champagne —" she names a quantity that makes Letitia, passing, stop dead.
> "That much?"
> "For four hundred, madam." The cook is serene. "The house has waited ten seasons for a supper like this. The larders are full. The cellars —" a glance at Mrs. Quick — "the cellars have been preparing for a decade, though they didn't know it."
> *(Rose approves the diagrams with a signature that feels absurdly like signing a treaty. The kitchens return to their chopping. Somewhere above, the house hums — the particular hum of a finished place about to be looked at — and the supper, like everything else, is going to be earned.)*

scenes.synopsis: the rose garden at evening — remembrance and the future, in flower language. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The rose garden at evening: the old bushes, the new plantings, the Hartwell rose's row standing budded and certain.)*
> *(She walks the rows with her hands behind her back — the posture Augusta taught her for gardens, the hands kept from touching — and reads the beds the way Bell reads a leader: for the thesis. Remembrance, in the rosemary at the borders. Faithfulness, in the violets edging the paths. And at the row's end, the Hartwell rose: the future, in bud.)*
> *(She does not touch the bud. The gardener was clear: it opens when it is ready, and not a day before. She respects the schedule. She has kept enough schedules in ten seasons to know that the best ones are the ones you don't rush.)*

scenes.synopsis: the family plate — the Dowager's silver; continuity, made visible. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The strong room, and Augusta supervising the laying-out of the family plate — the silver, the gilt, the pieces that survived Rackham's selling years by being hidden in the one place he never looked: the Dowager's own linen press.)*
> "This," Augusta lifts a salver, "survived your uncle. This —" a tureen — "survived your father. This —" the great epergne — "survived me hiding it from both of them." The spectacles lower. "The plate is the family's memory, child. It remembers what the people tried to forget."
> "And the ball?"
> "The ball gets all of it." Augusta sets the epergne down with finality. "Every piece. Let the ton eat off the survival. Let Drummond —" the rarest smile — "let the dragon dine off the things she thought were sold."
> *(They stand among the silver, two generations, and the strong room holds its candlelight. Continuity, made visible: the plate on the table, the house around it, the woman who kept both.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE FIRST NIGHT (who sleeps under the Park's roof first: the family, the oldest servant, or Rose alone). The finished house waits; decide its first night. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(Night, and the finished house quiet around her. The state bedrooms stand ready — the great bedchamber aired, the guest rooms dressed — and no one has yet slept in the Park as it now is: whole, complete, hers beyond challenge. The honor of the first night is hers to give, and the giving will be remembered.)*
> *(Letitia would say the family. Mrs. Quick would say the oldest servant, as the household's due. Her own heart says something quieter. The house waits. The candles burn low. Decide before the night decides for her.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The first night:*
- **The family first** — *blood, honored.* Augusta and Letitia take the state rooms; the house's first night belongs to the line. (Consequence: the Dowager weeps where no one sees, and the line is honored — but the night becomes ceremony, and ceremony is watched.)
- **The oldest servant first** — *the household's due.* The longest-serving soul below stairs sleeps in the great bedchamber; the house honors its keepers. (Consequence: the servants' hall never forgets — but the ton will hear of it, and the ton will talk.)
- **Rose alone first** — *the mistress, first.* She sleeps in the great bedchamber alone; the house's first night belongs to the woman who finished it. (Consequence: the quiet is absolute and entirely hers — but a housewarming begun alone is a statement, and statements get read.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: family, servant, or self. The house keeps the secret. The game does not.)*

scenes.synopsis: the night walk — the Park by moonlight; the finished whole, patrolled. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She walks the Park by moonlight — the waxing moon, ten days to full — with a shawl and no lantern, because she knows every path.)*
> *(The house behind her is dark except the library's one lamp. The lake holds the moon whole. The walled garden's wall is a line of silver. The cottages are dark, the stables dark, the pavilion a small lit lantern on the water's edge. It is all hers — beyond challenge, forever, Quill's word — and the ownership sits in her the way the shawl sits on her shoulders: warm, and not to be discussed.)*
> *(She walks to the canal and back. The night does what nights do at the finished Park: it behaves. Somewhere in London, Drummond is writing letters. Here, the only writing is the moon's on the water. She prefers this edition.)*

scenes.synopsis: the household's pride — the staff's stake in the ball; the two hosts. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Mrs. Quick finds her in the gallery at dawn — the housekeeper, immovable, with a list.)*
> "The staff's request, miss." The list is presented. "The footmen ask to wear the new livery for the ball — the full dress, not the undress. The maids ask for the afternoon off before, to do their hair. The kitchen asks —" a pause — "the kitchen asks for nothing, miss. The kitchen says the supper is its own reward."
> "Granted," Rose says. "All of it."
> "Thank you, miss." Mrs. Quick folds the list. "Miss Hartwell —" the immovable voice does something nearly warm — "we kept it for you. Through all of it. We're glad —" a stop — "we're glad it's finished."
> *(Rose watches her go — the straight back, the keys — and understands again what she understood at dinner: the housewarming has two hosts. Herself. And everyone who kept the place while she was earning it.)*

scenes.synopsis: London has heard — the town's talk turns to the ball; the war, joined. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The London letters, and Letitia reads them aloud with the particular relish of a woman reporting enemy movements.)*
> "'Miss Hartwell's housewarming,'" Letitia reads, "'is the talk of the town. Lady A. D. is said to be —' hmm — 'reserving her judgment.' Which means writing letters, darling. 'The Almerias have accepted. The Craykes have accepted twice, to be sure.'"
> "Twice?"
> "Enthusiasm, darling. Or insurance." She reads on. "'Miss Lavinia Crane has announced she will attend with a party, and the milliners are in despair.'"
> *(Rose takes the letters. The town's talk is a weather system, and it is turning fair — with a dragon-shaped cloud on the horizon. The war is joined. The ballroom, in three weeks, will fill or it will not, and every letter is a small battle.)*
> "Write back to them all," Rose says. "Personally. Every one."
> "Every one, darling?" Letitia reaches for a pen. "That's two hundred letters."
> "Then we'd better start."

scenes.synopsis: the first fitting, discussed — the gown's architecture; the atelier's triumph, begun. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The atelier, and the gown's architecture discussed over the sketch — Élise with her chalk, Rose with her questions, the three weeks laid out like a campaign.)*
> "The bodice first." Élise taps the sketch. "Ivory silk, the Park's stone at noon. The embroidery — the Hartwell rose, blooming — will take eleven days. The skirt —" she unrolls the measure — "the full moon's light on water. I have dreamed this gown, Miss Hartwell. Now I only have to make it."
> "Eleven days for the embroidery?"
> "Eleven days, six girls, and me." The chalk turns. "It will be the finest thing the atelier has ever made. I have told the girls. They are terrified." A sudden grin. "So am I."
> *(Rose looks at the sketch — the house, rendered in silk — and at the girl with chalk on her fingers who is going to make it.)*
> "Then be terrified together," Rose says. "It's the atelier's gown too."
> "It is." Élise rolls the sketch. "The modiste's girl is the ton's dressmaker now. Time to prove it."

scenes.synopsis: the eve of the war — the Park at night; the finished house, held. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The last night of the chapter: the Park dark, the house quiet, the moon waxing toward the ball.)*
> *(She stands at the library window with the guest list in her hand — the acceptances, the wobbles, the silences — and does the arithmetic she has done for ten seasons. Thirty acceptances. Four hundred chairs. A dragon writing letters in London. A ballroom, empty, forty paces of polished possibility.)*
> *(The arithmetic does not frighten her. Arithmetic never has. What frightens her — a little, in the honest dark — is how much she wants it: the full room, the lit candles, the ton seeing what she built. Wanting is the risk. She has always known that. She wants it anyway.)*
> *(She folds the list. Tomorrow the war-room opens at first light. Tonight the house holds her, finished and whole, and the wanting is hers to carry.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's verdict on the finished Park — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"Hartwell Park is finished, and London is invited to look. Ten seasons ago Miss Hartwell was ruined in a drawing room; she has since rebuilt the drawing room, the house around it, and — if the guest list holds — the Season itself. The Gazette congratulates the Park. It reserves judgment on the party."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (reserves judgment! the phrasing!), then the reckoning: the Park is pronounced finished in print as well as in person, and Bell has made the verdict formidable, which is Bell's way of making it permanent. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the house that is finished twice — in stone and in print — is finished for good.* — remembered: *the lesson: the house, finished twice, is finished for good.*
scenes.sting: Hartwell Park is finished, and London is invited to look. Ten seasons ago Miss Hartwell was ruined in a drawing room; she has since rebuilt the drawing room, the house around it, and — if the guest list holds — the Season itself. The Gazette congratulates the Park. It reserves judgment on the party.

scenes.synopsis: the first refusal — a polite, pointed no; the dragon's hand, glimpsed. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening post, and Letitia comes to the library with a letter held the way one holds a dead mouse — by the corner, at arm's length.)*
> "Read it, darling." The hawk's eyes are grave. "Aloud. I want to hear whether it sounds as bad as it reads."
> *(Rose reads: the Trelawneys — the wobbling Trelawneys — decline. With regret. With compliments. With the particular polish of a refusal that has been dictated by someone else. The phrases are Drummond's; she would know the cadence anywhere. Called-in debt, '09, paid in full — in refusal.)*
> "The first refusal." Letitia sits, suddenly. "Darling — it's begun. She's writing, and they're listening."
> *(Rose folds the letter with care. The war-room opens at first light. The dragon writes at night; they write at dawn. She looks at the guest list — the thirty acceptances, the four hundred chairs — and the arithmetic is suddenly simple: every chair is a battle, and the first battle has just been lost.)*
> *(She sets the letter down. The chapter closes on the refusal — polite, pointed, and entirely Drummond's — and the Season holds its breath.)*
**STATUS: FULL DRAFT** — awaiting Beth review.

scenes.synopsis: first light — the war-room opens; the Trelawneys' refusal, filed. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library at first light, and it is not a library today. The guest list lies spread across the desk in three columns — accepted, wobbling, refused — and the candles burn low against the dawn coming grey through the tall windows. Rose has been up an hour. The Trelawneys' refusal sits at the top of the refusals pile, which is presently a pile of one, and she means to keep it that way.)*
> *(She reads it a third time, though once was enough. The hand is the Trelawneys' secretary's, cramped and apologetic; the phrases are Drummond's. "With the greatest regret." "A prior and most pressing engagement." "The hope that Miss Hartwell will understand." Nobody in London hopes Miss Hartwell will understand anything. The '09 debt, called in like a loan at quarter-day. She refolds the letter along its original crease — paper remembers being folded — and sets it at the front of the refusals, under D for Drummond and under L for lesson.)*
> *(The lesson goes into the war-book's margin in her own hand: She does not forbid. She makes coming feel unwise. Underneath it, in fresher ink, the counter-lesson: Then we make it feel wise. One chair at a time. She blots it carefully. The sand-shaker hisses on the wet ink, a small domestic sound, and for a moment the war-room is only a woman writing at a desk before the household is up.)*
> *(She is ruling the day's columns when Letitia arrives — the address books under one arm, a cup of chocolate in each hand, the household's entire intelligence service wrapped in bombazine.)*
> "Dawn, darling." Letitia sets down the chocolate. "The dragon writes at night. We write at dawn. I have brought the books, the chocolate, and —" she produces a folded paper from her reticule — "the Craykes' direction in Mrs. Crayke's own hand, which I acquired by means I shall not disclose before chocolate."
> *(Rose takes the cup. It is thick and Spanish and unsweetened, the war-room's ration. The first sip burns pleasantly. Outside, the stable clock strikes six, and somewhere below stairs a door closes — the house beginning its day under her.)*
> "First light," she says, "and we begin."
> *(The candles gutter. The grey light strengthens through the windows and finds the columns — accepted, wobbling, refused — and the war begins the way all her wars begin: with better arithmetic and earlier hours.)*

scenes.synopsis: the dragon's order of battle — how Drummond empties rooms; the intelligence, mapped. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The war-room, mid-morning: Letitia's intelligence laid out on the desk like a campaign map — the letters in one pile, the debts noted in another hand, the absences marked with small black pins on the guest list. The chocolate cups stand empty. Letitia works the way generals work, Rose thinks, except generals rarely do it in a shawl with chocolate on their cuffs.)*
> "Three weapons." Letitia counts on her fingers, the chalk still on them from the atelier's errand this morning. "Letters — personal, flattering, full of concern about overcrowding. She writes as though the ballroom were a lifeboat, darling, and she is saving them a place on the shore. Debts — the '09 kind, the Trelawney kind, called in with smiles and remembered dinners. And absence —" she taps the list where the black pins cluster — "the cleverest. She doesn't tell them not to come. She tells them she won't be there. And half of London would rather miss a ball than miss Drummond's opinion of it afterward."
> "Within the rules." Rose studies the pins.
> "Perfectly." The hawk's eyes narrow. "That's what makes her good, darling. No whisper campaign. No lies. Nothing Bell could print and nothing Quill could sue. Just —" a gesture that takes in the letters, the pins, the whole elegant mechanism — "the gatekeepers' revenge. An empty ballroom is public humiliation, and she knows it the way you know the price of candles."
> *(Rose moves one of the black pins — the Fanes, wobbling — and considers the map. It is fought entirely in the open. And the open, she thinks, is where she has always won — because the open has witnesses, and witnesses remember who was kind.)*
> "Then we fight in the open." She sets the pin down. "Person by person. In daylight. With better stationery."
> "Person by person, darling." Letitia reaches for the fresh chocolate the maid has brought. "Pass the cups. Wars are thirsty work."
> *(Letitia pins the last black pin — the Aldingtons, cowardice engraved — and steps back. "Overcrowding," she reads aloud from the letters' margins, with the particular disgust of a woman who has survived actual crowds. "The ballroom holds four hundred, darling. The only thing overcrowded is her imagination.")*

scenes.synopsis: the first letter — Rose writes to the Almerias; gratitude, deployed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She writes the first letter herself — not the secretary, herself. Secretaries write invitations; mistresses write the letters that matter. The Almerias have accepted but they wobble — Drummond's letter reached them Tuesday, full of concern about overcrowding — and a wobbling acceptance is a refusal with better manners. So: her own hand, her own paper, her own ink.)*
> *(The pen moves, and she is careful with the particulars, because gratitude is only believed when it is specific. The kindness of '12, when the Almerias lent the house their name at the assembly where nobody else would be seen speaking to her. The loan of the carriage in '14, the winter the Park's own was in the coachmaker's hands and she had to get to London. The word in the right ear in '16 — Lady Almeria's quiet sentence to the patronesses, which opened three doors. She writes them all down. Thank you for coming. It matters that you come. The house is finished, and you are part of the reason.)*
> *(She has written thousands of letters in ten seasons. Threats, pleas, accounts rendered, love letters she never sent. This is the hardest kind: the honest one, with no weapon in it anywhere. She reads it over. It says what it means. She sands it, folds it, and seals it with the Hartwell crest, new-cut for the finished era — the rose, the oak, the whole of it, pressed into green wax.)*
> *(The footman takes the letter with the morning post — the green seal uppermost, the direction in her fair hand. She watches him go down the drive, the Almerias' letter riding among the bills and the tradesmen's accounts like a swan among ducks. One chair, secured with nothing but specificity and a new-cut crest. The seal is still warm from her hand.)*
> *(At the desk she inks the Almerias' name confirmed in the war-book's margin — the wobble stilled, the chair secured. Drummond's Tuesday letter, full of concern about overcrowding, answered by Thursday's gratitude, full of '12. The dragon writes worry. The mistress writes the truth. Specificity wins.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Dowager's recruits — Augusta writes her own letters; the old guard, mobilized. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta's morning room: the Dowager at her escritoire with a stack of her own correspondence, the old guard mobilized in her own shaky and absolutely legible hand. The room smells of the lavender water she has used since before Rose was born. Eleven letters, sealed and directed, lie in a finished row like soldiers on parade.)*
> "I have written to eleven." Augusta does not look up from the twelfth. "The Grevilles. The Sunderlands. Old Lady Micklethwaite, who owes me a debt from '88 that I have been saving like a good bottle." The pen scratches, steady despite the tremor. "They will come. They dislike Drummond more than they dislike excitement, which is saying a great deal about both."
> "Grandmama —" Rose picks up the top letter. The seal is the Ravencroft seal, older than the Hartwell crest, the wax the deep red of the last century.
> "It is not kindness, child. It is war." The spectacles rise. "The dragon empties your rooms with letters. I fill them with older letters. Mine are better written —" a pause — "and mine remember further back, which in this town is the same as being better armed. And Rose —" the spectacles lower again — "tell Letitia to stop looking so surprised when she hears. I have been fighting women like Agatha Drummond since before she was born. I was fighting them when her mother was in short skirts."
> *(Rose takes the eleven letters. Each is a small masterpiece of the form: warmth on the surface, duty underneath, and the faintest steel at the bottom, like a blade laid under silk. Augusta's hand shakes and her spelling never does.)*
> "The dragon writes at night," Augusta says, returning to the twelfth. "I write at dawn, like you. We shall see whose ink lasts longer. Ink, child, is a young woman's game only if the old woman lets it be."
> *(She carries the eleven letters to the post herself — not the footman, herself, down the drive in the morning air, the Ravencroft seals warm in her reticule. The post boy takes them with the deference due to eleven red seals, and she walks back up the drive past the limes thinking that Augusta's ink, shaky and exact, has just done what no army could: mobilized the old guard with stationery.)*

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry calls on the Craykes; the gift of attention, extended. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Henry calls in the afternoon with his cap in his hands and news, standing in the war-room doorway too large for it and entirely at home — the soldier's trick of being comfortable anywhere, learned in worse doorways than this.)*
> "The Craykes." He comes in, sets the cap on the desk's corner with care. "I rode over. They wobble — Drummond's letter reached them Tuesday, the lifeboat one. I told them —" he stops, the soldier's familiar awkwardness with social campaigns, the big hands worrying the gloves — "I told them the ballroom would be the poorer without them. Mrs. Crayke asked after the supper. I described the ices. I may have exaggerated the ices."
> "You exaggerated the ices, Major?"
> "Slightly." The smallest smile. "It was the truth, enlarged. I am practicing truths. The enlargement —" he considers — "is also a practice."
> "And the Craykes?"
> "They'll come." He picks up the cap again, turns it. "Mr. Crayke said the Park deserved a full room. Mrs. Crayke said —" a pause — "she said a host who sends a major to call is a host who means it. I didn't correct her about the sending. I thought the uncorrected version served better."
> *(She laughs — the first laugh of the war, startled out of her — and he looks absurdly pleased with himself, the way he looks after a well-executed maneuver, the way men look when the plan survives contact with the Craykes.)*
> "Henry." She comes around the desk. "That was — thank you. It was well done."
> "It was a small thing." He is already moving to the door, the errand discharged. "I am practicing small things. There will be more of them. The Craykes were today's. Tomorrow —" the cap goes on — "tomorrow is unassigned."
> *(Later she asks what exactly he said about the ices, and he describes them — the Hartwell rose ice, the confectioner's new flavors, the champagne — with the straight face of a man reporting troop positions. "Mrs. Crayke asked if the rose ice was real roses," he says. "I told her the garden grew them. It was the truth. The enlargement was only in the tone.")*

scenes.synopsis: the refusals pile — three more; the dragon's progress, measured. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and the refusals pile has grown: the Trelawneys, the Fanes, the Aldingtons — three refusals, each polite, each pointed, each with Drummond's cadence running underneath the compliments like a second handwriting. Rose reads them in order at the desk, the candles lit early against the grey evening, the way she reads accounts: for the pattern, because the pattern is the campaign.)*
> *(The Trelawneys: the '09 debt, called in. The letter thanks her "for the kind invitation" in the particular tone of people who have been told exactly which words to use. The Fanes: the '11 debt, older and heavier, the refusal dressed as a prior engagement that did not exist last month. The Aldingtons: no debt at all — worse. They fear the absence. Drummond won't be there, and they cannot bear to miss her opinion of the evening afterward. Cowardice, engraved on good paper.)*
> *(The Trelawneys' '09, the Fanes' '11, the Aldingtons' fear — the whole campaign in its Sunday clothes. She files them under D, in date order, the pile squared with her ruler: three letters, three chairs, three small public facts. The pattern is legible now, which is the first thing the pattern has ever done for her.)*
> *(The acceptances pile is taller — thirty-one, thirty-two, the Almerias confirmed twice, which Letitia counts as enthusiasm and Rose counts as one — but the refusals have a weight out of proportion to their number. Every empty chair is a fact the town can see. The war is fought in daylight, and daylight shows everything: the fullness, the gaps, the places where the dragon has been.)*
> *(She closes the war-book. Three refusals. The pile is small. It will stay small. She has decided this the way she decides everything in this war — early, in writing, before the candles are lit.)*
> *(Letitia comes in as she squares the pile, reads the three refusals over her shoulder, and makes a sound like a cat with a fishbone. "The '11 debt," she says of the Fanes. "Called in with smiles. Darling, I remember the dinner where that debt was incurred. The smiles were the most expensive part." She takes the Aldingtons' letter between finger and thumb. "And these — no debt at all. Just fear. Fear, engraved, at fourpence the sheet.")*

scenes.synopsis: counsel, precise — Octavia on the war's shape; the painter's eye for campaigns. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia arrives with the memorandum book and a painter's eye for the campaign's shape — she has been looking at the guest list the way she looks at a canvas, Rose realizes, for composition, for where the eye goes.)*
> "You are fighting the wrong war." She says it the way she says everything: precisely, without preamble, the brush-wiping cloth still in her hand. "Drummond doesn't need to empty the room. She needs to empty the idea of the room — to make coming feel like a wager on an uncertain night. You don't win by filling chairs. You win by making the chairs not matter."
> "The chairs are the whole war, Octavia."
> "The chairs are the arithmetic." Octavia opens the book. "The idea is the painting. Listen: the portrait hangs the week of the ball. The finished Park, the laughing woman, the whole of it — in paint, where no one can uninvite it. Let the town see what the ball celebrates before the ball happens. Let them come to a night that is already, in some sense, accomplished."
> "And the letters?"
> "Keep the letters. But —" a look, the precise voice softening by exactly one degree — "the daily devotions, Rose. Henry's small things. The Craykes came for the ices, not the invitation. They are winning you more chairs than the stationery. People come to be near warmth. The great houses can smell a cold campaign the way dogs smell weather. Remember that."
> *(Rose writes it down: the portrait, the week of the ball. Octavia closes the book with a snap.)*
> "You look tired," Octavia says.
> "I am fighting a dragon with stationery."
> "Then use better stationery." The precise smile, deployed like a signature. "Yours is better. It has your hand in it. Hers only has her secretary's."
> *(Octavia is already at the door when she turns back. "The sittings," she says. "Three more, in the right light — the morning light, the still-room's north window. Come tired, come as you are. The laugh won't pose." She picks up the memorandum book. "And Rose — the portrait hangs the week of the ball whatever the chairs say. The painting doesn't count. That's its virtue.")*

scenes.synopsis: Julian's recruits — the brother's old set; shame, converted to service. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Julian comes at dusk with a list of his own — his brother's old set, the fast young men of the Network years grown into cautious middle age, the ones who watched him fall and learned nothing from it until now. Twelve names, in his clerkly hand.)*
> "They'll come." He hands her the list across the desk. "I told them the truth — that I was the Network's instrument once, and that you knew, and that you kept me anyway. That you let me earn the mending instead of paying for the ruin." He stops, looks at the window. "It was not a comfortable conversation. There is no comfortable version of telling twelve men you were the villain of their youth and would like them to come to a ball."
> "Julian —"
> "The mended gloves." He turns them in his hands, the old familiar motion. "I told them about the gloves. About being mended. About the keeping, and the wearing, and the choosing to keep wearing." A quick, unguarded look. "They listened, Rose. Men like that — they don't listen to virtue. Virtue bores them. They listen to mending. Mending is something they have all needed and none of them have done."
> *(She takes the list. Twelve names, twelve chairs, twelve men who owe the Park nothing and Julian everything. The truth, deployed like artillery, and no apology anywhere in it.)*
> "Thank you," she says, and means the whole of it — the list, the telling, the discomfort spent like coin.
> "It was service." He puts the gloves away. "Shame, converted. It spends better than I expected. I may have more of it."
> *(The names stand in two columns — the Network years' fast young men, grown cautious, each one a small surrender of the past. She reads them twice, memorizing the order, and sets the list where the morning's calls will find it. Twelve chairs. Twelve men who have all needed mending and none of them have done — until now.)*
> *(She files the list with the war's other recruits — Julian's twelve, in the clerkly hand, between Augusta's eleven and Lavinia's multiplying sixes. Twelve men who were the Network's audience once, now the Park's guests. She rules the line, blots it, and the columns grow longer by one column.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE WOBBLERS (the undecided great houses: court, concede, or outflank). The list waits; decide the means. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The war-room, night: the wobblers' list — the great houses, undecided, the ball's true prize — spread under the candles, and Letitia with her pen poised and her shawl pulled close against the library's evening chill. The great houses will not be won by letters. Letters are what the dragon sends. The great houses require something else, something with a face on it.)*
> "The Sunderlands want a call," Letitia says, tapping the list. "Personal. The lady said as much to Augusta — she wants to be asked, not written to. The Grevilles want to be asked by Augusta, not by us — the Dowager's hand, the old seal, the whole century of it. And the Micklethwaites —" she taps harder — "want to be *convinced*. They've heard Drummond's version over tea. They want ours, in person, with better tea."
> *(Rose looks at the three names. Three houses, three vanities, three doors that only open from the inside. The candles burn low. Somewhere in London, the dragon is writing — or sleeping, or planning, or whatever dragons do at midnight. Here, the decision waits, and the waiting is the expensive part.)*
> "Three ways," she says. "Say them plainly."
> "Court them — you, in person, the mistress asking. Concede the form — Augusta's letters, the old guard's weight. Or outflank — Lavinia's set, the young and the glittering, and let the great houses follow the fun." Letitia sets down the pen. "All three are honest, darling. That's what makes it difficult."
> *(She studies the three names by candlelight — the Sunderlands' pride, the Grevilles' debt, the Micklethwaites' fear — and the war-room's night settles around the choosing. The mistress, asking; the Dowager, writing; the glitter, outflanking. The candles burn lower over the three names, and the list waits.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — The wobblers:*
- **Court them personally** — *the mistress, in person.* Rose calls on every great house herself; the Park's mistress, asking. (Consequence: the honor is immense and the days are long — but a personal call is a debt, and debts get repaid in attendance.)
- **Concede the form, keep the prize** — *Augusta's letters.* The Dowager's older, better-written letters do the work; Rose saves her strength. (Consequence: the old guard comes for Augusta, not for Rose — but they come, and the chairs fill.)
- **Outflank with the young** — *Lavinia's set.* The glittering young lead; the great houses follow where the fun goes. (Consequence: the ball gains brilliance and loses gravity — but brilliance fills rooms faster than duty.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: court, concede, or outflank. The means are hers, and the night will remember how they were won.)*
> *(Letitia waits, pen hovering, and the list holds its breath. Three names by candlelight. The candles burn, and the choosing is hers, and the night will keep her answer. Decide.)*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent's letter, answered — the Frenchman's recruits; charm, deployed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Laurent's answer comes — not a letter, Laurent; himself, on the doorstep, with the rain on his coat and the polish undimmed and Letitia already ordering chocolate as though Frenchmen materialized daily.)*
> "The émigré houses." He sheds the coat, kisses Letitia's hand, accepts the chocolate with the air of a man receiving tribute. "They wobble, your great houses? Mine do not wobble. They *vibrate* — it is a French specialty. I have told them —" the Gallic shrug, deployed like a fan — "that Drummond's absence would be noticed, and that my presence would be certain, and that Paris is watching. Paris is always watching. It is Paris's chief occupation, after lunch."
> "And they'll come?" Rose takes the list he produces — twenty names, the émigré houses, in a hand that makes the alphabet look decorative.
> "They will come to see whether I am as charming as I claim." The sudden, unpolished smile, the real one. "I am. It is my one reliable talent. The others are decorative." He sobers, and the polish drops the way a curtain drops — all at once, revealing the room behind. "Rose — the de Varennes were ruined by the same speculation that built your sin. The same paper, the same men, the same ruin with a French accent. We know what it is to be uninvited. I will not watch it happen to you. Not while I have a coat to shed on your doorstep."
> *(He stays for dinner. The émigré houses — twenty chairs — go onto the list in Letitia's best hand, and the war-room gains something it has lacked: the particular electricity of a Frenchman who has decided. Charm, deployed like cavalry, and behind the charm, the thing charm is usually covering — loyalty, with its coat off.)*
> *(At dinner he is in fine form — Paris's opinions dissected, the de Varennes' ruin and the Hartwell sin laid side by side like two maps of the same country. "The same paper," he says, refilling her glass. "The same men. We were uninvited together, Rose. We shall be welcomed together. It is symmetry. The French adore symmetry.")*

scenes.synopsis: the war-room's dress — fashion-selection; the campaigner's face for the calls. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The calls begin tomorrow — the great houses, the wobblers, the personal asking — and Letitia lays out the war-room's dress with a general's eye, three gowns across the bed like three strategies.)*
> "The campaigner's face, darling." She holds up the first. "Not the ball's. The war's. You are calling on great houses to ask a favor, and the dress must say: I am worth the favor, and I know it, and I am not going to grovel for it in bombazine."
> *(Rose looks at the three. The claret: the archive's color, the Ravencroft line stated, the heir's gown for houses that respect blood. The grey: the Park's stone at noon, the mistress severe and exact, for houses that respect certainty. The green: the garden's color, the builder's honest silk, for houses that respect work.)*
> "The great houses see the dress before they hear the ask," Letitia says, practical as a quartermaster issuing boots. "The Sunderlands will read the grey as respect. The Micklethwaites will read the claret as lineage. The Grevilles —" a pause — "the Grevilles will read anything Augusta tells them to read, but the green wouldn't hurt."
> *(She considers. The dress is not the ball's finery and not the morning's ease. It is the campaigner's uniform: the woman who asks favors and is worth them, rendered in silk. She chooses, and Letitia nods — the quartermaster's approval, given once and never repeated.)*
*Choices (no coin cost; the game remembers):*
- **Wear the claret, stated** — *the archive's color.* The heir's gown, the line declared; the great houses see the Ravencroft in her.
- **Wear the grey, exact** — *the stone's color.* The mistress's gown, severe and certain; the great houses see the Park in her.
- **Wear the green, honored** — *the garden's color.* The builder's gown, practical and honest; the great houses see the work in her.
> *(She chooses, and Letitia folds the other two away with the care of a woman putting up maps after the campaign. The choice is remembered — the game keeps such things. Tomorrow the calls begin, and the dress will say what the letters cannot.)*
> *(The maid lays the chosen gown out that evening — the campaigner's face, ready for the morning — and Letitia inspects it the way she inspected the maps: for weaknesses. "No rustle," she decrees. "No train. The great houses respect a woman who can walk into their morning rooms without bringing the drapery with her. Sleep well, darling. Tomorrow you are the ask." The gown waits on its hook; the morning waits beyond it.)*
