scenes.synopsis: the first call — the Sunderlands, convinced; the war, fought in person. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The Sunderlands' morning room: the great house, the wobblers' chief, all gilt and good carpet and the particular stillness of a room that has seen every kind of caller. Rose arrives in the war-room's dress — the choice made, the face set — with Letitia's briefing in her head and her own honesty in her mouth, which is the riskier of the two.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." Lady Sunderland receives her with the particular courtesy of a woman who has already decided and is enjoying the suspense, the way cats enjoy doorways. "We have had —" a pause, the tea things between them like a negotiating table — "letters."
> "So have I." Rose sits, uninvited and unhurried, and accepts the tea. "Lady Sunderland, I won't pretend I don't know what the letters say. Drummond thinks my ballroom will be empty, and she may be right. She writes beautifully, and she has the '09 debts, and absence is a weapon I can't disarm." A breath. "But the Park is finished — ten seasons, the whole of it, the stone and the garden and the people — and I would rather show it to a half-empty room of friends than a full room of the curious. Will you come?"
> *(The silence. The clock on the mantel ticks twice. Then Lady Sunderland laughs — a real laugh, startled out of her, the sound of a plan collapsing pleasantly.)*
> "Well." She rings for fresh tea, which is the morning room's equivalent of a treaty signature. "No one has ever asked me like that. No preamble, no flattery, no pretending the dragon doesn't exist." She pours. "Yes, Miss Hartwell. We will come. And —" the courtesy, suddenly warm — "we will bring the Micklethwaites. Old Lady Micklethwaite has been waiting for someone to give her permission to defy Drummond since '88. Consider it given."
> *(The drive home is short and the air is sweet, and Rose sits in the carriage with Lady Sunderland's laugh still in her ears and the Micklethwaites' defiance already arranged. The first call, won with honesty — the cheapest weapon in the house, and, it turns out, the sharpest. She makes a note in the war-book: Ask as yourself. It works.)*

scenes.synopsis: the arithmetic, at noon — sixty chairs; the war, half-won. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Noon, and the arithmetic: sixty chairs secured — the Sunderlands, the Micklethwaites in train, the émigré houses certain, Julian's twelve, Augusta's eleven, the Almerias twice-confirmed and counted once. She does the sums in the war-room with the noon light lying across the list in a clean white bar, the pen moving down the columns the way it has moved for ten seasons.)*
> *(Sixty of four hundred. The dragon's refusals: nine — the Trelawneys, the Fanes, the Aldingtons, and six more since, each polite, each pointed, each filed under D. The wobblers: forty, shrinking daily. The arithmetic is better than yesterday and worse than tomorrow needs it to be — which is the permanent condition of every war she has ever fought, and she has stopped expecting otherwise.)*
> *(Letitia brings sandwiches — cold beef, mustard sharp enough to clear the head — and they eat over the map, crumbs on the guest list, the quartermaster and the commander taking the noon ration like soldiers.)*
> "The Micklethwaites held," Letitia says through the sandwich. "Lady Sunderland's doing. The old lady told Drummond's caller —" she swallows — "told her the Park's supper was worth the drive. To her face."
> *(Sixty chairs. The afternoon's calls wait — the Grevilles, the clergy's edges, the young multiplying. The war is half-won, which in her experience is the most dangerous half: the point where people start believing it, and belief makes everyone careless.)*
> *(The evening post brings the Grevilles' direction in Augusta's train and two more acceptances from the émigré houses. Sixty becomes sixty-four before supper. The columns lengthen — and the dangerous half keeps its numbers moving the right way.)*
> *(Letitia rules the new columns with the ruler's edge — sixty-four, the ink still wet — and brushes the sandwich crumbs off the guest list with the side of her hand. "The Grevilles want the personal call," she says, consulting the margin. "The clergy's edges want paper. The young want glitter." She looks up. "We have all three, darling. Spend them.")*
> *(The afternoon's campaign waits, and the quartermaster's margin is ready, and the ink is still wet.)*

scenes.synopsis: Lavinia's set, deployed — the glittering young; brilliance, as strategy. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Lavinia arrives with her party of six and the energy of a cavalry charge — twenty-four, glittering, absolutely loyal, trailing perfume and the particular confidence of youth that has never lost anything.)*
> "Darling!" She surveys the war-room — the maps, the columns, the sandwich crumbs — with delight. "This is delicious. A campaign headquarters! I have brought —" she counts on her fingers — "six, as promised, and each of them has promised to bring six, which is —" she does the arithmetic with visible effort, the tip of her tongue caught between her teeth — "a great many. The young are coming, Rose. The young always come to the best party. It is our entire function. The old decide; we attend; the old then wish they had decided differently."
> "And Drummond?" Rose moves a sandwich plate out of the map's way.
> "Drummond is —" Lavinia's voice drops its glitter for a moment, the way a chandelier dims when the candles are snuffed — "yesterday's weather, darling. The young don't fear her. We never did. She can't blackball by absence when the absence is the point — we weren't going to her evenings anyway." The glitter returns, full force. "We are coming to *your* ball. Hers is the one that will feel empty. Imagine it — Drummond, at home, listening to the carriages go past to the Park. I almost feel sorry for her. Almost."
> *(She sweeps out, leaving perfume and six confirmed chairs and the war-room's morale visibly improved, the way sunlight improves a room. The glittering young: brilliance, as strategy, and strategy that enjoys itself.)*
> *(Letitia counts the six, then counts their sixes, then gives up and writes "dozens" in the margin with a flourish, underlining it twice. "The young," she says, "are a renewable resource, darling. They were waiting for someone to give them a better evening than Drummond's." The perfume lingers after Lavinia goes — orange-flower and confidence — and the war-room feels larger for it.)*
> *(The door closes on orange-flower — the maps' candle-smoke rising beneath it — and the war-room is brighter for it. Six chairs confirmed, and sixes behind them, multiplying beyond even Lavinia's already-generous count. "Dozens," Letitia says again, underlining it a third time, just for the pleasure of it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the war-room's face — dress the campaign's second week; direction + twenty 5-coin pins, story morsels between, reveal coda. (Turns: 21)
scenes.prose:
> **Occasion brief — The calls, continued:** "The great houses are being called upon in person. Dress for the woman who asks favors and is worth them — the campaigner's face, not the ball's. **Editorial criterion: purpose.**"
>
> **A. The Quartermaster** — Letitia's colors honored; warm brown, practical silk, the war-room's own uniform. Motif: the oak sprig at the cuff — the campaign, embroidered. Thread: **bronze** (the earned, stated) / **brown silk** (the practical, matched) / **cream** (the honest, lit). Colorway: warm brown + bronze + cream. Accessories: a bronze hair comb; the household keys, carried; brown kid gloves.
> **B. The Diplomat** — dove grey, exact; the Park's stone, the mistress's severity for the morning. Motif: feather-stitch, grey on grey — quietness with a spine. Thread: **silver** (the exact, edged) / **dove silk** (the stone, matched) / **pearl** (the certain, lit). Colorway: dove grey + silver + pearl. Accessories: a silver ribbon; no pendant — the throat, plain; grey kid gloves, immaculate.
> **C. The Heir** — claret, stated; the archive's color for the houses that respect the line. Motif: the Hartwell oak at the hem, restrained — the line, embroidered. Thread: **gold** (the landed, stated) / **claret silk** (the archive, matched) / **ivory whitework** (the declared, lit). Colorway: claret + gold + ivory. Accessories: the grandmother's pearls; pearl drop earrings; claret kid gloves.
>
> *(The dressing room, the campaign's second week: the campaigner's morning dress. She dresses the way the war has taught her: purpose, not display.)*
> (T1 · choice — the direction) *She commits: the quartermaster, the diplomat, or the heir — the campaign's thesis, remembered. The hair, composed. The accessories, exact. The mirror, to be consulted briefly. **Direction.** The great houses, in person — dress for the woman who asks favors and is worth them. **Editorial criterion.** Purpose — every choice must answer the campaign, not the ballroom.*
> *(System: commit to a direction — remembered for the campaign. Then the pins begin. Each pin costs 5 coins; no Crown SKUs; jewels from owned pieces only, never a ritual step.)*
> **Pin 1 (T2 · micro-decision) — Gown, chosen:** the caller's face — the brown practical, or the grey exact, or the claret stated — whichever the day chose, the purpose worn. *5 coins.*
> **Pin 2 (T3 · micro-decision) — Fit, exact:** the composed — no rustle for the morning room, no train for the campaign. *5 coins.*

scenes.synopsis: the paper's arithmetic — Bell on the guest-list war; the judge, observing. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Bell's note comes by the afternoon post — not a visit, a note, in the proprietor's own hand, the paper the Gazette's own stock, the seal plain. Rose opens it in the war-room with the afternoon light on the maps, and reads it twice, the way she reads everything from Bell: once for the words, once for the spaces between them.)*
> *"Miss Hartwell — The Gazette does not take sides in guest lists. It observes that Lady A. D. has declined to comment, that the Sunderlands have accepted, and that the town's talk has the particular quality of a tide turning. The paper will report the ballroom's fullness or emptiness as fact. — N. Bell"*
> *(The judge, observing: no favor, no warning, no thumb on the scale — just the fact of the observation, set down in the proprietor's dry hand. It is, she reflects, folding the note along its crease, the most useful thing anyone has sent her all week. A paper that reports fullness as fact is a paper the dragon cannot use. Drummond's whole campaign depends on the *feeling* of emptiness, the rumor of it, the fear of it. Bell has just announced that the Gazette will count chairs, not feelings — and feelings, confronted with counting, tend to evaporate.)*
> *(She files the note under B, for Bell, and under J, for judge, and pins the clipping to the war-room's wall beside the map — the tide, turning, in the proprietor's hand. Letitia reads it over her shoulder.)*
> "The paper will report it as fact," Letitia says. "Darling, that's better than a hundred letters. That's the town's memory, committed in advance."
> *(Rose looks at the note on the wall beside the map — the tide, turning, in the dry unhurried hand. Daylight fights it; print will record it. Two kinds of permanence, and the dragon has neither. Someday Harrow will want the wall for the history. Today it is only the truth, pinned where the fighters can see it.)*
> *(She straightens the clipping once, though it hangs straight already, and steps back to the desk. The wall is becoming the war's archive — the refusals under D, the judge under B and J, the black pins, the columns — and the archive, she thinks, is on their side.)*

scenes.synopsis: the daughter's intelligence — what the dragon is planning; Honoria's divided loyalty, stated. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Honoria comes at dusk, unannounced, and asks for the library — not the morning room, the library, where the maps are. She stands before the guest list like a general studying enemy dispositions, forty-eight and composed, the sponsorship's long debt paid in full years ago and the daughter's debt still being paid nightly.)*
> "She's writing to the clergy now." Honoria's finger traces the map's edge. "The bishops. Respectability's last redoubt. If she can keep the church away, she can call the ball —" a pause — "worldly. It's clever, Rose. It's her best move. The ton will brave a dragon, but the bishops — the bishops make the brave feel vulgar."
> "And you're telling me because?" Rose sets down her pen.
> "Because I am her daughter, not her soldier." The dry voice, dry as dust. "I have spent twenty years learning the difference between Mother and the dragon. The dragon is very good at this — the letters, the debts, the absence, all of it elegant and all of it within the rules. Mother —" a longer pause, and something moves behind the composure — "mother is tired. I don't think she knows it yet. I think she thinks she's fighting the war of '09 again, and she's not. She's fighting you, and you're —" a look — "you're not '09."
> *(Rose marks the clergy on the map — the new front, the bishops, a small black pin for each see. The evening light is going. Honoria moves to the door, then stops.)*
> "Thank you, Honoria."
> "Don't." She doesn't turn. "I am not on your side. I am on the side of —" she stops — "of the house being finished. It's the only side I've ever had. The bishops are yours to win or lose. I only report the weather."
> *(The door closes on the war's strangest courier. Rose stands at the map a long time — the clergy front, the black pins for the sees — and then moves the waverer's pin half an inch toward yes. Not hope. Intelligence: Quill's papers sent, the settlement's proof, the stone's evidence. The church respects paper. She has paper.)*

scenes.synopsis: the clergy front — Rose writes to the bishops; respectability, contested. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She writes to the bishops herself — three letters, in her best hand, the hand she uses for Quill and for royalty and for no one else. With each letter goes an enclosure: Quill's settlement papers, fair-copied — the entail's true history, the debt acknowledged and paid, the father's name cleared and cut in the Park's stone. Paper, for men of the book.)*
> *(The letters say, in essence, what the papers prove: the house is finished, the debt is paid, the Park stands on clean paper and a cleaner conscience. Come and see. It is not theology. She does not pretend it is theology. It is arithmetic — the debt rendered, the account closed, the stone cut — but arithmetic, presented properly on good paper with a solicitor's seal, has converted bishops before. Bishops are men, and men respect a closed account.)*
> *(She writes the three directions herself, in the fair hand: the waverer, the silent one, the one Honoria says is already half-convinced. Each letter gets the crest, the green wax, the full ceremony of the finished era. No groveling. No piety performed. Just the facts, the stone, and the invitation — respectability demonstrated, not pleaded.)*
> *(She holds each letter to the candle a moment, checking the seal's set — a seal is a signature you can touch, the way Augusta taught her. Then she sets the three with the evening post. The clergy front opens: not worldliness denied, but respectability demonstrated, on paper, with seals, in triplicate.)*
> *(The post bag takes them with the evening collection — three green seals among the franked letters and the tradesmen's bills. She watches the footman go down the drive, and the evidence goes with him: a clean account, in triplicate.)*
> *(The enclosures went in last — Quill's settlement papers, the proof of the clean account, folded once and slipped behind each letter. Paper for the church that respects paper: the debt paid, the conscience clean, the stone cut. Three bishops, three proofs, three green seals cooling on the desk — the clergy front's opening salvo, ready. The wax cools; the proof stands.)*

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry brings the garden's first sweet peas; attention, in flower form. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He comes with the evening post and a paper cone of sweet peas from the walled garden — the first of the season, cut that morning, the stems still wet. He presents the cone with the gravity of a man delivering dispatches, and the war-room, briefly, smells of the garden instead of ink.)*
> "The gardener said they were for the house." Henry sets the cone on the desk's corner, careful of the maps. "I told him the house could spare a cone. It was —" he considers, the soldier weighing a court-martial — "presumption. I am practicing presumption too. The small things were getting lonely."
> *(She takes the cone and puts the sweet peas in water herself — a glass on the library desk, where the war-room's maps can see them. Sweet peas: gratitude, in the flower language. Or possibly just sweetness. Henry would not know the language; he would only know the gesture, which is better. The gesture has no footnotes.)*
> "They're for the war-room, Henry."
> "Everything is for the war-room, these days." He watches her arrange them, the big hands folded behind his back. "When the war is over —" he stops, looks at the flowers.
> "Yes?"
> "When it's over, I'll bring them for the house." The smallest smile. "One practice at a time. Presumption today. The house tomorrow. The —" he stops again — "the rest, when it's earned."
> *(She looks at the sweet peas in their glass — the garden's first, the season's promise — and at the man practicing his way toward something he won't name. The devotion in the evening is the war's quietest front. It is also, she suspects, the one that will still be standing when the maps are retired.)*
> *(At the door she looks back once — the glass among the maps, the season's first sweetness where the war is planned. Presumption today, the house tomorrow; the rest, when it's over. She smiles, and goes up to dress.)*
> *(She goes up to dress, and the war-room keeps the sweet peas — the glass among the maps, the gesture among the plans — and the evening's quietest victory stays behind on the desk, footnoted by no one.)*

scenes.synopsis: the gown's progress — eleven days of embroidery, begun; the atelier's nerve. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The atelier, and the embroidery begun: six girls at the frames, Élise moving among them with chalk and corrections, the Hartwell rose blooming in silk on ivory — the buds done, the opening blooms underway, eleven days of work stretching ahead like a campaign.)*
> "Day two." Élise doesn't look up from the frame she is correcting. "The buds are done. The opening blooms —" she touches a petal with the back of her finger — "are fighting me. Silk doesn't open the way roses do. It has to be persuaded. Roses open because they must. Silk opens because a seventeen-year-old tells it to."
> "And the girls?" Rose looks down the frames — the bent heads, the flying needles, the particular silence of concentration.
> "Terrified." A grin, quick and young, there and gone. "And magnificent. Look —" she holds up a finished spray, the silk rosebud perfect — "Claudine did this. She's seventeen. Seventeen, Miss Hartwell, and she embroiders like the ton's dressmaker. Which she is. The ton just doesn't know it yet."
> *(Rose looks at the spray in Élise's hand — the rosebud perfect in silk — and at the girl bent over her frame, the needle flashing. Seventeen, and the ton's dressmaker already; the ton simply hasn't been told.)*
> "Tell her," Rose says. "Tell them all. The gown they're making is the finest thing the atelier has ever made — and when the ton sees it walk into the ballroom, they'll know whose hands did it. Names, Élise. I want their names in the Gazette's report."
> "I tell them daily." Élise returns to the frame, chalk in hand. "They don't believe me yet. They will. At the ball. Belief —" the warm voice, warm as ever — "belief is the last thing we embroider."
> *(The atelier's supper comes up from the kitchens at nine — the girls eat at the frames, needles down, the day's terror set aside for bread and cheese. Élise watches them with the chalk still in her hand. "Eat, all of you," she says. "Tomorrow we persuade the silk again." The frames rest till morning.)*

scenes.synopsis: the arithmetic, at dusk — one hundred and forty chairs; the tide, turning. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dusk, and the arithmetic: one hundred and forty chairs — the bishops wavering toward yes, the clergy front holding, Lavinia's young multiplying beyond even Lavinia's generous count, the Sunderlands' circle widening daily, the émigré houses certain. She does the sums in the war-room with the dusk lying on the list in a violet bar, and the numbers have the particular solidity of things earned the hard way.)*
> *(One hundred and forty of four hundred. The refusals: fourteen — stalled, no new ones in three days. The dragon's letters still go out nightly — Honoria's intelligence is exact, the desk in London still busy — but the acceptances are outpacing them now, person by person, in daylight, with better stationery and better tea and Henry's exaggerated ices. The tide Bell promised is not just turning. It is turned, and running.)*
> *(Letitia brings supper on a tray — the cook's pie, the war-room's ration — and they eat over the map, the candles lit against the dusk, the two of them companionable in the particular way of people winning.)*
> "The bishops' waverer," Letitia says, "asked Quill for the settlement papers. Quill sent them. The waverer is —" she consults her note — "reading."
> *(One hundred and forty chairs. The war-room holds its dusk. The dragon writes at night; they write at dawn — and dawn, it turns out, is winning.)*
> *(The waverer's note comes with the late post — Quill's papers received, read, "under consideration," the bishop's hand careful and noncommittal. Letitia reads it aloud with the air of a woman translating good news from a dead language. "Under consideration," she says, "is bishops' for yes, darling. They never say yes. They say 'under consideration' and then they come.")*
> *(Letitia folds the bishop's note into the war-book's margin — "under consideration," in the careful hand — and underlines it once. "Reading," she says. "The church reads slowly, darling. But it reads." The candles burn lower over the one hundred and forty, and the dusk holds its arithmetic.)*
> *(The dusk deepens on the list. She rules the final line, blots it, and lets the number stand — one hundred and forty, the columns verified, the refusals stalled, the tide running. The war's third week. Tomorrow will bring more.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE BISHOPS (the clergy's price: deference, hospitality, or principle). The church wavers; decide the means. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room: the bishops' replies — two yes, one waver, one silence — laid out on the table like cards, and Augusta with the particular expression of a woman who has managed clergy before and expects to manage them again. The morning light is kind to the room and unkind to no one, which is more than can be said for the conversation.)*
> "The waverer wants deference," Augusta says, tapping the second letter. "A personal call, the great bedchamber aired for his visit, the impression of piety — the full performance, child. The silent one wants hospitality — dinner, the cellar's best, no talk of the ball, let the wine do the asking. And the principle of the thing —" the spectacles lower — "wants you to invite them as equals and let them decide like adults. No performance. No cellar. Just the invitation, standing as written."
> *(Rose looks at the three replies. Three bishops, three prices, three doors. The waverer, the silent one, the principle. The church has always charged for its presence; the only question is the currency.)*
> "The deference would work," she says. "The hospitality would work. The principle —" she stops.
> "The principle," Augusta says, "is the only one that doesn't cost you anything afterward. Deference, once paid, is expected again. Hospitality without the ask can look like fear of the ask. But principle —" the rarest smile — "principle is the only currency the church can't spend twice."
> *(She looks at the three replies again — the waverer's careful hand, the silent one's blankness, the principle's plain ink. Deference would work; hospitality would work; the principle costs nothing afterward. The morning room holds its breath, and the bishops' prices lie on the table like cards in a game she intends to win.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The bishops:*
- **Deference, fully paid** — *the church, honored.* Rose calls in person, airs the bedchamber, performs piety. (Consequence: the waverer comes and brings his circle — but deference, once paid, is expected again.)
- **Hospitality, no strings** — *the table, laid.* Dinner, the best cellar, no mention of the ball; let gratitude do the work. (Consequence: the silent one thaws over the wine — but hospitality without the ask can look like fear of the ask.)
- **Principle, plainly stated** — *equals, invited.* The invitation stands as written; the church decides like adults. (Consequence: the respect is absolute — but adults sometimes decide no, and principle doesn't fill chairs.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: deference, hospitality, or principle. The bishops will remember how they were asked.)*
> *(Augusta waits, spectacles at the angle of counsel, and the three replies lie on the table between them. The church charges for its presence. The paying is the decision, and the decision is hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the dragon's silence — no letters for two nights; the quiet, priced. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Morning, and Letitia comes to breakfast with the overnight intelligence, the hawk's eyes puzzled over her chocolate.)*
> "Nothing, darling." She sets down the cup. "No letters for two nights. Honoria says the dragon's desk is —" she lowers her voice, though the breakfast room is empty — "quiet. She's not writing. Two nights, no letters, no callers reported, nothing."
> "She's planning." Rose butters her toast with the undue care of a woman thinking about something else.
> "Or she's —" Letitia stops. "Tired? Honoria said tired. Do dragons get tired, darling? I thought tiredness was something they inflicted."
> *(Rose considers the question with her chocolate. Two nights without letters. The refusals stalled at fourteen. The acceptances climbing daily — one hundred and sixty now, the columns lengthening. The dragon's silence could be exhaustion, or regrouping, or the worst possibility: a new weapon, not yet deployed, being sharpened somewhere out of sight.)*
> "We don't relax," Rose says. "Tired dragons are still dragons. A tired dragon is just a dragon who has stopped spending the cheap currency and started spending the dear kind."
> "Double the calls." Letitia reaches for the address books. "I do love a war. Especially one we're winning."
> "Double the calls," Rose agrees. "And Aunt — watch the quiet. The quiet is the thing she wants us to misprice."
> *(They double the watch the way they doubled the calls — Letitia's intelligencers alerted, Honoria's reports expected nightly, the breakfast table a council of war. The quiet gets priced daily now, like a stock: two nights, no letters. The price goes up every morning, and Rose pays it in vigilance, the one currency she has never overspent. Tired dragons are still dragons; they intend to be ready.)*
> *(Letitia writes the new watch-list in the war-book's margin — the intelligencers' names, the nightly reports expected, Honoria's hour marked with a star. The breakfast table, become a council of war: the address books open, the chocolate cooling. Honoria's reports expected nightly; the quiet, watched. By noon the watch-list is full, and the quiet has nowhere left to hide. The watch holds through the night.)*

scenes.synopsis: the historian's parallel — Harrow on the guest-list wars of the past; perspective. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Harrow finds her in the gallery, and walks with her among the portraits — the pensioner-historian, sixty-one, scarred and exact, his papers left behind in the library for once, his hands empty.)*
> "The '78 assembly." He nods at a Ravencroft, a woman with the family jaw and an unfashionable smile. "Your great-grandmother's ball. The same war — letters, debts, absence. The same dragon, different scales; the dragon of '78 was a Dowager with a grudge about a pew." A dry look. "She won, miss. The host. They always do — the hosts. Not because they're better. Because they're *there*. The house is there. The supper is there. The candles are lit. Absence is a weapon that only works until the night itself, and then the night has its own gravity, and gravity doesn't take letters."
> "And then?" They have reached the Park-drawn-whole, the frame at the gallery's end.
> "And then the room is either full or it isn't, and everyone sees which." He stops before the drawing — the whole, the complete, in his own careful hand. "History's lesson, miss, and it's the only one I charge for: Drummond can keep people away from the invitation. She can't keep them away from the night. Nobody ever could. The '78 dragon learned it. The '09 dragon learned it. This one —" a pause — "this one is learning it now, at the cost of her evenings."
> *(They walk on. The portraits watch — the whole long argument of blood, framed and dusted — and the historian's parallel settles over the campaign like dust settling after a charge: the hosts win, because they're there. It is not strategy. It is geography.)*
> *(They stand a moment before the drawing — the Park whole, in his careful hand — and the long light lies on the glass. "History," Harrow says, "is just the guest list, kept." He touches his cap, and goes back to his papers in the library.)*
> *("And the '09 dragon?" she asks. "The one whose debts we're still collecting?" Harrow smiles, the scarred gentleman's whole amusement. "The '09 dragon learned it too, miss — your mother's year. She kept the pews empty and the ballroom full, and the town remembered the ballroom. It's larger.")*

scenes.synopsis: the Hartwell rose, budding — the gardener's report; the bloom, on schedule. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The walled garden, morning: the gardener's report, delivered with soil on his hands and the particular pride of a man whose intelligence is horticultural.)*
> "The bud's coloring, Miss Hartwell." He shows her — the green tightness giving way to the first blush, the promise of the opening written in color. "A week. Ten days at most. It'll open for the ball, miss —" he grins, the soil deep in the lines of his hands — "roses have their own intelligence about these things. This one has been waiting ten seasons. It knows the date."
> "And the housewarming's flowers?" The cutting baskets stand ready by the wall.
> "Cutting starts in five days. Every stem Hartwell-grown." He straightens, and the pride is entire. "The ton'll walk through our garden, miss. Literally. I've planned the route — the terrace urns first, then the ballroom's great vases, then the supper room's low bowls. They'll breathe us in. They won't know they're breathing the Park, but they will be."
> *(She bends to the bud — the blush, the certainty, the tight green giving way. The legacy, literal and living, is on schedule. Ten days to the first bloom of the Hartwell rose. Ten days to the ball. The garden keeps its own calendar, and the calendar is holding, and the gardener stands beside her with soil on his hands like a general who has never lost.)*
> *(The cutting baskets fill as they talk — the gardeners moving down the rows, the secateurs flashing, the terrace urns' flowers first, then the ballroom's great vases. The gardener watches the baskets with the satisfaction of a quartermaster watching the wagons load. "Five days," he says, touching the bud. "The ball and the bloom. The garden keeps its promises, miss. It's the one thing here that never learned to lie.")*
> *(She walks the rows once more before leaving — the blush deepening, the baskets filling behind her. The gardener stays with his flowers, soil on his hands, a man who has never once been wrong about a rose.)*
> *(A blackbird scolds from the wall as she goes — the garden's own sentry, unimpressed by campaigns. Behind her the secateurs flash on, row by row, the baskets filling, and the bud on schedule behind them.)*

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry mends the war-room's map; service, in small things. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He finds her in the war-room at midnight — the map torn at the fold, the campaign's one casualty, the guest list's center split where it has been opened and closed a hundred times — and produces a needle and thread from his dispatch case without a word.)*
> "You carry sewing kit in a dispatch case, Major?"
> "I carry everything in a dispatch case." He threads the needle on the first try, the soldier's neatness, and begins mending the fold with small, exact stitches. "A map is an instrument. Instruments get maintained. The fold was going — another day and we'd have lost the clergy front to geography." He ties off, bites the thread, inspects the work. "There."
> *(She looks at the mended fold — the small exact stitches, the map whole again — and at the man who carries sewing kits in dispatch cases and mends campaigns at midnight, and the war-room's midnight feels suddenly, absurdly, like the safest place in England. Safer than the ballroom will be. Safer than anywhere with a dragon in it.)*
> "Thank you, Henry."
> "It was a small thing." He packs the kit — needle, thread, the little brass thimble — each to its place. "I am —" the smallest smile, there and gone — "practicing. The mending, the maintaining, the midnight. All of it."
> *(He goes, the dispatch case closed, the map whole. She pins it back on the wall herself and runs a finger along the stitches — the clergy front intact, the columns whole — and somewhere below, the stable clock strikes one over the war-room's midnight: the map, the candles, the mending, the safest place in England.)*
> *(Then she blows out the candles one by one, and the war-room's midnight settles over the mended campaign: the map whole, the stitches small and exact, the dispatch case closed, the man gone. The mending holds. She stands in the dark a moment — the war-room's midnight, the mended map, the campaign's one casualty repaired — and the quiet of it settles over everything before she goes up to bed, the map whole behind her.)*

scenes.synopsis: the arithmetic, at midnight — two hundred chairs; the war, being won. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Midnight, and the arithmetic: two hundred chairs — the bishops coming, the clergy front won, the young multiplying beyond Lavinia's already-generous count, the great houses steady, the émigré houses certain. She does the sums with the midnight lying on the list, the pen moving surely now, the columns no longer a battlefield map but a guest list with ambitions.)*
> *(Two hundred of four hundred. The refusals stalled at fourteen — no new ones in four days. The dragon silent for four nights now — Honoria's intelligence, exact and puzzling, the desk in London quiet. The acceptances climb like the Hartwell rose's bud: certain, on schedule, a little every day. The war is being won the way wars are won in daylight: visibly, and therefore undeniably.)*
> *(Letitia brings chocolate — the midnight ration, thicker than the morning's — and they drink it over the map, the two of them, the candles low. The war-room holds its midnight.)*
> "Two hundred," Letitia says. "Darling, do you remember when it was thirty? When the Trelawneys' refusal was the whole pile?"
> "I remember."
> "The pile's still small." Letitia taps the refusals — fourteen, squared with the ruler. "And the list —" she looks at the columns — "the list is becoming a ball."
> *(Two hundred chairs. The ball, ten days away, beginning to look like a ball — and the wanting, in the honest midnight, allowed to grow a little larger.)*
> *(The chocolate is thicker at midnight — Letitia's recipe, the war-room's own — and they drink it among the columns while the candles burn low. "Two hundred," Letitia says, trying the weight of it. "Darling. It's a ball. Say it.")*
> *(The house is quiet around them — the midnight's particular stillness. Two hundred chairs sit in the room like a third person at the table, and neither of them says goodnight for a while.)*
> *(Letitia refills the cups from the pot on the hearth — the midnight ration, thicker than the morning's — and the chocolate steams between them. "Ten days," she says. "Person by person, darling — I'd do it all again." She drinks. "Don't tell the bishops.")*

scenes.synopsis: the Dowager's assessment — the war, two-thirds won; the dragon's next move, anticipated. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta's morning room: the Dowager with the guest list, the refusals, and the particular stillness of a woman doing long arithmetic. The lavender water, the morning light, the spectacles at the angle of total attention.)*
> "Two hundred." The spectacles lower. "Of four hundred. The dragon silent four nights." A tap on the refusals. "She is not tired, child. Whatever Honoria sees — and Honoria sees truly, which is the pity of it — the tiredness is not the truth. She is waiting."
> "For what?" Rose pours the tea, the morning room's protocol.
> "For the ball to be inevitable." Augusta sets the list down with finality. "Agatha Drummond has never fought a lost battle in her life. She fights to the moment of decision, and then —" the rarest pause — "she decides. If your room fills, she will come. Not coming would be the concession, and she has never conceded anything, not in sixty years of evenings. She will come, and she will concede, and she will do it —" the spectacles rise — "in daylight, before the ton she tried to keep away. It is the only move she has left, and she knows it, and she is spending these quiet nights deciding how to make it look like victory."
> "Then we fill the room." She sets down the cup. "Past the point of argument."
> "Then we fill the room, child." Augusta returns to her letters. "It is the only war there is. Everything else — the letters, the bishops, the purple she is undoubtedly having made — is weather."
> *("The purple," Augusta says, returning to her letters as though the assessment were finished — which, with Augusta, means it is finished. "She is having it made. Purple. The deepest purple. Acknowledgment, dressed for daylight." The pen scratches. "Let her dress it beautifully, child. A beautiful concession is still a concession. The town will see the purple. The town will also see the room.")*
> *(Two hundred chairs. The room filling. The only war there is — and the numbers moving toward it, past the point of argument, toward the ball.)*

scenes.synopsis: the empty ballroom, revisited — forty paces; the stakes, restated. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Midnight, and the ballroom again: forty paces of polished possibility, the candle in her hand, the great room holding its breath the way it has held it every midnight she has come.)*
> *(She walks the floor's length — the steps counted, the arithmetic automatic now, forty paces there and forty back. Two hundred chairs. Four hundred wanted. Fourteen refusals, stalled. A dragon, silent, waiting for the moment of decision. The stakes restated in the candlelight, the old stakes, the only stakes: an empty ballroom is public humiliation; a full one is the verdict. Bell will count the chairs in print. The ton will count them in person. Everyone counts.)*
> *(She sets the candle down at the room's center and stands in the dark it makes around her — the flame's small circle, the great dark beyond. The wanting is still there — the honest dark, the wanting — and she lets it be there. Wanting is the risk. She has always known that, the way she knows the floor: exactly. She wants it anyway. She has wanted it since the first refusal, since the first letter, since the first dawn of the war-room.)*
> *(She snuffs the candle at the room's center and stands a moment in the complete dark — forty paces of it, the polished floor, the waiting air. The dark has a texture, the ballroom's own: beeswax, flowers not yet arrived, possibility. Then she takes up the candle again, relights it from the hall's lamp, and goes up to the war-room. The wanting walks with her, honest in the dark, and the dawn will find them both at the desk.)*
> *(She walks the forty paces again, slower this time — the polished floor cool through her slippers, the candle's small circle traveling with her. Two hundred chairs, and two hundred more to find. The room holds them all already, in the dark: the wanting, the waiting, the war's arithmetic done in footsteps.)*
> *(At the far end she turns and looks back down the room — the candle a single point of light in forty paces of dark. Two hundred chairs still to find, and the room already full of the wanting. She takes up the candle and goes, and the dark settles back into its waiting.)*

scenes.synopsis: the cottages' contribution — the tenants' gift; the house's two hosts, honored. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room, and the housekeeper's girl with a covered basket — the cottages' contribution, presented with ceremony, the girl's best apron on and her curtsy practiced to the point of pain.)*
> "From the row, miss." The girl curtsies, deep and careful. "The widows made the preserves. The girls did the posies. It's —" she lifts the cover with a flourish only slightly spoiled by nerves — "for the ball's supper room, miss. Our part. We wanted —" she stops, the rehearsed speech gone — "we wanted it to be there. Where they'll see."
> *(The basket: preserves in labeled jars — damson, blackberry, the row's own fruit — posies tied with ribbon, a card in a careful hand: "From the cottages, with pride." Rose looks at it for a long moment. The jars catch the morning light. The posies are sweet peas and rosemary — gratitude and remembrance, the cottages' flower language, whether they know it or not.)*
> "Tell them," Rose says carefully, "that the supper room will carry their card beside the epergne. Where the ton can see it. The great epergne, the family's grandest piece — and beside it, the cottages' card."
> "Oh, miss." The girl's eyes shine. "They'll —" she stops, curtsies again — deeper this time, from the heart — and flees, basketless, the apron flying.
> *(Rose sets the card on the desk, propped against the inkwell. The housewarming has two hosts — herself, and everyone who kept the place while she was earning it. The cottages' card goes beside the epergne. Where the ton can see it. Where the dragon, if she comes, will see it too.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick finds the card and reads it, and the immovable mouth does the extraordinary thing. "The epergne's foot, miss," she says. "The family plate and the cottages' pride, side by side." She holds the card a moment longer. "Ten years, miss. It's right." She stops, because housekeepers do not name these things — but the keys at her waist chime as she straightens, which says it for her.)*
> *(The card goes to the supper room that afternoon, carried by Mrs. Quick herself — not trusted to a girl, not this. She places it with her own hands, and the keys at her waist are silent this time. It is done properly, and it is done.)*

scenes.synopsis: the embroidery's crisis — a petal fails; the atelier's nerve, tested. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The atelier, and a crisis: a petal — the great opening bloom's central petal — has failed. The silk puckered in the night, the tension wrong, six days' work ruined in the one place the eye goes first. The frames stand silent. The girls stand around the ruined petal the way mourners stand around a grave.)*
> "It's ruined." Claudine, seventeen, stands before the frame with her hands twisted in her apron, the tears held back by force of will. "I — Miss Élise, I ruined it. The tension — I pulled too tight, I —"
> *(Élise looks at the petal for a long time. The atelier holds its breath. Then she picks up her scissors — the good shears, the ones she never lends — and cuts. One clean cut. The ruined petal comes free and falls to the floor like a dead thing.)*
> "Watch." She holds up the empty space in the bloom. "Silk fails. Hands don't." She turns to the girl, and the warm voice is warm and also iron. "You will do it again. Better. Because now you know how it fails, and knowing how it fails is the whole of the craft. The first petal was hope. The second will be knowledge."
> *(Claudine takes up the needle. Her hands shake once, then steady. The frame fills again — the petal, re-begun, the silk persuaded this time, the tension right. The atelier's nerve, tested, holds. The other girls return to their frames, and the particular music of the atelier resumes — needles, breathing, Élise's chalk.)*
> "Eleven days," Élise says to Rose, quietly. "Still eleven days. We don't lose days to fear. Fear —" she looks at the re-begun petal — "fear is the one thing we don't embroider."
> *(By evening the re-begun petal is half done — Claudine's needle flying, the tension right this time, the knowledge in the hands. Élise watches from her frame, chalk in hand, and nods once. "Better," she says quietly. "See? The better embroiderer." She turns back to her own frame before the girl can answer, and the atelier's nerve holds steady.)*

scenes.synopsis: the arithmetic, at dawn — two hundred and sixty chairs; the dragon's silence, broken. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dawn, and the arithmetic: two hundred and sixty chairs — and news, the kind Letitia delivers the way other people deliver thunder. The dragon's silence is broken. Not letters. A visit.)*
> "She called on the Micklethwaites." Letitia's intelligence is breathless, the chocolate untouched. "In person. Yesterday. An hour — a full hour, darling, with tea and everything. She's not writing anymore." The hawk's eyes are bright. "She's *calling*. The war's gone personal. The dragon has left her desk and taken the field."
> "And the Micklethwaites?" Rose is already reaching for the list.
> "Held." Letitia grins, fierce and delighted. "Lady Micklethwaite told her the Park's supper was worth the drive. To her face, darling. The old lady has been waiting since '88 to say something like that, and she said it over her own tea things. I would have paid money to see it. I would have paid a great deal of money."
> *(Rose does the sums: two hundred and sixty of four hundred. The dragon, calling in person — spending her presence now, the dear currency, the one that runs out. The letters weren't enough. The war's gone personal, which means they are winning.)*
> "Then we call too," Rose says. "Everyone. Today. If she wants it personal, we'll give her personal — ours is better. Ours has better tea."
> *(The calls go out that morning — everyone, everywhere, the whole alliance deployed: Rose to the wobblers, Augusta to the old guard, Henry to the Craykes' circle, Lavinia's young to the young, Laurent's charm to the émigré houses. The war-room empties by ten, the address books gone with their owners, the maps left in Rose's keeping. Personal. The dragon wants personal. Personal she shall have.)*
> *(The war-room empties by ten — the address books gone out with the callers, the maps in Rose's keeping, the lists divided street by street. She stands at the map with the morning on it, the dragon's silence broken and answered, and the counter-campaign's machinery turns: call for call, presence for presence, the daylight's answer to the dragon's night. The calls go out; the day answers.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE DRAGON'S CALL (answer Drummond's personal campaign: match, ignore, or preempt). The dragon calls in person; decide the counter. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The war-room, noon: the dragon calls in person now — the Micklethwaites held, but others may not, and the map shows the red marks of her visits spreading — and the counter must be decided. Augusta sits with her spectacles at the angle of war; Letitia with her pen poised; the noon light hard on the list. Three ways to answer a dragon who has taken the field.)*
> "Match her," Augusta says, tapping the red marks. "Call for call, presence for presence. You go where she goes, and you go first the second time. Ignore her —" a second tap — "the calls are nothing if the room fills. Dignity, and the arithmetic. Or preempt —" the rarest smile, the Dowager's whole mischief in it — "invite her to call on *you*. Here. At the Park. Let the dragon come and see what she's fighting — the finished house, the full room coming, the whole of it, in daylight."
> *(Rose looks at the map — the red marks, the columns, the war made visible. Three answers, each honest, each with its price. The candles are not lit; it is noon, and the decision is a daylight one. Somewhere in London, the dragon is ordering her carriage for the afternoon's calls.)*
> "Say the prices plainly," Rose says. "All three."
> "Matching burns you at her pace — dragons set a pace that kills. Ignoring risks the escalation — ignored dragons do the unpredictable thing. Preempting —" Augusta's smile again — "preempting is either genius or madness, and no one will know which, including the dragon, until she comes through your door."
> *(One last look at the map — the red marks, the columns, the daylight on both. Three answers, each honest, each with its price, and the choosing hers.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The dragon's call:*
- **Match her, call for call** — *presence for presence.* Rose calls in person on every wobbler Drummond visits. (Consequence: the days are endless and the victories personal — but matching a dragon's pace is how people get burned.)
- **Ignore the calls** — *the room, filling.* The campaign continues as planned; Drummond's presence is nothing if the chairs fill. (Consequence: the dignity is absolute — but ignored dragons escalate, and escalation is unpredictable.)
- **Preempt with an invitation** — *the dragon, invited here.* Drummond is asked to call at the Park, to see the finished house before the ball. (Consequence: the boldness is breathtaking — but inviting the dragon into the house is either genius or madness, and no one will know which until she comes.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: match, ignore, or preempt. The dragon will answer. Dragons always answer, and the answer will come in person now.)*
> *(The noon passes. The map waits — the red marks, the columns, the three answers. Augusta's spectacles catch the light. Letitia's pen hovers. Decide — the doing has already begun.)*

scenes.synopsis: the decision, executed — the counter-campaign, launched. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The decision executed before the ink dries: the counter-campaign launched — the calls redoubled, the letters flying, the war-room's maps updated with the dragon's movements marked in red, the red spreading like a rash across the guest list's edges. Rose works through the afternoon with Letitia's address books and Augusta's eleven and Julian's twelve and Lavinia's multiplying young — the whole alliance, deployed, every chair a small battle.)*
> *(The red marks spread across the map: Drummond's calls, answered chair by chair. The Micklethwaites held. The Grevilles — Augusta's eleventh letter, the '88 debt, the old seal — confirmed. The clergy front: two bishops firm, the waverer reading Quill's papers, the silent one thawing. The young: multiplying beyond counting, Lavinia's sixes becoming dozens. The great houses: steady, the Sunderlands' circle widening like ripples.)*
> *(She goes to the map before the candles are lit and takes down the day's red marks one by one — each pin lifted where an answer came, each column ruled where a chair was won. The dragon's morning calls, answered by evening: that is the whole of the counter-campaign, and the map shows it cleaner than any column. Fourteen red marks left. Fourteen refusals, stalled.)*
> *(At dusk the arithmetic: two hundred and eighty. The counter-campaign's first day, and the room fills faster than the dragon can empty it — the acceptances outpacing the calls. The war's shape is changing: from defense to advance, from holding to winning. She stands at the map with the dusk on it and allows herself, for one moment, the luxury of the numbers.)*
> *(She rules the final column, blots it, and sits back. Two hundred and eighty chairs, the red marks answered, the refusals stalled at fourteen. The dragon spends her dearest currency for nothing now — and both of them know it.)*
> *(Letitia brings the evening chocolate — the war-room's ration, thicker at dusk — and they drink it over the ruled columns. "Two hundred and eighty," the quartermaster says, savoring it. "Darling, the room is filling faster than she can empty it. Tomorrow we do it again." The candles burn low over the ruled columns.)*

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry walks the drive's lanterns; the moonlight, prepared. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(He walks the drive with her at dusk — the lanterns going up in the limes, the moon waxing toward full, the great trees holding the little lights like hands holding fireflies — and inspects each hanging with a soldier's eye, the big hands testing chains.)*
> "This one." He adjusts a lantern's chain, the metal clinking softly. "It'll swing in the wind. The drive's the ball's first impression —" he steps back, squints up — "it should be steady. A swinging lantern says the house is nervous."
> "You are hanging lanterns, Major?" She falls into step beside him. "The war-room's map is mended, the Craykes are converted, and now the lanterns?"
> "I am practicing useful things." He moves to the next, tests, adjusts. "The small devotions, Rose. The gift of attention, every day, on purpose." He tests the chain — steady — and nods. "Today the lanterns. Tomorrow —" the smallest smile — "whatever needs doing. There is always something that needs doing. I have started making lists."
> *(They walk the drive's length, checking lanterns, and the dusk does what dusks do at the Park: it behaves. The devotion in the evening is the quietest campaign of the war — no letters, no debts, no absence, just a man making sure the lights hang steady — and, she suspects, the one that matters most. Wars are won with arithmetic. Evenings are won with lanterns.)*
> "Stay for supper, Henry."
> "I had planned to." He adjusts the last lantern, steps back, satisfied. "It was in the dispatch case too. The supper plans. Filed under S."
> *(The last lantern goes up at the drive's end — the chain tested, the swing allowed for, the little light steady in the limes. Henry steps back, satisfied, and the drive holds its dusk: the lanterns going up like a constellation, the moon waxing toward full, the house lit behind them, and the ball's first impression secured.)*
> *(Walking back, the drive behind them is a constellation of small steady lights. "Every one," Henry says, satisfied. The devotion in the evening, complete: the lanterns hung, the supper planned, the moon doing the rest.)*

scenes.synopsis: the portrait's progress — the laugh, nearly caught; the unveiling, planned. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The still-room studio: the portrait nearly finished — the laugh, nearly caught, the Park behind her nearly breathing, the north light doing what Octavia has spent weeks persuading it to do. The smell of linseed and turpentine, the particular quiet of a room where something is being made.)*
> "Three more sittings." Octavia steps back, brush in hand, head tilted. "The laugh is —" she tilts further — "there. Almost. One more session in the right light and I'll have it — the picnic's light, the unguarded moment, the whole of it." She looks at Rose. "The unveiling — the week of the ball, as planned. In the west gallery. The finished Park, the laughing woman —" the precise voice softens, the way it does only here — "my half of the arrangement, Rose. Nearly done. Nearly true."
> *(Rose looks at the almost-laugh — her own joy, caught in paint, the mouth open, the eyes bright — and the war-room's arithmetic fades for a moment. Some victories are not counted in chairs. Some are counted in the exact angle of a laugh, caught by someone who loves the laugher.)*
> "It's the best thing you've ever made."
> "It's the truest." Octavia cleans her brush with the methodical care of a surgeon. "There's a difference. You taught me that — the difference between the best and the truest. The best is for the ton. The truest —" she covers the canvas — "is for the house."
> *(The brushes stand cleaned in their jar, the week's colors lined up like soldiers. Octavia covers the canvas herself, the cloth settling over the almost-laugh. "Thursday," she says. "The right light. Then it's true.")*
> *(She leaves Octavia to the studio's quiet — the covered canvas, the cleaned brushes, the north light going grey. Three more sittings. The laugh, nearly caught. The unveiling, the week of the ball. The devotion in the studio is the war's quietest front, and it is winning too — one sitting at a time, the truest thing Octavia has ever made, nearly true. The truest thing, nearly true — and Thursday will finish it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the cutting begins — Hartwell-grown flowers; the ton, to breathe the garden. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The walled garden, dawn: the cutting begun — the gardeners at work with baskets, the secateurs flashing, every stem Hartwell-grown, the rows giving generously.)*
> "The terrace urns first." The gardener directs like a general, the baskets lined up in campaign order. "Then the ballroom's great vases. Then the supper room's low bowls." He shows her the first basket — the blooms, the garden's own, the colors the ton will breathe. "They'll breathe us in, miss. The ton'll walk through our flowers and breathe the Park. They'll think it's the ballroom's perfume. It'll be the walled garden, ten seasons in the making."
> *(She walks the rows where the cutting has been — the neat gaps, the remaining blooms nodding in the morning breeze — and the garden gives generously, the way finished things do. The Hartwell rose's bud: blushing deeper, the color coming, on schedule. Five days to the ball. Five days to the bloom. The cutting baskets fill. The gardeners move down the rows like a harvest.)*
> "And the rose?" She stops at the row's end.
> "On schedule, miss." He touches the bud with reverence. "Five days. The ball and the bloom together. The garden keeps its promises."
> *(She takes a basket herself and walks it up to the terrace — the urns' flowers, the first cutting, the stems still cool from the morning. The gardener's boy runs ahead to open the door, and the house takes the garden's offering the way it takes everything this week: as a promise kept.)*
> *(The baskets go up to the house — the terrace urns' flowers first, the gardeners carrying them like offerings. The ton will breathe the Park without ever knowing its name — kept quietly, and exactly on time.)*
> *(By noon the terrace urns stand full — the Hartwell-grown flowers nodding in the great stone vessels, the week's first flowers in place. The cutting goes on behind her, row by row, and the baskets keep coming.)*
> *(Five days to the ball, five to the bloom. The garden gives; the house receives; the promises hold fast, and the baskets keep coming up the hill.)*

scenes.synopsis: the arithmetic, at midnight — three hundred and twenty chairs; the ball, becoming real. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Midnight, and the arithmetic: three hundred and twenty chairs — the counter-campaign's third day, the dragon's calls answered chair by chair, the room filling like the tide Bell promised. She does the sums with the midnight lying on the list, and the numbers have stopped being a war and started being a ball.)*
> *(Three hundred and twenty of four hundred. The refusals stalled at fourteen — no new refusals in six days, the dragon's personal campaign spending her presence and gaining nothing. The wobblers, won. The great houses, steady. The young, multiplying. The émigré houses, certain. The bishops, coming. The columns stretch down the page and onto the second sheet, and Letitia has started a third.)*
> *(Letitia brings chocolate — the midnight ration — and they drink it over the map, the candles low, the war-room holding its midnight the way it has held every midnight of the war.)*
> "Three hundred and twenty," Letitia says softly. "Darling, the ballroom holds four hundred. We have three hundred and twenty. Five days —" she looks at the list — "five days, and the wanting is allowed to become the expecting."
> *(Three hundred and twenty chairs. Person by person, in daylight, with better stationery. The ball, five days away, beginning to look inevitable — and the dragon, somewhere in London, doing her own arithmetic in the dark.)*
> *(Letitia starts the third sheet — the columns overflowing, the acceptances beyond the page's edge. "Three hundred and twenty," she writes, underlining it twice. "Darling, we're going to need a bigger list." The midnight holds: the chocolate, the candles, the quartermaster's delight. Five days to the ball, and the inevitable beginning to look — even to the dragon in London, doing her arithmetic in the dark — like a fact.)*
> *(Rose takes up the pen herself and rules the third sheet's first column — the quartermaster's work, shared at midnight. The acceptances flow beyond the page's edge, name after name, and the candles burn low over the columns. Three hundred and twenty chairs, and rising. The midnight holds, and the list grows, and the ball comes nearer.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's verdict on the war — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"Lady A. D. has been writing letters, and Miss Hartwell has been writing back — earlier, and better. The town's talk has the quality of a tide turning, and tides, as the Gazette has observed before, do not turn back. The ballroom's arithmetic favors the host."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (earlier, and better! the phrasing!), then the reckoning: the war is pronounced winnable in print as well as in person, and Bell has made the verdict formidable, which is Bell's way of making it permanent. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the war that is won twice — in daylight and in print — is won for good.* — remembered: *the lesson: the war, won twice, is won for good.*

scenes.synopsis: the dragon's answer — Drummond accepts; the concession's shape, glimpsed. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening post, and Letitia comes to the war-room with a card held the way one holds a live coal — carefully, and with respect for the burn.)*
> "Read it, darling." The hawk's eyes are wide. "Aloud."
> *(Rose reads: Lady Agatha Drummond accepts. The housewarming ball. With pleasure. The card is engraved, formal, perfect — and at its foot, in the dragon's own hand, three words: "Until the ball." Not a threat. Not a promise. Something rarer: an acknowledgment.)*
> "She's coming." Letitia sits, suddenly. "Darling — she's coming. Not coming would be the concession, and she —" she stops — "she's decided. Augusta was right. She fights to the moment of decision, and then she decides."
> *(Rose holds the card. The dragon's answer: acceptance, on terms, in writing. The war's shape changes — from emptying the room to entering it. What Drummond does at the ball, she does before the ton she tried to keep away.)*
> *(She sets the card on the map, at the campaign's center. The chapter closes on the acceptance — engraved, formal, and entirely the dragon's — and the Season holds its breath.)*

scenes.synopsis: the final week — 320 chairs; the arithmetic, nearly won. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dawn of the final week, and the arithmetic: three hundred and twenty chairs — the war's third week, the dragon's acceptance filed at the campaign's center like a captured flag, the engraved card with its three handwritten words — "Until the ball" — sitting on the map where every fighter can see it.)*
> *(She does the sums in the war-room with the dawn lying on the list. Three hundred and twenty of four hundred. The refusals stalled at fourteen — the dragon's fourteen, kept, hers. The great houses steady, the young multiplying, the émigré houses certain, the bishops coming. The ballroom, in seven days, will be full — or near enough to full that the difference won't signify, which Bell will confirm in print and the ton will confirm in person.)*
> *(Letitia arrives with chocolate and the week's orders — the household's lists now, not the campaign's: the flowers' cutting, the musicians' hire, the candles' last order, the purse shelf's honest costs. The war-room's maps are being retired, rolled up with their red marks and black pins, and the household's lists are taking their place on the desk.)*
> "The maps," Letitia says, rolling the last one, "go to Harrow for the history. The lists stay. Darling —" she ties the roll with ribbon — "the campaign is nearly won. What remains is the week. The week is for arriving unhurried, or not arriving at all. Augusta's doctrine."
> *(The final week begins the way the finished house begins everything: early, and with better stationery. Three hundred and twenty chairs. Seven days. The dragon's acceptance stays where it is — the captured flag at the campaign's center — and the wanting, in the honest dawn, is becoming the expecting, which has its own discipline, harder than the fighting.)*
> *(Letitia ties the last map with ribbon and sets it aside for Harrow's history — the red marks, the black pins, the whole campaign rolled up like a finished letter. "The history," she says, "will want to know how it was done. Person by person, in daylight, with better stationery." The week's orders take the desk. The war is nearly won. The week is the victory, administered.)*

scenes.synopsis: the last wobblers — won; the list, closed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning calls, and the last wobblers fall: the Grevilles, convinced by Augusta's eleventh letter — the '88 debt, the old seal, the Dowager's whole century of ink; the Fanes, re-won after the '11 debt is publicly forgiven, the forgiveness announced at the Sunderlands' tea where everyone could hear it; the Aldingtons, shamed into courage by Lady Micklethwaite's example, the old lady's defiance proving contagious.)*
> "Closed." Letitia draws the line under the wobblers' list with a flourish, the pen digging into the paper. "The list is closed, darling. Four hundred invitations, three hundred and forty acceptances, fourteen refusals, and the rest —" she taps the silences — "the rest are cowards, and cowards don't count. They never did. They only ever counted themselves."
> "Three hundred and forty."
> "Three hundred and forty, darling." The hawk's eyes shine. "The ballroom holds four hundred. We have three hundred and forty. The arithmetic —" she stops, because quartermasters don't weep, and reaches for the chocolate instead — "the arithmetic is beautiful. Look at it. Three hundred and forty chairs, person by person, in daylight."
> *(Rose looks at the closed list — the columns, the names, the ruled line under the wobblers. The letters, the calls, the debts forgiven, the courage shamed into being. The war, nearly won, and the list closed like a book.)*

> *(Rose runs her finger down the acceptances — the great houses, the young, the émigré houses, the bishops, the last wobblers won — and remembers the first light three weeks ago: a single refusal, a pile of one. scenes.synopsis: the dragon's preparations — Honoria's last intelligence; Drummond, dressing for the ball. (Turns: 8)

> "Acknowledgment." Rose turns the word over. "Of what, exactly?"
> "Of the room. Of the house. Of you." Honoria moves to the window. "She's preparing, not plotting. The desk is quiet. The letters have stopped — all of them, even the debt collections. Mother has fought to the moment of decision, and she has decided. What she does at your ball —" the dry voice, dry as dust — "she does as herself. I thought you should know. So you can —" a stop — "so you can be ready. Not armed. Ready. There is a difference, and she is counting on you to know it."

Rose turns it over the way Augusta turns things over: thoroughly, and without mercy. Preparation, not plotting. The desk quiet. The letters stopped. The dragon, dressing for the ball the way generals dress for parleys.)*

> *(She goes to dress for dinner, and the evening's first hour holds the purple the way the war-room held the maps: as intelligence, filed. By Saturday the whole town will know the color. The dragon's concession, tailored, is on its way.)*

scenes.synopsis: the embroidery's final days — the great bloom, nearly done; the atelier's last push. (Turns: 8)

Then —" she stops before the gown, and the young voice does something it rarely does — falters — "then it is the finest thing the atelier has ever made, and I will have to let it go. Eleven days, six girls, and me. And then it walks away."
> "You'll see it at the ball." Rose touches the ivory silk — the Park's stone at noon, rendered in cloth.
> "I'll see it —" the voice cracks, just slightly — "I'll see it walk into the ballroom, and the ton will see what the modiste's girl can do." She recovers, chalk turning. "Claudine finished the central petal. The re-begun one. Look."

> "Wake her gently," Rose says. "And Élise — the atelier's triumph is three days away. Rest when you can."
> "Rest." Élise laughs, the warm sound frayed at the edges. "At the ball, Miss Hartwell. We'll rest at the ball. The girls, the frames, the chalk —" she looks at the gown — "we'll all rest at the ball."

Élise moves among them — the young commander, the modiste's girl become the atelier's — and the great bloom opens in silk on ivory, petal by petal, the re-begun one perfect. Three more days, and the finest thing the atelier has ever made walks into the ballroom, under the candles, before the ton. scenes.synopsis: the Dowager's ball-week counsel — what the week is for; Augusta, exact. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta's morning room: the Dowager with the week's shape in her head, exact at seventy-two, the lavender water, the morning light, the spectacles at the angle of total counsel.)*
> "The week is not for the ball." The spectacles lower. "The ball will happen — the chairs are counted, the supper is planned, the gown is nearly done. The week is for you — to arrive at the night unhurried, unharried, and entirely yourself. Rest. Walk. Let the household do its work." A tap on the table. "The host who arrives exhausted has lost before the first dance. The host who arrives rested —" a pause — "the host who arrives rested has already won."
> "And the dragon's purple?" Rose pours the tea. "Acknowledgment, Honoria says."
> "Acknowledgment." Augusta considers the word the way she considers everything: thoroughly, and without mercy. "It means she has decided to concede, and she means to do it beautifully. Let her. A beautiful concession is still a concession — and a concession made beautifully is the only kind the town will remember kindly." The rarest smile. "And if it's a trap?"
> "Then it is the most beautifully dressed trap in the history of traps, and you will spring it in the finest gown the atelier ever made." The smile widens, just slightly. "Either way, child. You win. That is the virtue of having built the battlefield — every trap laid on it is laid on your ground."

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry oversees the terrace urns; the garden, presented. (Turns: 7)

They should be —" he searches for the word the way he searches for everything: thoroughly — "welcoming. But not eager."

> "It's a fine line." Unmoved, rotating another urn its quarter-inch. "I am practicing fine lines."

scenes.synopsis: the bud, blushing deeper — the bloom, days away; the garden's calendar, holding. (Turns: 7)

scenes.synopsis: the portrait, finished — the laugh, caught; the unveiling, planned for the ball's week. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The still-room studio at midday, and the north window doing exactly what Octavia said it would do when she commandeered the room — laying the Park out behind the sitter like a backdrop that refused to sit still. Eleven mornings of sittings, always before the household woke. Rose knows the easel's creak the way she knows the war-room's desk drawer; the linseed smell is the studio's own weather.)*
> *(The canvas stands covered, the cloth over it like a held breath. Octavia is wiping a brush that is already clean — the precise woman's one allowed imprecision, the tell that the work has cost her.)*
> "It's done." She doesn't look up. "The laugh. I caught it on the ninth morning — you were laughing at Letitia through the door, something about the bishops' secretary and a seating plan — and I have spent the two mornings since trying not to spoil it."
> *(She draws the cloth away. The Park breathes behind the painted woman — the lake, the limes, the whole finished argument of it — and the woman in front is laughing the way Rose laughs when she has forgotten to arrange her face. Not the ball's laugh. The morning's.)*

> *(The frame leans against the wall — oak, plain, the Park's own timber, chosen over gilt. Rose knows the argument happened in the memorandum book; the page lies open on the stand, the decision inked and underlined twice.)*
> "The oak," Rose says.
> "Gilt would have apologized for the laugh." Octavia caps the linseed oil — the small domestic sound of a finished thing. "Oak doesn't apologize."
> *(They stand before it while the north light moves a fraction across the paint — the laugh, the Park, eleven mornings compressed into one canvas. The arrangement was simple, and Octavia states it the way she states everything.)*
> "My half of the arrangement." She covers the canvas again — the practiced gesture, the laugh disappearing under the cloth like a secret kept. "Delivered. Your half —" she looks at Rose — "is the wall. Choose it well."
> *(At the door Rose looks back once — the covered shape, the north window, the painter wiping the already-clean brush — and the week's first choosing waits on her like the canvas waited on the painter. Thursday, the cloth comes off. The ton will see what Octavia sees.)*

scenes.synopsis: the last debt, paid — Julian's freedom, complete; the gloves, kept by choice. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The canal walk at dusk: Julian with the final receipt — the brother's last debt, paid in full, with money he earned — and the water holding the dusk the way the week holds its breath.)*
> "It's done." He hands her the paper — the figures, the clearance, the end of it. "The last of it. Tuesday's payment cleared. Quill has the accounts —" a quick look — "you'll check, I know. Check."
> "I won't."
> "You will." The real smile, the unguarded one. "It's your nature." He turns the mended gloves in his hands — the stitching, the wear, the kept thing. "I keep these, Rose. Not as penance — as choice. The mending held. I held." He looks at the terrace, at the Park whole below. "Free. The terrace, the gloves, all of it. Finally."

> "Walk me back," she says.

> *(They walk back along the water — the free man, the kept gloves, the terrace waiting below as a life. Not yet. Soon. The arrangement, offered freely for the first time: the arm, the walk, the always. The week's quietest freedom — the mending held, he held — settling like dusk on the canal.)*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent arrives — the Frenchman, for the ball; England, the subject, nearer. (Turns: 7)

> "The de Varennes are coming." He sheds the coat, kisses Letitia's hand, accepts chocolate with the ease of a man who has never been refused it. "All of them. Paris writes daily —" the Gallic shrug — "and daily I do not answer. England, Rose. The subject draws nearer."

For the housewarming. For —" he stops, the polish dropping entirely — "for the woman who finished the house. The rest —" a gesture at the future — "the rest we will decide. Later. > "The de Varennes," Rose says, "all of them."
> "All of them." He raises his chocolate. "To the housewarming. To the woman who finished the house." The unpolished smile. "To England — the subject, nearer."
> *(The rain dries on his coat by the fire. The post's letters wait unopened. The Frenchman is here for the ball — and the house, with him in it, is more itself.)*
> *(A footman takes the wet coat — the rain, the road, the Channel's weather still in the wool — and Laurent stands in the hall's light, unpolished and entirely at home. "The house," he says, looking around, "is finished. And its mistress —" he kisses Rose's hand — "is exactly on time.")*
> *(Dinner lengthens — the presence like music, the woman who finished the house across the table. The rest — the subject, the decision — deferred to the masquerade, the old world one more night.)*

scenes.synopsis: Lavinia arrives early — the glittering advance guard; the ball's brilliance, secured. (Turns: 7)

By supervise I mean —" she looks around, radiant, and the glitter drops for a heartbeat — "oh, Rose. It's *finished*. It's actually finished. I have seen houses built, and I have seen houses kept, and I have never —" the heartbeat passes — "I have never seen anything like this."

> "Our rooms had better be the best." The glitter returns, fully. "We are the advance guard, darling. The ball's brilliance, secured. The young have arrived. The rest will follow —" she counts her six, precise — "because we are here, and we are the future, and the future is always the best party."
> *(The house absorbs them — the laughter, the luggage, the life — the siege-luggage carried upstairs, the six installed, the advance guard in place. The ball's brilliance, secured three days early by the young, who are the future, and the future is the best party.)*
> "Supervise," Rose says, "is a strong word."
> "I am a strong woman." Lavinia is already moving toward the stairs. "The advance guard supervises, darling. It's in the name. Guard. Advance. Come, girls — we have a finished house to be brilliant in."
> *("We came early to help. By help I mean supervise." The glitter, the heartbeat's drop, the finished house seen truly for once: "I have never seen anything like this." The future, arrived early.)*
> *(Upstairs the siege-luggage is being unpacked under Lavinia's supervision — the best rooms, the brightest laughter, the six settled like glitter. Three days early, and the house already sounds like the future.)*
> *(The six follow her up — the chatter filling the stairwell, the laughter coming down long after the doors close. The finished house holds the sound the way it holds everything this week: as a promise of the ball to come.)*

scenes.synopsis: the household's final orders — the staff, ready; the two hosts, aligned. (Turns: 7)

She looks down the table — the footmen, the maids, the kitchen's own. "This house has waited ten seasons. We will not be the reason it waits longer."

The maids practice their curtsies in the corridor, giggling, then straightening when Mrs. Quick's keys chime. Behind them the copper gleams, the kitchen serene among it all.)*
> "Miss Hartwell. The house is ready." The immovable mouth does the extraordinary thing — it softens, just slightly. "We're proud, miss. All of us."
