> *(At the corridor's end the keys turn, the straight back going — and the household's final orders are given and taken: the flowers Thursday, the low bowls Friday, the linen twice-pressed. Ten seasons of keeping, aligned behind one week of showing.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick walks the servants' hall once more after the dismissal — the table cleared, the orders given, the week's machinery turning. She runs a finger along the table's edge, checking for dust that isn't there, and the keys at her waist chime faintly. The keeping, ready for its showing.)*

scenes.synopsis: the hanging — the portrait goes up; the woman, witnessed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Thursday morning, and the chosen wall waits with its nails in — the footmen in clean gloves, the plumb line swaying, the frame's oak catching the gallery's long light before the canvas is even up.)*

> *(The applause breaks it — the maids first, then the footmen, Mrs. Quick immovable at the back with her mouth doing the extraordinary thing. It is against all protocol, and therefore exactly right.)*
> "It's the best wall in the house," Rose says.
> "It's the best woman in the house," Octavia says. "The wall was the easy part." But the hand in Rose's is not precise at all — it is shaking, just slightly, with the week's quietest triumph.
> *(Rose holds the shaking hand and looks at the laughing woman on the wall — the Park behind her, the morning's laugh, the truest thing — and the light does what the north window promised: it finds the paint and the woman at once.)*
> *(From the stairs the gallery reads whole — the line of ancestors, the laughing woman hung among them or before them or above the war's old ground, the week's choosing made visible. Rose does not say which truth the wall tells. The wall tells it.)*
> *(The household disperses to its duties — the maids wiping their eyes and blaming the dust, the footmen straightening already-straight gloves. The cook pats Octavia's shoulder as she passes, a benediction in flour.)*
> *(Octavia stays a moment longer, adjusting nothing — there is nothing to adjust — and then she picks up the memorandum book, snaps it shut, and goes back to being precise. The portrait hangs. The woman is witnessed. Thursday has done its work.)*

scenes.synopsis: the final issue's shape — Bell on what the paper will print; the last word, planned. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Bell comes with the final issue's shape in her head — the proprietor, planning the last judgment, the notebook already half full of the week's certainties.)*
> "The ball gets the front page." She states it flatly — the soft voice, the sharp eyes, the mid-forties proprietor naming weather. "The verdict — unsparing and just — waits for the final assembly. But the ball —" the notebook opens — "the ball gets the reporting: who came, who didn't, what the dragon wore, what the gown —" a look — "what Élise's gown *did*. The town will read it Monday and argue about it for a year."
> "And the verdict?"
> "The verdict is written." The notebook closes. "I've been writing it for ten seasons, Miss Hartwell. The final assembly just gives me the last paragraph." She moves to the door — the straight back, the shut notebook. "One proprietor to another: whatever the ball costs you, it doesn't cost you the paper. The paper was never yours to lose."
> *(Rose watches her go — the straight back, the shut notebook — and the final issue's shape settles: the ball, reported; the verdict, waiting; the last word, on the paper's own terms. Ten seasons of writing, and the last paragraph still to come. The front page, the reporting, the town's year of argument.)*
> "The paper was never yours to lose." Rose turns the sentence over after the door closes. One proprietor to another — the strangest kindness of the week, and the most exact. The ball gets the front page. The verdict waits. The last word belongs to the paper, as it always has.
> *(The sentence goes with her back to the week's lists — "The paper was never yours to lose" — the strangest kindness of the week, and the most exact.)*
> *(The notebook goes back into Bell's reticule — the soft voice, the sharp eyes, the mid-forties proprietor carrying the week's certainties back to the Gazette. The final assembly waits for its last paragraph; the ball waits for its front page. Ten seasons of writing, and the verdict still to come — unsparing and just, when the assembly gives it the ending.)*

scenes.synopsis: the ballroom, dressed — Hartwell-grown flowers; the great room, in bloom. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The ballroom, Thursday: the flowers going in — the gardeners on ladders, the great vases filling, the forty paces transforming petal by petal.)*
> *(She stands in the doorway and counts the way she counts everything — fourteen vases down the room's length, the terrace urns' sisters come inside for the week, white lilies standing tall among the roses. Purity of intent, the lilies say in the flower language, and the room had better mean it.)*
> *(A gardener's boy drops a petal on the polished floor and is scolded softly; the petal stays where it fell, because the room is past the point where one petal signifies. The ladders shift. The vases fill. The chandeliers hang unlit above it all, waiting for Saturday's candles.)*
> "The candles go in Saturday at noon," the gardener says, reading her look upward. "The footmen with the long tapers. A hundred lights, miss, and the flowers underneath. You'll see."
> *(She walks the vases' line and checks the water in each — the levels, the clarity — topping the seventh with the ewer herself, the quartermaster's granddaughter's exactness. The stems stand straight. The lilies hold their tall white. The roses, Hartwell-grown, open a fraction wider in the room's warmth.)*
> "Friday for the low bowls," the gardener says, coming down his ladder with a fistful of stripped stems. "The supper room's. They'll want the cool of the morning, miss, or the roses sulk."
> "The roses sulk," Rose says.
> "Everything sulks before a ball, miss." He touches his cap. "It's the occasion. Even the flowers know."
> *(The supper room's low bowls wait their turn — Friday's work, done early in the morning's cool, when the roses don't sulk.)*
> *(She walks the forty paces among the ladders — the gardeners nodding, the vases filling — and the floor's wax smells of beeswax and crushed stems. In three days the ton walks through Hartwell's flowers and breathes the Park. The gardener's plan, executed.)*
> *(She touches one lily as she passes — the tall white, the intent — and the petal is cool and certain under her finger. The room is not decorated, she thinks. It is stated.)*
> *(At the far end she turns and looks back down the room — the fourteen vases, the lilies, the ladders, the unlit chandeliers — and the empty ballroom holds its flowers the way the week holds its breath: completely, and on purpose. Thursday. The flowers are in.)*

scenes.synopsis: the final tasting — the supper, approved; the Hartwell rose ice, attempted. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The kitchens: the final tasting — the savories laid in rows, the ices sweating gently in their molds, the champagne's quantity confirmed at two hundred bottles, counted twice.)*
> "The rose ice, Miss Hartwell." The confectioner presents it on a chilled dish — the pale cold, the floral, the garden's working roses rendered in sugar and frost. "Rosewater from the garden's roses. Not the Hartwell rose —" a glance toward the walled garden, though the walls are between — "the gardener was most particular. The legacy is for Saturday. The ice is for the sisters."
> *(She tastes: the cold first, then the floral, then the exact. It is the garden, frozen — the Park's summer, kept in a spoon. The sisters' rosewater, the Hartwell rose untouched, the legacy reserved for the bloom.)*
> "Approved." She signs the diagrams — the courses in order, the wines, the ice between the removes. "All of it."
> "It holds two hours out of the ice, miss." The confectioner wraps the dish again, brisk. "The supper's timing must mind it. Two hours, not three."
> *(She notes it — the ice's two hours, inked in the diagram's margin — and tastes the clear soup last, the kitchens' pride. It is exactly as it was at the first supper she ever ordered here, only better, the way the house is better: the same, and finished.)*
> *(The cook stands serene among the copper, arms folded, the week's whole campaign in her posture.)*
> "The supper is the house's argument," Rose says, "and the argument is won."
> "We've been making it for ten seasons, miss." The cook does not smile; she doesn't need to. "Saturday we serve it."
> *(The diagrams go back to Mrs. Quick's file, inked and dated. The confectioner returns the rose ice to the ice house with the week's own ceremony — the frozen garden, the sisters' roses, the Hartwell rose still on its stem out in the walled garden, blushing toward Saturday.)*
> *(She leaves the kitchens to their copper and their calm. Ten seasons of making it, and the making shows in every dish. Saturday, the serving, at last.)*

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry checks the moonlight drive; the ball's first impression, secured. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He walks the moonlight drive with her at dusk — the lanterns hung, the limes waiting, the full moon two days away — and tests each chain with his thumb, the soldier's quarter-inch neatness applied to light.)*
> "Steady." The chain holds. He moves to the next, the ladder creaking under his boot. "Every one. The drive's the ball's first impression —" the soldier's certainty — "and the first impression is the lanterns, the moon, and the house lit like —" he stops.
> "Like what, Henry?"
> "Like something that intends to be seen." He looks down the drive — the sixty lanterns, the limes hung with light, the house at the end with its windows lit. "I've watched you build it for —" another stop. "A long time. Saturday the ton sees it. I wanted the drive to be worthy."
> *(One chain was rusted through — he shows her the replaced link, the new iron bright against the old, the fault found and mended before the week could find it. The soldier's eye, exact to the link.)*
> *(The dusk turns cold off the lake, and she pulls her shawl closer — the week's first real cold, the year's turning. He offers his arm for the walk back without breaking stride on the chains, the soldier's courtesy automatic as the testing.)*
> *(The moths find the first lit lantern and begin their orbit — the week's smallest courtiers, arriving early. He watches them a moment with the grave attention he gives everything, then tests the next chain.)*
> "Saturday at five," he says, "the lighting begins. The porter's boys know the order. Dusk does the rest, and the moon does the rest after that."
> "Five," Rose says, noting the hour the way she notes everything. "The drive lights itself, with help."
> "With help." The smallest smile. "The moon is a guest, Rose. Guests like assistance."
> "The drive is worthy," Rose says.
> "The drive —" the thumb on the chain, the steady pull — "the drive is steady. Every one." The smallest smile. "Worthy is Saturday's word. Tonight the word is steady."
> *(They walk back in the dusk — the sixty lanterns steady behind them, the limes' long shadows, the moon two days from full rising over the Park. The gift of attention, every day, on purpose, in lanterns.)*
> *(At the house door he stops and looks back down the lit drive — the whole length of it, steady, every one — and nods once, the maneuver complete. The dusk deepens. The moon clears the limes. The drive waits for its guest.)*

scenes.synopsis: the arithmetic, at noon — 380 chairs; the room, full. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Noon, and the arithmetic: three hundred and eighty chairs — the final week's fifth day, the last acceptances in, the silences written off, the noon lying on the list like the week's own light.)*
> "Three hundred and eighty, darling." Letitia sets down the pen — the quartermaster's flourish, the ruled line under the last of them. "The ballroom holds four hundred. We have three hundred and eighty. The fourteen refusals —" the line drawn under those too — "are Drummond's, and they can keep each other company."
> *(The last acceptances came with the morning post — the bishops' household in the secretary's fair hand, the de Varennes' written confirmation with Laurent's flourish in the margin, the final wobblers' cards turned face-up at last. Rose does the sums with the noon on the list — the visible win/lose, won.)*
> *(An empty ballroom is public humiliation. A full one is the verdict. The verdict is in — not perfect, but full enough that the fullness is the fact, which Bell will confirm in print Monday and the ton will confirm in person Saturday.)*
> "The dragon's fourteen can have their evening," Rose says. "We'll have ours."
> "Ours, darling." Letitia closes the book — the snap, the verdict. "Ours is better."
> *(Rose runs her finger down the acceptances one last time and thinks of the margin's lesson, three weeks old: the pile of one, the chair at a time. The margin's wisdom stands — three hundred and eighty times over.)*
> "Ours is better," Rose says, "because it's ours."
> "Because it's ours." The hawk's eyes shine. "Three hundred and eighty reasons, darling. Count them Saturday."
> *(The ink is still wet on the last line, and Rose blots it herself — the sand-shaker hissing on the wet ink, the war's last administrative act.)*
> *(The closed book goes onto the shelf — the quartermaster's war, filed — and Letitia reaches for the chocolate, the war-room's ration become the week's. The noon holds on the ruled line.)*
> *(She goes to the window when the book is shelved — the Park whole below, the ballroom's forty paces waiting, the drive's lanterns unlit till Saturday. Three hundred and eighty chairs. The room will be full. Saturday, the counting.)*

scenes.synopsis: the dragon, in London — her preparations, reported; the purple gown, finished. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Honoria's last report before the ball — the dragon's preparations, complete, delivered in the morning room without emphasis.)*
> "The purple's finished." Honoria stands by the window — the composure, the ten seasons of divided loyalty, the week's last weather. "She tried it on yesterday. She looked —" a pause — "she looked like herself. The dragon, in full plumage."
> *(Rose waits. Honoria's pauses are load-bearing.)*
> "She asked me what I thought." The The dry voice. "I told her the truth — that acknowledgment becomes her. She —" the stop — "she almost smiled, Rose. Almost."
> "And the fourteen?"
> "The fourteen are hers. She won't release them — it would look like retreat." The dry voice softens, just slightly. "But she's coming, Rose. In purple. For acknowledgment. Whatever Saturday costs her —" a look — "she's paying it beautifully."
> *(The fitting room, reconstructed from the daughter's dry report: the candles, the modiste's pins, the deepest purple against the dragon's stillness — and the almost-smile, witnessed by exactly one person in ten seasons.)*
> "She stood like a statue and let them pin," Honoria says, as if Rose had asked. "Twenty minutes. Not a word. The modiste's hands were shaking. Hers weren't."
> "And you?" Rose says. "What will you wear Saturday, Honoria?"
> "Grey." The dry voice, dry as dust. "Someone in the family should look like the weather."
> *(Rose laughs — startled, genuine — and Honoria's mouth does something it rarely does in the morning room: it almost follows.)*
> *(Rose crosses to her — the morning room's light, the ten seasons between them — and takes her hand. "Thank you for telling me." "Don't." But Honoria's fingers close once, briefly, around Rose's — the daughter's whole divided heart in a single pressure — before she lets go.)*
> "She almost smiled," Rose says.
> "Almost." Honoria moves to the door. "In ten seasons, Rose —" a pause — "I have never seen her almost smile at anyone. You're the first." At the door: "Whatever Saturday costs her. She's paying it beautifully."
> *(The door closes. The purple stays — the deepest purple, the full plumage — and Rose sits with the war's end shaped in silk: the dragon, coming deliberately, to say whatever the purple means in daylight.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE RECEIVING (how Rose receives Drummond at the ball: at the door herself, with Augusta, or among the guests). The dragon comes; decide the receiving. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room: the receiving, planned — Drummond's arrival is the ball's true first moment, and the manner of it will be read by every guest in the room. Augusta's spectacles are at the angle of war; Letitia's pen is poised over the week's orders.)*
> "At the door yourself," Augusta says, "is honor — and courage. With me beside you is the line — the Ravencrofts, receiving together. Among the guests —" the rarest smile — "is equality. Let her find you among your people, as one of them."
> *(Rose weighs the three receivings. At the door herself: alone at the ballroom's doors, the courage absolute, the town seeing it — and the solitude, which dragons notice. With Augusta: the Dowager standing with her granddaughter, two generations, the line honored — and the night becoming the family's, not the woman's. Among the guests: the host among her people, one of the company, equality the message — and messages get missed, and the dragon may read it as evasion.)*
> *(The morning room's clock ticks — the decision's own time, the week's choosing. She looks from Augusta's spectacles to Letitia's hovering pen, from the pen to the ballroom's doors beyond the corridor. The manner of the meeting is hers to set down in ink.)*
> *(Letitia's practical notes run under the weighing like a ledger's ruling: the door wants the footmen briefed and the announcement timed; Augusta wants the Dowager's chair placed at the ballroom's doors and the old guard told; among the guests wants Lavinia's set to make room and the word passed quiet. Every manner has its machinery. The machinery is ready for all three.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: honor, lineage, or equality. The dragon will come. The receiving is hers.)*
> *(The purple will come up the drive Saturday; the acknowledgment will arrive in person. Augusta's spectacles lower a fraction — the war-angle eased, the counsel given — and Letitia's pen hovers, waiting for the word that will set the manner down in ink. Three manners, one arrival, and the choosing is now, and hers alone.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The receiving:*
- **At the door, herself** — *honor, and courage.* Rose receives Drummond at the ballroom's doors, alone. (Consequence: the courage is absolute and the town sees it — but alone at the door is alone, and dragons notice solitude.)
- **With Augusta beside her** — *the line, receiving.* The Dowager stands with her granddaughter; the Ravencrofts receive together. (Consequence: the line is honored and the dragon faces two generations — but the night becomes the family's night, not Rose's.)
- **Among the guests, as equals** — *equality, offered.* Rose lets Drummond find her among her people, one host among the company. (Consequence: the equality is the message — but messages get missed, and the dragon may read it as evasion.)

scenes.synopsis: the cottages' card — placed beside the epergne; the two hosts, visible. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The supper room: the cottages' card placed beside the great epergne — "From the cottages, with pride" — where the ton can see it, Mrs. Quick holding it low, like an offering.)*
> "Here, miss?" Mrs. Quick holds the card — the careful hand, the week's own placement. "Where they'll —"
> "Where they'll see it." Rose sets it herself, straightening it twice — the exactness, the host's certainty. "The housewarming has two hosts, Mrs. Quick. The ton should know both."
> *(The epergne rises above it — the great silver centerpiece, polished to the week's standard, the cottages' small card holding its ground at its foot like a footnote that refused the margin. It is the smallest thing in the supper room, and Mrs. Quick placed it as carefully as the silver.)*
> *(The card stands at the epergne's foot, and the supper room's long table holds it the way the house holds everything: as a promise kept. The cottages' preserves stand in their labeled jars along the sideboard — damson, blackberry, the autumn's whole keeping — the posies tied with ribbon, the card where Saturday's supper will surround it.)*
> *(Rose touches the card once, lightly, with one finger — the careful hand, the pride — and leaves it to do its work.)*
> "The preserves," Mrs. Quick says, "are the cottages' argument, miss. Labeled."
> "The cottages' argument," Rose says, "stands with the house's." She steps back — the card straight, the epergne great. "Both of us."
> *(The supper room's windows give onto the dusk garden — the week's flowers going up to the ballroom, the epergne's candles still unlit, waiting for Saturday. Mrs. Quick looks at the card a moment longer — the immovable mouth, the week's second softening — and then she nods, the keys at her waist chiming faintly, and goes back to the week's work. The two hosts, visible: the mistress, and the keepers.)*
> *(The card stands at the epergne's foot, straightened twice, waiting for Saturday's candles. Small, and exactly placed — the week's smallest thing, holding its ground. The smallest thing in the room, and the most exactly placed.)*

scenes.synopsis: the quartermaster's joy — Letitia, at the war's end; the aunt, herself. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia in the war-room at dusk — the maps retired, the lists closed, the quartermaster with nothing left to quartermaster — and the strangest expression on the hawk's face: peace.)*
> "It's done, darling." She sits among the retired maps — the red marks, the black pins, the rolled campaigns. "The war's over. We won." A pause. "I don't know what to do with my hands."
> "Rest them, Aunt."
> "Rest." She looks at her hands — the quartermaster's hands, steady through ten seasons. "Do you remember the first war-room, darling? The libel war. The maps. You, pricing names like ribbons." She laughs, suddenly — the accidental comedy, the warmth underneath. "We were so young."
> "We were."
> "And now —" she gestures at the finished house around them — "now the wars are over, and the house is finished, and I —" the voice does something uncharacteristic — it cracks, just slightly, toward love — "I'm proud, darling. Of you. Of us. Of the maps."
> *(Rose takes the quartermaster's hands — the steady hands — and the war-room holds its dusk. The aunt, herself: funny without trying, formidable without announcing it, cracking only toward love. Ten seasons of quartermastering, and the hands don't know rest — but the heart knows pride, and the pride knows its objects: you, us, the maps.)*
> "The maps," Rose says, "go to Harrow for the history."
> "The history." Letitia looks at her hands, then at the maps. "Let the history know, darling." The hawk's eyes shine. "Let it know we were —" she stops — "let it know we were magnificent."
> *("Let the history know we were magnificent." The hawk's shine. Ten seasons, and now the finished house, the won war, the proud aunt. The maps go to Harrow. The pride stays.)*
> *(The rolled maps lean in the corner, waiting for Harrow's history — the whole campaign rolled up like finished letters. Letitia looks at them, then at her hands, and laughs. "Magnificent," she says, trying the weight of it. The hawk's eyes shine, and the laugh is real. The quartermaster's hands, steady through ten seasons, rest.)*

scenes.synopsis: the musicians rehearse — the ball's music, heard first. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The ballroom, evening: the musicians rehearse — the strings tuning, the first dance tried, the great room learning its music.)*
> *(She stands in the doorway, unobserved, and listens. The tuning first — the A's passed down the line, the small disagreements resolved — and then the minuet, formal as a bow; the country dance, bright as the young will be; the waltz, which Lavinia's six will demand and the leader has plainly been warned about.)*
> "The waltz at half tempo first," the leader says, "then as written." The bow comes down, and the young's demand unfolds carefully — the turning three, the strings' sweetness finding its shape — before he lets them take it at the pace Saturday will require.
> *(The room sounds different full of music than full of flowers — the forty paces answering the strings, the unlit chandeliers catching the vibration. She has walked this room empty for ten seasons. Tonight, for three dances, it is not empty.)*
> *(The first violin's E string was replaced at the interval — the old one lies coiled on the music stand, the new one bright — and the supper-room doors stand open, the music leaking through to where Saturday's tables will wait. The whole house, tonight, is listening.)*
> *(The first dance ends. The leader taps his stand twice. The second begins. She stays for three dances, hidden in the doorway, counting the bars the way she counts chairs — the minuet's thirty-two, the country dance's figures, the waltz's turning three. The empty room practices being a ballroom, and the flower-dressed walls listen.)*
> *(The waltz falters once — the second violin late on the turn — and the leader stops them with a raised bow, the way Augusta stops a sentence. They begin again. This time it holds. Rose finds she has been holding her breath, and lets it go with the music.)*
> *(The third dance ends — the waltz's last turn, the strings' sweetness fading — and she slips away before the fourth, down the corridor with the music following. The ball's music, heard first: the privilege of the doorway, the rehearsal before the performance.)*
> *(Behind her the fourth dance begins — the leader's tap, the strings again — and the ballroom practices on without its witness. Saturday the room holds the ton. Tonight it holds the music. The corridor carries the waltz a little way, and then lets it go.)*

scenes.synopsis: the moon, waxing full — tomorrow, the full moon; the drive, to light itself. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The drive at midnight: the moon waxing toward full — tomorrow, the full moon — the lanterns hung steady, the limes waiting, the house at the drive's end holding its lights.)*
> *(She walks the drive's length in the almost-full light, her shawl pulled close against the year's turning cold. The lanterns burn steady — Henry's quarter-inches, the soldier's neatness, every chain tested at dusk. The gravel silvers under the almost-moon; her shadow walks beside her, long and certain.)*
> *(Letitia's words at the announcement, three weeks past: the moon is a guest too, and she'll want the good candles. The good candles are lit — sixty lanterns, the house's windows, the drive's whole length. The moon is invited. The drive waits for its guest.)*
> *(She counts her steps without meaning to — the quartermaster's granddaughter's habit, everything tallied — and gives it up at two hundred, the night too fine for arithmetic. Saturday the carriages will come up this drive under the full moon, the town watching. Tonight it is only hers.)*
> *(The stable clock strikes the half hour — the small domestic sound carrying across the Park — and the stars stand out between the limes' black branches. The gravel is cold through her slippers; she should have worn boots, and is glad she didn't. Midnight wants slippers, not sense.)*
> *(The porter's lodge shows a single lit window — the week's watch kept even at midnight. Beyond the limes the lake holds the moon's almost, broken into silver pieces. The Park sleeps the way it has slept all week: completely, and ready.)*
> *(She walks to the drive's end and back — the midnight's own promenade, the week's quietest walk. An owl calls once from the limes and does not call again. Tomorrow the moon does the rest — the ball's first impression, secured by the soldier and the sky together.)*
> *(Halfway back she stops and counts the lanterns toward the house — sixty small flames, steady, every one — and the week's arithmetic holds even at midnight. Then she turns for the house, and the drive keeps its watch behind her.)*
> *(At the house door she looks back — the lit length, the waiting limes, the almost-full moon clearing the trees. Midnight. The candles good.)*

scenes.synopsis: the wanting, restated — two days to the ball; the honest dark. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her bedroom, midnight: two days to the ball, and the window's honest dark.)*
> *(She sits at the window with the guest list — the 380 acceptances, the 14 refusals, the wobblers' line ruled and closed — and lets herself want it: the full room, the lit candles, the ton seeing what she built. The wanting is the risk. She has always known that. She wants it anyway.)*
> *(She does not re-read the fourteen — Drummond's fourteen, keeping each other company, filed and finished. She reads the acceptances' last page instead, the final wobblers turned face-up: the names, the houses, the person-by-person arithmetic of the whole war. Three hundred and eighty. The room will be full.)*
> *(The list is tied with tape, the wax long since broken; she unties it and reties it, the quartermaster's granddaughter's hands needing the work. The acceptances run in black ink, the refusals in red — the war-book's old colors, the fourteen red lines filed under D and finished.)*
> *(The Park is dark beyond the glass — the lake, the garden, the wall — and the Hartwell rose's bud is out there in the dark, blushing toward its opening. Two days. The bloom and the ball, together. The garden keeps its calendar. So does she.)*
> *(She opens the window a crack — the latch cold, the night air smelling of the garden's cut stems and the lake — and the week's whole growing comes in at once. The morrow's orders lie written on the desk behind her, the flowers and the musicians and the candles, waiting for morning.)*
> *(The glass is cold against her forehead. Below, the terrace urns stand welcoming-but-not-eager in the dark — Henry's quarter-inches, invisible and exact. The week has been administered. What remains is the wanting, and the waiting, and the two days.)*
> *(The candle gutters beside her — the week's own small weather — and she does not trim it. The house is quiet in the way finished houses are quiet: the stairs settled, the clocks agreed, nothing unfinished ticking anywhere.)*
> *(She sets the list down at last — the names, the numbers, the closed line — and pinches the candle out between finger and thumb, the way Augusta taught her. The dark takes the room whole. Two days. The wanting, allowed. The risk, taken. Midnight.)*

scenes.synopsis: London's verdict, pre-ball — the town declares the event of the Season. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The London letters, and Letitia reads them with triumph — the hawk's eyes shining, the week's vindication in the morning post.)*
> "'The housewarming,'" she reads, "'is the event of the Season. Lady A. D.'s acceptance is taken as —' hmm — 'as the town's verdict in advance. The ballroom will be full. The question is no longer whether, but how brilliantly.'"
> *(Three letters, the morning post's whole London — all saying the same thing in different hands, the town's shorthand doing its work. Lady A. D.: the dragon, initialed, the concession named without being named.)*
> "'The dragon's acceptance,'" Letitia reads from the second, "'has settled the only wager worth making.' Hmm. And the third —" she breaks the wafer — "the third only says the writer has ordered a new gown, which in London is the same as a verdict."
> *(The seals lie on the tray — a crest, a cipher, a plain wafer — and Letitia holds the cipher's letter to the light with the connoisseur's eye. "The cipher's hand is new," she says. "Someone's secretary has been practicing. The town is taking notes on itself, darling.")*
> *(Letitia reads the first line again, savoring it — "'the town's verdict in advance'" — and Rose hears the quartermaster's whole war in the savoring: the dawn letters, the black pins, the person-by-person arithmetic, all of it compressing into one borrowed sentence.)*
> "How brilliantly, Aunt?"
> "Very, darling." The hawk's eyes shine. "The town has decided. The war's over. What remains is —" she gestures at the finished house around them — "the brilliance. Which, I hardly need to tell you, is our department."
> *(Rose takes the letters — the town's hand, the verdict in advance. What remains is the night itself, and the dragon in purple, coming beautifully.)*
> "Their department," Rose says, "is the verdict. Ours is the brilliance."
> "Both decided, darling." Letitia folds the letters, the triumph filed. "The town will read about Saturday on Monday and argue for a year. We —" the shine — "we get to be there."
> *(The letters filed, the verdict in advance. The town has decided; the brilliance is their department.)*

scenes.synopsis: the embroidery, complete — the gown, finished; the fitting. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The atelier: the embroidery complete — the Hartwell rose blooming in silk on ivory, eleven days, six girls, and Élise — and the gown on the stand, finished.)*
> "It's done." Élise stands before it — chalk-stained and hollow-eyed and radiant, the young commander's triumph. "The finest thing the atelier has ever made. Look —" she turns the stand — "the rose, opening. The skirt, the moon's light on water. The bodice —" she touches it — "the Park's stone at noon."
> *(The fitting begins: the ivory, the embroidery, the fall of the skirt. Élise pins the hem herself — no one else's hands on the finishing — and the gown fits the way finished things fit: exactly. The whole house, worn.)*
> *(In the glass Rose meets Élise's eyes — the hollow ones, the radiant ones — and the girls watch from the frames, Claudine awake at last, the seventeen-year-old's perfect petal finished and gazed at like a small miracle.)*
> "Élise." Rose holds the gaze in the glass. "The modiste's girl is the ton's dressmaker now. After Saturday, everyone will know it."
> "After Saturday," Élise says, "I can sleep." A grin, sudden and young — the commander gone, the girl underneath. "After Saturday, Miss Hartwell, I am going to sleep for a week."
> "Sleep," Rose says, stepping down from the stand, "is earned."
> "Earned, darling." Élise touches the rose's last petal — the re-begun one, perfect. "Eleven days earned. A week of sleep —" the grin — "also earned."
> *(The girls are already tidying — the frames cleared, the silks folded, the chalk brushed from the worktables — with the dazed efficiency of soldiers after the battle. One of them laughs at nothing, and the laugh spreads, and the atelier fills with it: the week's youngest triumph, sounding exactly like relief.)*
> *(She leaves the atelier to its triumph — the gown on the stand, the house rendered in silk, the chalk dust settling in the afternoon light. Saturday the triumph walks into the ballroom. Tonight the atelier rests.)*
> *(Behind her the door closes softly on the finished work. Eleven days, six girls, one rose — and Saturday, the walking-away.)*

scenes.synopsis: the atelier's triumph, witnessed — the girls, the frames, the future. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She walks the atelier after the fitting — the frames empty now, the girls resting, Claudine asleep on the chaise with the finished petal in her lap.)*
> *(The afternoon light lies across the cleared worktables — the chalk dust settling, the silks folded, a thimble left on a frame like a small abandoned helmet. The pin cushions bristle, quilled with the week's hundreds. The air smells of pressed silk and chalk and the particular exhaustion of finished work.)*
> *(The atelier's triumph is not just the gown on the stand. It is the hands that made it — and the ton doesn't know yet what hit it. But the atelier knows, and the atelier is asleep.)*
> *(She covers Claudine with a shawl, gently — the sleeping girl, the needle down at last, the day's terror finally slept off. The girl doesn't stir. It lies perfect in the shawl's fold — the re-begun petal, the silk shaded petal by petal, knowledge embroidered over hope.)*
> *(A needle glints on the floorboards by the chaise — dropped in the final push, overlooked in the tidying. Rose picks it up and sticks it in the nearest cushion, the small domestic completion, and the atelier's eleven days are truly over.)*
> *(Élise sleeps in the corner chair — the young commander, the chalk still on her fingers, the genius at rest, her breathing deep and even. Rose does not wake her.)*
> *(Six frames stand empty — she counts them without meaning to, the quartermaster's granddaughter's habit — six frames, six girls, eleven days. The gown waits on its stand in the corner — the house rendered in silk, the rose opening — and the room's quiet gathers around it the way the week's quiet has gathered around everything finished: complete, and asking nothing.)*
> *(She stands a moment in the doorway — the sleeping girls, the empty frames, the folded silks — and the afternoon's stillness holds eleven days' work. Witnessed. Then the door closes softly, and the atelier keeps its quiet until Saturday. The chalk dust settles over the cleared tables, and the room holds its finished quiet.)*

scenes.synopsis: the pearls, restrung — the grandmother's pearls; continuity, worn. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta's bedroom: the pearls restrung — the grandmother's pearls, the Hartwell continuity made visible — and the Dowager's hands, shaky and exact, tying the final knot.)*
> *(Sixty-four pearls on new silk, each knotted apart from its neighbor — Rose counted while Augusta worked, the quartermaster's granddaughter's habit, the numbers steadying her. The old silk lies coiled in the pearl box, grey with age, frayed through at the clasp. Everything gets restrung, sooner or later.)*
> "For Saturday." Augusta holds them up — the pearls, the line, the weight of generations, the luster catching the lamplight. "They were my mother's. They'll be —" the spectacles lower — "they'll be yours after, I suppose. Everything is yours after, child. The plate. The pearls. The house." A pause — the rarest stop. "I am —" the voice, exact at seventy-two, does the unexact thing — "I am glad it's you."
> "When did you first wear them, Grandmama?"
> "The winter I came out." The spectacles rise, looking past Rose at something seventy years off. "My mother fastened them on me, the way I'm fastening them on you. I thought they were heavy then, too." The rarest smile. "I was wrong about a great deal that winter. Not about the pearls."
> *(Rose kneels — actually kneels — and lets Augusta fasten the pearls around her throat. The weight is familiar; the meaning is new. The clasp closes with the small sure click of the tongue finding the box. The Dowager's whole philosophy of tenderness, in a clasp.)*
> "Grandmama —"
> "Hush, child." The shaky hands, exact. "Saturday you wear the house. Tonight you wear the pearls. Both suit you."
> *(The old silk goes into the wastebasket without ceremony — grey, frayed, ten years past its duty. "Houses," Augusta says, as if Rose had spoken. "Pearls. Dowagers, on good days.")*
> *(She stands, and the glass gives her back the line: the grandmother's pearls, the mother's, the granddaughter's. Continuity, worn.)*
> "They're heavy," Rose says.
> "They're supposed to be." The spectacles rise. "Continuity has weight, child. Wear it well." The rarest smile. "You will. You do."
> *(At the door Rose looks back — the Dowager at her glass, the pearl box empty, the evening light on the lavender water — and the weight at her throat steadies her the way the week's arithmetic steadies her: completely, and without asking. "I am glad it's you." Given plainly. Kept.)*

scenes.synopsis: the first bloom — the Hartwell rose opens; the legacy, living. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dawn, and the gardener comes to the house himself — soil on his boots, reverence on his face, the week's most important errand.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." He can barely get it out. "The rose. It's —"
> *(She goes to the walled garden in her dressing gown, Letitia and Augusta behind her, and the Hartwell rose has opened in the dawn — the first bloom, the legacy literal and living: the petals the color of the Park's stone at noon blushing to rose, the form perfect, the scent — she bends — the scent like nothing she has ever smelled, like the garden's whole ten seasons in one flower.)*
> "Oh." Letitia's voice is small — the hawk, hushed. "Oh, darling."
> *(Augusta touches the bloom with one finger, gently — the Dowager's reverence, the line's own flower. The gardener stands with his cap in his hands. Rose looks at the first bloom of the Hartwell rose — her legacy, bred across the seasons, opened for the ball — and the wanting is there, and the joy is there, and they are the same thing.)*
> "Cut it," she says softly. "Carefully. It's for Saturday."
> *(The shears, the ceremony, the cutting — the gardener's hands, reverent, the bloom severed with the week's own rite. Ten seasons of breeding, and the first bloom opens for the ball: the petals, the color, the scent of the whole ten seasons. Cut carefully. For Saturday. The legacy, living — and now, carried.)*
> "The first bloom," the gardener says, cap still in his hands, "of the Hartwell rose, miss."
> "The first bloom." Rose holds it — the legacy, literal, living. "For Saturday."
> *(She carries it up to the house herself — the gardener's cap still in his hands behind her, the dawn holding over the walled garden.)*
> *(In the morning room the bloom goes into water — the glass, the stem cut fresh, the petals the color of the Park's stone at noon blushing to rose. The legacy, living, waits for its choosing. The glass stands in the morning room's light, and the bloom holds its color, waiting for Saturday.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE BLOOM (the first Hartwell rose: Rose's hair, the ballroom's great vase, or the stone). The bloom is cut; decide its place. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room: the first bloom in water — the legacy, living, cut with ceremony at dawn — and the decision of its place. Letitia holds it like a scepter; Augusta regards it like a fact.)*
> "Your hair," Letitia says, "is the woman — the legacy, worn. The ballroom's great vase is the house — the legacy, displayed. The stone —" she glances at Augusta — "is the debt. The father's name, cut in the Park's stone. The bloom on the stone says: remembrance, and the debt acknowledged in the flower language too."
> *(The scent rises as Letitia turns the glass — the Hartwell rose's own, like nothing in the garden, the ten seasons' breeding in a single breath. Augusta touches one petal with a fingertip, gently, the Dowager's reverence, and says nothing at all.)*
> *(Rose looks at the bloom in the glass — the petals, the Park's stone blushing to rose — and weighs the three places. Her hair: the woman crowned, the legacy worn where the ton will see it — and flowers fade, and the night is long. The great vase: the house displayed, the statement public and perfect — and the vase is the house's, while the bloom was the garden's. The stone: the debt honored, the remembrance absolute — and the ball wants the bloom, and the stone is quiet.)*
> *(Letitia's practical notes run under the weighing: the hair wants the pin placed before the gown and the bloom will fade by midnight; the vase wants the water changed and the stem cut fresh; the stone wants the walk and the weather considered. Every place has its keeping. The keeping is ready for all three.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: worn, displayed, or honored. The bloom will open once. The place is hers.)*
> *(The bloom waits in water — the petals opening wider even as they watch, certain. Letitia lowers the scepter-hand; Augusta's gaze doesn't move from the flower. The morning room holds the week's last choosing the way the ballroom will hold the town, and the choosing is now.)*
> *(The flower language, spoken where she chooses. Decide.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The bloom:*
- **Rose's hair, for the ball** — *the woman, crowned.* The first bloom goes in her hair with the ivory gown. (Consequence: the legacy is worn, and the ton sees it — but flowers fade, and the night is long.)
- **The ballroom's great vase** — *the house, displayed.* The bloom crowns the ballroom's central vase, where every guest sees it. (Consequence: the statement is public and perfect — but the vase is the house's, and the bloom was the garden's.)
- **The stone, in remembrance** — *the debt, honored.* The bloom is laid on the stone where Hugh's father's name is cut. (Consequence: the remembrance is absolute — but the ball wants the bloom, and the stone is quiet.)

scenes.prose:
> *(The decision executed: the bloom placed — in her hair, in the vase, on the stone, as she chose — and the legacy set.)*
> *(She looks at it in its place — the petals, the color, the scent — and the ten seasons compress into the flower: the entail found and settled, Hugh's father's name cleared and cut in the Park's stone, the Network's war closed and coda'd, Cecilia's war ended on Rose's terms. The sin answered, the debt paid — bred into this one opening.)*
> *(The gardener witnessed it — cap in his hands, the week's own rite completed — and nodded once, the ten seasons' work delivered. "Ten seasons, miss," he said. "And then Saturday." Letitia held the water glass steady. Augusta watched like a fact being recorded, and nodded once, and that was the whole ceremony after the ceremony.)*
> *(The sun reaches the bloom where it sits — the petals' edges taking the light, the Park's stone blushing to rose in the morning — and the garden's other roses nod in the breeze, the working roses, the sisters. The bees have begun. The placed bloom opens wider, certain, among its kin.)*
> *(She walks back to the house through the morning garden — the dew on the paths, the cutting beds already at work for Saturday. The day's orders wait on the desk. The bloom stays behind in its place, opening. The legacy keeps its own morning now; Saturday will find it ready.)*
> *(A bee finds the bloom within the hour — the garden's own inspection, thorough and unbribed — and works the petals' edges while the morning warms. The placed thing is accepted by the garden it came from. The legacy, living, is at home in its place.)*
> *(She passes the cutting beds on the walk back — the week's flowers gone up to the ballroom, the rows already filling again, the garden's abundance unembarrassed by the week's demands. The gardener's boy carries a basket of late roses toward the house and touches his cap. The morning goes on being the morning.)*
> *(At the garden door she looks back once — the placed bloom, the morning, the certainty of it — and the ten seasons' flower keeps its own morning without her.)*

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry brings the ball's eve post; the small things, continued. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He comes with the ball's eve post — the last letters, the last acceptances — and a sprig of rosemary from the garden's borders, the dispatch case under his arm, the evening's own gravity.)*
> "For remembrance." He presents it with the dispatch-case gravity — the sprig, the garden's, the week's. "The garden's. I thought —" he stops — "the week has been — I wanted you to have something that wasn't the ball."
> *(He cut it himself at dusk — she can see the clean angle of the stem, the soldier's neatness even in remembrance — from the border by the still-room, where the rosemary grows thickest.)*
> *(She takes the rosemary — remembrance, in the flower language — and the small thing lands the way his small things always land: exactly. The something-that-wasn't-the-ball, given at the week's end.)*
> *(She bruises one leaf between finger and thumb — the scent rising, sharp and green and certain — and the week's whole growing is in it: the borders, the dusk, the practiced hand that cut it.)*
> *(The post's last letters are all acceptances — the week's final arithmetic, closed — and the dispatch case holds the week's last papers, the brass corners worn, the cards squared. But the rosemary is the delivery that matters, and they both know it.)*
> "Thank you, Henry."
> "It was a small thing." He watches her put it in water — the sprig, the remembrance, the week's last quiet preparation, the glass set among the week's papers on the desk. "Tomorrow's the ball. Tonight —" the smallest smile — "tonight I practiced bringing rosemary. Tomorrow I'll practice something else."
> "Something else," Rose says, "is a broad practice."
> "Broad," he says, "as the garden's borders." The smallest smile, the steady one. "The devotion's eve, Rose. The rosemary, the remembrance. Tomorrow —" he stops — "tomorrow, the ball. Tonight, the small thing."
> *(At the door he stops — the dispatch case, the gravity, the smallest smile — and the week's last devotion is delivered entire: the post, the acceptances, the rosemary. "Tomorrow," he says, "I'll practice something else." He bows, the soldier's bow, and the hall's lamp lights his way out. The door closes. The sprig stands green in the glass.)*

scenes.synopsis: the household, ready — the staff's final report; the house, at its best. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Mrs. Quick's final report — the staff assembled in the hall at dusk, the housekeeper's immovable voice carrying the week's completion.)*
> "The ballroom's dressed, miss. The supper room's laid. The silver's out — all of it, miss, the epergne and the cottages' card. The livery's pressed. The linen —" the immovable voice, nearly warm — "the linen's pressed twice, miss."
> *(The keys hang at her waist — the whole house's iron, the decade's weight — and her back is straighter than the hall's columns. Ten years of keeping, and the keeping shows: in the straight back, the pressed linen, the shine that is the week's second.)*
> *(The staff stands in its ranks — the footmen in white gloves, the maids with their curtsies ready, the kitchen's calm behind them — the week's campaign complete, the week's rest about to begin. The hall holds them the way the house holds everything: as a promise kept.)*
> "Thank you, Mrs. Quick."
> "Miss Hartwell." The housekeeper's eyes shine, just slightly — the extraordinary thing, twice in one week. "Ten years. And Saturday —" she stops — "Saturday they see it. All of it. What we kept."
> *(Rose takes the housekeeper's hands — the keys, the work, the decade — and the two hosts stand together in the hall: the mistress, and the keeper. Saturday, the seeing.)*
> "They'll see it, Mrs. Quick. All of it."
> "All of it, miss." The keys, the work, the decade — the shine, just slightly. "The ballroom, the supper room, the silver. The card —" the cottages', the pride — "the card where they'll see it."
> *(She looks down the hall once — the dressed ballroom beyond, the laid supper room — and nods. "The house," she says, "at its best, miss." Then the extraordinary shine again, just slightly. "Ten years. Saturday.")*
> *(The staff disperses — the curtsies, the gloves — and the hall empties to its dusk quiet. The final report, given. The keeping, ready for its seeing.)*
> *(The keys chime faintly as she turns at the corridor's end — the whole house's iron, the decade's weight. Behind her the hall holds its dusk quiet: the dressed ballroom, the laid supper room, the silver out.)*

scenes.synopsis: the dragon's carriage, ordered — the last intelligence; Drummond, coming. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Honoria's last intelligence — the dragon's carriage, ordered for Saturday, delivered in the morning room.)*
> "The traveling carriage." Honoria reports dryly — the composure, the week's last weather. "The purple gown packed. She leaves London at noon Saturday —" a pause — "she wants the entrance, Rose. The full one. The town watching."
> *(A longer pause — the load-bearing kind.)*
> "She's bringing no party. Just herself." The dry voice drops. "And me. She asked me to come with her. I said yes."
> "Honoria —"
> "I'm her daughter." The dry voice, dry as dust. "Not her soldier. But her daughter." At the door: "Rose — whatever she says in daylight. Remember she chose to come. Remember the purple."
> *(The road, reconstructed from the report: the noon departure, the traveling carriage with the crest on the door and the lamps for the road, the purple packed in tissue. The dragon crossing the country to the Park the way generals travel to parleys — alone, but for the daughter.)*
> *(Rose crosses to her — the morning room's light, the ten seasons between them — and takes both her hands. "Ride carefully," she says, because there is nothing else to say to a daughter riding into her mother's war. "I will," Honoria says. "She drives fast when she's decided.")*
> "And you'll wear the grey," Rose says. "Someone in the family should look like the weather."
> "Someone should." The voice — and the mouth almost follows, the morning room's second almost of the week.
> "The noon departure," Rose says. "The full entrance."
> "She chose." The dry voice at the door. "The purple, the carriage, the noon. The entrance." A pause. "Remember it was a choice, Rose. Whatever she says in daylight —" the dust-dry voice — "remember she chose to come."
> *(Rose sends word to the porter's lodge herself — the traveling carriage Saturday at noon, the full entrance, the drive ready. The dragon comes alone but for the daughter. Not the soldier — the daughter, attending, because she chose too. The lodge's lamp will be lit; the gates will stand open. Whatever the dragon says in daylight, the Park will be ready to hear it.)*

scenes.synopsis: two days to the ball — the Park, ready; the woman, ready. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The ball's eve, and the Park ready: the flowers in, the supper planned, the gown finished, the bloom placed, the room filling.)*
> *(She walks the house at dusk — the ballroom dressed, the gallery hung, the portrait on its wall, the library ordered — and the finished whole holds her the way it has held her all week: completely, and without asking anything.)*
> *(The clocks strike the hour through the house — agreed, all of them, the week's small harmonies — and the stairs hold no footstep but hers. The household rests before Saturday the way the atelier rested: completely, and earned.)*
> *(The gallery's dusk finds the portrait — the laughing woman, the Park behind her, the laugh still there in the failing light — and the line of ancestors keeps its long watch around her. The week's first choosing, hung. The wall told its truth.)*
> *(The library's fire is laid and unlit — the war-room's desk ordered, the maps gone to Harrow, the columns ruled and closed. The ballroom's doors stand shut, the forty paces dressed behind them, and she lays her hand on the wood a moment without opening. Tomorrow.)*
> *(The wanting is still there — the honest wanting — and the readiness is there too. Three hundred and eighty chairs, person by person, in daylight. The room will be full.)*
> *(The dragon will come — in purple, at noon, for acknowledgment. The gown will walk in, the bloom will open where she placed it, the moon will rise. Everything the week promised, arriving on time.)*
> *(Below the window the drive lies ready — the sixty lanterns unlit, the limes waiting, the moon all but full rising over the Park. Tomorrow the carriages come up it under the full moon, the town watching. Tonight it is only hers, the eve's own promenade.)*
> *(She ends at the window — the Park dark beyond, the lake, the garden, the wall — and the eve lies ahead like the portrait's wall lay waiting: ready. The Park, ready. The woman, ready. The calendar, holding.)*
> *(The dusk deepens — the week behind, Saturday ahead, the wanting honest, the readiness complete.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's verdict on the full room — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"Miss Hartwell's ballroom will be full on Saturday — the Gazette has counted the chairs, and the count favors the host. Lady A. D. attends, in what is described as purple. The town's verdict, in advance: the Season's grandest occasion. The Gazette will report the night as fact."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (described as purple! the phrasing!), then the reckoning: the fullness is pronounced fact in print as well as in person, and Bell has made the verdict formidable, which is Bell's way of making it permanent. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the room that is full twice — in chairs and in print — is full for good.* — remembered: *the lesson: the room, full twice, is full for good.*
scenes.sting: Miss Hartwell's ballroom will be full on Saturday — the Gazette has counted the chairs, and the count favors the host. Lady A. D. attends, in what is described as purple. The town's verdict, in advance: the Season's grandest occasion. The Gazette will report the night as fact.

scenes.synopsis: the dragon's request — a private word before the ball; the Season, holding its breath. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and Letitia comes with a letter — not the post, a messenger, the dragon's own crest.)*
> "Read it, darling." The hawk's eyes are unreadable. "Aloud."
> *(Rose reads: Lady Agatha Drummond requests a private word — before the ball, at the Park, Friday afternoon. "There are things," the letter says, "better said before the candles are lit." The hand is the dragon's. The request is — unprecedented.)*
> "A private word." Letitia sits, slowly. "Darling — she's never asked for a private word in her life. Dragons don't ask. They —" she stops — "they summon. Or they strike."
> *(Rose holds the letter. The dragon's request: a private word, before the ball, at the Park. What Drummond wants to say before the candles are lit — the concession, rehearsed? The last weapon, unveiled? The Season holds its breath.)*
> *(She sets the letter down. The chapter closes on the request — engraved, formal, and entirely unexpected — and the Park waits for Friday.)*

scenes.synopsis: dawn of the eve — the ball tomorrow; the private word, today. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> She wakes before the maid knocks, which tells her everything about the state of her nerves. For a moment she lies still and listens to the house the way she used to listen to the war-room: for what's wrong. Nothing. The quiet is the finished kind, beeswax and cold ash and cut grass through the open casement, and somewhere below a door closes with the soft decision of someone who knows exactly where they're going.
> The day has two halves, and she does the arithmetic the way she always does, lying flat with the coverlet folded under her elbows. Three o'clock: the dragon, the library, the private word Drummond requested in her own hand — the handwriting like a fence. Nine o'clock tomorrow: the ball. Between them, the eve's dress, the final checks, the household moving through its paces like the well-drilled thing it is. She dresses for both halves at once, because that is what the day requires.
> At the window the Park lies in the dawn the way it has lain every morning this week, and she never tires of checking it: the lake flat as a held breath, the walled garden's geometry softened by mist, the drive swept to the color of wet stone. Last night's moon is still up, a pale coin in a blueing sky, and it occurs to her — unbidden, and she lets it stay — that the moon has watched every eve of this house for two hundred years, and this is the first one that belongs entirely to her.
> The maid, when she comes, finds Rose already at the window in her dressing gown, and does the professional thing: pretends this is normal. "The grey, miss? For the morning?" The eve's dress — dove grey, the Park's stone — laid out with the particular care of a woman who understands that today has two costumes and both matter. Rose dresses with the maid's quick hands, the laces, the pins, the plain pearl drops, and does the day's second arithmetic in the mirror: three o'clock, the library, the dragon; half past, tea; the household's final checks between.
> The ball's eve begins. She goes down to meet it.

scenes.synopsis: preparing for the dragon — the household's arrangements; Letitia's battle-stations. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> The morning room has been arranged the way Letitia arranges everything before a battle: with a quartermaster's eye and no survivors. The tea things stand in formation on the low table. Two chairs face each other across it at the exact angle of equals — or enemies, the geometry is the same. A third chair waits at a remove, near the window, where a person could sit and hear everything and be seen by no one.
> "Three o'clock." Letitia adjusts the third chair a quarter-inch and steps back to check the line of it. "The library, as decided — no, don't argue, darling, the library. Neutral ground with your maps on the walls. She'll look at them and remember what happened to the last person who stood in that room against you."
> "Aunt —"
> "Tea at half past. I will be —" Letitia gestures toward the window chair with the air of a woman describing her own funeral — "elsewhere. But close. Shouting distance."
> "You're arranging the exits."
> "I'm arranging everything." The hawk's eyes are grave and, underneath the gravity, entirely fond. "Dragons, darling. I've read about this. The parley before the battle. She'll come in tired and human and ask for terms you already decided, and you'll have to pretend to think. Be —" she stops, and does something rare: she says the true thing plainly — "be yourself, darling. It's the one thing she can't prepare for."
> "The seating," Letitia continues, warming to the campaign, "is the whole of it. You here, facing the door — no, don't argue, the light's better and she'll have the maps at her back. She'll look at them. They all look at them. It's the room where the war was fought, darling, and rooms have opinions." She moves the tea tray a quarter-inch. "And the exits — the terrace doors unlatched, the corridor clear. The appearance of not needing to flee. There's a difference, and dragons know it."
> "You've thought about this."
> "I've thought about nothing else for a week." The hawk's eyes, unrepentant. "It's what I'm for."
> Rose takes the quartermaster's hands, which are cold with the morning and with whatever quartermasters feel before parleys. The morning room holds its light. Three o'clock: the dragon, the library, the private word. Everything else is already decided except the weather.

scenes.synopsis: the Dowager's counsel on the private word — what dragons say alone. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> Augusta's morning room smells of rosewater and ink, and the Dowager is at her desk with the spectacles down and a letter half-finished, exact at seventy-two as at every age she has ever been. She does not rise. She gestures Rose to the chair and finishes the sentence first, because counsel given in a hurry is counsel wasted.
> "She will not threaten." The spectacles lower another fraction. "Threats are for the letters, child. Alone, she will —" a pause, and Augusta chooses the word with a jeweler's care — "she will be human. That is the danger. Dragons are easy to fight. Tired old women are not."
> "Honoria said she's tired."
> "Honoria is right." Augusta sets down her pen and folds her hands, and for a moment the armor is all the way off, which almost never happens. "Agatha Drummond has fought for fifty years — for her place, for her daughter, for her version of the world. She is tired, and she knows you won, and she has come to —" the rarest pause of all — "to arrange the losing beautifully. Let her. It costs you nothing, and it is the only courtesy she has left to give."
> "And if the terms are hers?"
> "The terms are never hers." The spectacles rise. The armor is back. "Whatever she asks, the answer is on your terms. Not hers. Yours. The house is yours, the ball is yours, the acknowledgment will be yours. She comes to the Park, child. People who come to the Park play the Park's game."
> "One more thing." Augusta rises — she does not rise for many people — and goes to the window, the spectacles catching the light. "Honoria will be with her. The daughter is the war's true casualty, child, and she has spent twenty years between the dragon and the world. Whatever happens at three o'clock, remember the girl at the door. She chose to come too, in her way." A pause. "And Rose — when Agatha Drummond is human at you, it will feel like winning. It is not winning. It is the parley. The winning was the ten seasons. Don't let the parley spend it."
> Rose takes the counsel the way she takes everything Augusta gives her: whole, and to be examined later in private. The dragon, human: the danger. The terms: hers. She kisses the Dowager's cheek — rosewater, papery skin, the faintest powder — and goes to prepare the ground.

scenes.synopsis: the gown, pressed — the ivory, the embroidery; tomorrow's armor, which is not armor. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> The dressing room is all candlelight and cedar, and the gown lies across the chaise like something the house dreamed. Ivory silk. The Hartwell rose blooming in embroidery across the bodice and down the skirt's border — eleven days of Élise's atelier visible in every petal, Claudine's central petal the still center of it all. The finest thing the atelier has ever made, and tomorrow it walks into the ballroom.
> She touches the embroidery the way she has touched it every day this week, because some things you check the way you check a pulse. The petals are silk thread on silk, the color the Park's stone when it blushes. A house rendered in silk: the argument made wearable, the ten seasons sewn into something a woman can walk in.
> The eve's dress waits on the wardrobe door — dove grey silk, feather-stitch grey on grey, the silver ribbon at the throat. Readiness, not armor: grey kid gloves, hair coiled and composed, the plain pearl drops. In the mirror, the mistress of the Park on the day before the ball — prepared, exact, unhurried. The grandmother's pearls stay in their case; today wants nothing but readiness, and readiness is the whole of the statement.
> The bloom waits in water in the cool of the pantry, at its peak, opening wider by the hour. She closes the wardrobe on tomorrow's statement, pressed and certain, and dresses for today.
> The fitting: Claudine's mouth full of pins, the ivory silk pooled at her feet, the stand-still and turn. The Hartwell rose climbs the skirt in embroidery, petal by petal — eleven days of the needle's persuasion. In the glass the gown is the house itself: ivory, exact, impossible to argue with.
> The grandmother's pearls — decided. The clasp repaired after the confrontation year, the rosewood case open on the dressing table. Not the diamonds; the pearls. The line's jewelry for the line's night. The maid fastens them, and their weight is the weight of every Hartwell woman who wore them to a ball and came home standing.
> She stands in the finished gown while Claudine fusses the hem, and the woman in the glass is the mistress of the Park entire. Two costumes for the day, both hers, both chosen — the ivory for the night, the grey for the hours that lead to it.

scenes.synopsis: the daily devotion — Henry's morning check; the small things, on the eve. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> He comes with the morning post, as he has come every morning for longer than either of them would admit to counting, and they walk the terrace together while he delivers the last intelligence. The household lists are closed — every name accounted for, every acceptance in, the arithmetic beautiful.
> "The urns held overnight." He reports like a scout returned from the line. "The lanterns are steady. The drive —" he looks down its length, the full pale sweep of it — "the drive is ready, Rose. Whatever today brings —" he stops, and the stop is the whole sentence.
> "The dragon, Henry."
> "The dragon." Unmoved, the soldier's stillness held in close formation. "She's one woman. You're —" another stop, and this one costs him something — "you're the Park. I'll be —" the smallest smile in the world — "elsewhere. But close. Shouting distance."
> "That's what Letitia said."
> "Letitia and I have an arrangement." He offers his arm for the steps, because the terrace is damp and he is Henry. "She arranges the exits. I arrange the lanterns."
> They walk the terrace's length while the post is dealt with — a letter from the Craykes, twice-confirmed, a gracious note from Old Lady Micklethwaite, the last acceptances stacked and filed. Henry carries the post like dispatches, and somewhere in the middle of it Rose understands that this — the morning walk, the post, the terrace — is the thing she fought the war for. Not the ball. The mornings.
> She laughs — the first laugh of the eve, and it startles them both, and then, just as quickly, it doesn't. "The drive is ready," she says. "Whatever today brings." The devotion in the morning is the steadiest thing in the house: the gift of attention, every day, on purpose. Today it stands in shouting distance, and it has never once failed.
> The terrace's flags are damp underfoot, the air smelling of wet stone and the lime trees. A thrush works the border, the gravel lies raked to corduroy, and the morning does its steady work around them. The devotion is not in the words, which are few. It is in the showing up, which is daily, and has never once failed.

scenes.synopsis: the Park's final walk — the finished whole, patrolled before the dragon. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> She walks the Park before three, because a woman about to receive a dragon in her library should know the exact state of her kingdom. The lake, flat silver under a thin sun. The walled garden, the cutting beds' neat gaps where the ball's flowers were taken, the remaining blooms standing like the ones who stayed behind to hold the line. The canal, the water moving. The lake pavilion, gleaming. The cottages, smoke going up straight from the chimneys in the still air.
> The stables smell of hay and leather and horse, and the greys have been washed twice and stand in their boxes like dandies. The Hartwell rose's bloom is opening wider on its stem — she checks it the way she checks everything, with her hands — certain, at its peak, keeping its appointment.
> It is all hers. Beyond challenge, forever, the lawyers said so and the ton is about to say so and the dragon is coming this afternoon to say so in her own way. The patrolling is love with a timetable, and she has kept it for ten seasons.
> The canal walk: the water moving black under the thin sun, the far bank's willows, the path she has walked ten thousand times. She stops at the bridge the way she always stops at the bridge, and looks back at the house — the house complete, the stone, the windows catching light — and the wanting rises in her the way it always does here: the honest wanting, the full room, the lit candles. She lets it rise and lets it settle. The timetable today says: the house at half past two, the dragon at three.
> The cottages: smoke going up straight, a child chasing a dog, a woman beating a rug with the particular violence of ball-week cleaning. The estate, living its life around the great event, unimpressed and essential.
> She returns to the house at half past two with damp hems and clear eyes. The library is arranged — the tea things, the seating, the maps on the walls like the war they were. Letitia is elsewhere but close. The dragon comes at three. The Park is patrolled. The woman is ready.

scenes.synopsis: the bloom, at its peak — the Hartwell rose, opening wider; Saturday, promised. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> The walled garden at midday is all green heat and the hum of bees, and the Hartwell rose stands at the bed's center like the answer to a ten-season question. The bloom is at its peak — the petals fully open, the color the Park's stone blushing to rose, the scent the garden's whole ten seasons folded into one flower.
> "For tomorrow, miss." The gardener stands back from it the way men stand back from altars, hands clasped, reverent. "It's at its peak. Another day and it'll be past — but tomorrow —" he grins, and the grin is all pride — "tomorrow it's perfect. Roses know, miss. I told you."
> "You did tell me."
> "Ten seasons, miss. This rose has been bred for ten seasons. It knows what it's for." He straightens, soil on his knees, certainty in his spine. "I mind the year we nearly lost the stock — the frost, the spring it snowed in April. Your aunt wanted to give it up." He shakes his head. "You said no. You said roses know what they're for." A beat. "You were right, miss. They do."
> She remembers the frost year. She remembers saying it. She doesn't remember believing it, quite — she remembers deciding to believe it, which is the same thing if you do it long enough. The bloom opens wider in the midday sun, certain, and the ten seasons sit between them like something solid.
> She bends to the bloom and breathes it in — the peak, the perfection, the legacy literal and living, keeping its appointment. Tomorrow the ton sees it: in her hair, in the vase, on the stone, as she chose. Today it opens for no audience but the garden and the gardener and her. Some things are only for the people who grew them, and this — before the ton gets it — is one.
> The gardener's hands, soil in the creases, lift the stem like a christening. "Bred for ten seasons, miss. This one knows its business." The petals give under her finger, the scent rising — the garden's whole argument in a single flower. The choosing is quick: the peak bloom, the perfect form, the legacy made literal and living.

scenes.synopsis: the gallery, ready — the portrait on its wall; the woman, witnessed daily. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> The west gallery holds the noon light the way it has held it for two hundred years, and the portrait hangs at its end on the chosen wall: the laughing woman, the Park behind her breathing, the paint barely dry. Octavia stands beside it with her hands folded, precise, watching the household pass.
> "They stop." The precise voice, quiet. "The maids, the footmen — they stop and look. The cook said —" and the precise voice does something it almost never does, it softens — "the cook said it's the first portrait in the house that looks happy."
> "The ancestors were painted to be looked up to," Octavia says, looking down the gallery's long line of owned faces. "You were painted to be looked at. They'll stand here tomorrow with their champagne and their opinions, and the laughing woman will look back at them, and something in them will recognize her before they understand it. That's what portraits are for." A direct look, plumb-line true. "Two houses, one shared life, Rose. My half of the arrangement — hung where they'll see it."
> A maid passes with a stack of linen, stops, looks at the portrait, smiles, goes on. The household's audience, daily, unpaid, unanimous.
> The gallery's light at midday: the skylights, the portraits in their long line, the laughing woman newest among the ancestors. A footman passes with a ladder, stops to look, grins, goes on. Octavia watches him go with the painter's satisfaction: witnessed, already, before the ton.
> Rose takes her hand — the painter's hand, paint still under the nails no matter how she scrubs. Tomorrow the ton joins the audience. Today the audience is the house, and the house has already decided.
> The frame: gilt, the Hartwell arms at the crest, hung at the gallery's end where the noon light finds it. Octavia supervised the hanging herself — precisely, and as if the wall might argue. It didn't. The laughing woman took her place among the ancestors like she'd always been there.
> The cook's verdict, delivered at noon with the nuncheons: "She looks like trouble, miss. The good kind." The household's verdict, delivered all week in stopped feet and smiles: the same. The ton's verdict comes tomorrow. The painter is precise about everything except the outcome, which she leaves to the light.

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE PRIVATE WORD (how Rose meets Drummond: the library as equals, the morning room as host, or the garden as women). Three o'clock approaches; decide the ground. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> Half past two, and the ground undecided. The library: neutral, the maps on the walls, the war-room's table between them — two powers, parleying, the room where the campaign was fought and won. She can feel the maps from here, rolled in their case in the corner, retired but not forgotten. Rooms remember, and the library remembers everything.
> The morning room: the host's ground. Tea and ceremony and the house's manners, the mistress receiving in her own house the way mistresses have received for centuries. The courtesy would be absolute. The courtesy is always absolute. But ceremony gives the dragon ceremony's weapons, and Agatha Drummond has been armed in ceremony for fifty years.
> The garden: the roses, the open air, two women without a room's armor between them. The honesty of it is disarming. The honesty of it is also the danger — the garden is the heart's ground, and she has put her whole heart into that ground for ten seasons.
> The tea things are ready for wherever they're wanted — Letitia saw to that, the quartermaster's contingency planning. The chairs wait. The clock moves. Half past two, and the ground undecided, and the deciding is the whole of it: where she meets the dragon says what the meeting is, before a word is spoken.
> Letitia waits elsewhere but close, shouting distance. Augusta's counsel sits in her, kept close: the terms are yours. Honoria's warning sits beside it: remember she chose to come. The clock moves toward three with the particular indifference of clocks. She decides the ground before the dragon decides it for her.
> The clock on the stair strikes the half hour, and the sound goes through the house like a starting pistol. The chairs are placed — the library's, the morning room's, the garden's bench brushed and waiting. Every ground is ready. Only the choosing remains.
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — The private word:*
- **The library, as equals** — *neutral ground.* The maps on the walls, the war-room's table; two powers, parleying. (Consequence: the equality is the message — but the library is where the war was fought, and rooms remember.)
- **The morning room, as host** — *the host's ground.* Tea, ceremony, the house's manners; the mistress, receiving. (Consequence: the courtesy is absolute — but ceremony gives the dragon ceremony's weapons, and she is better armed.)
- **The garden, as women** — *no armor.* The roses, the open air; two women, without a room between them. (Consequence: the honesty is disarming — but the garden is the heart's ground, and hearts are vulnerable there.)
> She makes the decision the way she makes all of them: the arithmetic first, the instinct second, the instinct winning. The footmen are told. The tea is ordered. Letitia takes her window chair, elsewhere but close, shouting distance. The ground is hers, and the dragon comes at three to stand on it.
