scenes.synopsis: the last dances — the ball's end; the musicians, playing on. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> The last dances: the ball's end, the musicians playing on. The final waltz, the final set, the night's close. The couples form for the last time — the tired and the true, the ones who stayed — and the first violin leads the last bars with his bow held like a torch.
> She dances the last, the night's meaning carried as she chose, and the ballroom empties the way great rooms empty: reluctantly, in twos and threes, with backward glances. The candles gutter. The flowers hold, tired and beautiful. The forty paces, danced to glass, shine in the low light.
> The floor turns slower. The dancers linger. The night is unwilling to end, and the musicians, professional to the last, play it out to the final chord, and the music's last note hangs in the candlelight like something you could touch.
> The ton goes home to tell the story. The carriages roll down the drive, the lanterns catching them, the house lighting their way out. The guests in the wings go to their rooms. The young drift toward the lawns, unwilling to let the night end, and Lavinia, awake now, glittering again, leads them.
> The ballroom stands empty and magnificent, the flowers breathing in the dark, the forty paces gleaming. The house stays, complete. The night is over, and the housewarming closes its doors on it.
> At the doors the master of ceremonies stands with his white gloves folded, the night's last official, and bows to her as she passes. "Three hundred and eighty, Miss Hartwell," he says quietly. "Not one left before the last dance. In thirty years I have never seen it." She thanks him, and means it.
> Mrs. Quick moves through the empty ballroom with her keys — the keeper's round, the immovable mouth — and the footmen begin the clearing, quiet as water: the trays, the glasses, the candles. The invisible work, resuming. Rose stands in the doorway a moment and watches them, and the ballroom, empty, magnificent, hers, holds the night's last warmth. The music's last chord is gone. The dawn is coming.
> The candles are snuffed one by one, and the ballroom's brilliance contracts to the grey of morning, and the forty paces gleam in the half-light. The night is over. The house stands. The meaning is carried into the dawn.

scenes.synopsis: the terrace at dawn — the night's end; the Park, lightening. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> The terrace at dawn: the night's end, the Park lightening. The sky pales in the east, the lake silvers, the garden wakes, the birds start. She stands on the terrace in the ivory gown, the triumph's morning, and the Park lightens the way the finished house lightens everything: early, and with light.
> The lake first, then the garden wall, then the drive, then the house. She stands a moment with the Park lightening before her and the ballroom dark behind her, and the dawn holds, and the daylight comes.
> Below stairs the kitchens are already waking — the beautiful chaos starting up, the breakfast room to be readied, the house party to be fed. The air is cold and clean, and she pulls her shawl closer around the ivory gown. The ball is over. The morning comes.
> The dragon's daylight waits: the morning room, the ton's witnesses, the acknowledgment. In an hour the purple will be changed for morning, and the two women will walk the gallery, and the concession will be spoken in daylight, as promised. The keeping of the word is the whole of it.
> The canal walk waits. The terrace waits, free, as a life. Julian's promise, kept in view all night through the ballroom's windows, moonlit and patient. She stands in the dawn's first light with the night behind her and the daylight before her.
> A footman comes out with her morning cloak, unasked, the invisible work anticipating, and she takes it with thanks. The ivory gown under the cloak, the pearls, the dawn. She walks the terrace's length once, the stone cold under her slippers, counting the balusters the way she counts everything when she is deciding something: forty, the same as the ballroom's paces. The house rhymes with itself.
> The bloom is still in its chosen place. She checks, the way she checks everything, with her hands. The terrace holds its first light, and she goes in to meet the day.
> The birds are loud in the garden now, and the air smells of the night's candles and the morning's cold, and the ivory gown moves through the dawn's first light like something the day has been waiting for. The night is behind her. The daylight is before her, and it is full.

scenes.synopsis: the guests, staying — the house party; the Park, holding its people. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> The guests, staying: the house party. The Park holds its people beyond the ball — the great houses in the guest wings, the young on the lawns, the émigré houses in the state rooms — and the Park becomes what the ball promised: a house that holds people.
> Lavinia's six are on the lawns at dawn, glittering even tired, the advance guard's last stand. The émigré houses settle into the state rooms, Paris's attention sated. The old guard takes the guest wings, conceding in comfort. The dragon is in the state rooms, the purple changed for morning, the acknowledgment waiting for daylight.
> They stay, and the staying is the argument: the house, finished, and the people, held. The breakfast room will be full. The lawns will be full. This is the legacy's first form — the Assembly foreshadowed, the annual convening taking shape, year after year.
> Mrs. Quick has the breakfast room's arithmetic in hand — the immovable mouth, the keys — and the kitchens are at full tide, and the house party will be fed the way the ball was fed: well, and as if it were easy. The cottages' card still stands at the epergne's foot, and the morning's guests will read it over breakfast, and the pride will do its work quietly, the way the best things do.
> The guest wings' fireplaces were lit at five — the maids' round, the hot water carried up in the brass cans, the invisible work going on around the sleepers. In the blue bedroom a bishop is already awake and reading his office by the window. In the rose bedroom two of Lavinia's twelve are sharing one bed and both pairs of shoes are under it, tangled. The house absorbs them all without comment, the way a finished house does.
> The dawn comes up, and the house party begins, and the morning is full: the breakfast room, the lawns, the people. The ball was the beginning, not the end, and the finished house holds them all, and the holding is the whole of it.
> The breakfast room's doors stand open, the silver laid, the cottages' card still at the epergne's foot from the night before. The morning's guests will read it over their chocolate, and the pride will do its work again, quietly.

scenes.synopsis: the dragon, at dawn — still here; the purple, waiting; daylight, coming. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> Drummond, at dawn: still here. The purple gown is changed for morning, the dragon in morning dress, exact, and daylight comes up over the Park. They pass in the gallery — the dawn's light through the tall windows, the portraits on the walls, the two women — and the acknowledgment waits for the morning room, the daylight, the ton's witnesses.
> "Miss Hartwell." Drummond inclines her head: the dawn's light, the exact courtesy, the fifty years. "In daylight. As promised."
> "In daylight, Lady Drummond." The returned courtesy, exact. "As promised."
> The gallery at dawn: the portraits in the first light, the ancestors witnessing, the laughing woman on her wall — Octavia's portrait, the truest thing in the house — watching the war's two generals walk to the parley's end. The state rooms behind them, the morning room ahead.
> Drummond walks with the dragon's straight back and the fifty-four-year-old woman's tired eyes. She has been awake since dawn, Honoria said, the daughter's vigil, and the rehearsal is behind her, and the daylight is before her. Come, waited, keeping.
> They pass the Hartwell brides' portraits, five generations in the dawn's light, and Drummond slows half a step at the last but one, the young duchess who died in the frost year, and Rose sees her see it. Fifty-four years, and the dragon looks at a dead duchess in morning dress and keeps walking. That is the whole war, Rose thinks: the dragon never stopped walking.
> The two women pass like ships, the courtesy exact, the promise between them. The morning dress is armor of a quieter kind. The gallery holds the strangest procession, and the morning room waits with its doors about to open.
> Rose walks beside her the length of the gallery, and neither speaks, because there is nothing left to say that the daylight will not say better. At the gallery's end the morning room's doors stand open, and the witnesses are gathering: Augusta, Letitia, Honoria, the old guard, the young. The two women go in together, the mistress and the dragon, to finish it.
> The gallery's dawn light follows them to the doors and stops there, the way the night has stopped. The morning room waits, the witnesses, the daylight. The dragon keeps her appointments, and this is the one that matters.

scenes.synopsis: Honoria, the morning's — the daughter's tension; the daylight, witnessed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> Honoria, in the morning's light: the daughter's tension, the daylight concession about to happen, witnessed. She finds Rose in the gallery with the dawn coming up, and the dry voice is quiet, and the hands are clasped, and the twenty years of soldiering are in the straight back.
> "She's ready." The voice is low, for the morning. "My mother. The morning room." She stops. "She rehearsed it, Miss Hartwell. In front of the glass. Again." The smallest smile, the daughter's pride and terror both. "The dragon, rehearsing. For daylight."
> "And you, Honoria?"
> "I'll be there." The daughter's eyes, direct, the soldier nowhere. "Her mother's daughter. Not her soldier." A breath, the morning's light. "In daylight. Witnessed."
> She has been awake since dawn, she says. She dressed carefully. She is, the word she doesn't say, afraid. For her mother. The dragon, about to be honest in public, in daylight, before witnesses, for the first time in fifty-four years.
> "Whatever she says in there," Honoria says quietly, "it's the truest thing she's ever said. Remember that." The daughter's eyes, direct, bright. "Not the purple. Not the ball. The truest thing."
> She unclasps her hands then, and Rose sees the fingers are white at the knuckles, and reclasps them, and the small unguarded movement says more than the dry voice ever has. Twenty years of carrying messages, and this morning the message is the mother's own, and the daughter has no part in carrying it. She only has to stand there and hear it.
> The corridor's morning light falls across the daughter's back as she goes: the straight back, the careful dress, the clasped hands. Rose watches her go toward the morning room — the daylight, the witnessing, her mother's daughter, not her soldier — and the honesty is about to be spoken, and the twenty years are about to end.
> The gallery holds the dawn a moment longer, empty now, the portraits witnessing nothing in particular. Rose stands alone in the morning light with the daughter's tension still in the air, and then she follows — the mistress, to the morning room, to the finishing of it.

scenes.synopsis: Bell's ball report — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read at dawn — the ball's edition, the ink still fresh. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"Last night Miss Hartwell's ballroom held the Season, and the Season — having seen the house, the gown, the bloom, and the dragon in purple — renders its verdict: magnificent. The Gazette has attended a great many balls. It has never attended the verdict before."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (the verdict! attended!), then the reckoning: the ball is pronounced magnificent in print as well as in person, and Bell has made the triumph permanent, which is Bell's way of making it true. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the night the Gazette calls the verdict is the night that was.* — remembered: *the lesson: the night the Gazette calls the verdict is the night that was.*
scenes.sting: Last night Miss Hartwell's ballroom held the Season, and the Season — having seen the house, the gown, the bloom, and the dragon in purple — renders its verdict: magnificent. The Gazette has attended a great many balls. It has never attended the verdict before.

scenes.synopsis: the morning room — daylight; the dragon asks; the concession, imminent. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dawn, full: the morning room fills — the ton's witnesses, the house party, the daylight pouring in — and Drummond asks for the company.)*
> *(She comes to Rose in the gallery — the purple changed for morning, the dragon exact — and the request is the concession's beginning.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The exact courtesy, the daylight's. "The morning room. In daylight. Before —" she glances at the witnesses gathering — "before the company. I would —" the rarest pause — "I would speak. Of the house. Of what was built."
> *(The morning room's doors open. The daylight pours in. The ton's witnesses gather — Augusta, Letitia, Honoria, the old guard, the young. Rose walks in — the ivory gown, the dawn's light — and the chapter closes on the threshold: the dragon, the daylight, the concession imminent — and the Season holds its breath.)*

scenes.animationNote: "The Housewarming" — the morning room, daylight; the concession imminent

scenes.synopsis: the morning room — daylight; the witnesses gather; the concession, about to be spoken. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room at half past nine, and the light does exactly what it promised at dawn: it comes through the east windows in solid bars and lays itself across the Turkey carpet like a thing with weight. The chairs are set in their rows, as for the ball's receiving, only now nobody is moving. The footmen hold the doors. The whole of the ton that stayed the night is here — the old guard, the young, the émigré houses, the bishops — and the talk, which was loud in the breakfast room, has gone very thin and very careful.)*
> *(She stands at the room's center. The ivory gown is gone — changed at seven, before the household was properly awake, for the morning's dress, the deep blue with the level line at the hem — and her hands, which were steady all through the night, have gone and turned honest at last: they want to shake. She lets them. Nobody is looking at her hands.)*
> *(Augusta is already seated, the spectacles on, seventy-two years of patience arranged in a chair. Letitia is by the windows, not sitting — the quartermaster never sits before a reckoning — turning her bracelet round and round her wrist. Honoria stands near the door, pale, the only Drummond in the room so far, and keeps smoothing a skirt that does not need smoothing.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." *(The footman, at the door, and the voice of him lands like a hammer on glass.)* "Lady Agatha Drummond."
> *(The room turns. Drummond enters — the morning's dress, deep purple again, because of course it is purple, the dragon exact in the doorway — and crosses to the room's center, where Rose waits. The two women face each other in full daylight, before the ton she tried to keep away, and the morning room holds its breath.)*
> *(She takes the room in as she has taken a hundred rooms: the chairs, the faces, the light. The bishops sit together, grave as rooks. The émigré houses cluster near the windows, already half-composing. Old Lady Micklethwaite has her lorgnette out, which means she intends to miss nothing and forgive everything. The footmen at the doors stand like sentries at a treaty signing, which is, Rose supposes, exactly what this is.)*
> *(Her heart is doing something unseemly under the morning's blue. Twenty-five, and the mistress of Hartwell Park, and her heart is hammering like a girl's. She lets it. The hands may shake and the heart may hammer; the voice, when it comes, will be level. It always is.)*

scenes.synopsis: the acknowledgment — spoken in daylight; the house, conceded. (Turns: 10)
scenes.prose:
> *(Drummond stops three paces from Rose. She does not look at the witnesses. She looks at Rose, and only at Rose — the same look she must have given her own mirror at dawn, rehearsing.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." *(The exact voice, the daylight's, no flourishes left in it.)* "Last night I attended your ball." *(A pause. The morning room's silence has a texture now, like stretched linen.)* "I saw the house — the ballroom, the garden, the bloom. I saw the ton — come, despite my efforts." *(Another pause, longer, the hardest kind.)* "I saw what was built."
> *(Rose says nothing. There is nothing to say yet, and she has learned, over ten seasons of mornings like this one, that the silence after a concession's first words is doing half the work.)*
> "Hartwell Park is magnificent." *(Drummond's eyes do not waver.)* "The house. The Park. The —" *(the word arrives, costed, paid for)* "— the achievement. I acknowledge it. Before the company." *(A breath, taken visibly, like a swimmer's before the cold plunge.)* "The war is over, Miss Hartwell. Genuinely."
> *(The words land in the room as the dawn's bars of light landed on the carpet: with weight, and everywhere at once. Somebody in the back — a young one, one of Lavinia's six — lets out a breath that turns half into a laugh before it is swallowed. Augusta does not move. The spectacles have gone very still.)*
> *(Rose hears, underneath the silence, the small honest arithmetic she always hears: the letters that will not now be written, the debts that will not now be called, the guests who will not now be warned away from her rooms. It is a long list. She lets it run its course and then sets it aside, because the list is not the moment.)*
> "Lady Drummond." *(Her own voice, level, the morning's.)* "The house thanks you. And I —" *(the direct look, the equal's)* "— I accept the acknowledgment. Genuinely."
> *(The hardest word hangs in the air — achievement — and Rose watches the room hear it. Augusta's spectacles have gone very still indeed. Letitia's bracelet has stopped. Honoria, by the door, has both hands pressed flat to her skirt, as though holding herself upright by main force.)*
> *(Drummond stands in the bars of light, the purple magnificent, and waits. The dragon does not fidget. The dragon has said the thing, and the thing is said, and now the room must do with it what rooms do.)*

scenes.synopsis: the ton, witnessing — the old guard, the young; the concession, seen. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The silence breaks. It does not break as applause breaks — nobody is so coarse as to clap — but in the particular sound of four hundred years of breeding trying to absorb a historical fact: the rustle, the shifted chair, the murmur that starts in the old guard's corner and spreads like tea through hot water.)*
> *(The old guard nods. Old Lady Micklethwaite nods first, the enormous nod of a woman who has been waiting to be proved wrong and is enjoying it, and the rest follow — the Grevilles, the Sunderlands, the bishops — the slow grave nodding of people who have seen everything and have just seen one more thing.)*
> *(The young stare. Lavinia's six stare openly, mouths in various stages of the unattainable, and one of them — the youngest, all elbows and brilliance — whispers something to her neighbor that makes the neighbor's eyes go round. They will talk about this for years. They will tell their daughters about it, inaccurately, and the inaccuracy will become the legend, and the legend will be better than the truth, and Rose does not mind. Legends are a kind of interest, and interest compounds.)*
> *(The émigré houses vibrate — the French murmur, the quick hands, the Parisian assessment of a scene's staging — and somewhere among them Laurent is smiling the particular smile of a man who has watched the English do something magnificent and is already composing the letter home.)*
> *(They will write it tonight: the letters, the journals, the talk. The dragon conceded in daylight, before the ton, the house acknowledged. The morning room, half past nine. The carpet's bars of light. What was built, conceded — and the ton, the whole ton, saw it.)*
> *(Bell is there — Mrs. Nance Bell, the Gazette's proprietor, in her own best dress, the notebook already in her hand — and Rose catches her eye across the room. Bell's mouth does the dryest thing. The sharp eyes say: I am counting the chairs. The mouth says: I am enjoying this enormously. The notebook says: the verdict, in the making.)*
> *(The murmur rises and falls, rises and falls, as the sea does against shingle. History, being recorded in real time, sounds remarkably like a tea party.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Dowager, watching — Augusta sees the dragon concede; the old enemies, the peace. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Afterward, when the room has emptied its breath and the witnesses have begun their careful drifting toward the doors — the old enemies do not rush — Augusta beckons. She has not risen. Seventy-two, and she has earned the right to receive her granddaughter sitting down.)*
> "Child." *(She takes Rose's hand in both of hers. The skin is thin and spotted and warm.)* "I have waited —" *(the voice does the extraordinary thing it does, the catch that is not weakness)* "— I have waited a very long time. Agatha Drummond, acknowledging. In daylight. Before the ton." *(The spectacles lower. The eyes behind them are bright in a way Rose has seen exactly twice before: once at the portrait's unveiling, once the night the house's roof went on.)* "The old guard, child, has seen everything now. There is nothing left to show them. We may —" *(the rarest smile)* "— we may rest."
> "Are you satisfied, Grandmama?" *(Rose keeps her voice low. The room is still full of people being careful.)*
> "Satisfied?" *(Augusta turns the word over as she turns everything: a jeweler with a stone.)* "Child, I am at peace." *(She squeezes the hand.)* "The war's over. The house stands. The line continues —" *(a glance toward the windows, the Park beyond, the daylight)* "— in stone, in flowers, in the woman." *(She holds the hand a moment longer than courtesy requires.)* "You did what I could not, child. I fought her with letters and pride, and she outlasted me. You fought her with the house, and the house —" *(the voice, steady)* "— the house did not need to outlast anyone. It simply stood."
> *(Rose bends and kisses the spotted hand. The Dowager's peace, witnessed: the oldest eyes in the room, satisfied at last.)*
> *(The room drifts on around them — the witnesses finding their groups, the talk resuming its careful pitch — and Augusta holds Rose's hand a moment longer, the spotted hand warm.)*
> "Seventy-two." *(Augusta says it suddenly, the spectacles direct.)* "I have been waiting since I was forty, child. Thirty-two years of Agatha Drummond." *(The rarest smile.)* "I shall spend the peace being magnificent at other people. It will be a novel sensation."
> *(Rose laughs — the first true laugh of the morning — and the Dowager's eyes shine, and the morning room holds them both in its bars of light.)*

scenes.synopsis: the quartermaster, witnessing — Letitia sees the peace; the maps, history. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia is at the windows still, where she was before it happened, and she has not moved since. The bracelet has stopped going round her wrist. Her eyes — the hawk's eyes, wet — are fixed on the place where Drummond stood, as though the words might still be hanging in the air there, visible, to be checked once more for forgeries.)*
> "Darling." *(She turns, and the laugh comes out wet and entirely unplanned, like all her best sounds.)* "She said it. In daylight. Before everyone. The exact words, darling — magnificent, the achievement, genuinely. I have had those words described to me in seventeen different letters over ten seasons, and every one of them was a wish. This one —" *(she gestures at the morning room, the emptying chairs, the carpet's bars of light)* "— this one happened."
> *(She takes Rose's hands, and her own are cold, which is how Rose knows the morning cost her more than she will ever admit. The quartermaster's hands are never cold. They were cold at the creditors' meetings and cold at the blackballing and cold every time the letters came, and they are cold now, at the peace.)*
> "The maps, Aunt." *(Rose says it gently, because somebody has to.)*
> "The maps." *(Letitia looks toward the library, through the walls, as she always has.)* "They go in the library. Framed. Every chair, every letter, every debt called or forgiven — the whole war, mapped, dated, annotated." *(The wet laugh again.)* "Harrow can catalogue them. He will enjoy it far too much. He will use his smallest handwriting." *(She squeezes the hands.)* "We did it, darling. You did it. The quartermaster merely —" *(the hawk's eyes shine)* "— the quartermaster merely kept the ammunition dry."
> *(The strategist, at rest: the peace, witnessed. Letitia Harrow, who mapped a war, stands in the morning's light and lets the maps become history.)*
> *(The morning room is emptying now — the witnesses off to their letters, the chairs being righted — and Letitia stands at the windows watching the drive, where the first carriages are already being brought round. The hawk's eyes are dry now. The wet was for the moment. The quartermaster does not waste ammunition on the aftermath.)*
> "Seventeen letters." *(She says it suddenly, half to herself.)* "I counted, darling, on the way in. Seventeen times I was told those exact words in a letter, and every one was somebody's hope." *(She turns, the real smile.)* "Eighteen's the charm."

scenes.synopsis: the daughter, witnessing — Honoria sees her mother concede; her mother's daughter. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Honoria is still by the door, where she stood through all of it, and she has the look of someone who has been holding her breath so long she has forgotten the mechanics of breathing. She finds Rose in the gallery afterward, among the portraits, and her hands are doing the thing with the skirt again, though the skirt is by now beyond smoothing.)*
> "She did it." *(The voice is quiet, and it keeps stopping: a carriage on a bad road.)* "In daylight. Before everyone. She —" *(a stop)* "— she rehearsed it, Miss Hartwell. In front of the glass. Three times. I heard her." *(The smallest smile, the daughter's, private.)* "The dragon, rehearsing. For daylight."
> *(They walk a little way down the gallery, past the ancestors, past the laughing woman on her chosen wall, and Honoria's steps are slow, as though she is still arriving at the morning's fact.)*
> "She's herself." *(Honoria stops before the portrait, the laugh, the light.)* "That's the thing. The honesty. It's —" *(another stop)* "— it's the most honest I've seen her, and I have seen her every day of my life. You did that." *(She looks at Rose, direct, the daughter's eyes clear.)* "Not the defeat. The honesty. Thank you. For the house. For —" *(a glance back toward the morning room, the mother, the daylight)* "— for letting her be herself in it. In the daylight. Her mother's daughter —" *(the breath, steadied at last)* "— and proud of it, for once. Not her soldier."
> *(The daughter's witness: the family's truth, spoken in the gallery's light. The concession's quietest work, done in a daughter's heart.)*
> *(They walk on, past the laughing woman, past the ancestors, toward the windows at the gallery's end, where the Park lies in its morning light. Honoria's steps are quicker now. The breathing has remembered itself.)*
> "She'll write to you." *(Honoria says it suddenly, the daughter's certainty.)* "My mother. Not a letter — a note. She writes notes when she means things. Letters are for —" *(the smallest smile)* "— letters are for war."
> *(Rose nods. The gallery's light falls across them both, the mistress and the daughter, and the morning holds its peace.)*

scenes.synopsis: Rose's terms — the reconciliation's terms, stated; equals, in daylight. (Turns: 9)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room empties slowly, as great rooms do after great moments — nobody wanting to be the first to break the spell, everybody wanting to be the first to write the letter. When the last of the émigré houses has murmured its way out, only the two of them are left: Rose, and Drummond, standing where they stood, the daylight pouring in around them like a third party to the conversation.)*
> "Lady Drummond." *(Rose says it with the exact courtesy, and means it.)* "The war is over. Genuinely." *(She looks at the dragon — fifty-four, exact, the purple magnificent in the morning light — and says the thing she decided, at dawn, watching the light come up over the lake, that she would say.)* "The terms are these. No humiliation — then, or now. The house acknowledged —" *(a breath)* "— and the peace, kept. Not as victor and vanquished." *(The direct look. The equal's.)* "As equals."
> *(Drummond turns the word over as Augusta turns words: the jeweler, the stone.)*
> "Equals." *(A pause. The morning room's silence is different now — the after-silence, the held breath let out.)* "Miss Hartwell —" *(the rarest thing: the formality, set aside, deliberately)* "— Rose. I tried to keep them away." *(The honest look, the dragon's, unarmored for the first time in Rose's experience.)* "The ton. From your rooms. I wrote the letters. I called the debts. I —" *(she stops, and does not finish, because finishing would be humiliation, and the terms are no humiliation)* "— they came anyway. The house deserved them."
> "The house deserved the daylight too." *(Rose says it quietly, and it is not a thrust. It is simply true.)*
> "It had it." *(The dragon's smallest smile.)* "This morning. In this room." *(She extends her hand — the exact hand, the glove immaculate — and the gesture costs her, Rose can see it cost her, which is what makes it worth having.)* "Equals, then. On your terms."
> *(Rose takes the hand. The clasp is firm, brief, and final. The daylight holds the two women: the dragon, and the mistress. The war, ended — on Rose's terms, as equals, in the morning's light.)*

scenes.synopsis: the war, ended — genuinely; the morning, after. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She walks the gallery alone, afterward, as she has walked it a hundred mornings — only this morning the portraits look different, or she does. The laughing woman is on her chosen wall, catching the gallery's light, and Rose stops before her as she always stops, but longer this time, because there is nowhere else she has to be.)*
> *(The reckoning runs, unbidden, as it always runs: no more letters to intercept, no more debts to settle before they are called, no more chairs to count against blackballing, no more maps to update in the war room. The war room. She smiles at the thought of it — Letitia's maps, framed, in the library, Harrow's smallest handwriting underneath — and the smile is the first one this morning that has not been a public instrument.)*
> *(The guest list, won. The dragon, reconciled. The ton, convened — the word she chose for the Assembly's imagining and the word that keeps coming back, the difference between being admitted to a room and being the reason the room fills.)*
> *(She walks on, past the ancestors, past the windows looking down to the drive where the carriages will soon be, past the whole finished house, and the war's end is the house's particular quiet: not the quiet of aftermath, which is hollow, but the quiet of a ledger balanced — the columns added, the totals agreed, the book closed with a clean hand.)*
> *(The morning after: the peace, genuine. The war — fought, not processed; won, not given; ended, genuinely — and the mistress walks her gallery in daylight, at rest.)*

> "Peace." *(Drummond's voice, quiet.)* "Genuinely."

The great houses first, the old guard's coaches rolling with the particular dignity of people who have witnessed history and are going home to write it down. Then the young, Lavinia's six last of all, hanging out of carriage windows and shouting promises to return for the Assembly.)*
> *(They go with the concession's talk in their carriages — the dragon, in daylight, the house acknowledged, the war ended genuinely — and the talk will spread as talk spreads: the letters tonight, the journals tomorrow, the clubs by week's end. London will know by Friday. Paris will know by the masquerade.)*
> *(Rose stands on the terrace and watches them go, as she has watched a hundred departures, only this time the watching is different: the drive empties, the gravel settles, the Park's quiet comes back up the drive like the tide coming in, and the exhale is the whole estate's — the house, the garden, the cottages, the keepers — one long released breath.)*

> *(Lavinia stays — the young, staying, her six camped on the lawns like a particularly glittering military encampment — and finds Rose in the gallery among the portraits, still in the morning's blue, the purple-apology gown retired to its box.)*
> "Darling!" *(She seizes Rose's hands, the glitter undimmed by the afternoon.)* "The concession! In daylight! Before everyone!" *(The joy, the real thing underneath it.)* "My six are still talking about it. The young have never seen a dragon concede, darling. It's —" *(she stops, the real voice surfacing for a heartbeat)* "— it's the best thing that's ever happened at a house party. Better than the ices. And the ices were —" *(the glitter returns)* "— the ices were remarked by a duchess, which is the highest praise known to nature."
> "And the purple-apology gown?" *(Rose asks it, because somebody has to, and Lavinia's wardrobe is a matter of public record.)*
> "Retired." *(She twirls, the morning dress flaring.)* "Its work is done. The dragon —" *(the real voice again, just for a heartbeat, the twenty-four-year-old underneath the brilliance)* "— the dragon was magnificent, Rose. In defeat. I'm glad she came. The ball needed her." *(She squeezes the hands.)* "You needed her. A victory without the dragon would have been —" *(a gesture)* "— it would have been a room full of people agreeing with each other. This was better. This was —" *(the glitter, the joy, the truth)* "— this was history, darling, and we were in the room."
> *(The advance guard stays — the young, the brilliance — and the aftermath holds its afternoon. Lavinia's final glittering beat: the ball needed the dragon, and the dragon came.)*
> *(The gallery's afternoon light slants across the laughing woman's portrait as they pass — the truest thing, catching the light — and Lavinia stops, the glitter arrested.)*
> "Darling." *(The real voice, sudden.)* "Ten seasons. Your house." *(She squeezes Rose's hands.)* "My six will glitter at the Assembly until we're grandmothers. It's arranged."
> *(They walk on — the glittering pair, the afternoon's light — and the advance guard's promise goes with them, glittering.)*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent, after the ball — the Frenchman, the masquerade nearer; Paris, writing. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(He finds her on the terrace in the late afternoon — the Frenchman, after the ball, the polish undimmed by the departures — and the unpolished promise lies closer to the surface than usual — the lake, after rain.)*
> "Paris is writing." *(He leans on the balustrade beside her, not quite touching, the Gallic ease.)* "Again. The third letter this month, and this one —" *(he taps his breast pocket, where the letter lives)* "— this one is the announcement, Rose. The masquerade. The old world's last night." *(The polish, and the promise underneath it, surfacing.)* "The date is set. The place is named. The émigré houses are —" *(the Gallic shrug)* "— the émigré houses are vibrating, which is their natural state, but this time with reason."
> "The last great masquerade." *(Rose looks out over the Park, the drive empty now, the quiet complete.)*
> "The last." *(The unpolished look, direct.)* "The old world, one more night. The mask off." *(He takes her hand — the Frenchman's hand, the promise in it.)* "England. After tonight —" *(he stops, corrects himself, because the ball is past and the truth is nearer)* "— after the announcement, the truth. I promised."
> *(He goes in, the letter in his pocket, the polish restored. The terrace holds the afternoon's last light. The masquerade, nearer: Paris writing, the old world's last night approaching, the promise kept in view.)*
> *(The terrace's afternoon light slants across them — the Frenchman, the mistress, the Park beyond — and Laurent's hand is warm on hers.)*
> "The émigré houses." *(He glances toward the house, where the last of them are departing.)* "They will all come. For the masquerade. Paris —" *(the Gallic shrug)* "— Paris is sending its best masks. And its worst." *(The unpolished look.)* "One more night of the old world, Rose. Then —" *(he lifts her hand, the smallest pressure)* "— then we are honest. All of us."
> *(Below, the last carriage turns at the gates — the émigré houses' final coach, the crests catching the light — and the drive is empty, and the afternoon is theirs.)*
> *(The émigré houses depart — the last of them, the carriages — and the terrace holds the Frenchman's promise, and the afternoon's light.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE PEACE'S TERMS (what Rose asks of the peace: nothing, the Assembly's first guest, or the war's history). The afternoon deepens; decide the asking. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The afternoon deepens — the drive empty, the house settling, the peace no longer new but not yet habitual — and the peace asks its question: what does she ask of it? The peace is complete in itself, and she could ask nothing, letting it be. Or she could give it form: the Assembly's first guest, the dragon convened annually, the reconciliation made into a tradition. Or she could give it truth: the war's history, written truly, the letters and the debts and the daylight set down.)*
> *(Nothing: the peace, complete, unasked-of. The Assembly's first guest: the dragon, convened, the peace made annual. The war's history: the true account, the peace made permanent in ink.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The peace's terms:*
- **Nothing** — *the peace, complete.* Rose asks nothing; the peace is enough. (Consequence: the peace is pure — but pures are fragile, and the future wants building.)
- **The Assembly's first guest** — *the dragon, convened.* Rose invites Drummond to the Hartwell Assembly, annually. (Consequence: the convening is the reconciliation's form — but annual is forever, and forever is long.)
- **The war's history, written** — *the true account.* Rose asks that the war be written truly — the letters, the debts, the daylight. (Consequence: the history is honest — but histories are read, and readings differ.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: nothing, convened, or written. The peace's terms, decided in the deepening afternoon, become the peace's future.)*
> *(The three askings wait — nothing, the dragon convened, the war written truly — and she gives them the single careful weighing she gives everything.)*
> *(Nothing would be the pure thing, and she has never trusted the pure things; they tarnish. The Assembly's first guest would be the formal thing, the reconciliation made annual — but annual is forever, and forever wants considering. The war's history would be the honest thing, the letters and the debts and the daylight set down — but histories are read, and readings differ, and Bell's Gazette has already written the first draft.)*
> *(The drive is empty. The house is settling. The peace is no longer new, and not yet habitual, and the asking will make it one or the other.)*
> *(The household book lies open on the desk — the guest lists, the dates, the machinery of convening — and the Assembly's first imagining waits beside the peace's terms, the future's two shapes side by side on the page.)*
> *(She runs her finger down the book's edge, the paper's deckled side, and the afternoon's light falls across the columns, and the three askings wait the way everything waits in a kept house: patiently, and in order.)*
> *(She thinks of the dragon's name in the household book — written in, underlined — and of the maps going up on the library's wall, and of the peace's quiet in the morning room. The terms will be hers. They always are.)*

scenes.synopsis: Julian, after — the free man; the canal walk, nearer. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(He walks with her in the garden as the afternoon cools — the free man, after the ball, the mended gloves in his pocket, the last debt paid — and the canal is there beyond the beds, flat silver, waiting as it has waited all season.)*
> "The concession." *(He says it quietly, to the path, the unguarded look.)* "In daylight. I watched from the back, Rose." *(A stop.)* "The dragon was honest. It was —" *(another stop, the ghost of the old smile)* "— it was the bravest thing I've seen. Braver than the ball. The ball was —" *(a gesture at the house, the whole triumph of it)* "— the ball was the house. This was the woman. Her." *(He looks toward the canal.)* "After the masquerade — the walk. The terrace, free, as a life." *(He takes her hand, the free man's hand, steady.)* "It's coming, Rose. When you're ready."
> "I'm nearly ready, Julian." *(She holds the hand, and the garden's evening cool comes up around them, and the canal waits.)*
> "Nearly." *(The ghost of the old smile, the unguarded look.)* "The ball's done. The daylight's done. The masquerade —" *(a glance toward the house, where Laurent's letter waits in a pocket)* "— then the walk. The life." *(He lifts her hand, the smallest pressure, and lets it go.)* "Take the evening, Rose. The peace is yours. The walk will keep."
> *(They walk on — the garden, the cooling afternoon — and the free man's patience holds, complete and unhurried, as the canal holds its water.)*
> *(The garden's evening cool deepens — the beds, the walls, the canal beyond — and they walk as they have walked all season: together, and unhurried.)*
> "The masquerade." *(He says it quietly, the unguarded look.)* "Then the walk." *(He stops, the ghost of the old smile.)* "The terrace has waited, and I have waited —" *(he looks at the canal, the flat silver)* "— badly, and with excellent manners."
> *(The canal waits — flat silver, the evening's — and the walk will keep.)*
> *(She laughs — the free man's joke, the unguarded — and the garden's evening cool holds them, and the canal's flat silver, and the waiting.)*

scenes.synopsis: Henry, after — the devotion, in daylight; the small things, continuing. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He makes the morning round with her — the lanterns down and stored, the urns checked, the drive walked — the soldier's after-ball inspection, conducted with the same care he gave the before-ball preparations, because the devotion does not distinguish between occasions.)*
> "All steady." *(He reports from the terrace, the smallest smile.)* "The drive, the lanterns, the garden —" *(a glance at the beds, the flowers breathing)* "— the garden, breathing. The peace —" *(the smile again, the soldier's, rare)* "— the peace, holding."
> *(They walk the terrace's length, and his step is the measured one, and hers has learned to match it over the seasons, and the afternoon's light falls across them as it falls across everything at Hartwell — all of it.)*
> "Henry." *(She stops him at the balustrade, the Park beyond.)*
> "It was a small thing." *(He bows over her hand — the soldier's bow, the ballroom's awkwardness gone from it, the devotion's own grace instead.)* "All of them. Every day." *(He straightens.)* "There'll be more. One practice at a time." *(The direct look, the steady one.)* "The war's over, Rose. The small things —" *(a glance at the lanterns, stored; the urns, checked; the drive, walked)* "— the small things continue. They don't need the war."
> *(The devotion, in daylight: the gift of attention, continuing past the victory. Every day, on purpose — after the war, too.)*
> *(The lanterns are stored — the great ones from the drive, the small ones from the urns — and Henry checks each one as he checks everything: to the wick. The soldier's hands are careful with the glass.)*
> "Tomorrow." *(He walks the drive's edge with her, the measured step.)* "The gravel wants rolling, after the carriages." *(The smallest smile.)* "Details, Rose. Details are my department."
> *(The wick-trimming done, he sets the last lantern in its store with the particular care of a man putting a campaign's weapons back in the armoury — cleaned, counted, ready.)*
> *(They walk the terrace's length again — the measured steps, the afternoon's light — and the soldier's care needs no announcement, then or ever.)*

scenes.synopsis: Octavia, after — the painter; the portrait, in daylight. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The portrait's wall, the afternoon: the painter, after — and the laughing woman in the gallery's westward light, the laugh caught mid-breath, the light exactly as Octavia mixed it.)*
> "They saw it." *(The precise voice, quiet, the satisfaction in it measured to the drop.)* "In the ball's light. The laugh." *(She stands before her work like a general before a won field — not triumphant, exactly, but confirmed.)* "Two houses, one shared life. My half —" *(a gesture at the portrait, the crowd's talk still hanging round it like perfume)* "— witnessed. In daylight, too." *(A pause. The precise eyes move over the paint, checking, always checking.)* "The finished portrait hangs, Rose. The picnic, unveiled." *(The precise smile, the real one, rare as the dragon's.)* "It's done."
> *(They stand together before it — the painter and the subject, the arrangement's two halves — and the gallery's afternoon light does what the ball's candlelight did: it finds the laugh, and holds it.)*
> "The cook was right." *(Rose says it softly.)* "The first portrait in the house that looks happy."
> "The cook —" *(Octavia's mouth does the precise almost-smile)* "— the cook has the best eye in the house. I've said so for years. Nobody listens to the painter about eyes." *(She looks at Rose.)* "Two houses, one shared life. The arrangement holds — in daylight, in paint, in the woman." *(The painter's after: the work, witnessed; the arrangement, kept.)*
> *(The gallery's westward light moves across the paint — the laugh, the light, the truest thing — and Octavia's precise eyes follow it, checking as she always checks.)*
> "The light." *(She nods at the painting.)* "It holds. In the ball's light, in the daylight, in this." *(The precise voice, the satisfaction measured.)* "I mixed it —" *(she stops, the painter's reticence)* "— I mixed it for the laughing. It took eleven tries."
> "Eleven." *(Rose looks at the laugh, the light.)*
> "Eleven." *(The precise smile.)* "The twelfth would have been despair. The eleventh was the laugh."
> *(Octavia looks at the laugh — the light, the eleven tries — and the precise face does the thing it does when the work is done: it rests.)*

scenes.synopsis: Élise, after — the atelier; the triumph's morning. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The atelier's morning — or rather, the atelier's afternoon, because nobody in the atelier saw the morning: Élise, hollow-eyed, chalk still under her fingernails, the commissions pouring in as the ton poured in at nine o'clock — in a tide.)*
> "Twelve." *(She can barely get it out, the young voice hoarse with the night.)* "Twelve commissions, Miss Hartwell. Duchesses. The —" *(she stops, the grin breaking through the exhaustion)* "— the ton's dressmaker. It's real." *(She looks at the ivory gown, hanging now, the triumph at rest.)* "The finest thing we've ever made. Walk like it." *(A laugh, the young one, sudden.)* "You did."
> *(The workroom around them is the beautiful wreckage of triumph — the silk scraps, the chalk, the pins in their cushions, Claudine asleep on a bolt of blush silk with a needle still in her hand — and Élise moves through it like a general through a won field: already planning the next campaign.)*
> "Sleep, Élise." *(Rose says it firmly, the mistress's voice, the one that is obeyed.)*
> "After." *(The grin, unabashed.)* "A week, Miss Hartwell. I promised." *(The warm eyes, the young ones, shining through the hollow.)* "The atelier's arrived, miss. Really arrived. The duchesses —" *(she stops, the wonder of it catching her)* "— the duchesses are coming to us."
> *(The atelier's morning: the triumph, real. The modiste's girl, arrived — and sleeping, eventually, when the mistress insists.)*
> *(Claudine stirs on the blush silk — the needle still in her hand, the beautiful wreckage around her — and Élise covers her with a length of muslin, as a mother covers a child.)*
> "She hasn't slept either." *(The young voice, fond.)* "None of us have. The atelier —" *(the grin, the hollow eyes)* "— the atelier doesn't sleep when there's triumph about. It's unprofessional."
> *(The commissions are pinned to the board — twelve of them, the duchesses' names, the ton's dressmaker's future — and Élise looks at them as Rose looked at the Assembly's book: the imagining, the pleasure.)*
> "Sleep, Élise." *(Rose says it again, the mistress's voice.)*
> "After." *(The grin.)* "A week. I promised." *(The warm eyes.)* "The duchesses can wait a week. Triumph —" *(she yawns, suddenly, enormously)* "— triumph is exhausting."

scenes.synopsis: the Park, the morning after — the finished whole, in daylight; the war's end, walked. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The Park, the late afternoon: the finished whole, in daylight — the lake flat silver, the garden walled in light, the house lit like intention — the war's end, walked.)*
> *(She walks the canal — the shawl, the daylight, every path known as her own hands are known — and the Park holds its afternoon as it has held her all season: asks nothing. The water beside her, the path under her feet, the whole estate breathing around her.)*
> *(She counts, as she always counts: the beds, done. The walls, done. The lake, done. The cottages, kept. The house, finished. The bloom, blooming. The ton, convened. The dragon, reconciled. The list runs its course, and she lets it, and then she sets it aside, The walk is the walk.)*
> *(The walk is the light on the water, the gravel under the slippers, the swans round the point with their unconcern, the garden's scent coming over the wall — rosemary for remembrance, the white lilies for purity of intent, the whole Park speaking its language of flowers in the afternoon's light.)*
> *(The canal's path is hers — the shawl, the daylight, the every-path-known — and she walks it longer than she needs to, as she did the gallery that morning, because there is nowhere else she has to be.)*
> *(A moorhen darts from the reeds. The swans come round the point. The water takes the afternoon and gives it back doubled, and the walk takes the afternoon and gives it back as the peace: the war's end, walked, the finished whole, in daylight.)*
> *(The gardener's boy is at the far beds with a barrow, and she stops to look at his work — the new edging, straight as a ledger's line — and nods, and he touches his cap, and the Park's ordinary goes on underneath the extraordinary.)*
> *(The lake's far shore is dark with the elms' evening shade, and a pair of swans comes round the point with the season's cygnets, grey and ungainly and entirely certain of their welcome.)*
> *(The rosemary's scent comes over the wall — remembrance — and the white lilies stand in the border — purity of intent — and the violets edge the path — faithfulness. The garden speaks its language, and the afternoon listens, and the mistress walks through the middle of the sentence.)*

scenes.synopsis: the household, after — the keepers; the ball's morning, the peace's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The household, after: the keepers — the maids, the footmen, the gardeners — moving through the afternoon with the particular ease of the day after a triumph: the ball held, the concession spoken, the war ended. The silver being polished without hurry. The linen going down to the laundry in the good baskets. The flowers from the ball being carried out to the cottages, the ball's beauty distributed as the house distributes everything: to its people.)*
> *(She walks through it — the still room, the kitchens' passage, the servants' hall — and the keepers look up, and nod, and go back to their work, and the nodding is the thing: not the ball's awe, which was public, but the household's acknowledgment, which is private and therefore worth more. They kept the house through the war. They are keeping it through the peace.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick passes in the passage — the immovable, the general — and inclines her head the exact inch that means, in the keeper's language, that everything is satisfactory. It is the highest praise the house bestows, and Rose receives it as it is meant: with gravity.)*
> *(The two hosts' house: the mistress, and the keeper — the afternoon after, the peace's. The household, at rest, like a crew after a long voyage: the work done, the ship sound, the harbor in sight.)*
> *(The laundry goes down — the good baskets, the ball's linen — and the maids carry it as they carry everything after a triumph: with care, and with stories. The footmen polish the silver and discuss the dragon's purple in low voices. The gardeners bring in the last of the ball's flowers for the cottages.)*
> *(The keepers keep — as they kept through all of it — and the peace is the household's, too.)*
> *(The house works as it always works: without waste. The ball held, the concession spoken, the war ended — and the keepers keep, as they kept through all of it. The mistress walks through the middle of the keeping, and the nodding follows her, and the peace is the household's, too.)*

scenes.synopsis: the keeper's verdict — Mrs. Quick, after the ball; the immovable, moved. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Mrs. Quick in the still room — the keeper, after the ball, among her jars and ledgers — and the immovable is moved, though she would deny it to her grave.)*
> "The supper, miss." *(The immovable voice, nearly warm — nearly, as the sun is nearly up at dawn.)* "The savories were magnificent, miss. The ices —" *(a pause)* "— the ices were remarked. By a duchess." *(The extraordinary mouth does something it has never done in Rose's experience: it almost smiles.)* "The champagne was sufficient, miss. Barely. But sufficient."
> *(Rose waits. The keeper's verdicts arrive in their own time, like the post, and cannot be hurried.)*
> "The house, miss —" *(Mrs. Quick looks at Rose, direct, the keeper's eyes)* "— the house was magnificent. The dragon conceded, miss. In daylight." *(The immovable voice, quiet.)* "I've kept houses, miss. A good many houses. I've never —" *(she stops, and the stop is the thing)* "— I've never kept the verdict before."
> "The house, Mrs. Quick?" *(Rose asks it gently, because the keeper deserves the asking.)*
> "The house, miss —" *(the rarest thing: the immovable voice, warm, entirely)* "— the house is the verdict. And the verdict —" *(she turns back to her jars, the conversation's end, the keeper's dismissal)* "— the verdict stands."
> *(The keeper's verdict: the house, magnificent. The immovable, moved — nearly warm, and entirely certain.)*
> *(The still room's jars gleam — the preserves, the cordials, the whole keeper's arsenal — and Mrs. Quick moves among them like a general among the troops: inspecting.)*
> "The rose ice, miss." *(She stops before a jar, the immovable voice.)* "The cook's. Forty years I have kept houses, miss." *(The extraordinary mouth.)* "Twice remarked. By a duchess." *(She moves on.)* "The jars are full. The house is fed. The peace —" *(the keeper's eyes)* "— the peace is kept."
> *(The still room's cat uncurls from the ledger's corner and inspects Rose with the particular indifference of the well-fed, and Mrs. Quick's mouth does its almost-smile again, unbidden.)*
> *(The keeper moves among her jars — the preserves, the cordials, the whole arsenal — and the verdict stands: the house, magnificent. The immovable, at rest.)*

scenes.synopsis: the supper's verdict — the cook, after; the house's argument, eaten. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The kitchens, the afternoon: the beautiful wreckage of the supper — the great coppers scrubbed and gleaming, the ranges cooling, the whole brigade moving with the particular languor of artists after the exhibition — and the cook, serene among it all, tasting something from a spoon with the air of a woman tasting victory.)*
> "A duchess, miss." *(The serene voice, the satisfaction in it deep and unhurried.)* "Tasted the rose ice. Twice." *(A pause.)* "Said she'd never eaten the house before." *(The serene smile.)* "The house, miss — the house was eaten. And praised." *(She sets down the spoon.)* "The argument was served. And won."
> *(They stand a moment in the kitchens' warmth — the mistress and the cook, the two women who fed the ton — and the ranges tick as they cool, and the coppers gleam, and the whole room smells of the night's triumph: butter, sugar, roses.)*
> "The ices, miss —" *(the cook's eyes, the artist's, bright)* "— the ices were the garden, frozen. I told the duchess so. She —" *(the serene laugh)* "— she asked for the receipt. I gave her the garden instead. Told her to grow her own roses." *(She picks up the spoon again, the conversation's end.)* "The house was eaten, miss. There's no higher praise. A house that's eaten is a house that's —" *(the pause, the artist's)* "— a house that's home."
> *(The supper's verdict: the house's argument, eaten and praised. The kitchens' peace: the triumph, digested.)*
> *(The ranges tick as they cool — the great coppers, the gleaming — and the brigade moves with the languor of artists after the exhibition.)*
> "The coppers, miss." *(The cook runs a hand along the great gleaming flank, the serene pride.)* "Scrubbed by noon. The brigade" *(the artist's eyes, bright)* "— the brigade outdid itself, and I permit myself the observation." *(She picks up the spoon, the conversation's true end.)* "Tomorrow, miss — tomorrow we begin again, ordinary. Tonight, the triumph digests."
> *(The kitchens settle — the coppers ticking, the brigade at rest — and the triumph digests, and the house is home.)*

scenes.synopsis: the garden's verdict — the gardeners, after; the flowers, praised. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The garden, the afternoon: the gardeners, after — the beds being tidied, the great bed's spent blooms deadheaded, the whole ten seasons' work receiving its after-ball grooming — and the head gardener waiting by the gate with his hat in his hands, as he waited the morning the first Hartwell rose opened.)*
> "The great bed, Miss Hartwell." *(He touches his forelock, though the hat is already in his hands.)* "Praised. By everyone, miss." *(A pause.)* "The bloom was the ball's flower. The garden was seen, miss — in the ball's light, and in the daylight." *(The rarest smile, the countryman's, slow.)* "Ten seasons, miss. They saw the ten seasons."
> *(They walk the beds together — the mistress and the head gardener, the two people who know every inch of the ground — and he points out the things the ton praised: the great bed's ordering, the cutting garden's abundance, the borders' succession. He names the flowers as a father names his children, and Rose listens as she always listens: wholly.)*
> "The rosemary's for remembrance, miss." *(He nods at the border, the grey-green spikes.)* "The white lilies — purity of intent. The violets —" *(the slow smile)* "— faithfulness. The garden speaks, miss. Always has." *(He puts the hat back on, the audience's end.)* "They heard it, miss. Last night, and this morning. The garden spoke, and the ton —" *(the forelock touched again)* "— the ton listened."
> *(The garden's verdict: the flowers, praised. The gardeners' peace: the ten seasons' work, seen at last.)*
> "The great bed, miss." *(He stops before it, the hat in his hands.)* "They stood here — the duchesses, the bishops — and they looked. Really looked." *(The slow smile.)* "Ten seasons, miss. They saw the ten seasons." *(He puts the hat on, takes it off again, the countryman's restlessness.)* "The bloom was the ball's flower, miss. But the garden —" *(he looks at the beds, the walls, the whole)* "— the garden was the ball's argument. And the argument —" *(the forelock touched)* "— the argument was won."
> *(The head gardener puts his hat on — the forelock touched — and the borders hold their afternoon: the succession, the ordering, the ten seasons, seen.)*

scenes.synopsis: the steward's accounts, after — Harrow; the ball's honest costs, reckoned. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Harrow in the estate office — the steward, after, the great book open on the desk, the afternoon's light falling across the columns — and the ball's honest costs are reckoned.)*
> "The accounts, Miss Hartwell." *(He lays the book open, the honest figures in the honest hand.)* "The supper. The music. The candles." *(A pause.)* "The triumph." *(The dry smile.)* "The house can bear it, miss. The Park is solvent —" *(he taps the page)* "— and magnificent. The two are not, as the City seems to think, incompatible."
> *(Rose looks at the columns — the neat figures, the honest totals — and the reckoning settles, cleanly.)*
> "The war's costs, Harrow?" *(She asks it, because the war had its costs, and honest houses reckon them.)*
> "Ended." *(He closes the book, the sound of it final.)* "Genuinely, miss. The letters stopped. The debts —" *(a gesture, the steward's, dismissive)* "— settled. The daylight —" *(the dryest smile)* "— the daylight was free." *(He looks up, the steward's eyes, the honest ones.)* "The Park's books are clean, Miss Hartwell. Ten seasons of war, and the books are clean. That's —" *(the pause, the dry voice warming)* "— that's the achievement nobody toasts, miss. But it's the one the steward toasts, in private, with the office sherry."
> *(The steward's accounts: the ball's honest costs, reckoned. The Park, solvent and magnificent — the books clean, the daylight free.)*
> *(The office sherry is produced — the steward's private toast, the honest books closed — and Harrow pours with the ceremony the occasion demands.)*
> "The books are clean." *(He raises the glass, the dryest smile.)* "The Park is solvent." *(He drinks.)* "And magnificent." *(The dry voice, warming.)* "The steward drinks to it, Miss Hartwell. In private. As is proper."
> *(The office clock ticks — the honest time, the steward's — and through the window the drive lies empty, the Park solvent in the afternoon's light, the columns and the landscape in agreement for once.)*
> *(Harrow corks the sherry with the ceremony of a man sealing a treaty, and the bottle goes back in its cupboard, and the great book waits for tomorrow's honest figures.)*
> *(Rose takes the glass — the steward's private toast — and drinks. The park, solvent and magnificent.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE WAR'S END (how Rose marks it: quietly, publicly, or not at all). The afternoon deepens; decide the marking. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The afternoon deepens — the drive empty, the letters going out, the house settling into its peace — and the war's end asks for its marking: the ten seasons, the dragon conceded, the peace genuine. How does she mark it? Quietly: the private act, the walk, the bloom, the woman's own. Publicly: the ton's witness, the toast, the history's record. Not at all: the peace unmarked, the future's, clean.)*
> *(Quietly: the private marking, the woman's, unseen. Publicly: the witnessed marking, the ton's, recorded. Not at all: the unmarked peace, the future's, unremembered — or remembered differently.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The war's end:*
- **Quietly** — *the private act.* Rose marks it alone — the walk, the bloom, the woman's own. (Consequence: the marking is true — but private is unseen, and the house loves witness.)
- **Publicly** — *the ton's witness.* Rose marks it before the company — the toast, the history's. (Consequence: the marking is recorded — but public is performance, and the peace was private.)
- **Not at all** — *the unmarked peace.* Rose marks nothing; the peace is the future's. (Consequence: the future is clean — but unmarked is unremembered, and the war was real.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: quietly, publicly, or not at all. The marking, made in the deepening afternoon, becomes the war's last act.)*
> *(The three markings wait — the private act, the ton's witness, the unmarked peace — and she weighs each once, and carefully, the weighing she gives everything.)*
> *(Quietly would be the true thing, the walk, the bloom, the woman's own — but private is unseen, and the house loves witness, and ten seasons have taught her that unseen things get rewritten. Publicly would be the recorded thing, the toast, the history's — but public is performance, and the peace was private, and she will not perform the thing she fought for. Not at all would be the clean thing, the future's — but unmarked is unremembered, and the war was real, and the real things want their mark.)*
> *(The afternoon deepens. The letters go out. The house settles. The war's end asks for its marking, and the marking will be hers.)*
> *(The letters go out in the carriers' bags — the night mail, the morning's post — and each one carries the war's end in its own hand, in its own words, and none of them will agree, and that is the nature of letters.)*
> *(She stands at the desk a moment, the pen lying where she left it, and the marking waits the way the peace waits: for her hand, and no other's.)*
> *(She thinks of the dragon's hand — the clasp, firm, brief, final — and of the morning room's bars of light, and of the bloom opening wider. The marking, or the unmarking — the war's last act is hers to make.)*
