scenes.synopsis: the letters — the ton writes; the aftermath's post; the concession, carried. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The evening: the letters — the ton writes, the aftermath's post — and the concession is carried across London on the night's mail.)*
> *(They write — the old guard, the young, the émigré: the dragon conceded in daylight, the house acknowledged, the war ended genuinely. Old Lady Micklethwaite writes four pages, both sides, the ink barely dry. Lavinia's six write in chorus, the letters contradicting each other on every detail but the essential one. The bishops write with gravity. The émigré houses write to Paris, and Paris — already writing about the masquerade — will read about the daylight concession in the same post.)*
> *(The post goes out — the carriers, the night mail, the whole machinery of London's talk — and the morning room's half past nine becomes the clubs' by Friday, the journals' by next week, the history's by next season. The concession, carried: the dragon, in daylight, the house acknowledged.)*
> *(Rose stands at the window and watches the last carrier go down the drive, the lantern swinging, and thinks of all the letters she wrote in this war — the answers, the deflections, the careful courtesies — and lays the pen down, in her mind, for good. The aftermath's post is other people's now. The history, written in letters, and the letters are no longer hers to write.)*
> *(She thinks of the morning room at half past nine — the witnesses, the daylight, the dragon's hand in hers — and the memory is the day's own, not the letters'. The post carries the news to London. The house keeps the day for itself.)*
> *(She stands at the window until the last lantern is gone, and then she turns back to the house — the keepers, the peace, the evening's quiet.)*
> *(The carriers go down the drive — the lanterns swinging, the night's mail — and London will read by Friday what the morning room witnessed at half past nine.)*
> *(The last carrier's lantern swings down the drive and out of sight, and the Park's dark comes up to meet the house, and the letters are gone beyond recalling.)*
> *(The evening's light fades. The house settles. The concession rides the mail — and the history is other people's now.)*

scenes.synopsis: the invitations — the Assembly's first seed; the annual convening, imagined. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The evening: the household book, the year's first imagining — and the Hartwell Assembly takes its first shape on paper.)*
> *(She sits with the book — the guest list, the dates, the whole machinery of convening — and the Assembly forms in her mind as the house formed: not all at once, but room by room. An annual house party and ball, convened by her, on her terms — the word she chose, and the word that holds: convening, not joining.)*
> *(The list begins — the old guard, the young, the émigré houses, the bishops, the dragon's name written in and then looked at for a long moment — and the imagining is the pleasure: the ballroom full again, the garden in its season, the bloom's anniversary, the whole Park convened as the ball convened it, only annually, and hers.)*
> *(She writes the dragon's name in. Then she underlines it. Then she sits back, and the evening's light falls across the book, and the Assembly's first seed is planted: the annual convening, imagined, the legacy's form taking shape on the page.)*
> *(She turns the page — the household accounts, the week's orders, the ordinary — and the Assembly's imagining sits beside them, the extraordinary beside the everyday, as it should in a kept house.)*
> *(The dates take shape beneath her pen: the garden's season, the bloom's anniversary, the ballroom's fullness. Annual. Convened. Hers. The legacy's form, taking shape on paper, in the evening's light.)*
> *(The bloom will be the Assembly's emblem — the anniversary, the season — and she circles the date twice, the pen certain.)*
> "Annual." *(She says it softly, to the empty room.)* "Convened. Mine." *(She looks at the dragon's underlined name.)* "The legacy's form — the word that holds."
> *(The evening holds its light on the page — the dragon's name, underlined — and the imagining is complete.)*
> *(The household book's leather is warm from her hands, and the pen lies across the page, and the evening's light goes amber on the ink, and the imagining sits complete beside the ordinary, the way the future always sits beside the present in a kept house.)*
> *(She closes the book — the year's first imagining, complete — and the Assembly's first seed is planted.)*

scenes.synopsis: the bloom, the morning after — the rose, opening wider; the legacy, living. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The bloom's corner, in the evening's last light: the sheltered place where the first Hartwell rose opened, the day's whole daylight behind it, the petals looser than they were at dawn — opening wider, overnight and all day, as though the flower had decided the concession deserved an answer.)*
> *(She checks it as she has checked it every day since it opened — the petals, the form, the scent — and runs the check in order, and honestly. The petals: further along, the edges just beginning to turn back. The form: true, the cup holding. The scent: the evening's already, the perfume coming up off the bloom before she has properly bent to it.)*
> *(Drummond stood here this morning, in this exact spot. The dragon's hand hovered near the petals and did not touch — the exact hand, the glove immaculate, held back by the one scruple the dragon apparently owns. The exact eyes ran out of exactness. The honest word was spoken, costed and paid for: magnificent.)*
> *(The bloom did not know it was being looked at. That is the thing about the bloom — the thing the dragon finally saw, perhaps, without quite understanding it: the petals do not distinguish between a duchess and a gardener's boy, between daylight and witness. They open. That is the whole of the arrangement.)*
> *(The evening's light moves across the petals, and the Park's stone blushes deeper to rose behind them — the wall taking the flower's color as it has taken it all season, the garden's own tribute, unconscious and complete. The bloom holds the light the way the house holds everything: steady, and without comment.)*
> *(The scent rises as the light goes — the rose's evening perfume, stronger at dusk than at noon, the ten seasons' breeding distilled into the air between her and the wall. A blackbird scolds from the espalier and thinks better of it. The garden holds its breath for the night's beginning.)*
> *(She touches it — one fingertip to the outer petal, very gently, exactly where the dragon's hand did not touch at all — and the petal gives back the day's warmth, held all day, returned now. Indifferent. Returning. The two things the bloom does, and the two things it was bred for.)*
> *(She leaves it to the dusk — the corner darkening, the stone cooling, the petals holding the last of the light a moment longer than anything else in the garden.)*

scenes.synopsis: the portrait, in daylight — the laughing woman, the morning after; the truest thing. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The gallery, the morning after the ball: the house quiet in a way it hasn't been for weeks — no florists on ladders, no musicians tuning, only the clocks and the doves — and she stops on her way to the morning room because the portrait catches her, the way it always does, sideways.)*
> *(It hangs on its chosen wall, the laughing woman, Octavia's work: the laugh caught mid-breath — not posed, not arranged, the mouth open, the eyes narrowed with it — and Octavia refused to soften a line of it. The laugh lines stay. The amusement stays. The woman in the frame is twenty-five and looks it, and looks glad of it, which no other face on this wall manages. The admirals frown down in their gilt. The judges weigh. One very severe bishop disapproves of everything, including, presumably, laughter. She laughs anyway. It changes the whole wall.)*
> *(The cook was right — said it first, in the kitchens, with a spoon in her hand: the first portrait in the house that looks happy. Rose had laughed when she heard it, and then stopped, because it was true. The admirals never smiled. The judges never smiled. Whoever sat for these walls sat for posterity, which is the enemy of amusement. This one sat for Octavia, which is a different thing entirely.)*
> *(Octavia never said what the joke had been. Rose never asked. That is the arrangement between them: the painter paints exactly what she sees, and the sitter does not interrogate the seeing. Precision is Octavia's tenderness. It is also, Rose has learned, her mercy — she could have painted the triumph, and chose the laugh instead.)*
> *(The daylight does the rest. Last night the portrait hung in candlelight, one more beautiful thing among beautiful things. This morning the sun comes in at the side and finds it honestly — no flattery in the light, none in the paint — and the laughing woman holds it. Drummond acknowledged the house; that was yesterday's business, done in daylight, witnessed. This is the woman's own acknowledgment, done months ago in paint, without witnesses at all. The two stand side by side now — the house, acknowledged; the woman, laughing — and the laughing one is the truer, because nobody had to be convinced of it.)*
> *(She stands a little longer than she meant to. Then the clocks strike the hour, the house remembers its day, and she goes on to the morning room — the dragon's daylight, the lists, the rest of it — with the laugh at her back, holding the wall.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, after the war — Rose, in daylight; the mistress, at rest. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her bedroom, the evening: the curtains not yet drawn, the Park beyond the glass going from silver to blue, and the mistress at the window in the daylight's memory — the war behind her, the room quiet in a way it has not been for ten seasons.)*
> *(The reckoning runs once, unbidden, as it always runs at day's end: the concession, spoken. The terms, stated. The garden, walked. The peace, kept. The letter — Laurent's, the masquerade's — waiting downstairs. The day holds its own account, and for once she does not run it twice to check.)*
> *(She does not reach for the pen. The desk is there, the ink, the paper, the whole machinery of answering — and her hands stay in her lap. The letters are other people's now: the ton's, the journals', the history's. Hers is the window.)*
> *(The house's windows light one by one across the Park — the keepers' evening, the lamps carried room to room — and each lit window is a small held thing, the night's work beginning. A carriage passes on the drive, the lamps' brief flare on the gravel, the last of the evening's departures, and the dark takes the Park back after it.)*
> *(The bloom's glass is dark now — the conservatory's silhouette against the night's blue — and somewhere inside it the day's flower rests, the petals closed on the day's warmth. She cannot see it from here. She does not need to.)*
> "At rest." *(She says it softly, to the window, to the darkening Park.)* "The woman after the war — at rest, whole." *(The night comes on.)* "The daylight's memory, kept."
> *(The dressing room's door stands open on the unlit room beyond — the day's dress laid across the chair, the walking boots by the door, tomorrow's ordinary waiting — and the sight is a pleasure, the war's end in furniture.)*
> *(A night bird calls from the elms — the Park's own voice, uninterrupted — and the mistress at the window smiles, because the night is hers in a way it has not been for ten seasons: unguarded, and entire.)*
> *(The night deepens, and the mistress sits at the window, and the house's lit windows hold their small fires against the dark.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's verdict on the concession — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"Yesterday, in daylight, before the ton she once tried to keep away, Lady Agatha Drummond acknowledged Hartwell Park. The Gazette — having counted the chairs, the flowers, and the dragon's purple — finds the war ended, genuinely, and the peace magnificent. The verdict stands."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (the dragon's purple! counted!), then the reckoning: the concession is pronounced genuine in print as well as in person, and Bell has made the peace permanent, which is Bell's way of making it true. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the peace the Gazette calls genuine is the peace that holds.* — remembered: *the lesson: the peace the Gazette calls genuine is the peace that holds.*
scenes.sting: Yesterday, in daylight, before the ton she once tried to keep away, Lady Agatha Drummond acknowledged Hartwell Park. The Gazette — having counted the chairs, the flowers, and the dragon's purple — finds the war ended, genuinely, and the peace magnificent. The verdict stands.

scenes.synopsis: the letter from Paris — the masquerade, announced; the old world, one more night. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and Laurent comes with the letter — the seal, the French hand, the masquerade announced — and the old world asks for one more night.)*
> "Rose." The Frenchman, the unpolished look. "It's —" he holds the letter — "it's announced. The last great masquerade. The date —" he names it — "the place —" he names it — "the old world, one more night. Paris —" the polish returns, but thinner — "Paris is coming, Rose. To London. For the masquerade."
> *(She takes the letter — the seal, the French hand — and the masquerade is announced: the old world's last night, in London, the mask off, England chosen.)*
> "The last great masquerade." She looks at Laurent — the promise, the truth, the coming. "Then —" she stops — "then the mask off."
> "Then the mask off." The Frenchman's eyes, direct. "England. I promised."
> *(The chapter closes on the letter — the seal, the French hand, the announced night — and the Season turns toward the masquerade: the old world, one more night — and the Season holds its breath.)*

scenes.synopsis: the walk's day — the morning; Julian's note; the promise, kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning: the walk's day — and the note came with the breakfast tray, as his notes have come all season, in the free man's unguarded hand.)*
> *(The note: "The canal. Ten. The walk." Nothing more. It does not need more. The promise was made seasons ago — the canal walk, the terrace free as a life, the final debts paid — and this morning is the promise's day, as the ball was the house's night.)*
> *(She dresses for the walk — the canal's dress, the walking boots, the warm shawl — and the dressing room holds its morning light, and the mirror is passed quickly, because the walk is not about the mirror. The walk is about the water, the path, the two walkers, the ten o'clock.)*
> *(The household knows. Mrs. Quick has the still room ready for the return, whatever the return brings. Harrow has the receipts laid out in the office, the paper done. Letitia — the quartermaster, the aunt — kissed her at the garden door and said the thing she says when she means it: nothing, only the hawk's eyes, warm.)*
> *(Nine o'clock: the breakfast tray cleared — the chocolate drunk, the toast hardly touched, the morning's appetite all for the walk — and she stands at the window in the canal's dress, the walking boots laced, the warm shawl over her arm. The Park holds its morning: the lake's silver, the garden's walls, the canal's flat line beyond the beds. The walk's day, begun.)*
> *(The note sits on the dressing table — "The canal. Ten. The walk." — the free man's hand, the unguarded letters. She has kept every note he ever wrote her, filed in order, as Harrow keeps his receipts. The whole season's promise, in paper. This one she puts in her pocket. The walk's day, carried.)*
> *(The stairs are cool under her hand, the house quiet around her, and the morning holds its breath the way the Park held it at the ball: before the beautiful thing.)*
> *(Half past nine. The household moves around her — the keepers, the morning's work — and the mistress goes down to the garden door, where Letitia waits with the hawk's eyes, warm, and the kiss that says what the quartermaster never says aloud.)*

scenes.synopsis: the canal — the walk begins; the water, the path. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The canal, ten o'clock: the walk begins — the water flat silver, the path known, the morning's mist burning off the banks.)*
> *(He waits at the canal's head — the free man, the mended gloves in his pocket, the last debt paid — and he is early, because he has been early for everything this season — a man is early for the things that matter. He turns at her step on the gravel, and the unguarded look does the thing it does, and the ghost of the old smile follows it.)*
> "Rose." *(He offers his arm, the free man's arm, steady.)* "The canal. The walk." *(A stop, the unguarded look.)* "The terrace, free, as a life — it starts here. On foot."
> *(She takes the arm. The path is the one she has walked a hundred mornings — the canal's length, the water beside, the whole Park holding its morning — only this morning the walking is different: it is the walk, the promised one, the tentpole's, and every step is the keeping of it.)*
> *(The mist burns off as they walk — the banks emerging, the reeds, the whole canal's length revealing itself step by step — and the morning's light comes down the water like a thing poured.)*
> "Ten o'clock." *(He says it quietly, the unguarded look.)* "I have imagined this morning —" *(he stops)* "— I have imagined it for seasons, Rose. The canal. The walk. The —" *(another stop, the ghost of the old smile)* "— the ten o'clock."
> *(A coot skitters off the far bank as they pass — the splash, the scolding — and Julian laughs, the free man's laugh, unguarded and sudden.)*
> "The canal remembers us." *(He says it lightly, the ghost of the old smile.)* "Every scheme I ever walked off was walked here, Rose. The water has heard worse confessions than this morning's."
> *(She holds the arm — the free man's arm, steady — and the path takes their steps, and the water takes the light, and the walk takes the morning. The promise, kept: on foot, together, at ten o'clock.)*

scenes.synopsis: the water — the canal's quiet; the walk's medium. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The water: the canal's quiet — the flat silver, the light coming off it in sheets, the walk's medium — and they walk beside it as they have walked beside everything this season: together, and unhurried.)*
> *(The canal holds its morning as it has held every morning: flat, silver, certain. The swans are round the point, unconcerned. A moorhen darts from the reeds with the particular urgency of a creature with somewhere to be. The water takes the light and gives it back doubled, and the path takes their steps and gives them back as the walk.)*
> *(She thinks, walking, as she always thinks: in logistics, in ledgers. The debts: paid. The gloves: kept. The terrace: free. The columns add. The totals agree. And underneath the arithmetic, as underneath every ledger there is the thing the ledger is for, the image she would never say aloud: the two of them, old, walking this path, the water still flat silver, the promise still kept.)*
> *(The canal's quiet is the walk's argument: the free life, stated in water, walked on foot, at ten o'clock, together.)*
> *(A kingfisher goes past — the blue flash, the water's jewel — and is gone before the eye has properly had it. The canal keeps its beauties as it keeps its water: flat, and certain, and without announcement.)*
> *(The light comes off the water in sheets — the morning's coin, spent freely — and the path takes their steps and gives them back doubled — the canal's exchange: everything returned stilled, and certain.)*
> *(The towpath's gravel gives underfoot, the honest sound, and the reeds stand in their ranks, and a water vole plops from the bank with the particular embarrassment of the interrupted.)*
> *(He walks with his hands behind his back — the free man's new posture, the debts' weight gone from the shoulders — and the morning's light catches the mended gloves in his pocket, the leather's honest scars.)*
> *(She thinks of the ton's mornings — the late risings, the chocolate in bed, the day begun at noon — and then she sets the thought aside, because the ton is not the canal, and the water is the morning's own argument.)*

scenes.synopsis: the free man — Julian's story; the final debts, paid. (Turns: 9)
scenes.prose:
> *(They walk, and he tells it — the free man's story, the final debts paid — to the water, to the path, to her.)*
> "It's done." *(He says it quietly, to the water, the unguarded look.)* "The last of them. The City —" *(he stops)* "— the City has been paid, Rose. Every creditor. Every note." *(Another stop, the ghost of the old smile.)* "The final debts — paid. All of them."
> "How, Julian?" *(She asks it, because the asking is the honoring, and the paying deserves its witness.)*
> "The season." *(The ghost of the old smile, the real one underneath.)* "The work. I earned it, Rose. Every pound." *(He looks at the water, the flat silver.)* "No shortcuts. No —" *(the unguarded look)* "— no more debts. The free man walks free." *(He touches his pocket, the gloves' pocket, the gesture unconscious.)* "Harrow has the receipts. The paper's done. The City —" *(a stop)* "— the City has no more of me."
> *(They walk on, the water beside them, and the story settles as true stories settle: without flourish, as the canal settles after the swans have passed. The final debts, paid: the free man's story, told to the water. Every creditor settled. Every note honored. The walk, free.)*
> *(The water takes the story — the City, the creditors, the notes — and gives it back as the quiet, as the canal takes everything and returns it stilled.)*
> "Harrow's hand shook." *(He says it softly, the wonder in it.)* "The old steward — forty years of other men's reckonings — and his hand shook on the last receipt. He told me to walk free, Rose. As if it were an order."
> *(A barge's wake rocks the far reeds — the coal boat from the village, the Park's ordinary commerce — and the water settles, and the story settles with it, and the morning goes on being the morning.)*
> *(She listens — the creditors, the notes, the paying — and the numbers run underneath, quiet: every creditor settled, every note honored. The story settles without flourish. The walk, free. The morning, the water's.)*

scenes.synopsis: the mended gloves — the choice; kept, not needed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He shows her the gloves — the mended gloves, from the pocket — and the choice is visible in the morning's light: the mending, the wear, the history, the whole of the free man's past held in his hands.)*
> "I kept them." *(He holds them out, the unguarded look.)* "I don't need them, Rose. The debts are paid. I could buy new. A dozen." *(The ghost of the old smile.)* "But I kept them. By choice." *(He turns them over — the mended seams, the worn leather, the places where the needle went in and the life came back.)* "They're —" *(a stop)* "— they're the proof, Rose. Not of the debts. Of the mending."
> *(She takes one — the leather soft with wear, the mending neat and honest — and holds it a moment, feeling the history in it: the seasons of owing, the season of paying, the morning of freedom.)*
> "The mended gloves." *(He takes it back, gently, and puts them both away — not in the pocket, this time, but in his hand, carried openly.)* "Kept. Not needed. Chosen."
> *(The morning's light moves across the leather — the mended seams, the worn places — and the gloves hold it as the canal holds the light: steady.)*
> "The proof." *(He turns them over, the unguarded look.)* "Not of the debts. Of the mending." *(He looks at her.)* "I was —" *(he stops)* "— I was a man who owed, Rose. For seasons. And now —" *(the ghost of the old smile)* "— now I am a man who mends. The gloves —" *(he holds them out)* "— the gloves are the mending, kept."
> *(The leather is warm from his pocket — the body's warmth, the morning's — and the mending runs along the seams like handwriting, the honest script of the season's work.)*
> "The left one wore through first." *(He touches the seam, the unguarded look.)* "All that winter of owing — the City, the notes, the counting. I mended them myself, Rose. Badly, the first time. The second time" *(the ghost of the old smile)* "— the second time I had learned."

scenes.synopsis: the terrace — free, as a life; the walk's end, the life's beginning. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The walk's end comes as the canal comes to its head: gradually, and then all at once — the banks widening, the path turning, and there beyond the last of the water, the terrace, the stone, the light, the Park beyond it.)*
> *(They come up the last of the path and the terrace takes them: the stone warm in the morning's sun under their boots, the balustrade running its length, the view back to the house across the lawns, the whole Park holding its light like a held breath let out.)*
> *(He stops at the terrace's edge and turns to her — the free man, the debts paid, the mended gloves in his hand — and does the thing he has done all morning, which for him is the rarest posture: he stands still. The unguarded look does the thing it does.)*
> "The terrace." *(A breath.)* "Free. As a life." *(He looks at her, the whole of it.)* "Rose — the walk was the promise." *(a stop)* "The terrace is the life." *(another stop, the ghost of the old smile)* "Ours — if you'll have it."
> *(The stone is warm underfoot — the morning's sun full on it — and she looks past him at the terrace, the free life's ground, and then back at him, and the morning holds them the way the canal held its water this morning: full, and asking nothing.)*
> *(Behind them the canal lies flat and silver to the morning, the walk's length walked, the mist gone off it, the water keeping its quiet.)*
> *(She thinks of the masquerade to come — the masks, the old world, one more night — and then she sets it aside, because the masquerade is Laurent's, Paris's, the old world's. The terrace is this morning's.)*
> *(The terrace's flagstones are warm through her bootsoles, the stored heat of the morning's sun, and the balustrade's shadow lies in neat bars across the stone, and the Park's whole light seems to have gathered here, at the walk's end, on purpose.)*
> *(A rook goes over toward the elms, the morning's black punctuation. The balustrade holds the light. He waits — the free man, the debts paid, the gloves in his hand — and the life stands offered on the warm stone, and the morning does not hurry them.)*

scenes.synopsis: the life — the offering; the future, stated. (Turns: 9)
scenes.prose:
> *(The terrace: the life, offered, the future stated, and the free man's whole heart in the morning's light, the unguarded look, the gloves in his hand.)*
> "I have nothing —" *(he starts, then stops, the honesty catching him as it always does)* "— no. That isn't true anymore. I have the terrace. The walk." *(He looks at the Park, the whole of it, the finished complete.)* "The Park, if you'll share it. The life, free, Rose. The debts paid. The gloves kept." *(He takes her hands, the free man's hands, steady.)* "The life is yours, if you'll have it. Free. As a life."
> *(She looks at him, the free man, the paid debts behind him, the terrace beneath them, the morning's light falling across the two of them without favor, and the future is stated the way the canal stated everything this morning: quietly, and for good.)*
> "The life." *(She holds his hands, the direct look.)* "Free. Yes, Julian."
> "The gloves are yours to keep." *(He presses them into her hand, the leather warm from his pocket.)* "Not to wear —" *(the unguarded look)* "— unless you want the walk again. The terrace" *(he looks at the stone, the light)* "— the terrace is yours regardless."
> *(She holds the gloves a moment, the mending, the wear, the history, and then she gives them back, because they are his choice, not hers to keep. He puts them in his hand, carried openly, and the terrace holds its morning light, and the promise, kept, becomes the life.)*
> *(A rook goes over toward the elms, the morning's black punctuation, and the Park holds its light, and the two of them stand on the terrace's warm stone with the whole free life in front of them, unoffered no longer, unrefused.)*
> *(The morning's sun is full on the terrace now, and the stone gives back the warmth, and somewhere below in the garden a thrush is having the last word about something, repeatedly, and the free man laughs — the unguarded sound — and the terrace keeps it a moment.)*
> "Free." *(She says it again, tasting the word the way she tastes everything: to make sure it's real.)* "As a life." *(The direct look, the woman's.)* "Yes."

scenes.synopsis: the past — the debts' story, fully told; the paying, honored. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(They sit on the terrace — the stone warm, the morning's sun full — and the past is fully told, the debts' story honored in the telling.)*
> "Tell me." *(She says it quietly, the direct look.)* "All of it. The debts. The paying."
> *(He tells it — the creditors, the notes, the season's work, the earning — the whole of the paying, honored in the telling. The City's ledgers, the notes honored one by one, the last receipt, the paper done. He tells it as he told the walk's beginning: quietly, to the light, the unguarded look never leaving her face.)*
> *(She listens as she has listened all season — the whole of her attention. The settled names run underneath — the creditors, the notes, the clear name — and underneath them, the image she would never say aloud: the man beside her, free, the mended gloves in his hand, the past paid and the future open.)*
> "It's done." *(He finishes, to the Park, the ghost of the old smile.)* "The past is paid, Rose. All of it."
> *(The past, told: the paying, honored. The debts' story, finished — and the future, beginning, on the terrace's warm stone.)*
> *(The terrace's stone warms under them — the morning's sun full — and the past is told as the walk was walked: quietly, and to the end.)*
> "The City." *(He looks at the Park, the whole of it.)* "The ledgers. The notes." *(He tells it — the creditors one by one, the paying season by season — the unguarded look never leaving her.)* "It's done, Rose. All of it."
> *(The terrace's stone is warm through her skirt, and the morning's sun has moved past the balustrade's shadow, and the Park lies below in its ordered green, and the past — told, honored, finished — sits between them like the third person at the table, quiet at last.)*
> "The last note was the hardest." *(He says it to the water, the unguarded look.)* "Not the largest — the hardest. A man I had wronged in the old days, before the owing began. I paid him first, Rose. Before the creditors." *(He stops.)* "It seemed the honest order."

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE WALK'S PACE (how Rose walks it: slowly, briskly, or stopping often). The walk deepens; decide the pace. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The walk deepens — the canal's length ahead, the water's quiet beside — and the question of the pace waits: the walk is the promise, but the pace is hers. Slowly: the savoring, every step a kept thing. Briskly: the eagerness, the future pulling. Stopping often: the seeing, the Park witnessed step by step.)*
> *(Slowly: the savoring, the step's. Briskly: the eagerness, the future's. Stopping: the seeing, the patience's.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — The walk's pace:*
- **Slowly** — *the savoring.* Rose walks slowly; every step, savored. (Consequence: the walk is complete — but slow is lingering, and the future wants arriving.)
- **Briskly** — *the eagerness.* Rose walks briskly; the future, eagerly. (Consequence: the eagerness is honest — but brisk is hurrying, and the walk wants savoring.)
- **Stopping often** — *the seeing.* Rose stops often; the Park, seen. (Consequence: the seeing is the reward — but stopping is pausing, and the walk wants walking.)
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: slowly, briskly, or stopping. The pace, decided on the canal's bank, becomes the walk's rhythm.)*
> *(The three paces wait — the savoring, the eagerness, the seeing — and she turns them over carefully, once, as she turns everything over.)*
> *(Slowly would be the complete thing, every step a kept thing — but slow is lingering, and the future wants arriving. Briskly would be the honest thing, the future eagerly — but brisk is hurrying, and the walk wants savoring. Stopping often would be the rewarding thing, the Park seen — but stopping is pausing, and the walk wants walking.)*
> *(The canal's length waits. The water's quiet holds. The pace will be hers, and the walk's rhythm will be the morning's rhythm, and the morning's rhythm will be the life's.)*
> *(The path narrows past the willows — the branches trailing, the shade cool — and they slow without speaking, the pace adjusting itself, the walk's own wisdom.)*
> "Savoring." *(He says it suddenly, the unguarded look.)* "That was your word, Rose. At the ball. The savoring, the eagerness, the seeing." *(The ghost of the old smile.)* "I have savored nothing in ten seasons. Teach me."
> *(She takes his arm — the free man's arm, steady — and the willows trail their branches, and the pace is the teaching, and the morning is the lesson.)*
> *(A dragonfly hovers at the path's edge — the iridescent industry — and the canal's quiet holds, and the pace waits to be chosen the way the morning waits to be lived: once, and personally.)*
> *(The willows trail their fingers in the water — the green shade, the cool — and the question of the pace is the morning's own, asked gently.)*

scenes.synopsis: the canal's length — the walk, walked; the pace, kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The canal's length: the walk, walked, the pace kept as she chose, and the water beside them, the path under their feet, the morning's light going with them like a third walker.)*
> *(They walk, slowly, or briskly, or stopping often, as she chose, and the canal's length is the walk's body: the water, the path, the two walkers, the pace. The reeds bend in the morning's breeze. A moorhen darts from the bank with its particular urgency. The swans come round the point, unconcerned, going about the canal's business around the walk's.)*
> *(The light comes off the water in sheets, the morning's coin spent freely, and the path takes their steps and gives them back as the walk, and the canal keeps its beauties the way it keeps its water: flat, and certain, and without announcement.)*
> *(She counts the bridges as they pass them, the near one, the far one, the crown's arch, and the counting is the walk's own arithmetic, the honest kind, the kind with no owing in it. Three bridges, the canal's length, the morning's whole account, and every column adds.)*
> *(The far bank rises, the path climbing, the view opening, and the canal's length lies behind them like a held breath, the water flat silver, the morning's work done. The walk, walked: the pace, kept. The promise, kept in every step.)*
> *(He walks beside her, the free man, the mended gloves in his hand, the patience, and the question the morning asked at the canal's head is answered in the walking: this is how the free life walks. At the pace she chose. On foot. Together.)*
> *(The towpath's stones are worn smooth in the middle, the ten seasons' treading, and the water runs beside with its particular business, and the walk goes on.)*
> *(At the second bridge they stop, because she wants to look down the canal's length both ways, and the looking is the walk's own business. Upstream the water runs flat to the morning's brightness; downstream it bends out of sight behind the alders. He waits without speaking, the patience, and a kingfisher goes past low over the water, too quick for more than the blue, and she laughs out loud at the quickness of it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the water's life — the swans, the light; the canal, living. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The water's life: the swans, the light — the canal, living — and the walk's beauty, witnessed step by step.)*
> *(They pass them — the swans, the light on water, the whole canal's society — and the canal is living: the moorhen's urgency, the dragonflies' industry, the fish rising in the shallows with the particular discretion of creatures that have somewhere to be. The water takes the morning and gives it back doubled, and the walk takes the morning and gives it back as the life.)*
> *(She watches the swans — the unconcern, the grace, the ten seasons of unconcern — and the image comes unbidden, as the true images come: the free life, stated in swans. Not the debts, not the paying, not the paper done — the living, the morning's, the water's.)*
> *(The canal, living: the water's life, the light. The walk's beauty, witnessed — and the free life, stated in the morning's own language.)*
> *(The dragonflies work the reeds — the industry, the iridescence — and the canal's society goes about its morning around the walkers, indifferent to tentpoles.)*
> *(She watches the water's life — the swans, the light, the fish rising — and the walk's beauty is the morning's own: not staged, not performed, simply there, as the free life is simply there when the debts are paid.)*
> *(A heron stands in the shallows — the grey patience, the stillness — and the walk's beauty is the morning's own, unstaged, unperformed, simply there.)*
> "The free life, stated in swans." *(She says it softly, the morning's.)* "That was my thought, earlier. The debts, the paying, the paper done — none of it is the living." *(She watches the heron.)* "This is the living. The water's. The morning's."
> *(The heron strikes — the quicksilver flash, the fish — and the morning's language is fluent in hunger, too, and the walk witnesses it all.)*
> *(The moorhen returns to the reeds with its particular urgency discharged, and the dragonflies resume their industry, and the water's life goes on around the walkers as it went on before them: unconcerned, and complete.)*
> *(The water's life goes on — the swans, the light, the fish rising — and the walk's beauty is witnessed, and the morning speaks fluently.)*

scenes.synopsis: the bridge — the crossing; the walk's middle, passed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The bridge: the canal's stone arch, the water running under it, the steps worn hollow in the middle by ten seasons of crossings — his, mostly, the schemes walked off and the schemes walked home.)*
> *(They cross it, and the climb is the walk's own small labor: the arch rising under their boots, the worn steps, the parapet cool under her hand. At the crown the canal gives them both ways — the length behind, the water flat silver, the morning's mist gone off it now; the length ahead, bending toward the terrace's direction, the afternoon's promise in the light.)*
> *(From the crown she can see the far bank's alders, a gardener's boy's barrow left mid-lawn, a swan's white wake stitching the water behind it. The whole morning laid out below like the estate books laid open — walked, this time, instead of added.)*
> "Halfway." *(He stops at the crown, the free man's hand on the stone.)* "The canal's middle. The morning's middle." *(The unguarded look.)* "Every scheme I ever walked off turned around here, Rose. This walk" *(he looks at the terrace's direction)* "— this walk goes on."
> *(He takes her hand — the free man's hand, steady — and they stand a moment at the crown with the water under and the Park both ways, and the arch holds them the way the morning has held everything: without asking.)*
> "The middle." *(He says it softly, the ghost of the old smile.)* "The past behind, the future ahead." *(A stop.)* "The best place, Rose. The between."
> *(The parapet's stone is cool under her palm, the old cool, the ten seasons' cool, and the water runs under the arch with its particular business, and the crown holds them a moment longer than the crossing strictly requires.)*
> *(A swan comes under the bridge — the white wake, the unconcern — and passes beneath them, and is gone round the bend, and the arch keeps the small sound of the water a moment after.)*
> *(They go down the far side, the steps worn hollow, the parapet cool, and the bridge gives them back to the path — crossed, the middle passed — and the water runs under the arch behind them, and the walk goes on toward the terrace.)*

scenes.synopsis: the far bank — the view back; the Park, whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The far bank: the view back, the Park whole, and the walk's reward, the seeing.)*
> *(They stand on the far bank and look back: the house on its rise, the garden walls, the lake's silver beyond, the cottages' roofs past the trees, the ten seasons' work laid out in the morning's light like the estate books laid open. The walk's reward is the seeing: the Park, whole, from across the water.)*
> *(She looks at it, and the reckoning runs, unbidden, the way it always runs: the beds, done. The walls, done. The house, finished. The bloom, blooming. The dragon, reconciled. The debts, his, paid. The list runs its course, column by column, and she lets it run, and then she sets it aside, because the list is not the view.)*
> *(The view is the whole Park in the morning's light, the free man beside her, the mended gloves in his hand, the terrace ahead. The house on its rise. The garden walls. The lake's silver. The cottages' roofs. The finished complete, seen from the far bank, and the columns have added, and the totals agree, and none of it is the point.)*
> *(A gardener's boy crosses the far lawn with a barrow, the estate's ordinary morning going on underneath the tentpole's, and a dog barks once from the cottages, and the Park is living its life around the walk, unimpressed and essential, the way it lived it around the ball.)*
> "The ball was the seeing from inside." *(She says it quietly, the morning's.)* "The chandeliers, the music, the ton. This" *(she looks at the Park, whole)* "— this is the seeing from outside. The house, the garden, the water. All of it mine. All of it kept."
> *(She names the roofs for him, the way the mistress knows her estate: the home farm's, the dairy's, the cottagers' row past the trees, the walled garden's glass. He listens, the free man, learning the Park the way he never learned it as a boy, when it was his father's and then his burden. Now it is simply the view, and the view is simply the morning's.)*

scenes.synopsis: the return — the walk back; the terrace, nearer. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The canal's end: the return, the turning back toward the house, the walk completed.)*
> *(They turn at the canal's end, or at the point she chose, or at the terrace's first stone, and the walk becomes the return: the same water, the same path, the steps given back. The turning is the walk's own form, the way a waltz turns.)*
> *(The light has moved while they walked, the morning's hand across the water shifting, and the canal on the return is the canal made new: the reflections altered, the reeds' shadows longer, the swans elsewhere about the canal's business. Same water. Different walk.)*
> *(The boots are muddy now, the hems, the petticoats, the morning's honest marks, and the free man walks beside her with the mud on his own, the mended gloves in his hand, the day's beginning in his bearing. The return is not the walk undone; it is the walk confirmed, step by step, water by water.)*
> *(The house rises before them, the terrace, the morning room's windows catching the light, the finished house whole in the morning's full strength. The walk completes itself toward the house the way the ten seasons completed themselves toward the ball.)*
> *(She walks the return with the future in front of her, stated, hers, the terrace, the life, free, and the walk's completed steps are the promise's first payment: this is how the free life walks. Back to the house. Together.)*
> "The terrace." *(She says it as they approach, the house rising.)* "Free." *(The free man, beside her.)* "As a life." *(The morning's full strength, the windows catching it.)* "Yes."
> *(The return's light is different on the water — the morning's hand moved, the reflections altered — and the canal gives back the walk in reverse, the same beauties in a new order, and the boots are muddy, and the morning is nearly done being morning.)*
> *(A gardener's boy touches his cap as they pass the beds, and she stops to ask after the new edging, and the boy answers with the particular pride of the young workman, and the free man listens, learning the estate's small business the way he learned the morning's large one: by standing beside her while she does it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the terrace, arrived — the walk's end; free, as a life. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The last of the path is gravel — the crunch underfoot, the sound of arrival — and the terrace rises ahead of them, the stone, the light, the balustrade, the morning's promise made solid and walkable.)*
> *(They stand at its edge — the canal walked, the terrace reached, the water's quiet behind them and the life's ground beneath them — and the terrace is free: the stone warm, the view to the house, the Park holding its late-morning light.)*

The line can stand him." *(The dry voice, dry as ever, and underneath it something Rose has heard perhaps twice in her life: warmth, undisguised.)* "I am glad, child. Do not make me say it again."

> *(He sits with her, the free man, the columns done together, the mended gloves on the desk's edge, and the planning is the two of them's: the annual convening, the house that holds people, the terrace offered daily, the Park offered yearly.)*
> *(The notes grow: the guest list's first names, the ball's date, the bloom's showing, the cottages' part. The Assembly takes shape on the page the way the house took shape in stone: gradually, and completely.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick brings the breakfast room's arithmetic, the keys, the immovable mouth, and the household's part is the planning's: the menus, the rooms, the staff, the invisible work, all of it costed, all of it honest.)*
> *(The dragon's name is on the guest list's first page, because the daylight concession is behind them and the morning room's witnessing, and the old guard follows where the dragon leads. Augusta's name is beside it, the spectacles, the lineage. Letitia's, the hawk's eyes, the quartermaster. Lavinia's twelve, glittering. The list grows the way the house grew: name by name, stone by stone.)*
> *(She writes the ball's date in the margin, the same week next year, and the committing of the date is the planning's own ceremony, the way the laying of a foundation stone is. The annual convening, dated. The house, holding people, yearly.)*
> *(The ink is barely dry on the ball's date, and the page holds the year's shape, and the morning room's light falls across the notes, and the Assembly's first planning sits complete beside the household's ordinary.)*
> "The Assembly." *(She looks at the notes, the planning's shape.)* "Annual." *(The free man beside her.)* "The house, holding people. Year after year."

scenes.synopsis: the creditors, settled — the City, paid; the past, closed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The evening: the creditors, settled — the City, paid — and the past is closed, as the estate office's file is closed.)*
> *(The letters went out — the paid stamps, the honored notes — and the City received them: the creditors settled, the past closed. Julian's name — the free man's — clear in the City's books, as Hartwell Park is clear in the ton's.)*
> *(She thinks of the City — the ledgers, the notes, the whole machinery of owing — and then she sets it aside, because the City is not the terrace, and the ledgers are not the life. The past is paid. The arithmetic is done. The book is closed with a clean hand.)*
> *(Harrow's file sits closed on the estate office desk — the receipts within, the paid stamps, the creditors' marks — and the office's quiet is the City's quiet, filed.)*
> *(Somewhere in London a clerk draws a line through Julian Hartwell's name — the last line, the final account — and the City's machinery, indifferent, turns to its next debtor.)*
> *(The City's evening is coal-smoke and lamplight — the ledgers closing, the clerks going home — and Julian Hartwell's name is clear in the books, the past paid.)*
> *(A clerk's pen scratches in her mind's ear — the final line, the name struck — and then the sound fades, because London is miles off, and the evening is here.)*
> "The book is closed." *(She says it softly, to the evening.)* "The counting is done." *(She looks at the terrace — the stone, the light, the free life's ground.)* "The life is not the ledger. The evening" *(the woman's voice, the certain one)* "— the evening is the terrace's."
> *(The estate office's lamp is lit, and Harrow's file sits closed, and the City's machinery turns to its next debtor, indifferent, and the evening is the terrace's.)*
> *(The terrace's stone holds the day's last warmth underfoot, and the Park darkens beyond the balustrade, and the past — paid, filed, closed — is miles off in London, and the evening is here.)*
> *(The evening holds its quiet — the terrace, the stone, the free life's ground — and the past is the ledger's, and the ledger's only.)*

scenes.synopsis: the gloves, on the terrace — the symbol, in the dusk; the choice, sitting in light. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She stands with the bloom, the morning's, the gardener's pride in the room with her though the gardener is in the walled garden where he belongs. The first bloom, opening, certain, the ten seasons' breeding, the legacy living.)*
> *(The Park's stone blushing to rose, the form perfect, the scent rising in the morning's warmth. The bloom keeps its appointment the way the house keeps its: completely. The living proof no ton can refute, no column can total.)*
> *(She looks at it with the morning's eye, the gardener's, the mistress's, and the reckoning runs, the way it always runs, and she lets it run, and sets it aside, because the bloom is the point, not the list: the first bloom, witnessed.)*
> *(He stands with her, the free man, the mended gloves, and the bloom is the two of them's now, the free life's own flower, the living legacy, witnessed together.)*
> *(A bee works the bloom's heart, the morning's own business, unimpressed and essential, and the bloom holds its opening, certain, and the Park holds its morning, and the two of them hold their free life.)*
> *(She bends to the bloom the way the duchess bent to it at the ball, with actual curiosity, and the scent is the garden's ten seasons in a single breath, and the petals are the Park's stone blushing, and the form is the breeding's whole argument. The gardener's ten seasons, visible, in one bloom.)*
> *(She thinks of the frost year, the April snow, the near-loss of the stock, and the bloom is the answer to all of it, opening, certain. The deciding to believe, made petal. The living legacy, witnessed, and the witnessing is the morning's own business.)*
> "Every year." *(She says it, the bloom's certainty.)* "Roses know what they're for." *(The free man beside her.)* "The legacy, living."
> *(The morning's warmth rises from the soil, and the walled garden holds it, and the bloom's scent deepens, and the gardener will come at noon to check the staking, and the living legacy goes on being living, whatever the morning brings.)*
> *(The bloom stands in its chosen place, opening, certain, and the living legacy is witnessed, and the morning holds them, and the first bloom keeps its appointment.)*

scenes.synopsis: the canal, at dusk — the water, the light; the walk's memory. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The household: the day's business, done, the invisible work honored, the keys.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick moves through the house with her keys, the immovable mouth, the day's arithmetic complete, and the household's business is done the way it always is: well, and as if it were easy. The invisible work, honored.)*
> *(The footmen, the maids, the kitchens, the gardeners: the Park's people, going about the day's business, the ordinary, unimpressed and essential. The mistress's rounds have been walked. The orders given. The business done.)*
> *(She stands with Mrs. Quick in the morning room, the desk, the books, the columns added, the totals agreed, and the look between them is the household's own: the keeper and the mistress, the arithmetic shared, the honest kind.)*
> *(The house party's guests are at the lawns, the breakfast room, the Park's morning going on around the tentpole's, and the household holds them all, the finished house, the living world.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick's keys are the day's own music, the turning, the locking, the opening, and the mistress knows the sound the way she knows the estate's books: by heart. The keeper's round, the morning's, the afternoon's, the night's. The invisible work, going on.)*
> *(She walks the kitchens with Mrs. Quick, the week's menus, the house party's numbers, the Assembly's first costs, and the cook shows her the week's ordering, and the mistress checks it the way she checks everything: with her hands, with her eyes, the arithmetic shared.)*
> *(The larders are full, the pantries, the stillroom, the house party fed and the household fed, and the plenty is the planning's own, the honest kind, with no owing in it. The invisible work, honored, the keys, the keeper, the mistress.)*
> *(The keys' turning is the day's own music — the morning's, the afternoon's, the night's — and the mistress knows it the way she knows the estate's books: by heart, and with pleasure.)*
> *(The larders' plenty is the planning's own, the honest kind, and the house party is fed, and the household is fed, and the invisible work goes on, honored, whether witnessed or not.)*
> "The household." *(She says it, the day's business done.)* "The invisible work." *(Mrs. Quick's keys, the immovable mouth.)* "Honored."

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE FREEDOM'S MEANING (what Julian's freedom means: the past paid, the future open, or the choice itself). The dusk deepens; decide the meaning. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dusk, and the terrace to herself: the gloves on the balustrade where he left them, the canal flat and darkening below, the day's columns closed. The question she has been carrying since morning comes clear now, the way the canal came clear this morning — flat, certain, without announcement.)*
> *(She lays it out the way she lays out everything: three columns. The past, paid — the reckoning honored, every creditor, every note, the City ledgers closed behind him like a finished book. It is the cleanest column, the most provable. But pasts are past, and she knows what the consequence line already told her: the meaning wants the future.)*
> *(The future, open — the terrace free as a life, the walk daily, the unbuilt years. It is the largest column and the emptiest, which is its honesty: nothing in it yet but the promise. Futures are unbuilt, and the meaning wants the built.)*
> *(The choice itself — the gloves, kept, not needed, chosen. The emblem column. It is the smallest and the sharpest: a man who mends, a woman who asked, the mended thing carried openly. But emblems are symbols, and the meaning wants the living.)*
> *(The KEY DECISION's approach: the freedom's meaning, coming clear, the morning's fullness, the free life's own question.)*
- **The past, paid** — *the reckoning, honored.* The freedom means the debts paid — every creditor, every note. (Consequence: the reckoning is complete — but pasts are past, and the meaning wants the future.)
- **The future, open** — *the life, beginning.* The freedom means the terrace — free, as a life. (Consequence: the future is the gift — but futures are unbuilt, and the meaning wants the built.)
- **The choice itself** — *the gloves, kept.* The freedom means the choice — kept, not needed, chosen. (Consequence: the choice is the emblem — but emblems are symbols, and the meaning wants the living.)
> *(The three columns stand in the dusk — the paid, the open, the chosen — and none of them is wrong, which is what makes it a decision and not a sum.)*
> *(Behind her the house lights its first lamps — the library, the morning room — and the Park's dusk deepens around the lit windows the way it deepened around the ball's candles. Augusta's voice from this morning comes back to her, uninvited and exact: the line can stand him. The approval, given once, never repeated. It sits in the columns too, though it belongs in none of them — the past's arithmetic, the future's promise, the choice's emblem, and over them all the Dowager's dry warmth, undisguised, twice in a lifetime.)*
> *(The canal darkens. The gloves wait on the balustrade. The terrace holds its evening light, free as a life, and the meaning waits for her to name it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the evening — the walk's end; the Park, darkening. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The evening: the walk's end — the Park darkening, the lanterns lit along the terrace, the day complete as the ball's night was complete.)*
> *(She walks in from the garden as the light goes, and the walk's day is accounted: the canal walked, the terrace free, the debts paid, the gloves kept, the life offered, the meaning decided. The evening takes the book and closes it — gently, the way Mrs. Quick closes the still room at night.)*
> *(The household settles — the keepers, the night's work, the lamps carried room to room — and the house holds its evening as it held the morning: full. The walk's day, complete: the promise kept, the life begun.)*
> *(The rooks go over to the elms — the evening's black parliament — and the lake gives up its last silver, and the garden's walls go dark section by section.)*
> *(She walks the terrace once, the stone cooling under her step, the lanterns lit in their row, the gloves lying on the balustrade where he left them — and the day's walk is in her legs, the good ache of the kept promise.)*
> *(The bats come out — the evening's second parliament, silent — and the first stars prick through over the lake, and the garden's walls are dark.)*
> *(She touches the gloves as she passes — the leather cool now, the day's warmth gone out of it — and the balustrade is cool under her hand, and the night is the day's own, come round at last.)*
> "Complete." *(She says it softly, to the night, to the darkening Park.)* "The walk walked. The debts paid. The gloves kept. The terrace free." *(The woman's voice, the certain one.)* "The life offered — and the meaning is the keeping."
> *(The lanterns burn in their row, small held fires against the dark, and the gloves lie cool on the balustrade, and the day's walk is in her legs, the good ache, and the night keeps what the day promised.)*
> *(The night comes on. The house settles, the keepers at the night's work, the lanterns burning in their row along the terrace — and the walk's day is done, and the dark keeps it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the dinner — the family, after the walk; the line, the love. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The dinner: the family, after the walk — Augusta, Letitia, Rose — and the line, the love, the candlelight.)*
> "To the walk!" *(Letitia raises her glass, the warm look.)* "To the terrace! To the —" *(the hawk's eyes shining)* "— to the free man, free!"
> "To the terrace." *(Augusta raises hers — the spectacles, the seventy-two.)* "Free. As a life." *(The rarest smile.)* "To the woman —" *(she looks at Rose)* "— who walked it."
> *(They drink — the family, the line, the love — and the dinner holds its candlelight, and the walk's day is honored the family's way: the toast, the love, the line.)*
> "To the life." *(Rose raises hers, the direct look.)* "Free."
> "Free." *(The family, entire — the Dowager, the quartermaster, the mistress — and the dinner's candlelight holds them, the line, the love.)*
> *(The candles burn lower — the dinner's second hour — and the talk turns to the morrow: the household's ordinary, the garden's season, the masquerade's approach.)*
> "The masquerade." *(Letitia refills her glass, the hawk's eyes bright.)* "Paris sends masks, darling. We shall send —" *(the warm look)* "— we shall send ourselves. Unmasked, and magnificent."
> "Unmasked." *(Augusta's rarest smile.)* "At a masquerade. The Hartwells —" *(the spectacles)* "— the Hartwells never could resist a contradiction."
> *(The dining room glows — the candles, the silver, the three women's faces — and the dinner is the walk's day's crown.)*
> "To the keeping." *(Rose raises her glass once more, the direct look.)* "Every day. On purpose." *(She looks at the Dowager, the quartermaster.)* "The line taught me the stone. The garden taught me the flowers." *(The woman's voice, the certain one.)* "The walk taught me the rest."
> "To the morrow." *(Letitia raises her glass once more, the hawk's eyes bright.)* "The household's ordinary. The garden's season." *(The warm look.)* "The masquerade — and ourselves, unmasked, and magnificent."
> *(The candles gutter in their sockets, and the silver throws back the last of the light, and the three women's faces are warm in it, and the night holds them, and the walk's day is honored.)*
> *(They laugh — the family, the line, the love — and the candlelight holds the laughter, and the night holds them.)*

scenes.synopsis: the night — the terrace, moonlit; the free life, the moon's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Night, and the terrace to herself: the moon high, the stone silvered, the Park laid out below in the moon's own arithmetic — the lake a coin, the canal a ruled line, the garden walls dark hedges of shadow.)*
> *(She has sent the household to bed and kept the night for herself, the way she used to keep the war-room after midnight in the early seasons — the mistress's hour, when the house stops asking and starts simply being. Her shawl is wool, plain, the one Letitia knitted years ago and pretends not to have knitted. The stone is cold through her slippers. She doesn't mind. Cold is honest.)*
> *(Below, the canal keeps its level in the moonlight, undisturbed by anything but the moon. This morning it carried the walk; tonight it carries the reflection. Same water. The thought arrives uninvited and stays: that is what the day has been — the same water, carrying something different by evening than it carried at dawn.)*
> *(She thinks of Julian asleep — or not asleep, but quiet — in the guest wing, a free man under her roof for the first night of the rest of it. The debts are paid. The gloves are kept. Tomorrow the walk again, the rounds again, the arithmetic again. The future, unbuilt, waiting like the moonlit Park: all shape, no demands yet.)*
> *(An owl calls from the elms. The doves are silent. The house behind her ticks and settles, the finished complete, holding its people the way the night holds the Park — without effort, because that is what it is for.)*
> *(She counts without meaning to — the walk, the rounds, the arithmetic, the Assembly's planning, the bloom, the household, the dragon's daylight answered — seven columns, and every one of them adds. Letitia would laugh at her, counting on the moonlit terrace. Letitia counts in daylight and calls it quartermastering; Rose counts at midnight and calls it nothing at all. The totals agree either way. The day is the honest kind, with no owing in it anywhere she can find.)*
> *(She stands until the cold finds her properly, and then a moment longer, because the night is the free life's too — not just the days, with their columns and walks, but this: the moon, the stone, the hour that belongs to no one. Then she goes in, the shawl close, the terrace keeping its moonlight behind her.)*

scenes.synopsis: the gloves, kept — the final image; the choice, the night's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The terrace, in the evening's approach: the light going the way it went on the walk's return — shifting, the afternoon's hand moving across the Park, the stone keeping the day's warmth underfoot a little longer.)*
> *(She stands on the terrace with the day behind her — the walk, the promise, the rounds, the arithmetic, the Assembly's planning, all of it done — and the evening is the day's own reward, come up the steps unannounced.)*
> *(He stands beside her, the free man, the mended gloves in his hand, the day's fullness in his bearing — and the evening is the two of them's now, the way the morning was: offered, accepted, lived.)*
> *(The Park holds the evening — the finished complete, the garden walls in the low light, the lake's silver going gold — and the bloom is closing for the night in its chosen place, and the terrace is free in the evening's light the way it was free in the morning's.)*
> *(Below, the canal runs dark between its banks, the day's silver gone out of it, the water keeping the evening the way it kept the morning — flat, and certain, and without announcement.)*
> *(A rook goes over toward the elms, the evening's black punctuation. The light holds a moment longer on the balustrade, and then it doesn't.)*
> *(She thinks of the evening's business waiting — the dinner, the household, the night's own — and sets it aside for one more minute, because the evening is the day's reward and the reward wants its minute.)*
> "The evening." *(She says it, the day's close.)* "The terrace." *(The free man beside her.)* "Free."
> *(The terrace's stone gives up the day's warmth slowly, and the balustrade is cool under her hand, and the Park's dark comes up the lawns, and the evening is the day's own, come round at last.)*
> *(The first stars are out over the lake, and the bats are about their silent business, and the house's windows light one by one, and the night begins its own watch.)*
> *(She stands a moment longer — the free woman, the evening's light going gold and then going — and then she turns toward the house, and the day is behind her, complete, and the evening is hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, after the walk — Rose, the night's; the mistress, the free life's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The evening walk done: they came up the terrace steps together in the last of the light, and he left her at the top with the gloves in his hand and the promise kept in her legs — the good ache of the walked walk — and now she is alone with the night's business waiting.)*
> *(Dinner is laid below. The household has its evening orders. Mrs. Quick's keys have made their final round. All of it goes on — the kept house, the kept promise — and she stands a moment at the balustrade where the gloves sat this afternoon, looking out at the Park going dark in sections: the garden walls first, then the canal, then the lake giving up its last silver to the dusk.)*
> *(She thinks of the morning's Julian — the debts, the offering, the unguarded look — and the evening's Julian — the walk, the pace, the patience — and they are the same man, which is the whole of it. The free man, free in the morning and free at night, the mending holding.)*
> *(The rooks go over to the elms, black against the blue. The first stars come out over the lake. The terrace stones give back the day's warmth under her slippers, the last of it, and she stands in it a moment — the mistress, the woman, the free life's — before the night's business calls her in.)*
> *(Tomorrow: the walk again. The rounds again. The arithmetic again. The thought doesn't tire her the way thoughts of tomorrow used to. It steadies her, the way the canal's level steadies the water — kept, daily, on purpose.)*
> *(The balustrade is empty where the gloves sat this afternoon — he took them with him, carried openly, the mended thing no longer needing the stone's keeping. She touches the spot where they lay, the stone still faintly warm from the day, and the smallness of the gesture surprises her: all season the terrace has been the promise's place, and now it is only a terrace again, stone and light, holding nothing but the evening. Which is, she realizes, exactly what free means.)*
> *(She goes in to dinner with the dusk at her back, and the house receives her, lit and warm, and the day closes the way good days close: complete, unforced, the promise kept and the night waiting its turn.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's record — the City's books; arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"The City's books record the settling of certain long-outstanding notes, and the Gazette — having followed the debts as faithfully as the ballroom — notes the ledger closed. A free man walks the terrace at Hartwell Park. The Gazette approves of paid debts."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (the ledger! closed!), then the reckoning: the freedom is recorded in print as well as in the terrace's light, and Bell has made the paid debts permanent, which is Bell's way of making them true. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the debt the Gazette calls paid is the debt that's done.* — remembered: *the lesson: the debt the Gazette calls paid is the debt that's done.*
scenes.sting: The City's books record the settling of certain long-outstanding notes, and the Gazette — having followed the debts as faithfully as the ballroom — notes the ledger closed. A free man walks the terrace at Hartwell Park. The Gazette approves of paid debts.

scenes.synopsis: the masquerade's preparations — Paris, arriving; the old world, one more night. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and Laurent comes — the masquerade's preparations, Paris arriving — and the old world asks for its night.)*
> "Rose." The Frenchman, the unpolished look. "Paris —" he holds the letters — "Paris is coming. The émigré houses —" he names them — "the —" another name — "all. For the masquerade." The polish returns, thinner. "The old world's last night —" he takes her hand — "the mask off. England. It's —" he stops — "it's nearly here, Rose."
> *(She takes the letters — the French hands, the arriving — and the masquerade's preparations are the old world's: Paris, coming to London, for one more night.)*
> "The last great masquerade." She looks at Laurent — the promise, the truth, the nearly. "Then —" she stops — "then the mask off."
> "Then the mask off." The Frenchman's eyes, direct. "England. I promised."
> *(The chapter closes on the letters — the French hands, the arriving — and the Season turns toward the masquerade: the old world, one more night — and the Season holds its breath.)*
**STATUS: FULL DRAFT** — awaiting Beth review.

scenes.synopsis: the masquerade's eve — the preparations; Paris, arrived. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The day before the masquerade, the house learned a new arithmetic. Rose walked the hall at four o'clock and counted: forty-two masks hung along the gallery wall, each tagged with a guest's name in Harrow's clerkly hand. Six hundred candles ordered, four hundred already in the sconces, the rest in the butler's pantry under cloths. Three musicians' stands by the east windows, tuned and waiting. She counted because counting steadied her, and because somebody had to know whether the night was ready.)*
> *(Paris had arrived before luncheon. The émigré houses came up the drive in a procession of hired carriages, the ladies with their jewel cases on their laps the way women carry things they do not trust to servants, the gentlemen bowing to the Park as if it were a person they were pleased to meet again. Harrow had put them in the guest wings, French beside French, and the corridors filled with a kind of French that Rose's schoolroom French could follow if she did not think about it too hard.)*
> *(In the hall the footmen were hanging the last of the candle branches. The wax smelled of honey and heat. A boy on a ladder reached too far and Harrow said, "Steady," without looking up from his list, and the boy steadied.)*
> *(Laurent found her by the great doors, watching the light come through the fan window in a shape like a hand.)*
> "It is nearly a ballroom," he said.
> "It was a ballroom last Tuesday," Rose said. "It has an excellent memory."
> *(He laughed, and the laugh was the unpolished one, the one that had taken him ten seasons to let her hear.)* "Tomorrow night," he said, quieter. "The old world's last night. And then, Rose —" He stopped, and looked at the masks on the wall, all those painted faces waiting. "Then the truth. I have worn the other thing so long I have forgotten where it ends and I begin."
> "Then it is a good thing it comes off," Rose said.
> "Yes." He took her hand and kissed it, not the Frenchman's flourish but something plainer. "Midnight. You will see."
> *(He went to write his letters to Paris, and Rose stood a while in the hall that smelled of wax and French soap, and counted the masks again. Forty-two. The old world, all present, one more night.)*
scenes.animationNote: "The Masquerade" — the masquerade's eve; the old world's last night approaches

scenes.synopsis: the masks — the choosing; the old world's ritual. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The masks were laid out on the long table in the morning room, on white cloths, like surgical instruments or jewels. Rose had asked for them brought down at noon, and Mrs. Quick had supervised the laying-out with the air of a woman arranging evidence.)*
> *(There were the three she had asked to see. The first quoted the S1 triumph: ivory silk, the same gold embroidery Élise's girls had stitched along the brow, the ribbon ties replaced because the old ones had gone soft with age. The second was the Hartwell rose, blush silk massed with small fabric roses at the temple, the work of it so fine Rose could see the stitches only if she held it to the light. The third was a plain black domino, unadorned, the silk so dark it seemed to take the light out of the room.)*
> *(She lifted each in turn. The triumph mask was light as a breath and smelled faintly of the cedar chest it had slept in. The rose mask was heavier, the little roses catching at her glove. The domino was nothing at all, weightless, honest.)*
> *(This was the old world's ritual, she supposed: choosing the face you would wear to the farewell. The Frenchwomen would have opinions. Letitia would have opinions. Octavia would look at the three and see something about Rose that Rose had not yet seen herself, and say it precisely, and be right.)*
> *(She held the domino up to her face and looked at herself in the glass over the mantel. A black oval, two eyes. It told nothing. It promised nothing. She set it down and picked up the triumph mask, and the gold embroidery caught the noon light, and for a moment she was twenty again, in the S1 gown, terrified and glittering, with the whole Season ahead of her like a road she could not see the end of.)*
> *(She put them all back on their cloths in a row. The choosing could wait for the night. That was the ritual's mercy: the masks would keep.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick folded the cloths' corners back with a precision that suggested she disapproved of indecision as a moral category. "Miss," she said, which was Mrs. Quick for everything else she was not saying, and withdrew.)*

scenes.synopsis: the gown — the S1 triumph gown, quoted, transformed; the atelier's memory, worn. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Élise's fitting room smelled of chalk and hot irons and the orange-flower water Élise kept in a blue bottle for her own nerves. The gown hung on the stand like a held breath: ivory silk, the S1 triumph's lines, the embroidery requoted in gold along the hem and bodice where the old gown had carried it, the neckline lowered a fraction because Rose was twenty-five and not twenty, and knew the difference.)*
> *(Élise stood back with pins in her mouth, which made her look nineteen instead of twenty-two, and studied the hang of the skirt the way a general studies ground.)*
> "The triumph," Élise said around the pins, and took them out. "Quoted, Miss Hartwell. Transformed." She smoothed the silk over Rose's shoulder, and her chalk-stained hands were gentle. "The S1 gown was the beginning. Everybody remembers the beginning." She stepped back, head tilted. "This is the becoming. Walk like it."
> "I am standing still," Rose said.
> "Then stand like it." Élise smiled, and the hollow look she had worn all season was gone from her eyes. "The atelier's memory is in every stitch. The girls stayed late three nights. One of the girls cried over the hem." She adjusted a fold at the waist. "Happy tears. I told her to cry over the hem, it improves the drape."
> *(Rose laughed, and the gown moved with her, and it was true: the beginning, become. The ivory caught the lamplight and threw it back softened, like the gown was remembering something kind.)*
> *(On the worktable lay the bouquet, quoted too: the S1 triumph's flowers, transformed. White lilies for the purity of the intent, and among them small blush roses, the Hartwell's own. Élise had tied it with ivory ribbon and left the ends long.)*
> "For midnight," Élise said, following her look. "When the mask comes off. You will want something to hold."
> *(Rose picked up the bouquet. The lilies were cool against her gloves. She thought of the S1 ball, the terror, the glitter, and set the thought aside the way Élise set pins: carefully, and for later.)*
