scenes.synopsis: dawn — the masquerade's end; England's morning. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dawn came up over the Park the way it always had, unimpressed by masquerades: the sky paling, the lake flat silver, the gardens dark and then less dark.)*
> *(Rose stood in the emptying hall and watched the footmen move quietly among the wreckage — glasses collected, champagne bottles borne off, the shed silk gathered. The candles were out, the chandelier dark, the masks gone to the morning room. The hall looked larger without its candlelight, and younger, like a face without paint.)*
> *(She had not slept. She did not want to sleep. There are nights after which sleep feels like ingratitude. Her feet ached in the thin slippers. Her hair was coming down. She had never been less fit to be seen, and never less inclined to care. The house had seen her at every hour for ten seasons; the dawn shift was only the latest.)*
> *(Harrow came through with his list, the night's accounting.)* "Forty-two masks, miss. All kept. Six hundred candles, burned." He consulted the list. "The champagne —" A pause. "The cellar reports adequately."
> "Adequately, Harrow?"
> "The cellar's word, miss. Not mine." The dry smile. "The night is complete, Miss Hartwell."
> *(She looked at the empty hall, the dawn in the tall windows.)* "The night is complete, Harrow. Thank you — for the candles, the champagne, the everything."
> "It was the house's honor, miss." *(He bowed, and went on with his list, and his footsteps faded down the corridor.)*
> *(She walked to the tall windows and looked out at the Park. Forty-two masks, six hundred candles, one unmasking, one choosing. The arithmetic closed. She had learned, over ten seasons, that the best nights were the ones where the accounts balanced without anyone seeing the ledger — and Harrow, she suspected, had known that all along.)*
> *(The dawn came through the tall windows in long pale bars, laying light across the danced floor like a clean page. The hall stood empty and true, ready for whatever the new world asked of it next. Rose stayed a while, watching the light move. Somewhere upstairs a guest laughed in their sleep, and a door closed softly, and the house exhaled into morning.)*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent, at dawn — the Englishman; the mask off, permanently. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(She found him on the terrace, where he had come after waking from the chair by the windows. He was rumpled — the shawl's creases in his coat, his hair uncombed — and he had never looked less like the Frenchman and more like himself. The polish had slept off him. What remained was the man, in the dawn, with his hands in his pockets against the cold.)*
> "England." He looked at the Park, pale and waking. "The first morning, Rose. Unmasked." The direct look. "The Frenchman was the mask. The Englishman —" He took her hands. "Is the morning."
> "The mask off," Rose said. "Permanently."
> "Permanently." He breathed the cold air like a man tasting it. "The letters are written. Paris will know by week's end." He looked at her. "And then?"
> "And then the Park. The future. Here." She smiled. "We practiced this."
> "We did." *(He held her hand, and they stood in the Englishman's first morning, and the question needed no more answering than that.)*
> *(The borrowed shawl was still folded over his arm — the émigré lady's, returned with thanks at dawn. He carried it carefully, the way he had carried the mask: a thing that had served honorably.)*
> *(He looked back at the hall, dark now, the night's candles out.)* "One more night. The old world had it. It was a good night to give." The truth's look, steady. "The new world is the morning. Ours."
> "Chosen, Laurent," Rose said.
> "Chosen."
> *(Her breath showed; his showed. Two small clouds in the cold air, mingling. It struck her as the most honest conversation they had ever had without words.)*
> *(A blackbird began in the lime walk — the first of the morning, insistent, English — and the Park answered in small stirrings: a hare on the lower lawn, mist lifting off the lake. Behind them the house stood dark-windowed, catching the sun one pane at a time, waking.)*
> *(No performance, no audience. Only the terrace, the dawn, and her. The night was over — the farewell, the becoming, the unmasking, all of it — and what remained was this: a cold terrace, a blackbird, a man with his hair uncombed, holding her hand as if he meant to keep holding it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Park, the morning after — the new world; the whole, unmasked. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(At seven she walked the Park, the whole of it: the lake, the gardens, the house behind her catching the sun one window at a time.)*
> *(The lake was flat silver, the gardens dewed, the terrace stones still cool from the night. A blackbird sang from the lime walk, insistent, English, as if it had been appointed to the post. The dew came through her slippers at once. She did not mind. The Park at dawn asked nothing of her but presence, and presence was the one thing the night had taught her to give without counting the cost.)*
> *(The gardeners were out already, moving among the beds with the day's first barrows. The head gardener touched his hat as she passed, and she nodded, and neither of them mentioned the masquerade, which was the country way of acknowledging it completely.)*
> *(A hare ran across the lower lawn, startled, white tail flashing, gone into the mist that was rising off the lake in slow ribbons. She walked the terrace's length — the mended gloves' terrace, Julian's free life — and thought of the masquerade's eve, the counting, the masks on the gallery wall, and of how the night had kept every promise it made. That was rare enough to be worth noting, even at seven in the morning with wet feet.)*
> *(Behind her the house woke fully: smoke from the kitchen chimneys, a window thrown open, somebody laughing in the servants' hall. The night's guests would want breakfast. The new world, she reflected, began with breakfast, like everything else worth doing.)*
> *(She passed the terrace doors where Julian had gone out hours before, his footprints still faint in the dew. The free life, the walk continuing. The Park held his walk and Laurent's morning and her own, and did not choose between them, and neither did she.)*
> *(She stopped at the lake's edge. The water was flat, the sky in it, the morning doubled — the world, and the world's reflection, both true. She stood a while, and the Park stood with her, and the blackbird sang, and the new world began under her feet, steady as the ground.)*

scenes.synopsis: the letters — Paris writes; the old world, informed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Before breakfast they wrote: the émigré, at the writing desks in the morning room, the quills scratching, the sealing wax heating. Paris would read these letters at breakfast, days hence, and learn what the hall had learned at midnight.)*
> *(The marquise sealed hers with a shaking hand, caught Rose's eye in the doorway, and patted the air in Rose's direction — the patting universal, a benediction — and Rose inclined her head, grave, honored.)*
> *(The younger lady with the tired eyes wrote swiftly, page after page, and sanded them with care. Rose guessed Paris would get its truest account from her: the fury, the shrug, the story becoming itself in the telling.)*
> *(An old gentleman sealed his with extra wax, as if the choosing needed the sealing. The vicomte wrote standing up, too restless to sit, blotted a page, swore softly in French, and began again. Each letter was the night retold; each retelling was a little different; all of them were true. Rose thought of ten seasons of paper — the Network's paper, Rackham's paper, all those careful lies — and was glad this paper told the truth, or as much of it as ink could hold.)*
> *(Harrow collected the letters for the post, weighing the bag in his hand.)* "Paris, miss. The old world —" A glance at the bulging bag. "Informed."
> "In writing, Harrow."
> "In writing, miss." *(He tucked the bag under his arm.)* "The choosing is carried."
> *(Rose thought of all the letters that had crossed that Channel in ten seasons — invitations, warnings, lies in fair hands — and of how this bag differed from every one of them: it carried nothing but the truth, and the truth, for once, was good news.)*
> *(The quills kept scratching behind her as she went in to breakfast, where Letitia was already holding forth on the night to anyone who would listen, which was everyone. The choosing was carried, in French, across the Channel: England, chosen, before witnesses, permanently. Somewhere in Paris, days hence, somebody would read it over coffee and put the cup down carefully, and the old world would know.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, after the masquerade — Rose, the dawn's; the mistress, the new world's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her bedroom, the morning after: Rose sat at the window in the ivory gown, quoted and transformed, the embroidery catching the morning light. She should change. She did not change. The gown was the night's, and the night was hers, and the morning could wait a little for its mistress.)*
> *(On the dressing table lay the quoted bouquet — the white lilies, the blush roses. For midnight, Élise had said. You will want something to hold. She had held it. The ribbons were a little crushed. It was perfect, the way used things are perfect.)*
> *(Her maid came in, stopped, smiled, said nothing, and went about laying out the morning dress with the particular gentleness servants use for mistresses who have not slept. The ivory gown would be brushed and put away. The night would be kept, not worn — Mrs. Quick's distinction, and a sound one.)*
> *(The maid's hands were gentle with the morning dress, laying it out as if the day were a guest to be welcomed. Rose watched her in the glass: the quick competent movements, the bitten-back smile. The house had its own way of celebrating, quieter than champagne, and no less real.)*
> *(She thought of the masks sleeping under their cloths, the letters crossing the Channel, Laurent's morning on the terrace, and of the meaning she had named in the small hours, quietly, to the empty room. The night had been all three things at once. The morning was the fourth thing: the living with it, unmasked, daily.)*
> *(Later there would be breakfast, and the guests' departures, and the ordinary business of the house reasserting itself like tide coming in. Later the gown would go to the cedar chest with the S1 things, and the mask with it. But not yet. For now the window, the Park, the light — and the rare, unrepeatable luxury of having nowhere to be but here.)*
> *(The Park woke below — the gardeners at their beds, the lake silver, the house stirring. The woman at the window watched it all and did not look away. The masquerade was over. The woman remained, watching, in the ivory gown, in the dawn's light, and the morning came on.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's masquerade report — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"At midnight last night the masks came off at Hartwell Park, and one — a Frenchman's — did not go back on. The Gazette — having attended the old world's last night — reports the becoming: England, chosen. The unmasking was permanent. The Gazette approves of truths that keep."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (the becoming! reported!), then the reckoning: the choosing is pronounced permanent in print as well as in the dawn's light, and Bell has made the Englishman true, which is Bell's way of making him last. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the truth the Gazette calls kept is the truth that holds.* — remembered: *the lesson: the truth the Gazette calls kept is the truth that holds.*

scenes.synopsis: the picnic portrait — the unveiling, announced; the painter's triumph, coming. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Morning, and Octavia comes — the picnic portrait, the unveiling announced — and the painter's triumph is coming.)*
> "Rose." The precise voice, the precise look. "It's —" she holds the letter — "it's ready. The finished portrait. The picnic." The painter's eyes, bright. "The unveiling —" she names the day — "the Park. The —" she stops — "the finished portrait, unveiled. And hung." A breath. "Two houses, one shared life. My half —" the precise smile — "my half, witnessed. In the Park."
> *(She takes the letter — the painter's hand, the announcing — and the unveiling is the next tentpole: the finished picnic portrait, unveiled and hung in the Park.)*
> "The unveiling." She looks at Octavia — the promise, the triumph, the coming. "Then —" she stops — "then the Park holds the portrait."
> "Then the Park holds it." The painter's eyes, direct. "Forever."
> *(The chapter closes on the letter — the painter's hand, the announcing — and the Season turns toward the unveiling: the finished portrait, hung in the Park — and the Season holds its breath.)*

scenes.synopsis: the unveiling's day — the morning; the Park, prepared. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The unveiling's day dawned clear, the Park prepared, the light the particular gold of early autumn. Rose walked the grounds at seven and found everything as it should be: the chosen place swept, the portrait's wall washed, the gardeners moving among the beds with the quiet industry of men who had been told this day mattered and had decided to believe it.)*
> *(The painter's triumph, approaching. Octavia had been awake since five — Rose knew, because the studio lamp had been lit when she passed, and because Octavia on the day of a triumph slept the way generals sleep before a battle: not at all.)*
> *(She walked the Park's length, the morning, the prepared. The lake flat, the gardens dewed, the terrace stones cool. The finished picnic portrait waited under its veil in the chosen place, and the Park held its breath the way the hall had held its breath before midnight, politely, completely.)*

scenes.synopsis: the free man, on the portrait — Julian, the unveiling's; the terrace, the painted. (Turns: 8)

> "Two houses," Rose said. "One shared life."
> "The arrangement." He touched his pocket, the gloves. "The arrangement is the life, painted. Proof, if anyone wanted it." The ghost of the old smile. "Nobody will want it. They'll see the laugh and stop there, which is as it should be."

It suited him, she thought, to approve a portrait for its background. Julian's own portrait would never be painted — he would refuse to sit, and the refusal would be the whole of him — but here he was anyway, in the background of someone else's happiness: the slope, the distance, the free life, kept in paint without his permission. > *(They stood before it together, the free man and the laughing woman, and Rose thought of the terrace, the walk, the decade of Julian's quiet tending — the gloves mended, the path walked — and of how he had come through the seasons to this: standing before a portrait of happiness, approving it, and meaning it.)*
> "The walk continues," he said, low. "The terrace is free. And this —" a gesture at the paint — "this is the proof. The happy, hung."

> *(He bowed over her hand, and went to stand on the terrace, and Rose watched him go — the free man's back, straight, unhurried — and the laugh in paint watched too, and the morning went on, and it was all true at once.)*

What he was really doing, she understood, was standing guard over the laugh. Someone had to. The portrait couldn't watch itself.)*
> *(She had seen him that morning, before the company came, straightening the portrait's hanging wire with a pocket level, though the wire had been perfectly straight. That was Henry: the devotion didn't pause for unveilings.)*
> *(The company milled around them, the toasts beginning, the afternoon going gold, and Henry stayed at his post through all of it — not aloof, exactly, but stationed, the way he was stationed everywhere: the still point, the kept light. Rose thought the portrait was lucky to have him. The laugh would need guarding, in the years to come, from dust and damp and indifference. Henry guarded things the way other men collected them: completely, and without being asked.)*
> *(She thought of the lanterns, the daily round, the devotion that was not a season's but a life's, and of how the two of them stood at opposite ends of the same truth: Octavia had caught the laugh on a summer afternoon, and Henry kept the light by which it could be seen in winter.)*
> *(He went back to his post at the company's edge, and the laugh shone in the paint, and the morning deepened around them both. The smallest smile stayed on his face all the way back to his post — which, for Henry, was practically a speech.)*

scenes.synopsis: the picnic, remembered — the day painted; the story, told. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(In the afternoon, with the company gone to the gardens, Rose stood before the portrait in the empty chosen place and let the day come back.)*
> *(The blanket on the Park's slope, the lake below. The cook's hamper, unpacked with ceremony: the cold chicken, the veal pie, the gooseberry fool, the bread still warm from the ovens. The wasps, arriving like uninvited guests, and Letitia declaring war on them with a napkin, and winning. Laurent's story — the one about the Paris tailor and the runaway poodle — and the laugh, the one that had escaped her before she could catch it, her head thrown back, the joy unguarded.)*
> *(Octavia had been sketching all afternoon, quiet at the blanket's edge, the charcoal moving, and nobody had paid her much mind. That was Octavia's gift: to be unnoticed while seeing everything. The sketches had become the studies, the studies had become the portrait, and the portrait was now hung, witnessed, and true — and Rose, who had been too busy laughing to notice the sketching, was in it forever, twenty-five and joyful.)*
> *(She stood before the painted day and remembered the real one: the grass warm under the blanket, the gooseberry fool sweet on the tongue, the wasps persistent, Letitia's napkin warfare, the poodle story, and the laugh Octavia had chased for months and caught in a single afternoon. The day had been perfect in the way perfect days are: unplanned, unrepeatable — and, it turned out, paintable.)*
> *(That was the joke of the portrait, she thought, touching the frame lightly: the painter had worked for months to catch what the afternoon had given away free. The day had done the living; the paint would do the keeping. Neither owed the other an apology.)*
> *(The afternoon light moved over the varnish, and the picnic shone — the grass, the hamper, the laugh — and the chosen place was quiet, and Rose stood alone with the painted day and was, for a minute, completely happy, which was the one thing the portrait had been trying to tell her all along. She stayed until the light changed, and then she went to find the company in the gardens, carrying the painted day with her like a warmth.)*

scenes.synopsis: the two houses — the arrangement, witnessed; the shared life, painted. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The company had gone to the gardens, and the chosen place was quiet, and Rose and Octavia stood before the portrait in the afternoon light with the odd privacy of two people left alone with a thing they had made.)*
> *(Octavia pointed with a clean finger — the paint washed off, the nail still rimmed faintly green — at the two houses on the hill.)*
> "There," she said. "Yours. And there, mine. The distance is exact. I measured it."
> "You measured the distance between our houses?"
> "Three hundred and twelve yards. For the painting." *(The precise voice, warm.)* "The arrangement, surveyed."
> *(Rose laughed, and the painted laugh laughed with her, the two of them caught in the same hour of the afternoon.)*
> "Three hundred and twelve yards of shared life," Rose said. "I will have Harrow check your arithmetic."
> "Harrow will find it correct. Harrow always finds me correct. It is our only quarrel."
> *(Rose did the ledger-mind's arithmetic: seven minutes at a walk, four if she hurried, which she never did. On clear days the studio's chimney was visible from the Park's west terrace, and Octavia a speck at the studio door, waving or not waving, depending on the painting.)*
> "Seven minutes," Rose said. "That is the arrangement, measured in shoes."
> "Seven minutes," Octavia agreed. "And the coal on your account, and the gardeners mowing both lawns on the same round, and my maid borrowing your laundress on Tuesdays."
> "The cheapest arrangement in England. Two houses for the price of one and a half."
> "Romance," Octavia said, "is wasted on you."
> "Romance is your department. Mine is the coal bill."
> *(Octavia leaned her shoulder against Rose's, briefly, the painter's version of an embrace.)* "My half," she said, looking at the paint. "Delivered. In the Park. Forever."
> "Your half, received." *(Rose looked at the two houses, the exact yards, the shared life.)* "Three hundred and twelve yards. I like the number. It sounds like a promise with the paperwork done."
> *(The afternoon light moved over the canvas, and the two houses stood on their hill in paint, separate roofs, one landscape, and the distance between them — measured, exact — held the shared life the way a frame holds a picture: not by touching it, but by being exactly where it should be.)*

scenes.synopsis: the painter's speech — Octavia, the precise, the public; the triumph, spoken. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia stood before the company in the chosen place, the portrait behind her, her hands steady, and spoke — briefly, precisely, and in the wrong order, the way she did everything that mattered.)*
> "The picnic." The precise voice, carrying. "The day —" She stopped, and smiled, crooked. "The laughing woman." A breath. "Two houses. One shared life." She looked at Rose, and the precise voice did something unprecise: it warmed. "I painted the truest thing I know. The happy." A gesture at the canvas. "The arrangement, witnessed. In the Park." A breath. "Forever."
> *(She stopped. The speech was over — short, halting, perfect — and the company applauded, and Octavia stood in the applause the way she stood before a canvas: seeing it, storing it, the painter's eyes bright.)*
> *(It was the most words Rose had ever heard Octavia speak at once, and the fewest she had ever needed. The painter had said the whole of it in six breaths, and the afternoon held them. The speech had been rehearsed — Octavia had paced the chosen place at dawn, muttering to the dust sheets — and the rehearsal had not survived first contact with the company, which was why it had been perfect. The precise voice, unprecise with feeling, had said more in its stumbles than fluency could have managed.)*
> *(The marquise nodded, slowly. The vicar beamed. The young officer clapped loudest, his hands red. Henry, at the company's edge, applauded with his hands held low, the soldier's applause, and Rose saw him blink once, hard, the way he did when the devotion got the better of him. Even Harrow, by the door with his list, had stopped writing to listen — and Harrow never stopped writing. And Letitia wept, openly, and offered the biscuit tin around as if grief and biscuits were related — which, for Letitia, they were — and the company took the biscuits, moved, and the applause went on.)*
> *(Rose went to Octavia and embraced her, hard, and the company applauded harder, and the laugh in paint shone on behind them.)* "You were magnificent," Rose said into her shoulder.
> "Don't," Octavia said. "I shall cry, and the precise voice does not cry in public." *(She cried, a little, and the company loved her for it, and the afternoon held the moment.)*

scenes.synopsis: the toasts — the portrait, honored; the company, the glasses. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The toasts began, and the chosen place turned golden.)*
> *(To the painter: Octavia, precise, triumphant, blushing to the ears. To the portrait: the picnic, the laugh, the truest thing. To the picnic: the day, forever. To the arrangement: two houses, one shared life, witnessed. The glasses rose, the company standing, the champagne properly cold.)*
> *(Somebody was still seeing to the champagne — refilling, rechilling, invisible — and Rose made a note, the ledger-mind automatic, to find out who and thank them properly, and then forgot the note in the toasting, which was as it should be. The triumph's day did not want ledgers. It wanted toasts.)*
> *(Augusta raised her glass, the spectacles catching the light.)* "To the truest thing," she said. "The line drinks to it."
> *(Letitia raised hers, the biscuit tin at last set down.)* "To the happy, hung! The first in the house!"
> *(Laurent raised his.)* "To the painter, who sees."
> *(Julian raised his, quiet at the company's edge.)* "To the terrace's view," he said, "kept in paint." *(Henry raised his.)* "To the light," he said, "by which it's seen." *(The company drank to both, and the toasts went on, and nobody was in a hurry, and the champagne stayed cold, and the afternoon deepened like a held note.)*
> *(The young officer proposed a toast to the wasps, who had made the picnic memorable, and the company roared, and Letitia brandished her napkin in salute, and even Augusta's mouth twitched — which those nearest her would talk about for weeks.)*
> *(They drank, and the laugh in paint drank with them in its way — permanent, shining, unspillable — and the afternoon went gold around the edges, and Rose thought that this was what the day had been for all along: not the hanging, not the speeches, but this, the glasses raised, the people she loved standing in a lit room, drinking to the truth. It was the first completely happy hour she could remember in the chosen place — no strategy, no sting, no ledger — and she intended to remember it exactly this way: gold, and loud, and true.)*

scenes.synopsis: Lavinia, on the portrait — brilliance, the unveiling's; the glittering, the true. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Lavinia arrived late, glittering, apologetic, radiant — and went straight to the painting, and stood before it, and was quiet, which for Lavinia was the equivalent of a scream.)*
> "Darling!" The glitter turned on Rose, bright as ever. "The portrait! The picnic! The —" She stopped, studying the laugh in paint, and the glitter fell away, just for a heartbeat, and the real voice came through, quiet. "The laugh, darling. It's the truest thing, Rose." The glitter returned. "Two houses, one shared life. The arrangement is the bravest thing, darling. Painted." She took Rose's hands. "I am so proud I could spit."
> "You are late, Lavinia," Rose said.
> "I am never late, darling. I am dramatic." The glittering smile. "The portrait is magnificent. Octavia is magnificent. You are magnificent. I am —" she struck a pose — "also here."
> *(The company laughed, and Lavinia basked, and Rose held her hands — the glittering, the loyal — and saw the heartbeat's real beneath the brilliance, and loved her for it. The glitter was Lavinia's armor and her gift; the real underneath was the loyal friend of ten seasons, who had arrived late and dramatic and exactly on time.)*
> *(She swept off to charm the émigré, glittering, and the laugh in paint shone after her. From across the room Rose could hear her already: "The arrangement, darling, is the bravest thing —" holding the émigré ladies spellbound, the glitter doing its work, the truth smuggled inside it like a letter in a bouquet.)*
> *(She had been the same at every crisis of the ten seasons, Rose reflected: arriving late, glittering, saying the true thing sideways so it didn't frighten anyone, and then working the room like a general. The ton called it brilliance. Rose, who had seen the heartbeat underneath, called it courage, and left it at that.)*
> *(Rose thought that brilliance, done kindly, was its own kind of devotion — and that Lavinia's, for all its noise, had never once been unkind. The glitter settled over the afternoon like sun on water, and the portrait held the laugh, and Rose held her friend's hands in memory — warm, bejeweled, loyal — and the unveiling went on, brighter for her being in it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the émigré, on the painter — Paris, the unveiling's; the old world, the new. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The émigré came to the portrait with the particular admiration of the exiled for the true — they knew about arrangements, having lived the distance, the exile's own arrangement — and Paris approved, in its way, which was all at once and in French.)*
> *(The marquise stood before the laugh in paint and nodded, slowly, the patting hand stilled at last. The vicomte with the scarred cheek studied the two houses on the hill and said something low to his wife, and she nodded. They understood two houses, one shared life. They had lived it across a Channel, in letters and visits and the long arithmetic of absence.)*
> *(A quiet woman in grey spoke to Octavia in rapid warm French, and Octavia answered in her careful schoolroom French, and the woman laughed, delighted, and kissed Octavia's cheeks, and Octavia glowed the particular glow of the precise praised in public — the glow of a woman who is usually the one doing the seeing.)*
> "What did she say?" Rose asked.
> "She said —" Octavia's precise voice, pleased — "she said the laugh is French. I told her the laugh is English." The precise smile. "We agreed the laugh is universal."
> *(The émigré ladies gathered, and the French flowed, and the painter stood in the middle of it, precise and pleased, and the marquise patted Octavia's hand — the patting universal, a benediction — and Rose thought that the afternoon had given Octavia what ten seasons never had: a room full of people who saw her seeing, and said so, in three languages.)*
> *(The quiet woman in grey stayed longest, standing before the laugh with her hands folded, and when she left she touched the frame the way one touches a church door. The exiled, Rose thought, knew a home when they saw one — even, especially, in paint. They had spent years learning the exact shape of what they missed, and here it was, hung on a wall: the day, the laugh, the shared life, kept.)*
> *(By evening the émigré had written the portrait into their letters already — Rose could see them composing over the desks, the laugh described in French, the arrangement approved — and she thought of the masquerade's letters to Paris, which had carried a choosing, and of these, which would carry a seeing. Paris would read them at breakfast and nod, slowly, like the marquise, and the old world would know: the laugh, universal, hung in the Park.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE PORTRAIT'S TITLE (what the portrait is called: the picnic, the two houses, or the laugh). The afternoon deepens; decide the naming. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The afternoon deepened, and the portrait asked its title. The company had seen, the toasts were drunk, the laugh shone in the chosen place, and the naming waited.)*
> *(The Picnic: the day, named. The blanket, the hamper, the wasps, the laugh — the painted day, forever. But days pass, and the portrait is forever, and the naming should be the forever's, not the day's.)*
> *(The Two Houses: the arrangement, named. Two houses, one shared life, the thesis in paint. But arrangements are private, and the portrait is the Park's, and the Park is everyone's, and the naming should hold the Park too.)*
> *(The Laugh: the truth, named. The truest thing, the happy, caught mid-flight. But truths are many, and the portrait is the one, and the naming should hold the one — the particular laugh, the particular day.)*
> *(Octavia stood by the portrait with the plaque blank in her hands, waiting. The plaque was brass, small, the size of a calling card. It would hang beneath the portrait for as long as the house stood, and longer than anyone in the room. Titles outlive their namers; that was the whole of the weight, and the whole of the honor.)*
> *(The lettering would come — the brass, the permanent — and the title would shape the portrait's memory, and the memory would shape the years. The company watched, quiet. Each name was true. Each name was incomplete. That was the difficulty with names: they were like frames, they held the thing and cut off the world.)*
> *(Rose stood before the portrait — the day, the houses, the laugh — and weighed the names the way she had weighed the masks at noon: for beauty, for courage, for truth. The picnic would date it. The two houses would claim it. The laugh would free it. She thought of the wasps, the gooseberry fool, the head thrown back — and of the line, the Park, the shared life — and the names turned in her mind like cards dealt face down.)*
> *(The naming was hers, as the portrait was Octavia's, as the day had been everyone's. The afternoon held its breath, the way afternoons do when something permanent is about to happen.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The portrait's title:*
- **The Picnic** — *the day, named.* The portrait is called the picnic — the painted day. (Consequence: the naming is the day's — but days pass, and the portrait is forever.)
- **The Two Houses** — *the arrangement, named.* The portrait is called the two houses — the shared life. (Consequence: the naming is the arrangement's — but arrangements are private, and the portrait is the Park's.)
- **The Laugh** — *the truth, named.* The portrait is called the laugh — the truest thing. (Consequence: the naming is the truth's — but truths are many, and the portrait is the one.)
> *(She drew breath, and named it — quietly, for the plaque, for the years — and Octavia took up her tools, and the afternoon held still.)*

scenes.synopsis: the title, lettered — the plaque; the naming, permanent. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(They lettered the plaque in the afternoon light, and the whole company watched a painter write. Octavia sat on a stool the footmen had brought, the small brush in her hand, and worked the way she worked a canvas: precisely, without hurry, the tip of her tongue just showing at the corner of her mouth, which Rose had never seen her do and filed away.)*
> *(The plaque was brass, no larger than a lady's hand, and it would sit beneath the portrait in the chosen place, and it would outlast them all. That was the point of brass. Octavia's hand did not tremble. The letters came up one by one, black on gold, each one perfect before the next was begun.)*
> "Do not breathe on it," Octavia said, without looking up.
> "I am not breathing," Letitia said, breathing on it.
> *(A ripple went through the company, and Octavia finished the word, and sat back, and examined it the way she examined paint, head tilted.)*
> "There," she said. "Named."
> "Named," Rose agreed.
> *(Harrow stepped forward with his book, and wrote the title in it, and the date, and the wall. The house's record. The plaque would be permanent; the book would be the proof. Rose watched him write, and felt the ledger-mind's satisfaction: the day's last entry, the account closed, the triumph filed.)*
> *(The company came forward in ones and twos to read it. The marquise patted the air. The vicar bent close and nodded. The young officer read it aloud, slowly, as if the words were heavier than they looked, and then laughed, and the painted laugh laughed with him.)*
> "It will dry by evening," Octavia said, standing, and the footmen took the stool away, and the plaque stayed, the letters wet and black on the brass.
> "And no one is to touch it," Rose said.
> "No one is to touch it," Octavia agreed, and looked at Letitia.
> "I never touch anything," Letitia said.
> *(The afternoon moved toward evening, and the titled portrait shone, and the plaque shone beneath it, the name lettered in the painter's hand. The other two titles went unlettered, unmourned. A portrait could only be called one thing, the way a day could only be lived once, and both were done.)*
> *(She read the plaque once more, the black letters on the brass, the name exact. It would be read by people not yet born, in a light not yet fallen. That was the brass's promise, and the afternoon held it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the gardeners, on the hanging — the Park, the portrait's; the keepers, the witnessed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(They came in the afternoon, the keepers, to see the hung: the head gardener and two younger men, caps in their hands, their boots clean for indoors and their faces set in the solemnity of men visiting a church.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The head gardener touched his hat — the gesture of a man addressing something larger than the room. "The portrait. Hung."
> "You hung it," Rose said. "I saw the ladder marks."
> *(The younger men shifted, and one of them — the tall one with the smudged thumb — looked at the corner of the frame, where his thumb had been, and where his sleeve had wiped it clean, and said nothing.)*
> "The level," the head gardener said. "Borrowed. Returned." A pause. "Straight."
> "It is straight," Rose agreed. "The painter measured it herself. Twice."
> *(They stood before the laugh in paint, the three of them, caps in hands, and looked at it the way men look at a thing they have lifted with their own hands: with ownership. Their hands had been on the frame. Their ladder had leaned against the wall. The garden was proud, and the pride had come indoors with them.)*
> "The garden's proud, miss," the head gardener said at last, and it was the longest sentence he had spoken all season.
> "The garden did its part," Rose said. "The slope, the lake, the light. She painted what you keep."
> "We keep it, miss." He touched his hat again. "The Park. And now —" a glance at the portrait — "the portrait."
> *(Rose thought of the Park they kept — the beds, the borders, the lawns mowed on the round — and of the laugh they had lifted onto its wall, and of how the keeping had widened by one portrait without anyone signing a paper. That was how the Park grew: by the keepers' hands, one hung thing at a time.)*
> "Thank you," she said. "All three of you. The company saw it at eleven, but you saw it first."
> *(The tall one with the smudged thumb colored to his ears. The head gardener nodded once, the matter settled, and they put their caps back on, and went out to the afternoon's work, the beds, the borders, the triumph's ground.)*
> *(Rose watched them go across the terrace, caps on, the tall one's stride a fraction prouder than it had been. The Park was the portrait's frame, and the keepers had fitted the picture into it, and the afternoon glowed, and the beds waited, and the laugh hung straight on its wall.)*

scenes.synopsis: the keeper, on the portrait — Mrs. Quick, the unveiling's; the immovable, the true. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(She came in the late afternoon, when the company had thinned, and stood before the laugh in paint with her hands folded and her keys quiet at her waist, and was — for Mrs. Quick — voluble.)*
> "The portrait, miss." The immovable voice, nearly warm. "Hung." A pause, the housekeeper's pause, shorter than the Dowager's but nearly as final. "The laugh." Another pause. "The truest thing."
> *(Rose stared. Mrs. Quick's mouth — the extraordinary mouth, the immovable — had done something extraordinary: it had softened at the corners, like wax near a flame.)*
> "The house," Mrs. Quick said, "has never looked happier, miss."
> "Thank you, Mrs. Quick," Rose said, and meant it, and did not know what else to say to a miracle.
> "The veil was straight," Mrs. Quick said. "I supervised."
> "The veil was straight. Perfectly."
> *(Mrs. Quick nodded, once, the matter closed, and her hands stayed folded, and she did not touch anything, and Rose understood that this was the housekeeper's whole economy: to feel everything and adjust nothing, and to let the feeling show exactly once, at the hour of her choosing.)*
> "Ten seasons, miss," Mrs. Quick said. "The veils. The hangings." She looked at the laugh in paint. "This one —" she stopped — "this one was worth the straightening."
> *(It was the longest speech Rose had ever heard her make, and the warmest, and she stored it the way Octavia stored light: completely, and without comment, because comment would have ended it.)*
> "The evening's rounds, Mrs. Quick," Rose said.
> "The rounds, miss." *(The keys stirred at her waist, the immovable restored, the warmth folded away like a cloth into a drawer.)* "The house is settled."
> *(She withdrew, upright, unhurried, and the chosen place was quiet, and the laugh in paint shone on, and Rose stood before it and smiled, and thought that the day's greatest triumph had not been the unveiling at eleven but the housekeeper at five, moved by a laugh in paint, and saying so, once, before the rounds.)*
> *(The late afternoon light moved over the canvas. Mrs. Quick's footsteps faded down the corridor, the keys quiet, the rounds begun. The portrait held its laugh, and the house held its happiness, and the immovable had said her piece, and gone.)*

scenes.synopsis: the cook, on the painting — the picnic's, the painted; the kitchen, the witnessed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She came in the evening, serene, the kitchen's own, to see the day she had fed, hung. The cook stood before the portrait in her clean apron, her hands folded over it, and studied the painted picnic the way a general studies ground.)*
> "The picnic, miss." The cook was serene. "Painted."
> "You cooked it," Rose said.
> "I cooked it, miss. The cold chicken. The veal pie." She leaned a fraction closer. "The gooseberry fool." A pause, the serene's pause. "There." She pointed — not touching — at the painted hamper. "The veal pie, miss. In the paint. Forever."
> *(Rose looked, and there it was: the veal pie, golden, in the corner of the picnic, rendered in oil, immortal. The cook's crust, the cook's doing, hung on the Park's wall. Rose had never considered that a pie could be a legacy, and the cook had considered nothing else.)*
> "It looks exactly like your veal pie," Rose said.
> "It is my veal pie, miss. The painter ate two slices before she painted it. For accuracy."
> *(Rose laughed, and the painted laugh laughed, and the cook's serene smile said that accuracy had been worth the two slices.)*
> "You said it first," Rose said. "At the picnic. The first portrait in the house that looks happy."
> "I said it, miss." The cook nodded. "And I was right." She looked at the laughing woman in the paint. "You look happy, miss. In the paint. It is a good likeness. The painter got the laugh right, and I got the pie right, and between us —" the serene, complete — "between us, miss, the day is kept."
> *(Rose thought of the hamper, unpacked with ceremony on the Park's slope, the food that had fed the day the portrait painted. The kitchen's wisdom had seen it first: that a happy day, cooked well, could be painted, and that the painting would keep the cooking.)*
> "Tomorrow's menu," Rose said. "Have you planned it?"
> "The menu is planned, miss. The kitchen does not rest on its laurels." The cook looked once more at the immortal veal pie. "Though the laurels," she said, "are nice."
> *(She went back to the kitchen, serene, and Rose stood before the portrait, and was — in the paint, and out of it — happy. The evening came on, and the chosen place glowed, and somewhere below, the kitchen planned tomorrow, and the veal pie shone in the paint, golden, forever, accurate.)*

scenes.synopsis: the steward, on the arrangement — Harrow, the unveiling's; the honest, the painted. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(He came in the evening, the dry voice, the books, and stood before the laugh in paint with his hands behind his back and his head tilted at the precise angle of a man checking a sum.)*
> "The arrangement, Miss Hartwell." The dry voice, the honest. "Two houses. One shared life." A pause. "The honest account."
> "The honest account," Rose agreed.
> *(He looked at the portrait a moment longer, and Rose looked at him, and thought of all the ledgers of ten seasons: the debts, the payments, the reckonings, the columns of figures that had been the house's true biography. This was the first ledger that had been painted instead of written, and it balanced.)*
> "The truest ledger," Harrow said. "Painted."
> "Harrow," Rose said, "that is exactly right."
> "I am occasionally right, miss." The dry smile, there and gone. "The hanging is complete. The plaque is lettered." He consulted nothing; he knew. "The company is satisfied. The veil —" a glance — "was straight. Mrs. Quick supervised."
> "Mrs. Quick supervised everything today, Harrow. Including, I suspect, you."
> "Mrs. Quick," Harrow said, "supervises the supervision. It is her genius." He looked back at the laugh in paint. "The debits and credits of happiness, miss, and the account is honest. Two houses. One shared life. The painter has done the arithmetic, and it —" the dryest pause — "it comes out even."
> *(Rose felt the ledger-mind's kinship, the two of them before the painted account, and understood that Harrow loved the portrait the way he loved a balanced book: not for the beauty of it, though the beauty was there, but for the honesty. Nothing hidden. Nothing carried forward. The day, stated truly.)*
> "The books are balanced, Harrow?"
> "The books are balanced, miss." He bowed, the steward's bow, and withdrew, and the evening deepened around the portrait, and the painted ledger shone in the chosen place, and the account was honest, and the Park held it.
> *(She stood a while longer before the truest ledger, the laugh in paint, the honest account. The evening light moved over the canvas, and the numbers held: two houses, one shared life, the painter's arithmetic, even. The books were balanced, and the day was filed, and the steward had said his piece, dryly, and gone.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Park, the unveiling's afternoon — the whole, the hung; the triumph's ground. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(At five she walked the Park alone, the unveiling's afternoon going gold around her, and took the slope where the picnic had been — the real slope, not the painted one. The blanket was gone. The hamper was gone. The grass had risen again where they had sat, the way grass does, indifferent to history.)*
> *(She sat down where the blanket had been. The grass was cool through her skirts. Below, the lake lay flat, catching the light; above, the house stood on its hill, the chosen place's windows catching it too. Between them, the two houses on the hill, exactly where Octavia had put them — three hundred and twelve yards apart, the painter's eye true even in the distance.)*
> *(The light was going from gold to amber. A blackbird sang in the lime walk, insistent, as if the day needed a second announcing. The gardeners were finishing the beds, their figures small and bent. Somewhere a door closed. The Park had the particular stillness of late afternoon: the work nearly done, the evening not yet begun.)*
> *(She thought of the picnic itself: the wasps, Letitia's napkin, Laurent's poodle story, the laugh that had escaped her before she could catch it. Octavia had chased it for months. Rose had not chased it at all. It had simply happened, on a slope, at luncheon, unguarded. That was the joke of the portrait: the painter had worked for months to catch what the afternoon had given away free.)*
> *(The painted picnic would last. The real one was already gone — the grass risen, the crumbs taken by the birds, the gooseberry fool a memory. That was the arrangement between days and paintings: the day did the living, the paint did the keeping, and neither apologized to the other.)*
> *(A hare ran the slope's edge, startled by nothing, gone into the long grass. The amber deepened on the lake. Rose thought of the morning's terror — the veil straightened five times — and of the afternoon's gold, and of how the day had asked everything and given more. The slope had held the picnic; the wall would hold the paint; the Park would hold them both, the way it held everything, without comment.)*
> *(She stood, brushed the grass from her skirts, and walked home through the gold, the terrace stones warm under her feet. The slope stayed behind her, empty, the grass cool — the day's real picnic gone, the painted one forever — and the light went amber on the lake, and the Park held it.)*

scenes.synopsis: Octavia, after — the painter, the triumph's; the precise, at rest. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She found Octavia in the evening before the hung portrait, quiet, the paint-stained hands folded in her lap, the bright eyes on the laugh in paint. The company had gone to dress for dinner. The chosen place was hers again, the painter's, the way it had been at five in the morning with the veil.)*
> "It's done," Octavia said, without turning. "The picnic. The —" she stopped — "the truest thing."
> *(Rose sat beside her on the bench the footmen had left. The evening light was soft on the canvas. The laugh shone, unguarded, permanent.)*
> "Your hands are empty," Rose said.
> "They are." Octavia looked at them, the paint under the nails, the charcoal gone. "I do not know what to do with them. All day they have had the brush, the level, the veil. Now —" she opened them, closed them — "nothing. It is the strangest part of a triumph. The finishing."
> "You could rest them."
> "I am resting them. It is terrible." *(The precise smile, crooked.)* "I chased it for months, Rose. The laugh. It would not sit still." A pause. "Nothing true sits still. That is the whole of painting. The chasing."
> "You caught it."
> "I caught it." The painter's eyes, bright, on the paint. "It is there. Forever."
> *(They sat a while, the painter and the subject, and the evening moved over the portrait, and Rose thought of the studio lamp at five, the veil straightened five times, the terror of the morning, and of this: the painter at rest, the hands empty, the triumph complete. The price had been paid in full, and the purchase was hanging on the wall.)*
> "Two houses," Octavia said quietly. "One shared life." The precise voice, the quiet. "My half, Rose. Forever. In the Park."
> "Your half, delivered." *(Rose put her arm around Octavia's shoulders, and the painter leaned into it, briefly, and then straightened, and they sat before the laugh in paint, and the day closed, golden.)*
> *(The chasing was over. The catching was forever. The evening held them, and the portrait held its laugh, and the painter's hands — empty, paint-stained, at rest — lay folded in her lap, and did not reach for anything.)*

scenes.synopsis: Rose, after — the subject, the seen; the woman, the painted's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Later, alone, she stood before the hung portrait in the evening light, the subject regarding herself, and did the strange arithmetic of being seen: the living woman, the painted woman, the two of them meeting across the varnish.)*
> *(She looked at the laughing woman the way one looks at a stranger in a glass: first the surprise, then the acceptance. The surprise was the laugh's — the head thrown back, the mouth open, the joy unguarded. The acceptance was the woman's. Yes, she thought. That is me. I had not known.)*
> *(The cook was right. The first portrait in the house that looked happy, and the happiness was true, and it was hers. The ancestors were solemn on the gallery walls, two hundred years of oil-paint gravity, the Hartwells unsmiling. This one laughed. It laughed in the chosen place, in the evening light, permanently, and the solemnity had not stopped it.)*
> *(She thought of the S1 portrait, the frightened girl, the terror and the glitter, the whole Season ahead of her like a road she could not see the end of. The girl had been presented to the ton. The woman had been painted by a friend. Ten seasons lay between them, and she had walked every yard.)*
> *(The evening light moved over the paint. She was happy, in the paint — happy in a way the S1 girl had not dared to be, happy in a way the seasons between had taught her to be, carefully, and then all at once, on a slope, at luncheon, unguarded. The frightened girl had become the laughing woman, and the paint held the becoming, and the becoming was true.)*
> *(She stood a while, and then she went to dress for dinner, and the portrait stayed, and the Park held it. The day had been the triumph's, and the evening was hers, and the laugh was forever, and the woman — the painted and the living, the surprised and the accepting — went up the stairs in the day's dress, which she would change, eventually, when the evening required it.)*
> *(Behind her the chosen place was quiet, and the laugh shone in the evening light, and the woman in the paint laughed on, twenty-five, joyful, unguarded, and the woman on the stairs smiled, once, to herself, and went to dress.)*

scenes.synopsis: the portrait, in the evening light — the hung, the lit; the chosen place, the glow. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She saw it at dusk from the doorway, unobserved, and understood that Octavia had planned for this: the hanging's height, the wall's angle, the light's fall. The painter's precision, serving the triumph long after the brush was down.)*
> *(The evening light came through the windows low and gold, and the portrait caught it, and the laugh in paint shone. The picnic, the two houses, the shared life: glowing, in the chosen place. The varnish gave back the day, and the room glowed, and Rose stood in the doorway and watched the light do the painter's last work.)*
> *(She had hung it for the morning, for the unveiling's eleven o'clock sun. But she had placed it for this: the dusk's low gold, the laugh lit from the side, the two houses on the hill catching the last of it. The chosen place had been chosen twice — once for the company, once for the light — and the light was the truer choosing.)*
> *(The gold deepened. The painted lake caught it first, then the painted grass, then the laughing woman's face, last and brightest, as if the day were ending inside the picture in the proper order. Rose watched the light move over the paint the way she had watched it move over the real Park an hour before, and the two movings were the same, and different, and both true.)*
> *(Octavia had said, that morning, that the laugh needed the light, and that the laugh was the whole of it. She had been right about the morning. She had been righter about this. The dusk's gold found the painted laugh and held it, and the portrait did not just hang in the evening light. It received it, the way a face receives a compliment: fully, and without surprise.)*
> *(The light faded, gold to rose to grey, the way light does, unhurried. The portrait held its shine a little longer than the room, the varnish giving back the day after the day had gone. Then it too went quiet, and the chosen place was dark, and the portrait slept, hung, and the dusk was over, and the painter's planning was complete.)*
> *(Rose stood in the dark doorway a moment longer. The day's last light had been the portrait's own, and the painter had hung the triumph where the dusk could find it, knowing the dusk would come. That was the precision, she thought, and it held. She went in to dinner, and the chosen place was dark behind her, and the laugh slept in the paint, waiting for the lamp.)*

scenes.synopsis: the laugh, in paint — the truest thing, permanent; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She had a lamp brought, late, and studied the laugh by lamplight, close, the way Octavia had studied it with the brush.)*
> *(The lamplight moved over the varnish, and the laugh shone back, warm and near. By lamplight the paint showed its work: the brushstrokes in the grass, the layered gold in the sky, the quick sure strokes of the laughing mouth — laid down last, Octavia had said, because the laugh had to be the freshest thing on the canvas.)*
> *(She thought of the ancestors in the gallery, the solemn, the unsmiling, their forever the stern and the posed. They had had lamplight too, in their day — the candles, the oil — and their paint had held the gravity. This forever was different. This forever laughed, and the lamplight found the laugh, and the room was warm with it.)*
> *(The laughing woman would be twenty-five forever, joyful forever, the Park behind her forever, the two houses on the hill forever. The paint would not age. The varnish would yellow, in time — Octavia had said so, honestly, the way painters do — and the yellowing would be the years, and the laugh would shine through the years. That was the arrangement, and it was a good one.)*
> *(She thought of the morning's terror — the veil straightened five times, the painter's hands trembling — and of this: the laugh, permanent, shining. The terror had been the price. The lamp was the receipt.)*
> *(She set the lamp on the table beside the portrait and stepped back, and the laugh shone in the lamplight, and the chosen place was quiet. The ancestors looked down from the gallery with their stern forever, and Rose looked up at them — the laughing woman, twenty-five — and did not look away. Let them stare. The house had room for both kinds of forever.)*
> *(She touched the frame lightly with one gloved finger — a benediction, or a promise — and took up the lamp, and left the chosen place. Behind her the laugh stayed, shining in the dark after the lamplight, the way true things stay after the light that found them. The night could come. The laugh would be there in the morning.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE PORTRAIT'S MEANING (what the portrait means: the arrangement, the laugh, or the Park). The evening deepens; decide the meaning. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The evening deepened, and the portrait asked its meaning. The company gone, the lamplight lit, the laugh in paint shining, and the meaning waited.)*
> *(The arrangement: the shared, honored. Two houses, one shared life, the bravest thing, witnessed, hung. But the shared is private, and the portrait is the Park's, and the meaning should hold the Park too — the whole, the home.)*
> *(The laugh: the true, kept. The joy unguarded, the head thrown back, the mouth open, the eyes bright — permanent. But truths are many, and the portrait is the one, and the meaning should hold the one: the particular laugh, on the particular day.)*
> *(The Park: the whole, hung. The grounds, the light, the frame and the heart, the triumph's ground. But the whole is vast, and the portrait is a day, and the meaning should hold the day — the slope, the hamper, the wasps, the gold.)*
> *(She stood before it in the lamplight — the subject, the seen — and the portrait asked, and the evening waited. Each meaning was true. Each was incomplete. The meaning would shape the portrait's forever, and the forever would shape the years, the way the title had shaped the plaque that afternoon.)*
> *(The lamplight moved over the paint. The laugh shone, patient as ever. She thought of Julian before it that morning, and Henry at the company's edge, and Bell's sharp eyes, and the quiet woman in grey touching the frame like a church door — and understood the portrait had been collecting meanings all day, the way the lake collects light. Hers would be one more. That was the way of hung things: they belonged to everyone who stood before them. She had named the title that afternoon, for the plaque, for the years. The meaning was the quieter naming — the one the plaque wouldn't carry, the one the room would keep. Titles were for the house. Meanings were for the woman who had laughed.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The portrait's meaning:*
- **The arrangement** — *the shared, honored.* The portrait means the arrangement — two houses, one shared life. (Consequence: the meaning is the shared — but shareds are private, and the portrait is the Park's.)
- **The laugh** — *the true, kept.* The portrait means the laugh — the truest thing, the happy. (Consequence: the meaning is the true — but trues are many, and the portrait is the one.)
- **The Park** — *the whole, hung.* The portrait means the Park — the whole, the hung, the ground. (Consequence: the meaning is the whole — but wholes are vast, and the portrait is the day.)
> *(She named it silently, to the empty room — the way one names a ship, for luck — and the naming was a settling, and the laugh shone on, whatever the room had heard.)*

scenes.synopsis: the night — the portrait, the chosen place's; the hung, the dark. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She left it at last and closed the door softly, and the portrait slept in the chosen place, unseen — and the laugh was there anyway.)*
> *(That was the thought she carried up the stairs: that the laugh continued in the dark, unobserved, the way the Park continued in the dark, the way the lake lay flat whether or not anyone stood at its edge. The paint did not need the seeing. The linen and the oil were there, holding the picnic, the two houses, the shared life, whether the room was lit or not.)*
> *(The house settled around her with the night's sounds: the fires ticking down, the beams settling, a door closing somewhere below, Mrs. Quick's keys quiet on the rounds. She had spent the day watching the portrait in every light — the morning's gold, the afternoon's white, the dusk's amber, the lamp's warm near — and now there was no light, and the portrait held. That was the permanence: the staying, when the shine was gone.)*
> *(On the landing she met Mrs. Quick, finishing the rounds, the keys quiet at her waist. They inclined their heads to each other — the mistress and the keeper — and neither spoke, because the day had said everything. The housekeeper's eyes, usually immovable, were nearly warm. The portrait had done that. The laugh, hung, had thawed even Mrs. Quick.)*
> *(The morning would come, and the light with it, and the laugh would be there in the paint — twenty-five, joyful, unguarded. It would not have moved in the night. It would not have faded. The varnish would hold, the brass plaque would hold, the wall would hold.)*
> *(She went up to bed, and the house settled, and the chosen place was dark behind its closed door, and the portrait slept, hung, and the laugh was there in the dark — present the way true things are present in the dark: completely, and without needing to be seen.)*
> *(The door was closed. The night was the portrait's. The morning would come, and the laugh would be there — and so, she thought, climbing the stairs with the day's tiredness in her bones, would she.)*

scenes.synopsis: the letters — the portrait, reported; London writes. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(In the evening the company wrote, and the chosen place's desks were full, and the quills scratched, and London would read in the morning what the Park had seen at eleven.)*
> *(The marquise wrote in French, rapid, the patting hand at last employed with a quill, page after page. The vicar wrote to his sister — the unveiling described, the laugh praised, the light noted — in a clergyman's careful hand. The young officer wrote to his mother, and blotted a page, and began again, and the second attempt was the truer for the blotting.)*
> *(The ton wrote, the curious and the kind, who had watched for ten seasons and wanted the watching set down. The émigré ladies wrote, the French flowing, the arrangement approved in three languages. The desks were full, the lamplight warm, the sand shakers busy, the sealing wax heating — and the portrait shone in the chosen place while the letters piled.)*
> *(Rose walked among the desks, unobserved, and read over no one's shoulder — the letters were the writers', not hers — but she saw the marquise's rapid pages, and the vicar's careful ones, and the young officer's blotted one, and thought of the masquerade's letters to Paris, which had carried a choosing. These would carry a seeing. The laugh, reported. The truest thing, in writing.)*
> *(She thought of all the letters that had left this house in ten seasons — invitations, warnings, lies in fair hands, the Network's paper, Rackham's paper — and of how this evening's bag differed from every one of them: it carried nothing but the truth, and the truth, for once, was good news, and the news was a laugh.)*
> *(Harrow came through with the evening's bag and collected the letters, weighing it in his hand.)* "London, miss. The portrait —" a glance at the bulging bag — "reported."
> "In writing, Harrow."
> "In writing, miss." The dry smile. "The witnessing is carried."
> *(He tucked the bag under his arm and went out to the post, and the quills kept scratching behind him — the last letters, the late thoughts, the postscripts. Rose went up to bed past the empty desks, the lamplight out, the letters on their way. The portrait had been seen, and the seeing had been written, and the writing would be read, and London would know by morning what the Park had known at eleven.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell, attending — the Gazette, the unveiling's; the reporting, the dry. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Mrs. Nance Bell came in the evening, unannounced, and stood before the laugh in paint with her hands behind her back, and said nothing for a full minute — which, from Bell, was a speech.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The voice soft, the eyes sharp on the paint. "The finished picnic. The laugh."
> *(Rose looked at her — the proprietor, the independent, soft-voiced, sharp-eyed — and thought of ten seasons of stings: the debts, the ballrooms, the reckonings, all of it archived in Bell's dry voice, all of it true, or true enough to print. The Gazette had reported everything. Now it stood before the laugh.)*
> "You will write it true, Mrs. Bell," Rose said.
> "I write what I see, Miss Hartwell." Bell's eyes moved over the canvas — the picnic, the two houses, the shared life. "I see the laugh. I see the two houses." A beat. "I see the first happy portrait in this house. The Gazette sees it too."
> "You came all this way to look at a painting."
> "I came all this way to look at the truth, Miss Hartwell. The painting is where it happened to be hung." The sharp eyes warmed, just for a moment, the way lamplight warms a room. "Ten seasons, Miss Hartwell. I have written the debts and the dances and the disasters. I have not often written the happy." A pause. "It is harder. The unhappy writes itself."
> *(Rose thought of the stings — the arch, the precise, the reward-only — and of the woman behind them, standing before a laugh in paint in the evening, doing the harder writing in her head. It struck her that Bell, who had made a living out of other people's worst hours, had ridden out in the evening for this: to stand in a quiet room and look at joy, and get it right.)*
> "Write it well, Mrs. Bell," Rose said quietly.
> "I write it true." Bell nodded once, the matter settled, and went to find a desk — and the laugh in paint shone on, witnessed at last by the sharpest eyes in London. Tomorrow the Gazette would print it — the laugh, the two houses, the happy — and London would read it over breakfast, and the truest thing in the house would be true in print, which was the only immortality Bell could offer, and it was enough.

scenes.synopsis: the household, on the triumph — the keepers, the unveiling's; the peace's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The household moved through the evening with the particular ease of people whose great work is done: the night's work, done well, by people who had done it before and would do it again.)*
> *(The footmen banked the fires in the hall, the coals settled, the guards on. The maids turned down the beds, the curtains drawn, the ewers filled. The cook planned tomorrow's menu at the kitchen table, serene — the veal pie immortal upstairs, the next day's dinner mortal below — and from the servants' hall came the low sound of the staff at their own supper, the day's triumph discussed in the servants' own tongue, which Rose did not speak and did not need to.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick made her rounds, the keys quiet at her waist, nearly warm still from the portrait, and found everything in order, or as near to order as evenings ever are. The immovable face, passing Rose on the stairs, inclined its head a fraction lower than protocol required. From Mrs. Quick, that was a speech.)*
> *(Rose walked the hall in the quiet. The chosen place was dark, the portrait sleeping. Nobody hurried. Nobody fussed. The day had asked everything of them — the hanging, the company, the veils, the straightening — and they had given it, and the giving was over, and the evening was theirs.)*
> *(She passed the morning room: the desks stood empty, the letters gone to London. She passed the hall: the fires banked, the coals glowing under the guards. The house settled around her like a dog turning in its sleep, content, and Rose thought that the household had its own unveiling that day — not the portrait, but the proof: that the place could do a great thing greatly, and then bank the fires, and sleep.)*
> *(It struck her, climbing the stairs, that the house had two triumphs that day: the one in the chosen place, witnessed and toasted, and this one — the banked fires, the turned beds, the quiet keys — witnessed by no one, and no less complete. She was not sure, all things weighed, which of the two she loved more.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, after the unveiling — Rose, the evening's; the mistress, the portrait's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her bedroom, the evening: she sat at the window in the day's dress — she should change, she did not change — and the Park darkened below, field by field, the lake going from silver to slate, and the chosen place held the laugh in paint, and the day was the woman's quiet.)*
> *(On the dressing table lay the program from the unveiling, printed that morning: the company's names in a column, the toasts listed beneath. She had kept it. She picked it up and read the names — Augusta, Letitia, Laurent, Julian, Henry, Lavinia, the marquise, the vicar, the young officer, the émigré, the neighbors — and folded it once, neatly, and put it in the desk box where she kept the season's papers.)*
> *(The ledger-mind, filing the day. The unveiling: eleven o'clock. The toasts: the painter, the portrait, the picnic, the arrangement. The plaque: lettered, brass, permanent. The day balanced, the way honest accounts balance: completely, and quietly. She ran a finger down the column of names, and each one brought its hour back: Augusta's toast, Letitia's napkin, Laurent's poodle story, Julian's quiet, Henry's post, Lavinia's glitter, the marquise's nod. The program was a poor thing, ink on paper — and it held the whole day, the way a pressed flower holds a summer.)*
> *(The dress would go to the maid in the morning to be brushed and put by, and the day would stay filed in the desk box, the program folded, the names in their column. Some days you lived; some days you filed. This one, she had done both, and the filing was the pleasure, not the duty.)*
> *(The finished unveiled, the hung, the meaning decided — whatever the room had heard. The day behind her, complete. The evening ahead, quiet. She sat at the window and watched the dark come on over the Park, and did not look away.)*
> *(She sat a while longer, watching the last light go, and then she rang for her maid, and the evening began. The program was filed, the dress was the day's, the laugh was permanent — and the woman changed her dress, and the night went on, ordinary and welcome, like bread after cake.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's unveiling report — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"Yesterday the finished picnic portrait was unveiled and hung in the Park at Hartwell, and the Gazette — having seen the laugh in paint — finds it the truest thing in the house. Two houses, one shared life: the arrangement, witnessed. The portrait stays."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (the laugh! in paint!), then the reckoning: the triumph is pronounced true in print as well as in the chosen place's light, and Bell has made the hung permanent, which is Bell's way of making it forever. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the portrait the Gazette calls true is the portrait that stays.* — remembered: *the lesson: the portrait the Gazette calls true is the portrait that stays.*
scenes.sting: Yesterday the finished picnic portrait was unveiled and hung in the Park at Hartwell, and the Gazette — having seen the laugh in paint — finds it the truest thing in the house. Two houses, one shared life: the arrangement, witnessed. The portrait stays.

scenes.synopsis: the small things, gathering — Henry's devotions, the next chapter; the quiet, coming. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and Henry comes — the small things, gathering — and the devotion's chapter is coming.)*
> "Rose." The soldier, the evening round. "The lanterns —" he checks them — "the urns —" another check — "the —" he stops, looking at the chosen place, the hung portrait. "The portrait —" the smallest smile — "the truest thing, Rose." He bows over her hand. "The small things —" he straightens — "continue. Every day." The unguarded look. "Tomorrow —" a breath — "tomorrow, the —" he stops — "the counting, Rose. The small things —" another breath — "counted."
> *(She watches him go — the straight back, the evening round — and the small things gather: the devotions, the daily, the quiet — coming.)*
> "The counting." She looks at the hung portrait — the laugh, the forever. "Tomorrow —" she stops — "tomorrow, the small things, counted."
> *(The chapter closes on the evening round — the lanterns, the urns, the straight back — and the Season turns toward the devotions: the small things, counted — and the Season holds its breath.)*
