scenes.synopsis: the letter, answered — Rose replies; the planning, begun. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library before breakfast, and the night post lying on the desk like a small white accuser. Rose sorts it the way Letitia taught her — the bills at the bottom, the interesting at the top — and the interesting is Lavinia's letter, which announces itself before she opens it: cream paper, handwriting slanted at a gallop, the seal pressed crooked because Lavinia never could wait for wax to cool.)*
> *(She reads it twice. The first time for the sense, the second time for Lavinia, who is in every line the way perfume is in a room. A final fête, the letter says. Her last. The Season's young are restless, she writes, and they want one last brilliance before the summer ends, and who better to give it them than she? The pen has underlined* brilliance *twice, and there is a blot where she changed her mind about the form and then changed it back.)*
> "Well," Rose says aloud, to no one, which is how she has conducted most of her important correspondence for ten seasons. She takes out her own paper — the Park's, plain, the watermark a small oak — and answers in the hand Quill once called "the only honest thing in Chancery." The reply is short. It says yes before it says anything else. It says the Park will open its doors and its cellars and its ballroom and whatever else a final brilliance requires. It says: come and plan it with me, and do not bring your modiste's nerves, only your ideas.
> "Lavinia's final," Letitia reads over her shoulder, and the hawk's eyes sharpen. "Darling, you have written* candles *in the glory column. Candles are cost."
> "For Lavinia's last, they are glory." Rose does not look up. "You taught me the difference. Glory is what the ton remembers. Cost is what the household book forgives."
> "The household book," Letitia says, sitting down with the air of a general opening a campaign, "forgives nothing. It merely waits." She uncaps her pen. "But for Lavinia —" the pen pauses — "for Lavinia, it will wait beautifully. Now. The musicians. How many, and how loud, and whether the young will dance until the candles gutter, because they will."
> *(The planning begins then, in the library, over chocolate going cold: the musicians, the flowers, the supper, the form of the thing still undecided and therefore still perfect. Outside, the Park does its morning work — the gardeners at the beds, the grooms at the yard — unaware that inside the house, at the library desk, the last brilliance of the Season is being built, one column at a time.)*

scenes.synopsis: Lavinia arrives — the glittering, the planning; the loyal's, the final's. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The drive at eleven, and a carriage coming at a speed that makes the head groom wince from the yard. Lavinia arrives the way weather arrives — all at once, and with opinions. She is out of the carriage before the steps are properly down, her maid following with three hatboxes and the air of a woman who has given up arguing, and she crosses the gravel with her arms already open.)*
> "Darling!" The embrace smells of orange-flower water and the London road. "The fête! I have had seventeen ideas since dawn and rejected eleven of them, which leaves six, which is —" she holds up her fingers, counting — "too many. Rose. Darling. We must plan it *properly*. A final brilliance is not thrown, it is —" she searches the air — "it is *composed*. Like music. Like war."
> *(They walk up the steps arm in arm, and Lavinia talks the whole way — the young are restless, she says, the Season has been thin, the last weeks before summer want something to remember — and Rose listens the way she has learned to listen to Lavinia: for the heartbeat under the glitter. It comes as they cross the hall, sudden and quiet:)*
> "They were good to me, you know." Lavinia's voice drops, and the glitter goes with it, just for a breath. "The young. When I was —" she does not finish. "This is for them, really. For the house." She squeezes Rose's arm. "For you." Then the sparkle is back, bright as a struck match. "Now. The form, darling. I have been *agonizing*. A breakfast? No — too early, the young are never awake. A rout? Too crowded, one loses the — the —" she gestures — "the *shine* of it."
> "A ball," Rose says.
> "A ball." Lavinia stops dead in the middle of the hall, and the footmen go around them the way water goes around a stone. "Yes. Darling, yes. The night, the candles, the floor. The young want the night — they always have." She takes both of Rose's hands. "We will give it them, darling. The last brilliance. Glittering. Loyal." A pause, and the real voice again, quick as a slipped stitch: "Final."
> *(They stand there a moment, hands joined, in the hall of the finished house — the elder at twenty-five and the younger at twenty-four, though no one who saw them would guess which was which — and the planning of Lavinia's final fête moves from the library's columns into the air between them, where all of Lavinia's best plans have always lived.)*

scenes.synopsis: the plan — the final brilliance; the fête's form, imagined. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room, given over to the campaign. Lavinia has commandeered the long table, the map of the Park's state rooms, and all of Letitia's pencils, and she paces before it like a commander who has mislaid her army but remembers exactly where she left it.)*
> "The ballroom, obviously." She slaps the plan. "Forty paces, darling, I measured it in my head on the drive down and I am *never* wrong about floors. The supper in the dining room, the cards in the —" she waves — "the small saloon, the one with the green curtains. And the terrace for the intervals, because the young will want air and the night will want them."
> "The music?" Rose asks, taking notes in the margin of the plan.
> "Twelve." Lavinia does not hesitate. "No — fourteen. Darling, one cannot economize on *fiddles*. The young dance until the candles gutter, Letitia says, and she is right, they do, I have *seen* them." She stops pacing. "The flowers. All Hartwell-grown — the gardener will weep with pride, I have decided he will. And the supper —" she closes her eyes — "the supper must be the kind they talk about in October. The ices. The — the —" she opens her eyes — "Rose. *Ices in the shape of roses.* Can the cook do it? Tell me the cook can do it."
> "The cook," Rose says carefully, "can do anything except be hurried."
> "Then we shall not hurry her. We shall *worship* her." Lavinia drops into a chair, suddenly serious — the glitter thinning, the heartbeat showing through. "Darling. Listen." She leans forward. "I want it perfect. Not grand — perfect. The young will remember this night when they are old and married and dull, and I want them to remember —" she stops. "I want them to remember it was *kind*. That someone gave them a last brilliance and asked nothing for it." The glitter returns like a curtain dropping. "Also the ices. The ices are *essential*."
> *(Rose writes* ices, rose-shaped *in the household book, underlining it twice the way Lavinia underlines everything, and the fête takes its form on the page: the ballroom, the terrace, the fiddles, the Hartwell flowers, the supper they will talk about in October. The plan is Lavinia's. The ink is Rose's. Between them, the final brilliance is imagined whole.)*

scenes.synopsis: the young — Lavinia's six, the twelve; the advance guard, the restless. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The saloon at four, and Lavinia's young arriving in a clatter of hooves and laughter — the advance guard of the fête, come down early to be useful and staying to be delightful. Lavinia's own circle at the core, and more orbiting, and they fill the saloon the way swallows fill a sky: all motion, all noise, all grace.)*
> *(Rose watches from the doorway a moment before going in, and what she sees is something other than the restlessness Lavinia described — a kind of held breath. They are young in the particular way of people who have survived a war's ending and do not quite know what the peace is for. They perch on the furniture their mothers would forbid, they argue about the ball's supper with the gravity of diplomats, and when Lavinia sweeps in they rise like a wave.)*
> "My dears!" Lavinia opens her arms to the room. "My *advance guard*. You are early, you are loud, and you are *exactly* what the fête requires. Now —" she claps — "the ballroom must be walked. The floor must be judged. I need opinions on candlelight, and I need them *honest*."
> *(They follow her out in a flock, and Rose follows the flock, and the ballroom receives its first inspection: the young pace the forty paces, test the floor with their slippers, stand where the musicians will stand and declare the acoustics — one of them, a girl with a laugh like a bell, actually sings a scale — and pronounce the room, by acclamation, perfect.)*
> "It wants," says a young man with more hair than sense, standing in the center of the floor with his arms spread, "it wants *us* in it."
> "It shall have you," Lavinia promises, "and it shall have the candles, and the fiddles, and ices in the shape of roses." A cheer goes up that the housekeeper will hear in the still-room and smile at. "But first —" Lavinia's voice drops into conspiracy — "first you must swear. The fête is *secret* until the invitations go. Not a word in London. Not a whisper."
> *(They swear it, hands stacked in the middle of the ballroom like conspirators, and the oath dissolves immediately into laughter, and the laughter into a reel danced without music on the perfect floor. Rose stands at the ballroom door and watches the advance guard take possession of the night before it happens, and understands what Lavinia meant about loyalty: it is not given to houses. It is given to people, and then the houses get it too.)*

scenes.synopsis: the preparations — glittering; the Park, the brilliant's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The Park, three days before the fête, and the whole house tilted toward the preparations like a ship under full sail. Rose walks the grounds with the household book and finds the brilliance being built everywhere she looks — the gardeners cutting for the ballroom, the footmen carrying chairs to the terrace, the still-room a battlefield of preserves for the ices.)*
> *(In the ballroom, the chandeliers come down for cleaning, and the maids polish each crystal with the tenderness of nurses. The candles arrive from London in crates marked* FRAGILE *in a hand that suggests the sender did not believe it. Letitia receives them in the hall with the air of an admiral taking on powder, and counts every one — twice — while the footman waits with the respectful patience of a man who has learned that the quartermaster's arithmetic is not to be hurried.)*
> "Every candle," Letitia announces, closing the household book on the count. "The ballroom, the terrace, the stairs. Darling, if the ton complains of the light, they are complaining of the *sun*."
> *(In the kitchens, the cook has been visited by Lavinia — a state visit, with presents — and has agreed to the rose ices on condition of absolute sovereignty over the menu. "The young," the cook tells Rose, serene among her coppers, "will eat what is put before them, miss, and be grateful, miss. The ices are the crown. The rest is the —" she searches — "the setting." Rose does not argue with sovereignty.)*
> *(On the terrace, the gardeners arrange the tubs of orange trees, and the evening rehearses itself: the stone still warm from the day, the Park lying green beyond, the first stars considering whether to come out. Rose stands at the terrace edge and does the arithmetic Letitia taught her — once for the sum, once for the nerve — and finds the sum is large and the nerve is steady. Every room is being polished, provisioned, or counted. The Park is ready to glitter.)*
> *(She writes it in the household book that night, in the column Letitia calls glory: the ballroom, the terrace, the fiddles, the candles, the rose ices. Underneath, in smaller hand, she adds what the book cannot hold: that the house has never looked more itself than it does tonight, three days from a party, humming like a hive.)*

scenes.synopsis: the gowns — the young's; brilliance, the dressed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her bedroom, the afternoon of the fête, and the gowns laid out on the bed like a hand of cards — Lavinia's doing, of course, who arrived with her maid and three bandboxes and the firm conviction that Rose could not be trusted to choose alone. "Darling," she had said, "you dress for *battles*. This is a *brilliance*. Different theatre entirely.")*
> *(Rose stands before the bed in her petticoat and regards the options the way she regards everything: as a problem of logistics. The blush silk — Lavinia's choice, scattered with the small bright embroidery that catches candlelight. The deep blue — severe and true, the color of a night that keeps its promises. The ivory — plain as a vow.)*
> "The young," Lavinia says, draped over the chaise with a fashion plate she is not reading, "will wear *everything*. Muslins like foam. Silks like armor. One of them —" she lowers her voice — "one of them told me her gown cost more than her brother's horse. Darling, the *gowns* are the fête's first brilliance. Before the candles. Before the fiddles."
> "And what will you wear?" Rose asks.
> Lavinia sits up. "The silver." She says it the way other women say a prayer. "The gown, not the hair, darling, I am *twenty-four*. It has waited long enough for a night worthy of it." The glitter thins, just for a breath. "This is the night. My last brilliance. It should see me —" she stops — "as I was. As I am." The curtain drops back. "Also it makes my eyes look *enormous*."
> *(They dress together, the way sisters do, with the maid running between them and the pins flying. Lavinia laces Rose and Rose hooks Lavinia, and the bedroom fills with the particular intimacy of women preparing for a night that matters — the shared mirror, the borrowed pearl, the honest verdict.)*
> "There," Lavinia says at last, stepping back. "Darling. *There*." In the glass, Rose sees the gown she chose and the woman the house chose, and they are — for tonight — the same person. "You are dressed," Lavinia says softly, "and the night had better look sharp."

scenes.synopsis: the music — the young's; the brilliant's sound. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The ballroom at seven, empty before the guests, and the musicians arriving with their instruments like a small invading army — fourteen of them, led by a first violin with the bearing of a field marshal and a cello player who keeps apologizing to his own instrument. They tune in the gallery, and the sound falls into the empty ballroom like rain into a well.)*
> *(Rose stands in the middle of the forty paces and listens. The tuning resolves — the field marshal taps his bow — and the first violin sings a phrase alone, testing the room. The ballroom answers: the plaster, the glass, the waxed floor give the note back warmer than it came. The cello player stops apologizing and smiles.)*
> "The air," says the first violin, coming down to the floor with his bow still raised, "the air in this room, madam —" he bows to Rose — "it *carries*. We shall not have to force it. The room does half our work."
> "The room," Rose tells him, "has had ten seasons of practice at carrying things."
> *(They rehearse the opening set — a quadrille, then a waltz, then the country dances the young will demand when the night is old — and the ballroom fills with it: the fiddles bright as cut glass, the cello underneath like a heartbeat, the flutes threading through like light through leaves. In the kitchens below, the cook's staff moves faster without knowing why. On the stairs, a footman pauses with a tray and listens.)*
> *(Lavinia arrives mid-rehearsal, already dressed, the silver gown catching the unlit chandeliers' ghosts. She stands beside Rose and does not speak — for Lavinia, an extraordinary discipline — until the waltz ends.)*
> "Darling," she says then, very quietly, the real voice, no glitter at all. "That is the sound the Season has been missing." She takes Rose's hand. "Thank you for letting me —" she stops. "For the *fiddles*, darling. Fourteen of them. You are *magnificent*." The glitter returns, bright as the violins. "Now. The candles must be lit at half past eight *precisely*. I have told Letitia, but tell her again — the quartermaster respects *repetition*."

scenes.synopsis: the supper — glittering; the young's feast. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The kitchens at eight, and the supper in its final staging — the cook's sovereignty on full display. Rose descends, as she always does before a great night, to pay her respects to the true power of the house, and finds the kitchen in the ordered frenzy of a well-run war: the coppers steaming, the pastry cooks flour-white as ghosts, the footmen lined up for the trays like troops for inspection.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The cook receives her among the steam with the serenity of a commander who has already won. "The supper." She gestures, and the gesture takes in the whole gleaming length of preparation: the raised pies, the jellies trembling in their molds, the cold fowls, the fruits, and at the center — on a bed of ice, in state — the ices. Roses, in ice — blush-pink, perfect, melting even as they are admired.
> "They are," Rose says, "impossible."
> "They are," the cook agrees, "the crown." She lowers her voice. "The young will eat them first, miss, before the soup if we let them. I have instructed the footmen —" a glance at the line — "the ices go out *with* the champagne, not after. A brilliance must be *timed*, miss."
> *(Rose tastes nothing — the cook's rule, never taste before the guests — but she walks the length of the tables and does the other arithmetic, the one Letitia taught her: enough for the expected, and enough again for the unexpected, because the young bring friends the way the tide brings shells. There is enough. There is more than enough — the tables are laid, the trays are lined up, the night is fed before it begins.)*
> *(On her way up, she meets Letitia on the stairs, carrying the last of the seating cards.)*
> "The supper," Letitia says, "smells like victory." She fans herself with the cards. "Darling, I have seated the dragon's —" she catches herself — "I have seated *everyone* where they will be happiest, which is to say where they will cause the least trouble. The young are together. The old are together. The dangerous are —" she smiles the quartermaster's smile — "separated by at least two chairs and one footman."
> *(They climb together toward the light and the music beginning above, and the house smells of wax and orange-flower and roasting fowl, and the fête — three days planned, a lifetime imagined — is ready.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE BRILLIANCE'S FORM (the fête's form: a breakfast, a rout, or a ball). The day deepens; decide the form. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library at dusk, three days before the fête, and the brilliance asking its form. Rose stands at the window with Lavinia's letter in one hand and Letitia's household book in the other, and the day deepens around the question the way dusk deepens around the Park: gradually, then all at once.)*
> *(A breakfast: mornings, and glitter. She pictures it — the young arriving sleepy and laughing, the terrace in morning light, chocolate and rolls, the fête done by noon. It would be *charming*. It would also be over before the candles were ever lit, and Lavinia's brilliance — she knows this the way she knows her sums — was never a morning thing. Mornings are for planning. Lavinia does her glittering after dark.)*
> *(A rout: evenings, and noise. The crush, the whole ton pressed into the state rooms like flowers in a book. It would be *grand*. It would also be — she pictures her young lost in the crowd, Lavinia's toast drowned in the general roar — the opposite of loyal. A rout belongs to everyone. This fête belongs to *someone*: to Lavinia, to the young, to the last brilliance.)*
> *(A ball: night, and the final hours. The forty paces, the fiddles, the candles, the ices in the shape of roses going out with the champagne. The young dancing until the candles gutter. Lavinia in silver, at the center of it, glittering to the last. It would be grand — grander than a breakfast, grander than a rout — and grandeur has its own cost, measured in candles and nerve.)*
> *(Letitia comes in with the evening post and reads the indecision off Rose's face the way she reads everything: at a glance, and aloud.)*
> "Darling." The hawk's eyes, amused. "You are standing at a window holding my household book like a *novel*. Decide."
> "Breakfast wastes the candles," Rose says. "A rout wastes the *toast*. A ball —" she turns from the window — "a ball spends both, and asks the night to pay it back." She opens the book. "Write it down, whatever it is. The ink will decide when I have finished talking."
> "The ink," Letitia agrees, uncapping her pen, "is a coward. It only writes what you tell it." The pen hovers. "Well, darling?"
> *(The form is chosen — and the fête takes its shape in the household book: the hours, the dancing, the small hours of the morning. Outside, the Park darkens into its evening order, unaware that inside the library, the last brilliance has just been given its hours.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: breakfast, rout, or ball.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — The brilliance's form:*
- **A breakfast** — *the morning, glittering.* The fête is a breakfast — the morning's, the young's. (Consequence: the form is the morning's — but mornings are early, and the brilliance wants the night.)
- **A rout** — *the evening, brilliant.* The fête is a rout — the evening's, the glittering's. (Consequence: the form is the evening's — but routs are crowds, and the loyalty wants the intimate.)
- **A ball** — *the night, final.* The fête is a ball — the night's, the last brilliance. (Consequence: the form is the night's — but balls are grand, and the fête was the young's.)

scenes.synopsis: the fête — the glittering, held; the final's, the night's. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:

scenes.prose:
> *(One o'clock, and Lavinia claims the room once more. The musicians lower their bows. The dancers find the edges. The ballroom does what it has done all night for her: it listens.)*
> "Darlings." She stands in the center of the floor, the silver gown still bright though the candles have burned two inches. "The final brilliance." She looks at the young — the six, the twelve, the orbiting dozens, all her dears. "The Season gave us the house, darlings." Her voice drops, and the glitter thins — the real voice, the heartbeat's. "The Park. The —" she looks at Rose — "the woman."
> *(A breath, held by the whole room. Then the glitter returns, but thinner now, like gold leaf — you can see through it to the true thing beneath:)*
> "The young were the ball, darlings." She raises her glass, and her hand is steady. "The young *are* —" she stops. "The young are the future, darlings." The real voice again, the final one, quiet enough that the back of the room leans in. "For the house, darlings. For Rose." She breathes, and the whole room breathes with her. "Loyal —" the word lands like a bell — "loyal, to the last."
> *(The cheer that answers is the night's heart — the young crying "Loyal! To the last!" with their glasses high, the ton joining, even the footmen at the doors standing straighter. Lavinia bows to them all, the hostess's deepest curtsy, and when she straightens, her eyes find Rose across the floor.)*
> *(Lavinia steps down from the center of the floor, and the young close around her — her dears, her circle — and for a moment the hostess is simply surrounded, the way a queen is surrounded, the way a mother is.)*
> "Miss Lavinia." The bell-laugh girl, very grave. "We shall *never* —" she stops. "That is all. We shall never."
> "Darling." Lavinia touches the girl's cheek — the real voice, the heartbeat's, held for all to hear. "That is *enough*. That is the whole of it." She looks around at their young faces. "Be *glittering*, my dears. And be *loyal*. The two are not —" she stops herself, smiling — "the two are not enemies, whatever the old may tell you."
> *(Rose bows back — the small bow, the true one — and between them, across the candlelight and the forty paces, the speech settles where the night's best things settle: into memory. The toastmistress has said the true thing, and the room will remember it longer than the ices.)*

> *(After the speech, and the advance guard gathers — drawn to the terrace by something older than the dancing. Rose follows, curious, and finds them at the balustrade in the dark beyond the candlelight, very quiet, very young.)*
> *(One of them — the girl with the bell laugh — is speaking, low and fast, and the others listen the way the ballroom listened to Lavinia. She sees Rose and stops, flushing.)*
> "Go on," Rose says.
> "We were —" the girl glances at her friends — "we were swearing, Miss Hartwell. An oath." She lifts her chin. "That we will be —" she searches — "that we will *deserve* this. The house. The night." Another glance. "That when it is our turn to — to *convene* things —" she stumbles on the word, then firms — "we will do it *loyally*. Like Miss Lavinia."

She thinks of ledgers, because she always thinks of ledgers when she is moved: an oath, entered. The young, debited joy, credited loyalty. The account will balance. It always does, if the keeping is honest.)*
> "Then swear it properly," she says, and holds out her hand.
> *(One of the young men — quiet, the thoughtful one of the six — speaks up from the dark, his voice low.)*

She stands among the Ravencrofts and the Hartwells, the whole long argument of her blood, and listens to the fête go on without her for three minutes.)*
> *(It goes on beautifully. That is the discovery: the brilliance does not need her. Lavinia's night has its own momentum now — the young dancing, the ton charmed, the candles burning at exactly the rate Letitia calculated. She thinks of the west gallery at dawn in the first chapter — the inventory, the counting — and understands the last item on the list: the ballroom, *celebrated*. A house that throws its own parties without being supervised — the last item on the list, and the best.)*

scenes.prose:
> *(Three o'clock, and the small hours — the brilliance unwinding, the fête's long beautiful exhale. The musicians play slower now, the country dances giving way to the dreamy sets the tired young love best, and the ballroom's light has gone golden at the edges where the candles burn low.)*
> *(Rose sits out a set with Octavia, who has spent the evening in corners, watching — the painter's habit, the precise eye storing the night the way other people store wine.)*
> "The light," Octavia says, not looking at Rose, looking at the room. "At three, the candles do something they do at no other hour. The faces go —" she gestures, precise — "soft at the edges. The young look *kind*. The old look *young*." She turns, the precise smile. "I am memorizing it, Rose. For *later*. Some nights should be kept."
> "Will you paint it?"
> "I am painting it *now*." Octavia taps her temple. "The truest canvas. No one can buy it, no one can hang it, and it will not fade." She looks at her friend. "The unwinding, Rose. It is the most honest hour. The glitter —" a nod at the room — "the glitter is tired, and what is left is the *loyal*. Watch."

The small hours strip the night to its frame, and the frame is sound.)*
> "Lavinia," Octavia says, very quietly, watching the silver gown move through the golden light. "At three in the morning, the glitter is *tired*, and what is underneath —" the precise voice, certain — "is the *structure*. Like a painting. The varnish thins, and you see the drawing." She turns to Rose. "Her drawing, Rose, is *true*. I have looked all night. It is the truest thing in the room."
> *(Rose follows the painter's gaze, and sees what Octavia sees: Lavinia bending to the old lady, Lavinia pressing the girl's cheek, Lavinia — caught between dances — standing perfectly still for three seconds with her eyes closed, simply *being* in the music. The drawing, true.)*
> *(The musicians play the final waltz of the unwinding — not the last waltz of the night, but the last of the height — and the remaining dancers move through it like swimmers in deep water, slow and certain. The fête unwinds, beautifully, the long exhale, and lets itself be tired at last.)*

scenes.prose:
> *(Half past three, and the ballroom emptying — the guests thinning to the terrace, the carriages, the last dances. Rose finds Lavinia in the small saloon, alone for the first time all night, the silver gown dimmed to moonlight, a glass of champagne untouched in her hand.)*
> *(She stops in the doorway, not wanting to break it — but Lavinia looks up, and the glitter is gone. Not thinned, not slipped: gone. What is left is the real voice, the heartbeat's own, and it is twenty-four years old and exhausted and incandescent.)*
> "Darling." Lavinia holds out her hand, and Rose goes to her. "The fête —" she stops. "The final brilliance, darling." She takes both of Rose's hands in hers. They are cold. "The young —" another stop — "the young were —" the real voice, steady, unadorned — "the young were the joy, darling. All of it. Every season I glittered, it was *for* them. So they would have —" she breathes — "one person in the ton who was *glad* to see them."
> "They know," Rose says.
> "Do they?" The true look, held. "Then it was enough." Lavinia's fingers tighten. "The loyalty, darling." She says the word like a vow. "Loyal —" a breath — "loyal, to the last. For the house, darling." The glittering eyes are wet, and she does not hide it. "For *you*."
> *(They sit together in the small saloon while the fête ends around them — the last carriages called, the musicians packing their instruments, the footmen moving through the ballroom with the quiet efficiency of men restoring a world. No glitter. No performance. Two women, one night spent, the true thing between them like a third person in the room.)*
> *(Rose takes the cold hands and chafes them gently, the way she has seen nurses do, and the small saloon holds its quiet.)*
> "It was *enough*, Lavinia." She says it plainly, no glitter, the real voice answering the real voice. "Not the fête. *You*. Ten seasons of it. The young will carry it —" she thinks of the terrace, the stacked hands — "they are carrying it already. You gave them the *shape* of it. Glittering, and loyal, and —" she stops — "and *kind*."
> "Kind." Lavinia turns the word over like a coin. "Darling, no one has ever called me *kind*." The true look, wet and bright. "Say it again."
> "Kind," Rose says. "To the last."
> *(When Lavinia finally rises, the glitter comes back — a shrug, a sparkle, the curtain — but Rose has seen underneath, and will keep what she saw the way she keeps everything that matters: entered, accounted, never spoken of, never forgotten.)*

scenes.synopsis: Letitia, on Lavinia — the aunt, the fête's; the quartermaster, the brilliant. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room at breakfast — very late breakfast, the shutters half-closed against a sun the night does not deserve — and Letitia presiding over the wreckage of the fête with the satisfaction of a general reviewing a won field. The household book lies open. The candles are counted. The ices are history.)*
> "Darling." Letitia looks up as Rose comes in, and the hawk's eyes are warm. "The fête." She gestures at the book, at the columns, at the whole accounted brilliance. "The final brilliance, darling." She closes the book with a small, decisive sound. "The quartermaster —" a laugh — "the quartermaster *salutes*, darling."
> "Salutes whom?" Rose pours the chocolate. "Lavinia? The young? The cook's sovereignty?"
> "All of them." Letitia leans back, cradling her cup. "But mostly —" the warm look, the grave one underneath — "mostly Lavinia. Darling, I have known that girl since she was *twelve* and glittering at her first ball. I have watched her spend herself like —" she searches — "like candlelight. For the young. For the ton. For anyone who needed a little *shine*." She sips. "Last night she spent the last of it. And do you know what, darling?"
> "What?"
> "It was *enough*." Letitia's voice does something unusual: it wobbles, once, and recovers. "The advance guard —" she looks toward the windows, the Park beyond — "all those seasons of fighting, darling, and *this* is what the war was for. A night like last night. The young, dancing."
> *(Rose reaches across the table and covers her aunt's hand with her own, and Letitia — who has never in her life accepted comfort gracefully — accepts it, for once, without a joke.)*
> "The household book," Rose says, "forgives nothing. It merely waits. Your words, darling."
> "My words." Letitia turns the book so Rose can see the fête's final column — the sums, the candles, the fiddles, the ices, all accounted. "And see how beautifully it has waited." She taps the margin, where she has written in the small hand: *Lavinia — the last brilliance. Paid in full.* "There are expenditures, darling, and there are *investments*. The book knows the difference, even if the ton does not."
> "Which is this?"
> "Oh." The hawk's eyes gleam over the chocolate. "This, darling, is the *one* entry in ten seasons that the book will never regret. Frame *that*."
> *(The quartermaster's salute stands. In the household book, under the fête's final column, Letitia has written, in her smallest hand:* Lavinia — the last brilliance. Paid in full.*)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE LOYALTY'S KEEPING (how Lavinia's loyalty is kept: in the young, in the house, or in Rose). The night deepens; decide the keeping. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The small saloon at four in the morning, the fête ended, and the loyalty asking its keeping. Rose sits where Lavinia sat — the chair still holding the ghost of the silver gown's warmth — with the night's noise gone quiet around her, and the question settles the way dust settles after dancing: everywhere, and softly.)*
> *(In the young: the advance guard's hands still warm on hers from the terrace, the society with rules, the bell-laugh girl's four pages crossed out to a single line. Kept in them, the loyalty would live on — handed down, convened by hands younger than hers. But futures are unbuilt, and oaths — she has kept enough of them to know — are only as strong as the remembering. The young will remember. She believes they will. Belief is not keeping.)*
> *(In the house: the ballroom dark now, the forty paces holding the night's geometry in their wax, the stone that outlasts every candle. Kept in it, the loyalty would sit permanent and unforgetting, entered in the record like a deed. But stones are cold, and what Lavinia gave was warm: the hand on the elbow, the kiss on the girl's cheek, the* I am tired, darling *in the small saloon. Stone cannot keep warmth. Stone can only keep shape.)*
> *(In Rose: the mistress, the convener, the one who watched from the ballroom door and the terrace edge and the gallery — the images unentered, unaccounted, hers. Kept in her, the loyalty would live where it was witnessed, carried in one woman's memory like a candle through the dark. But hearts are one, and this loyalty belonged to the many — the young, the ton, the household, the whole glittering room crying "Loyal! To the last!")*
> *(She sits in the quiet saloon and does the arithmetic she always does — once for the sum, once for the nerve — and finds the sum will not resolve to a single column. The loyalty is not *in* one place. It is in the young's oath and the house's stone and her own kept images, all at once, the way the fête was in the ballroom and the terrace and the small hours all at once.)*
> *(But the night asks, and so she answers, knowing, as she writes it in the household book's margin in the first grey of dawn, that keeping is daily work: the work Lavinia did, given freely, annually, loyally, to the last.)*
> *(She closes the book. The household stirs toward morning below, and the kept loyalty goes with her up the stairs like a candle carried through the dark.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: young, house, or Rose.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The loyalty's keeping:*
- **In the young** — *the future, kept.* The loyalty is kept in the young — the advance guard, the future. (Consequence: the keeping is the future's — but futures are unbuilt, and the loyalty was the now.)
- **In the house** — *the stone, kept.* The loyalty is kept in the house — the Park, the stone. (Consequence: the keeping is the stone's — but stones are cold, and the loyalty was the warm.)
- **In Rose** — *the heart, kept.* The loyalty is kept in Rose — the woman, the heart. (Consequence: the keeping is the heart's — but hearts are one, and the loyalty was the many's.)

scenes.synopsis: Augusta, on the glittering — the Dowager, the fête's; the line, the brilliant. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta's morning room, the day after the fête, and the Dowager receiving Rose with the air of a judge who has already written the verdict and is merely waiting for the defendant to sit down. The spectacles are on. Seventy-two years, fully deployed.)*
> "The fête." Augusta sets down her correspondence. "Sit, child." Rose sits. "I watched it." A pause. "All of it. From the gallery door, where the old may observe without being *expected* to dance." The spectacles lower. "The final brilliance, child."
> "And your verdict, Grandmama?"
> "Lavinia —" another pause, longer — "the glittering, child, the —" the rarest smile touches the severe mouth — "the loyal, child." Augusta removes the spectacles — a twice-yearly event — and looks at Rose with unguarded eyes. "I have seen a great many *brilliances* in my seventy-two years. Most of them were —" she searches — "expenditure. Noise, purchased." She replaces the spectacles. "Hers was *loyalty* — given entirely, and never counted."
> "She did it for the young," Rose says.
> "She did it for *you*, child." The dry verdict, delivered without mercy. "The young were the excuse. The house was the reason." Augusta takes Rose's hand — the old hand, the rings, the weight of it. "The line —" the voice does something extraordinary, going soft at the edges — "the line honors the loyal, child. Glittering —" she stops, and for a moment the Dowager is simply a very old woman who has seen a young one be brave — "glittering, to the last."
> *(Rose holds the old hand and does not speak, because there is nothing to add to a verdict, and Augusta — who has pretended not to see tenderness for seventy-two years — looks out of the window at the Park instead, which is the Dowager's entire philosophy, deployed one final time.)*
> "Grandmama." Rose hesitates — then asks it, because the morning room is quiet and the verdict is given and there will not be a better hour. "The young. The advance guard. What do you make of *them*?"
> "They are," she says at last, "what we were, before we learned to be *careful*." The dry verdict, without mercy and without malice. "The girl with the bell laugh will be a force. The quiet young man of the six will be a *power*, if no one ruins him." She looks at Rose. "They are *yours* now, child. Lavinia has made you their —" she searches — "their *standard*. Do not," the spectacles lower, "be careful with them. Be *exact*."
> *(Augusta's honoring stands, witnessed and entered into the record. As Rose leaves, Augusta returns to her correspondence, but she does not pick up her pen for a long time.)*

scenes.synopsis: Julian, on Lavinia — the free man, the fête's; the terrace, the brilliant. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The terrace at noon, the day after, and Julian waiting there with the air of a man who has been waiting some time and does not mind. The fête's wreckage is gone — the footmen have been miraculous — and the terrace is itself again: stone, sky, the Park beyond.)*
> "The fête." Julian falls into step beside her, unguarded, the night's formality shed like a coat. "The —" he stops, searching. "The final brilliance, Rose." The ghost of the old smile. "Lavinia —" he touches his pocket, where the mended gloves live — "glittering, Rose. Loyal, Rose."
> "You danced," Rose observes. "Three sets. I counted."
> "I did." He looks surprised at himself. "The advance guard —" the direct look — "they salute, Rose, and I salute back." He bows over her hand, the free man's bow, unforced. "Do you know what I thought, watching them? The young." He straightens. "I thought: I was never *that*. At their age I was —" he touches the pocket again — "mending. Always mending."
> "And now?"
> "Now —" the ghost of the smile becomes something realer — "now I dance at fêtes, Rose. The debts are paid. The gloves are kept." He looks out at the Park. "The free life. It turns out to be —" he searches — "mostly *mornings*. Good mornings. Like this one."
> *(They stand at the terrace edge together, and the Park lies below them whole — the finished house, the dressed grounds, the lake pavilion gleaming — and Julian stands unguarded in the noon light, the loyal saluting the loyal.)*
> "The gloves." Rose nods at the pocket, where his hand has gone again. "You touched them four times during the fête. I counted that too."
> "Did you." The ghost of the old smile. "They are —" he takes them out, the mended gloves, worn soft as skin — "evidence, Rose. That a man can be mended." He turns them in his hands. "Last night, dancing —" he stops — "I did not think of debts. Not once. Three sets." He looks up, unguarded. "Do you know how long it has been since I did anything for three *sets* without counting the cost?"
> "Tell me."
> "I *can't*." He laughs, surprised at himself. "That is the whole of it. I can't remember. The free life, Rose —" the direct look — "it turns out to be *forgetting* the arithmetic. Now and then. On *purpose*."
> *(As they turn to go in, Julian says, very quietly, almost to himself: "She was magnificent, wasn't she. Lavinia." And Rose, who has no answer that would not be too small, only nods — and the nod is enough, because some verdicts need no words.)*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent, on the brilliant — the Englishman, the fête's; the unmasked, the glittering. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library in the afternoon, and Laurent waiting among the shelves with a book he is not reading — the Englishman at ease in the house that is, in some way he no longer troubles to define, also his. He looks up as Rose comes in, and the direct look is there before the smile.)*
> "The fête." He sets the book down — unmarked, she notes; he never could bear to dog-ear. "The —" a pause, the English careful and chosen — "the final brilliance, Rose." The truth's look. "Lavinia — glittering, Rose. Loyal, Rose."
> "Your English," Rose says, sitting opposite, "gets better every season. It is becoming *dangerous*."
> "My English —" the direct look warms — "my English is the least of what you have taught me." He takes her hand, the unmasked gesture, no performance in it. "I salute the advance guard, Rose." A breath. "When I came to this country I wore —" he touches his face — "a mask. For years. Last night, dancing the waltz with *you* —" the truth's look, held — "I could not remember where I had put it."
> "Perhaps," Rose says, "you never needed it here."
> "Perhaps," he agrees, "I never did." He rises, and bows over her hand — the English bow he has earned: plain, direct, true. "The mask off, Rose. *Loyally*."
> "You left a book." Rose nods at the unmarked volume he set down. "Yours?"
> "The library's." He picks it up, turns it over. "French. Poetry." The direct look, wry. "I brought it to —" he stops — "to *appear* occupied, if the afternoon proved dull. Old habits." He sets it down again, deliberately. "The afternoon is not dull. The mask —" he touches his face, then lets the hand fall — "the mask is off, Rose. Even the *props* are retired."
> "Keep the book," Rose says. "The library lends to the unmasked. It is the *rule*."
> "Then I am *ruled*." He bows, the English bow, plain and true — and takes the book, and the afternoon, and the unmasked life, with him.
> *(He leaves her among the shelves, and the library holds the afternoon the way it holds everything: patiently. Rose sits a while longer with the unmarked book he left behind, thinking of masks, and of the people who no longer need them, and of the house that taught them so.)*

scenes.synopsis: Octavia, on the loyal — the painter, the fête's; the precise, the brilliant. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The still-room at dusk — Octavia's studio, the north light going grey — and the painter cleaning her brushes with the methodical calm of a woman who has spent the fête working. Rose finds her there, and the almost-finished picnic portrait stands on the easel with a new study pinned beside it: the ballroom, in washes of gold and silver, the dancers suggested in three brushstrokes.)*
> "The fête." Octavia does not look up from the brushes. "The precise observation, Rose, is this." She sets a brush down. "The final brilliance. Lavinia — glittering, Rose. Loyal, Rose." The precise voice, warm underneath the precision.
> "You painted it," Rose says, looking at the study. "Already."
> "I *saw* it. The painting is —" Octavia gestures at the washes — "later. Years, perhaps." She looks at her friend directly. "The painter sees the truest thing, Rose." She stops, and the precision does something rare: it hesitates. "Glittering." A breath. "She spent it all, didn't she. The shine. On *them*."
> "On all of us."
> "On all of us." Octavia picks up the study, holds it to the failing light. "I will paint it true, Rose. Not the glitter — the *loyal*. The gold leaf over the real. That is the painting." She pins the study back. "Two houses, one shared life. The arrangement holds. The painter keeps her half of it."
> "Show me," Rose says.
> *(Octavia holds the study to the light — the ballroom in washes of gold and silver — and points with the clean end of a brush: three strokes, and there is Lavinia, silver gown, arms open to the young.)*
> "The hands." The precise voice, quiet. "See. I have painted them *open*. Not raised, not commanding — *open*. That was the night, Rose. Not the glitter." A pause, the precision doing its rare hesitation. "The *giving*."
> *(Rose looks at the three brushstrokes that are Lavinia's hands, open, and feels the peculiar vertigo of being seen accurately — not herself, this time, but the night, the true thing under the gold leaf.)*
> "Paint it true," she says.
> "I *always* paint it true," Octavia says. "It is my only *flaw*."
> *(Rose leaves the painter to her north light, and in the corridor passes the ballroom doors — closed now, the candles out — and hears, very faintly, the ghost of the waltz, or only the house settling. Either way, it is enough.)*

scenes.synopsis: Henry, on the fête — the soldier, the night's; the devotion, the brilliant. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room at breakfast, two days after the fête, and Henry arriving with the post as he does most mornings — the daily devotion, uninterrupted by brilliance. He hands Rose the London letters on the terrace steps, sorted: the interesting at the top, the bills at the bottom, the way she likes it.)*
> "The fête." He stands very straight, the soldier's posture even in a morning coat. "The final brilliance, Rose." The smallest smile. "Lavinia — glittering, Rose. Loyal, Rose."
> "You came," Rose says. "You stayed until two. I saw you."
> "I did." He bows over her hand. "The small things continue, Rose. The devotion salutes, Rose."
> "The devotion," Rose says, "danced twice. I counted that too."
> "The devotion —" the smallest smile deepens, fractionally — "was *ordered* to dance. By a lady in silver." He looks toward the drive, where the morning post came from, where the world goes on. "She told me the young should see that even soldiers *dance*, Rose. So that they know the peace is —" he searches — "real. Used. Not merely declared."
> "The post." Rose nods at the bag. "Anything interesting at the top today, Major? Or only bills at the bottom?"
> "A letter." He produces it, sorted as promised. "From London. The young." The smallest smile. "The bell-laugh girl, I believe. Four pages." He hesitates — then adds, the unguarded look brief and bright: "She writes that the twelve have formed a *society*. With rules."
> "Letitia will want to see that."
> "Letitia," Henry says gravely, "will want to *audit* that." The smallest smile deepens. "The small things continue, Rose. The post. The sorting." He bows over her hand. "The *devotion*. Even —" a beat — "especially after brilliance."
> *(They climb the steps together, and the letter goes into the house with them, and the post goes unread for once, and the morning does what mornings do at the Park now: it behaves. Rose understands, not for the first time, that Henry's daily devotion is its own brilliance — quieter than Lavinia's, steadier, and built — like everything at the Park — to last.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Park, the glittering's morning — the whole, the brilliant's; the light. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The Park, the morning after the morning after — two days on, and its own dawn. Rose walks early, before the household is up, and the grounds hold the fête the way a field holds the memory of rain: invisibly, and everywhere.)*
> *(The terrace is swept. The ballroom windows are open to the air. The drive shows the faintest twin lines where the last carriages went, already softening into the gravel. The gardeners are at the beds, cutting the spent blooms, and the roses — the Hartwell rows — stand in their restored order, indifferent to brilliance, loyal to the season.)*
> *(She walks to the lake pavilion and back, the long way, past the stables where the strings are going out in the mist. The head groom touches his hat. "A good night, miss," he says, which from him is oratory. The greys are being washed — once, this time, not twice; the fête is over, and the yard has returned to its professional calm.)*
> *(At the walled garden, the gardener shows her the buds without being asked — the Hartwell rose, still tight, still certain. "Another week, miss. Perhaps two." The same verdict as always, delivered with the same pride. Some things at the Park do not hurry for fêtes. Rose finds this restful.)*
> *(At the lake pavilion she finds the night's leavings: a lady's glove on the step, kid, blush-pink, the mate presumably waltzing somewhere in London by now. Rose picks it up — small, damp with dew — and holds it a moment. Somewhere a young woman is missing a glove and not minding in the least. She sets it on the pavilion's ledge, where the household will find it, and where — she knows the household — it will be kept until claimed, pressed in tissue, labeled in Mrs. Quick's immovable hand.)*
> *(Inside the pavilion, the air smells of last night's orange trees and this morning's lake. She stands at the window and looks back at the house — the whole, the complete, the finished — and thinks of Lavinia's letter, weeks ago now: the pen underlining* brilliance *twice, the blot where she changed her mind about the form. The form was a ball. The brilliance was Lavinia. The blot — Rose smiles — the blot was the *truth*, showing through.)*
> *(She completes the circuit and stands at the gallery window, looking at the whole — the morning light doing what light does in a finished house: staying. The fête is over. The Park remains. She counts, once for the sum, once for the nerve: intact, and hers, and quietly, completely, hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the letters — the young write; London, the glittering's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library at noon, and the letters — the young write, as the young do, in the fever of the morning after. They come by the midday post, a whole packet of them, addressed in hands still learning their own confidence, sealed with everything from proper wax to a button pressed into candle grease.)*
> *(Rose reads them at the desk, one by one, and they are — without exception — the same letter: the night was the most brilliant thing, ever; Miss Lavinia was magnificent; the ices were beyond description; may they come again; will there be another; please. One of the twelve has drawn the ballroom in the margin, the chandeliers as small exploding suns. Another — the girl with the bell laugh — has written four pages and crossed out three of them, leaving only:* Thank you. I will remember. *)*
> *(Letitia comes in mid-packet and reads over her shoulder, uninvited and indispensable.)*
> "London," she says, "will hear of this." The hawk's eyes scan the bell-laugh girl's single line. "Darling, *this* one. Four pages crossed out. That is the letter of a young woman who has understood something." She sits. "The fête, reported. The final brilliance, loyal and glittering — all of it, in hands still learning confidence."
> "Shall I answer them?" Rose asks. "All of them?"
> "You shall answer *three*." Letitia holds up three fingers. "The quartermaster's arithmetic: three answers, and the rest will hear of it. Choose the truest letters." She rises, pausing at the door. "And darling —" the warm look — "keep the drawing. The chandeliers as exploding suns. Frame it. The Park should own its own *mythology*."
> "Read it aloud," Rose says. "The four pages. The crossed-out ones especially."
> *(Letitia holds the bell-laugh girl's letter to the light like a general studying dispatches.)*
> "'Dear Miss Hartwell.'" The hawk's eyes move down the page. "'The night was —' crossed out. 'I cannot describe —' crossed out. 'You will think me foolish —' crossed out." She looks up. "Darling, this is the *bravest* letter of the packet. She wrote the truth four times and was *afraid* of it four times." She folds it carefully. "And then —" the warm look — "then she wrote the one true line, and sent *that*. The young are *learning*, darling."
> "The truest letters," Rose says, "are the shortest."
> "The truest letters," Letitia corrects, "are the ones that *survive* the crossing-out."
> *(Rose answers three — the bell-laugh girl first, the drawing second, the button-seal third — and files the rest in the letter file, under* Fête, Lavinia's, final. *London writes, and the witnessing goes into the Park's paper memory, to outlast the candles.)*

scenes.synopsis: the household, the brilliant's — the keepers, the fête's; the peace's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Below stairs at midday, and the household at rest after the fête — the keepers' own peace. Rose descends, as she does after every great night, and finds the servants' hall in the particular peace of a job magnificently done: the long table cleared, the silver back in its baize, the footmen drowsing in the sun by the area steps.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." Mrs. Quick finds her by the dresser, forty-four and immovable, and permits herself — the extraordinary mouth — something very close to satisfaction. "The fête." A pause. "The household —" another pause — "the household showed them, miss. The silver the way it should be. The linen pressed twice."
> "Twice, Mrs. Quick?"
> "For the ton, miss." The immovable mouth does the extraordinary thing again. "They saw what a house looks like when it's kept."
> *(The cook emerges from the kitchen, serene among the wreckage of her sovereignty, and accepts Rose's thanks with the gravity of a crowned head receiving tribute. "The ices, miss," she says. "They went with the champagne. Timed." She allows herself a small smile. "The young ate them *first*, miss. Before the soup. I saw." She does not sound displeased.)*
> *(Rose walks the length of the hall, and the keepers nod — the footmen, the maids, the boot boy who carried candles up three flights without breaking one — and the peace of the house settles over her like a well-cut coat. Two hosts, she thinks, remembering the first chapter: herself, and everyone below stairs who kept the place while she was earning it.)*
> "And the boot boy, miss." Mrs. Quick permits herself the full extraordinary mouth. "Candles, up three flights, and not one *broken*. I have —" she stops, the immovable voice doing something unprecedented — "I have commended him. *Personally*."
> *(Rose finds the boot boy by the area steps, drowsing in the sun with the footmen, and commends him again — personally, as is now the custom — and he goes scarlet to the ears and forgets to bow, which the footmen will tease him about for a month.)*
> "Miss." He manages it at last, very low. "The fête. Was it —" he searches — "was it *brilliant*, miss? Truly?"
> "Truly," Rose tells him. "And you carried the *light* of it. Remember that."
> *(She climbs back to the daylight with the noise of the hall gone quiet behind her, and the house, whole and held, hums underneath her feet like something alive.)*

scenes.synopsis: Lavinia, departing — the final; the loyal's farewell. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The drive at noon, and Lavinia departing — the final farewell, the glittering's last. The carriage stands ready, the hatboxes loaded, the maid already inside with the air of a woman who has survived worse departures. Lavinia herself lingers on the steps, bright as ever, and not quite ready.)*
> "Darling." She takes Rose's hands — the glitter there, but thin now, the real voice underneath it like light under water. "The fête —" she stops — "the final brilliance, darling." She looks at the Park — the whole, the complete — then back at Rose. "The young —" another stop — "the young go, darling. Back to London. Back to —" she gestures vaguely — "the Season's thin end."
> "And you?" Rose asks.
> "I —" Lavinia stops, and the glitter drops entirely — the heartbeat's real, the true look held. "I am *tired*, darling." She says it plainly, no performance. "Ten seasons of glittering. It is —" she breathes — "enough. The loyalty, darling." The vow again, quieter. "Loyal —" the true look — "loyal, to the last. For the house, darling." Her fingers tighten. "For *you*."
> *(She embraces Rose then — the real embrace, not the hostess's, fierce and brief — and Rose holds her, and the drive is very quiet, and the Park does not move.)*
> "The last brilliance, darling." Lavinia steps back, and the glitter comes up like a curtain — bright, practiced, perfect. "Mind the young for me. They are *yours* now, you know. The advance guard." She climbs into the carriage. From the window, the silver flash of her smile: "Be *glittering*, darling. Someone must."
> *(At the carriage door, Lavinia turns — the glitter bright, the real voice just underneath, the way light is underneath water.)*
> "Darling." Very low, for Rose alone. "The charter." She sees Rose's surprise and smiles — the true smile, unadorned. "Oh, I *know*. A house like this does not end with a fête. It *begins* with one." She squeezes Rose's hands once more. "Convene them, darling. Not the ton —" the glitter flashes — "the *young*. Convene them *annually*, and be —" the real voice, the last word — "be *loyal*."
> "Loyal," Rose promises. "To the last."
> "I *know*." Lavinia climbs in, and the door closes, and the silver flash of her smile is the last brilliance of the morning.
> *(The carriage rolls. Lavinia does not look back — she never looks back; it is her one superstition — and Rose stands on the steps until the dust settles, holding the farewell the way she holds everything: entered, accounted, and aching.)*

scenes.synopsis: the farewell — glittering, the last; the drive, the carriages. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The drive at one, and the farewells — the young departing in a long glittering line, the carriages called in order of precedence that no one observes. The young, in their dozens, all of Lavinia's dears, going back to London with the night still in their eyes.)*
> *(Rose stands on the steps and takes each farewell as it comes: the bell-laugh girl, curtsying so deep she nearly topples; the young man with more hair than sense, bowing over Rose's hand with sudden, surprising gravity; the drawing girl, pressing a folded paper into Rose's hand — another ballroom, more exploding suns.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The bell-laugh girl holds Rose's hands. "The oath." Very low. "We *meant* it. The terrace."
> "I know," Rose says. "Keep it the way you'd keep —" she searches — "a gown. Carefully. And wear it often."
> *(The girl laughs through something very like tears, and runs for her carriage, and the line moves on. The carriages roll down the drive in their dust, the wheels loud on the gravel, then softer, then gone around the bend where the oaks stand. The last brilliance, departing — the young carrying it back to the world.)*
> *(Letitia joins Rose on the steps as the last carriage rounds the bend — the quartermaster, the final count, the household book under her arm.)*
> "Carriages." She closes the book with the small decisive sound. "Fiddles. Candles." The hawk's eyes, warm. "One *fête*, darling. Final." She looks at the empty drive. "The young have gone. Lavinia has gone." A pause. "And we —" the warm look — "we remain. As is *proper*. Someone must keep the house they were all so *glittering* in."
> "The keepers," Rose says, "remain."
> "The keepers," Letitia agrees, taking her arm, "remain. Come inside, darling. The chocolate is *hot*, the morning is *ours*, and the household book —" the quartermaster's smile — "the household book has *room* for whatever comes next."
> *(They go in together, and the drive holds its emptiness behind them, the shape of everything that left it. Rose stays until the last dust settles, and the house receives its keepers without comment, the way houses do when they know.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE BRILLIANCE'S MEANING (what the brilliance meant: the youth, the loyalty, or the joy). The morning deepens; decide the meaning. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dawn on the drive, a week after the fête, and the brilliance asking its meaning. Rose walks alone — the carriages long gone, the dust settled, the gravel raked smooth by the gardeners — and the morning deepens around the last question the way the first dawn deepened around the west gallery in the first chapter: early, and not to be hurried.)*
> *(The youth: the advance guard's oath, the society with rules, the bell-laugh girl's four pages crossed out to a single line. If the brilliance meant the youth, it meant the future — the many, the convened, the going-on. But futures are unbuilt, and the brilliance — she saw it, she *held* it — was the now: the candles at their brightest, the waltz at its height, Lavinia in silver at the center of the breathing crowd.)*
> *(The loyalty: the oath on the terrace, the household book's margin, her own unentered images. If the brilliance meant the loyalty, it meant the keeping — the held, the sworn, the practiced. But the brilliance was never held. It was spent: Lavinia spending herself like candlelight, the ices with the champagne, the kiss on the girl's cheek. The brilliance was the given, gloriously, entirely, on purpose.)*
> *(The joy: the forty paces turning, the young demanding the waltz again, the small hours golden at the edges. If the brilliance meant the joy, it meant the dancing — the glittering, the beautiful, the night in motion. But the joy was the vehicle, not the cargo. Underneath it ran the true thing: the* I am tired, darling *in the small saloon, the hand stacked on hands on the terrace, the loyalty underneath the glitter like the drawing under the paint.)*
> *(She walks the drive's length and back, and the Park does its morning work around her — the strings going out, the gardeners at the beds, the house waking — and the question walks with her, unhurried, the way the first dawn walked with her in the west gallery.)*
> *(At the drive's end, where the oaks stand, she stops and looks back at the whole — the house, the Park, the morning's light — and decides what the brilliance meant: the youth who will carry it, the loyalty that will keep it, or the joy that carried it there. The answer goes into the morning like a coin into a purse — hers, and spent on purpose.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: youth, loyalty, or joy.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The brilliance's meaning:*
- **The youth** — *the future, meant.* The brilliance meant the youth — the young, the future. (Consequence: the meaning is the future's — but futures are unbuilt, and the brilliance was the now.)
- **The loyalty** — *the kept, meant.* The brilliance meant the loyalty — the loyal, to the last. (Consequence: the meaning is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the brilliance was the given.)
- **The joy** — *the danced, meant.* The brilliance meant the joy — the glittering, the danced. (Consequence: the meaning is the danced's — but danceds are nights', and the brilliance was the loyal's.)

scenes.synopsis: the Park, after — the whole, the quiet's; the brilliance's memory. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The west gallery at dawn, three days after the fête, and the Park holding its brilliance the way the sky holds yesterday's weather: as memory, not as storm. Rose walks the gallery before the household is up, and the portraits hang straight in the morning light.)*
> *(She counts, because she always counts — once for the sum, once for the nerve. The ballroom: restored to order, the candles out, the floor waxed. The terrace: swept, the orange trees back in their places. The kitchens: calm, the sovereignty intact. The household: rested, the keepers at their posts. The young: gone to London, sworn. Lavinia: gone — three days down the road, the last carriage.)*
> *(At the gallery's end, the window gives onto the drive, and the drive is empty, and the empty asks its old question — now that the brilliance is over, what is it for? — and this time Rose has the beginning of an answer. Something *annual*. Something convened on her terms. She turns the thought over the way she turns a coin, feeling for the true weight of it.)*
> *(In the library, she takes down the household book — not the fête's pages, the *new* pages, the blank ones at the back — and opens them on the desk. The charter. She has not written it yet. She has barely *thought* it. But the thought has the weight of a coin, true metal, and she turns it over: an annual house party and ball. Convened by her. On her terms.)*
> "Not joining the ton, darling." She hears Lavinia's voice — the glittering's last lesson, given at a carriage door. "Convening it." She looks at the heading a long moment — then closes the book, gently, the way one closes a door on a guest not yet arrived. *Not yet*, she thinks. *The charter will keep. The heading is the promise. The promise is enough, for this morning.*
> *(She walks back toward the stairs, and the gallery holds its beeswax smell, and the light does what light does in a finished room: it stays. On the library desk, under a closed cover, the next thing waits: two words, in ledger-hand, patient as dawn.)*

scenes.synopsis: the young, after — the advance guard, the future's; the loyal's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room, and a letter from London — the young, after, writing in the week following the fête. The bell-laugh girl again, the hand more confident already: the Season's thin end is somehow less thin, she writes; the twelve have formed a *society*, with rules; the first rule is loyalty, the second is glitter, the third is that no one may be dull at dinner.)*
> *(Rose reads it twice — the first time for the sense, the second time for the joy — and shows it to Letitia, who reads it once and snorts.)*
> "A society." The hawk's eyes gleam. "With *rules*. Darling, we have created a *monster*." She taps the letter. "The first rule is loyalty. *Lavinia's* rule. The girl has understood everything."
> "The advance guard," Rose says, "is organizing itself."
> "The advance guard," Letitia corrects, reaching for the household book, "is *institutionalizing* itself. There is a difference, darling, and the difference is *stationery*." She writes in the book's margin, in the small hand: *The young, after — the society, the rules. Loyalty, kept.* "They will need a patron, you know. Societies always do."
> "They have one," Rose says.
> "They have *two*." Letitia does not look up. "Lavinia, in spirit. And you —" the pen pauses — "in *fact*. The future's patron, darling. The keeping kind." She closes the book. "The young go on. That is the whole of it. They go on, and they take the loyalty with them, and one day —" she looks out at the Park — "one day they will convene things of their own, and we shall be the old guard, and we shall *complain* about the music."
> "Stationery." Rose seizes on it. "The difference between a society and a *mob* is stationery."
> "Precisely, darling." Letitia is already writing — the quartermaster's hand, swift. "I shall send the girl a *ream*. Hartwell paper. The watermark oak." She looks up, the hawk's eyes gleaming. "With a note. *From the patron*."
> "And what will the note say?"
> "It will say —" Letitia considers, pen poised — "it will say: *The first rule is loyalty. The patron approves. The second rule is glitter. The patron insists. The third rule —* " she writes it with particular satisfaction — " *no one may be dull at dinner. The patron will be watching.* "
> *(They laugh together, the aunt and the niece, and the morning's promise stands: the advance guard, going on, glittering, into whatever the peace turns out to be for.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, the glittering's — Rose, the morning's; the mistress, the loyal's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her bedroom at dusk, and Rose alone at the window in the evening's quiet after the morning's business. The Park lies beyond the glass, whole and dimming, and the room holds the day's last light the way a shell holds the sea.)*
> *(She sits in her petticoat, the fête's gown hung away, her hair still pinned from the morning's business, and does the accounting she always does when the house is quiet: the columns, the sums, the nerve. The fête: held, and paid for, and true. Lavinia: gone, and spent, and *enough*. The young: sworn, and writing, and going on. The loyalty: kept — as she chose, in the young, in the house, in herself, in whatever measure the night decided.)*
> *(But the ledger is not where she feels it. The ledger is where she *thinks* it. What she feels is an image she would never say aloud: Lavinia in the small saloon at half past three, the glitter gone, saying* I am tired, darling *— and the advance guard on the terrace, stacking their warm young hands on hers — and Augusta's old hand in hers, the rings, the weight — and the ballroom at midnight, the whole room breathing as one.)*
> *(She lets the images stand, unentered, unaccounted. Some things the household book cannot hold, and she is learning — at twenty-five, mistress of the finished whole — to let them stay unheld. The mistress, whole.)*
> *(She thinks of the charter heading, closed under its cover in the library —* The Hartwell Assembly *— and of Lavinia at the carriage door: *Convene them, darling.* The thought has the weight of a coin. She turns it over once more, feeling for the true metal: an annual house party and ball. Convened by her. On her terms. Not joining the ton. Convening it.)*
> *(The images stand, unentered — Lavinia in the small saloon, the stacked hands on the terrace, Augusta's rings, the ballroom breathing as one — and now, among them, the heading: two words, in ledger-hand, waiting. The mistress, whole — and underneath it all, the convener, not yet spoken aloud.)*
> *(Below, the Park's lamps are lit one by one, and the house settles into its evening order, and Rose sits at the window a while longer, watching the light go out of the sky and come on in the windows — the brilliance kept exactly where it belongs: in memory.)*

scenes.synopsis: the loyalty, kept — the final beat, the permanent; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library at night, and the loyalty kept — the final beat. Rose takes down the household book and turns to the fête's pages, and there it all is: the columns, the sums, the quartermaster's small hand in the margin —* Lavinia, the last brilliance. Paid in full.*)*
> *(She reads the pages the way she read Lavinia's letter at the chapter's start — twice, once for the sense, once for the person — and the keeping settles over her like the evening: as she chose, in the young who swore on the terrace, in the house that held the night, in herself, the woman who convened it all without ever quite hosting it.)*
> *(She writes one line more, in her own hand, under Letitia's: not a sum, not a column. A sentence, which the household book has never held before and will never hold again:)*
> *She gave the Season its last brilliance, and asked nothing for it. The books balance.*
> *(She turns the pages slowly — the columns, the sums, the quartermaster's marginalia — and each entry is a small lit window into the night: the candles; the fiddles; the ices, roses in ice, gone before the soup. The sums are large. The nerve — she checks, once for the sum, once for the nerve — is steady.)*
> *(She thinks of Lavinia's letter, weeks ago: the cream paper, the galloping hand, the pen underlining* brilliance *twice. She thinks of the reply she wrote —* yes *before anything else — and of the two columns, cost on the left, glory on the right. The glory column has overflowed its margins. Letitia will pretend to disapprove. Letitia has already framed the page in her mind; Rose can tell.)*
> *(She writes the sentence —* She gave the Season its last brilliance, and asked nothing for it. The books balance. *— and the nib scratches, and the ink shines wet, and for a moment the library is very quiet, the way the small saloon was quiet at half past three, the way the terrace was quiet under the stacked hands.)*
> *(She closes the book. The fête's heart goes into the Park's keeping, where stone and paper and memory do what they have always done: hold.)*

scenes.synopsis: the house, the loyal's — the Park, the glittering's memory; the whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Midnight, and the house walked in its own loyal hours, midnight and after. Rose takes a candle and walks the Park's state rooms the way she walked the west gallery at dawn in the first chapter: the ballroom, dark now, the chandeliers hung like sleeping bats; the dining room, the long table bare; the small saloon, where Lavinia sat at half past three with the glitter gone.)*
> *(She stands in the small saloon a moment, the candle held high, and the room gives back nothing but itself — chairs, curtains, the pianoforte closed. It does not need to give back more. The memory is not in the room. The memory is in *her*, entered, accounted, the one entry the household book will never see.)*
> *(The gallery next, the portraits in their dark order, Harrow's plan at the end — the Park drawn whole, every zone inked. She holds the candle to it and reads the date in Quill's clerkly script, and thinks of Lavinia's letter —* the final brilliance *— and of the charter she has begun to imagine — the annual thing, the convening, the Hartwell Assembly taking its first breath.)*
> *(At the bedroom door she sets the candle down and stands a moment in the dark, listening to the house. It gives back nothing but itself: the settled timber, the banked fires, the breathing of the keepers below stairs. It does not need to give back more.)*
> *(She thinks of the charter heading under its closed cover — two words, in ledger-hand — and of Lavinia's last lesson at the carriage door, and of the young, sworn, going on. The whole — the complete — held in the dark the way the day holds it in the light: entirely, and without effort.)*
> *(She walks home to bed through the sleeping house, the candle guttering, and the whole goes with her. At the bedroom door she blows out the candle, and the dark takes the house, and the house — she knows this the way she knows her own sums — keeps everything. The morning's light will find it all exactly where she left it.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's glittering report — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"Last night the young held their final brilliance at Hartwell Park, and the Gazette — having attended the glittering from the first — finds it loyal to the last. The advance guard salutes the house. The Season's joy, recorded."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (the glittering! recorded!), then the reckoning: the fête is pronounced loyal in print as well as in the night's light, and Bell has made the final brilliance permanent, which is Bell's way of making it last. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the brilliance the Gazette calls loyal is the brilliance that's true.* — remembered: *the lesson: the brilliance the Gazette calls loyal is the brilliance that's true.*
scenes.sting: Last night the young held their final brilliance at Hartwell Park, and the Gazette — having attended the glittering from the first — finds it loyal to the last. The advance guard salutes the house. The Season's joy, recorded.

scenes.synopsis: the charter — the Assembly's founding, begun; the annual convening, the imagined. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and she sits with the household book — the charter, begun — and the Hartwell Assembly takes its shape.)*
> *(She writes — the charter, the founding — the annual house party and ball, convened by her, on her terms: the Assembly's founding, begun.)*
> "The Hartwell Assembly." She writes the name — the charter's first line. "An annual —" she stops — "house party and ball. Convened —" another stop — "by me. On my terms." She looks at the Park beyond — the whole, the quiet's. "Not joining the ton, darling." She hears Lavinia's voice — the glittering's last lesson. "Convening it."
> *(The chapter closes on the charter — the household book, the begun — and the Season turns toward the Assembly: the annual convening, founded — and the Season holds its breath.)*
