scenes.synopsis: the year's turning — the rose's year; the garden, the seasons. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The walled garden in March, and the beds still wearing their winter straw — the Hartwell rose's row standing bare-caned and patient under a sky the color of wet slate. Rose walks it before the household is up, her boots leaving the first prints of the day in the damp path.)*
> *(The gardener's boy is already at work, raking back the mulch with a care that suggests he has been told exactly what hangs on each cane. She watches him a moment from the gate — the small, deliberate movements, the way he checks each bud as he uncovers it, the way the work is really a kind of listening.)*
> *(She counts the way she counts everything now: one year since the rose was budded onto its stock. One year since she stood here and chose the charter's flower. The ledger in her head turns its own page — planted, tended, wintered — and the arithmetic is simpler than any she has ever kept: wait, and watch, and do not rush.)*
> *(She kneels, heedless of the damp, and touches a cane the way Augusta taught her to touch accounts: firmly, and expecting an answer. The cane is alive under her thumb — green beneath the brown, stubborn as the family. She stands, brushes the straw from her skirts, and walks back to the house through the cold, already planning nothing — which is, for her, a kind of luxury.)*
> *(The head gardener comes up the path with the empty barrow, and he stops when he sees her kneeling in the damp, and his face does the complicated thing it does when the mistress is doing the boy's work.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." He touches his hat. "The year's plan, miss, if you've a moment. The manure for the rose bed — the well-rotted, from the home farm — and the new labels. The old ones have weathered past reading."
> "Order the manure. And have the labels cut fresh — boxwood, not pine. Pine rots."
> "Boxwood." He makes a note in his head, where he keeps everything. "And the Assembly's garden party, miss — the ton'll walk this row. Shall I —" he gestures at the bare canes — "shall I make it pretty, miss? Extra mulch, the edges trimmed sharp?"
> "Make it honest, not pretty." She stands, brushing the straw from her knees. "The ton can see a working bed. They've seen enough pretty."

scenes.synopsis: the spring — the buds, the year's; the tending, the gardeners'. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(April, and the head gardener has summoned her the way other men summon a magistrate — with a look across the breakfast room that says this cannot wait. She finds him in the rose bed with the pruning knife in his hand and the Hartwell rose's first buds fattening on the canes like small green promises.)*
> "Look at the graft, miss." He bends a cane toward her with the tenderness of a man handing over a child. "The join's healed proper. You can see where the bud's worked onto the stock — see? Clean. It wintered sound. The straw did its work, and the frost never bit deeper than the mulch."
> *(She looks where he points, and the scar of the grafting is a pale line, closed and firm, the bud above it swollen and certain. Two years ago she stood here and chose the charter's flower. Last spring she watched the boy rake back the straw. Now this.)*
> "How many?"
> "Eleven canes, thirty-four buds. I counted twice." The rarest smile cracks his weathered face. "It's the charter's, miss, so I counted a third time, to be sure."
> *(The boy comes with the new labels — boxwood, cut fresh, the old ones weathered past reading — and a hank of twine. He ties each label to its cane with a knot he checks twice, tongue out, and stands back.)*
> "Eleven canes," he announces. "Thirty-four buds, miss. I counted."
> "Twice?"
> "Three times, miss." He grins. "It's the charter's. To be sure."
> *(The head gardener inspects the boy's knots the way Augusta inspects a settlement, and finds one crooked, and re-ties it himself with the square knot, and the boy watches, and learns. Ten seasons the old man has watched her learn the garden's grammar. Today she is finally fluent.)*
> *(She walks the beds' length with him, and the buds are green and tight and absolutely certain of themselves, the way only young living things can be. The spring is doing what spring does in a walled garden: arriving all at once, everywhere, as if it had never been away.)*
> *(The thrush is arguing on the north wall, making the same case it made last year. She leaves the gardeners to the watering, and the April light does the rest.)*

scenes.synopsis: the tending — the garden's; the woman, the tending's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She comes back at noon with her gardening gloves on — the plain leather pair, not the kid — and the head gardener looks at her for a long moment, and then hands her the trowel without a word.)*
> *(The work is simple and it is not. She weeds the rose bed's edge, her hands in the cold loam, and the soil gets under her nails and up her sleeves, and somewhere in the third row her thoughts stop being a ledger and become something older: the rhythm of the work, the give of the earth, the small clean snap of a weed's root coming free.)*
> "Not too deep, miss." The gardener's boy, hovering. "The rose's roots run shallow. You'll want to —" he mimes the angle — "like that."
> "Like this?" She adjusts the trowel.
> "Yes, miss. Like that." He nods with the authority of fourteen years. "You've the hands for it."
> *(It is the nicest thing anyone has said to her all week. She works the row to its end, and the sun warms the back of her neck, and the Hartwell rose's canes stand over her work like a congregation. She thinks — the image she would never say aloud — of all the paper she has moved in ten seasons: settlements, charters, invitations. This is the first thing she has ever made with her hands that she cannot file. She likes the feeling more than she intends to admit.)*
> *(The midday bell rings from the stables, and the boy brings her water in a tin cup, and she drinks it standing in the row with the soil on her hands and her back aching in the honest way.)*
> "Miss." The boy hesitates. "The blisters — shall I fetch the salve?"
> *(She looks at her palms. The plain leather gloves have not saved her.)*
> "No." She flexes her hands. "Blisters are the receipt, boy. You pay for the garden in skin."
> *(He grins and goes back to his barrow, and she works the last of the row in the noon heat. When the head gardener inspects her weeding he nods — once — the way he nods at everything she does now, and she carries the nod back to the house like a verdict. Luncheon is cold, and Letitia scolds her, and she does not mind in the slightest.)*

scenes.synopsis: the summer — the blooming, the year's; the first, the promised. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(June arrives the way June always does at the Park — all at once, with the hayfields going gold and the bees working the garden like it owes them money. And in the rose bed, the first color shows: the Hartwell rose's buds swelling, the green giving way at the tip to something deeper, richer, not yet open.)*
> *(She finds the head gardener there before her, which does not surprise her. He is crouching beside the best bud, and he does not look up when she comes, because some moments are too private for looking up.)*
> "The first." He nods at the bud. "It's the promise kept, miss. Days now. Not weeks. Days."
> "It'll open when it's ready, I know. And not a day before."
> "Aye, miss." He straightens, and his knees crack, and he does not care. "Roses are like the ton. They bloom on their own terms."
> *(She laughs, because he said it to her once before, years ago, when the rose was only an idea. The bud is the size of a thumbnail and it is the most important thing in the Park. She bends to it, close enough to see the veins in the petal-tip, and the color there is — she has no word for it, which annoys her, because she has words for everything.)*
> *(She does not touch it. Some things you earn by not touching. The boy brings the watering can and pours with the ceremony of a priest, and the June light does the rest.)*
> *(She walks back to the house through the heat, and the whole garden hums behind her, and the promise of the thing is almost — almost — better than the thing.)*
> *(She comes back at dusk, unable to stay away, and the bud is fuller, the color deeper, the green nearly gone at the tip. The boy is there before her, caught in the act of checking it himself.)*
> "Miss." He goes red. "I was just — the watering's done, but I thought —"
> "You thought you'd keep an eye."
> "Yes, miss." He stands his ground. "It's the charter's, miss. Someone ought to."
> *(She gestures at the path, and they walk the row together, and he tells her about the bees — the hive by the orchard wall, the queen, the honey — with the authority of fourteen years. The bud holds the dusk light. She leaves the boy to his watch and goes in to dress for dinner, and the garden keeps the evening.)*

scenes.synopsis: Letitia, the blooming — the quartermaster, the rose's; the strategy, the flower's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia finds her in the rose bed at the height of the morning, and the aunt stands at the gate in her garden hat with the household book tucked under her arm like a weapon.)*
> "Darling." The hawk's eyes sweep the beds. "Do you know what it costs to keep a rose bed? I do. I have the figures." She taps the book. "Manure — the well-rotted, four loads from the home farm. Straw for the winter. The boy's wages —" she names a figure that makes Rose blink — "the knife-sharpening, the twine, the boxwood labels."
> "You sound like you're building a case."
> "I am always building a case, darling. That is the whole of being me." The warm look. "And the case here is this: it is worth every penny, which is not a sentence I say often."
> "You say it about the kitchens."
> "I say it about nothing, darling, and you know it." She bends — careful of her skirts — and puts her nose to a bud, and her face does something entirely unguarded. "Oh. Oh, that's going to be magnificent."
> *(Rose watches her aunt breathe in the future, and the household book hangs forgotten at her side. Even Letitia, quartermaster of everything, has been conquered by a bud.)*
> *(Letitia opens the book then and there, balancing it on the gate, and does the arithmetic aloud with her pencil, and underlines the return twice: a flower that exists nowhere else on earth, the ton walking the row at the Assembly, and the Gazette writing it up. She snaps the book shut.)*
> "And it costs less than the kitchens spend on ices in a week." She pats Rose's cheek, leaving a smudge of pencil lead. "A sound investment, darling. The quartermaster has spoken."
> "Darling." The aunt stops at the terrace steps. "When it opens — the first bloom — I want to be here. Not told about it. Here."
> "You shall be."
> "Good." The smudge stays there all through luncheon, and nobody mentions it, which is the household's whole protocol for Letitia. By supper it has faded to a grey ghost, and Rose has decided to leave it there a little longer.

scenes.synopsis: Augusta, the blooming — the Dowager, the rose's; the line, the flower's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta comes at the hour she always comes to the garden — late afternoon, when the light is honest — and she walks the rose bed's length with her stick and her spectacles and the particular stillness of a woman who has waited a very long time to be unsurprised.)*
> "The bloom." She stops before the best bud. "The rose's." She bends — seventy-two years bending — and looks at it through her spectacles with the attention she once gave to settlements. "The charter's flower —" the voice does something extraordinary, something soft at the edges — "the line's flower, child."
> "Grandmama."
> "I have seen roses come and go in this garden for sixty years, child." She straightens with effort, and Rose moves to help and is waved off. "Your grandfather planted the first Hartwell bed. Your father let it go to briar. Rackham —" a pause — "Rackham would have sold the soil if he'd found a buyer." She looks at the bud. "And now this. The legacy, child. Yearly."
> *(Rose watches the Dowager's face, and Augusta pretends not to be moved, which is the Dowager's entire philosophy of tenderness. But her hand — the old, ringed hand — rests on the cane a moment longer than botany requires.)*
> "It will be beautiful, Grandmama."
> "Of course it will be beautiful, child. It is ours." The spectacles rise. "See that it opens where the ton can see it. A victory no one witnesses is a rumor. A rose no one witnesses is —" the rarest smile — "merely a rose."
> *(They walk back toward the house together, slowly — Augusta's pace, the stick tapping the gravel — and the Dowager talks, which she does rarely, and only in gardens.)*
> "Your grandfather's rose bed stood where the potting shed is now." The stick taps. "The old Hartwell rose — not this one, the one before. Damask. Scented like —" she stops — "like a church, child. He cut one for me every June, without fail, for forty years. Your father let the bed go to briar in a single season. Men." The spectacles lower. "They build, and they neglect, and they call it fate."
> "And we, Grandmama?"
> "We tend, child." The rarest smile. "Mulch, wait, trust. Your gardener's whole philosophy in three words, and sounder than any settlement I ever signed."
> *(They reach the terrace, and Augusta stops, and looks back at the rose bed — the buds, the row, the kept year standing in the afternoon light.)*
> "And Rose —" at the door, without turning — "it will be beautiful. I have seen sixty Junes in that garden. I know."
> *(The door closes. The stick taps down the corridor. The Dowager has spoken, and the garden keeps the verdict.)*

scenes.synopsis: the autumn — the cutting, the year's; the gardeners', the tending. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(October, and the garden has turned the color of old gold. The head gardener is waiting by the rose bed with the pruning knife and the year's reckoning in his face, and the Hartwell rose's canes — spent now, the season's glory gone to hips and leaf-fall — stand ready for their rest.)*
> "Cut back hard, miss." He touches his hat. "The rose wants its sleep, and the sleeping's half the blooming. You know that now."
> "I know that now." Ten seasons of watching have taught her what no book could: the garden keeps a different calendar than the ballroom, and it does not negotiate.
> *(He works with the knife, and the cuts are clean and sure, and the canes fall in neat bundles. The boy gathers them. She holds the basket, because there is no rank in October, only the work.)*
> "Mulch, wait, trust." The old man wipes the blade. "It's the whole of gardening, miss. Mulch, wait, trust."
> *(She carries the basket of cuttings to the compost, and the garden smells of leaf-mold and coming rain. The cuttings go on the bonfire behind the potting shed, and the smoke rises straight in the still air, and the garden smells of burning rosewood — sharp, sweet, final.)*
> *(The straw waits in the cart. They tuck the bed together, neat handfuls, the gardeners' whole philosophy in the doing of it. The rose is asleep. The year has been kept.)*
> *(The basket of hips goes over her arm — the gardener's wife will make syrup — and the boy walks with her to the still-room door, carrying the straw.)*
> "Miss." He hesitates. "Next year — will it be bigger? The blooming?"
> "The head gardener says roses remember the tending."
> "They do, boy." The old man doesn't look up from the straw. "And this one's been tended. You'll see."
> *(She stays till the fire burns low, and walks back to the house through the falling leaves, and the mulch-wait-trust of it settles into her like a lesson she has finally learned, and the bones are content. Behind her, the garden folds itself for winter, and it knows exactly what it is doing.)*

scenes.synopsis: the winter — the sleeping, the year's; the garden, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(December, and the walled garden is a study in white. Snow lies on the straw mulch, and the Hartwell rose's canes — pruned, tucked, sleeping — are small dark lines against it, like writing on a clean page.)*
> *(She walks the bed's length alone, her breath making brief clouds in the still air. The garden is at its most honest now: nothing blooming, nothing promised, nothing to be admired. Just the kept ground, and the kept rose, and the kept year.)*
> *(She thinks of the drawer she cannot open by force. The rose is dreaming under the straw — she knows it the way she knows the house's moods, which is to say she knows it without evidence and is never wrong. Somewhere under the snow, the roots are doing the winter's slow work, and no one can hurry them, and no one needs to.)*
> *(A robin follows her down the row, hopeful. She has nothing for it. The garden in winter gives nothing away — it keeps, and that is enough. She stands a long time at the row's end, looking at the sleeping canes, and the cold gets into her boots, and she does not mind.)*
> *(The image comes uninvited, as her real thoughts do: the rose is the one thing she has made that does not need her. The house needs her. The Assembly needs her. The rose only needs the seasons, and the seasons keep their own counsel. She walks back through the snow, and the prints of her boots are the only writing on the page, and the garden keeps its counsel too.)*
> *(The head gardener comes down the path with extra straw on the barrow, and he stops when he sees her, and touches his hat.)*
> "Miss Hartwell. The hard frost last night — I thought the bed might want another layer. The canes are sound, but there's no harm in —" he pats the straw — "in being certain."
> "Be certain." She steps aside. "I'll watch."
> "The dreaming, miss." The old man straightens, brushing straw from his coat. "The rose dreams under there. You can feel it, if you put your hand down. Warm. Like a sleeping dog."
> *(She puts her hand down into the straw, and it is warm — impossibly, against all the cold — and she looks up at him, and he nods, and neither of them says anything, because some things are too true for talking.)*
> *(She leaves him to the barrow, and walks back through the snow, and the warmth stays in her palm all the way to the house, like a kept secret.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE ROSE'S LESSON (what the rose teaches: the patience, the tending, or the returning). The year deepens; decide the lesson. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year turns, and the rose asks its lesson in the plain evidence of the seasons. Rose walks the walled garden in the year's late light, and the bed is mulched and waiting, and the question sits in her the way the dusk sits on the lawn: early, and not to be hurried.)*
> *(The head gardener's boy has left the watering can by the gate, and the labels are all tied square, and the straw lies neat over the sleeping canes. Everything in its place. The garden in late light is the most orderly thing she owns, and she walks it the way Augusta walks an account — slowly, and expecting it to add up.)*
> *(Patience, the gardeners say — mulch, wait, trust, forty years with a pruning knife in the hand. Tending, her own hands say — the blisters, the soil still under her nails from October, the noon rows worked in the leather gloves. Returning, the rose itself says — it came back from winter, and it will come back again, because that is what roses do when they are kept.)*
> *(She thinks of the strongbox drawer she cannot force. She thinks of the ledger, and the boy's grinning arithmetic, and the head gardener's warm straw, and Augusta's ringed hand on the cane. The garden has taught her all three lessons. It does not care which she names first — but the naming matters, because the name will shape how she remembers the year, and the year is the one she is going to keep.)*
> *(The thrush is still arguing on the north wall. The dusk comes on, and the garden holds it, and the rose bed is a dark line under the straw. The question will not be hurried. She stands at the row's end until the light goes entirely, and then she turns for the house, and she decides the way she decides everything now: firmly, and for good.)*
> *(Behind her, the watering can stands by the gate where the boy left it, and the labels stir faintly in the evening air. The garden does not applaud a decision. It simply keeps what is given it, and waits, and trusts, and the lesson — whichever name she has given it — walks beside her up the path like a companion.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — The rose's lesson:*
- **The patience** — *the season, taught.* The lesson is patience — the waiting, the season. (Consequence: the lesson is the season's — but seasons are weather's, and the rose is the tended.)
- **The tending** — *the hands, taught.* The lesson is tending — the hands, the gardeners. (Consequence: the lesson is the hands' — but hands are workers', and the rose is the year's.)
- **The returning** — *the yearly, taught.* The lesson is returning — the year, the yearly. (Consequence: the lesson is the yearly's — but yearly's are time's, and the rose is the bloomed.)

scenes.synopsis: the second spring — the buds, the returning; the lesson, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The second spring arrives, and the garden does not bother with ceremony. One morning the straw is raked back, and there are the buds again — green, fat, certain — the Hartwell rose beginning its year as if the winter had been a rumor.)*
> *(She walks the row with the head gardener, and he is trying not to look proud, and failing.)*
> "It remembers, miss." He touches a bud the way other men touch money. "Roses remember the tending. You can see it in the canes. Strong. Eager." He stops, embarrassed by his own poetry. "It remembers."
> *(She bends to the best of them, and it is already showing the year's ambition — the green splitting, the color waiting underneath. The lesson she named in the late light sits in her like a kept promise, and she does not say its name aloud. Names are for choosing, not for talking about. She straightens, and the spring air is full of the garden's business, and the year begins again.)*
> *(The boy runs past with the watering can, late as always, grinning. The thrush is back on the north wall, making the same argument as last year. The year's first bumblebee finds the row by midmorning, and the boy announces it like a herald.)*
> "Miss! The first bee! On the charter's row!"
> *(The head gardener inspects the labels, and finds one tied crooked, and re-ties it himself with the square knot, and the boy watches, and learns. Some instruction is never finished, only repeated.)*
> *(She walks the row once more before going in — the buds, the labels, the bee — and the garden is the proof of whatever she decided. The rose came back because it was kept. She goes in with the spring on her boots, and the breakfast bell is ringing, and everything — for once — is exactly on time.)*
> *(At the terrace door she stops and looks back, the way she has done every spring since she was a girl. The row stands green and certain in the morning light, and the boy is already late with the watering can, and the old man is already finding fault with the knots. Nothing has changed. Everything has changed. She carries the spring into the house on her boots and leaves it in the hall for Mrs. Quick to sweep up, which the housekeeper does with the air of a woman disposing of evidence.)*

scenes.synopsis: Julian, the rose — the free man, the flower's; the terrace, the blooming. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She finds him in the rose garden at the hour when the light goes gold — Julian, standing before the Hartwell rose's row with his hands in his pockets, looking at the buds the way he used to look at the terrace: like a man measuring something he is afraid to want.)*
> "The charter's flower." He does not turn. He touches a bud, gently, with one finger. "The only thing here that doesn't know who I was. It only knows who I am now. That's —" he stops — "that's restful, Rose."
> "You come here often?"
> "Most mornings." The unguarded look, the garden's light on it. "The terrace is yours, and the house is yours, and the whole Park is yours —" the ghost of the old smile — "but the rose is neutral ground. It has no opinions about mended gloves."
> *(He takes the mended gloves from his pocket — the gloves, mended years ago, kept ever since — and turns them over in his hands the way he always does when he is thinking about the free life.)*
> "The last of the brother's debts. Paid in March. With money I earned." The direct look. "Your money never touched it — you'll have Quill check, I know. Have him check."
> "I won't."
> "You will." The ghost of the smile again, warmer now. "It's your nature. It's why the rose blooms."
> *(They stand together in the gold light, and the garden holds them the way it holds everything: without judgment. He does not offer his arm. He offers his company, which is rarer, and she takes it.)*
> *(They walk to the terrace together, slowly, and the Park lies below them — the lake, the woods, the whole kept year — and Julian stops at the terrace's edge the way he always does, like a man who has finally been given permission to look. "Free," he says quietly. "The terrace. The gloves. All of it. Nearly." The word hangs in the gold light, and he does not take it back, and she does not ask him to. Nearly is honest. Nearly is further than he has ever got.)*
> *(The gloves go back in his pocket. The light fails. They walk back through the gold light together, and neither of them hurries.)*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent, the rose — the Englishman, the flower's; the unmasked, the blooming. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Laurent finds her at the rose bed the next morning, and he is carrying two cups of chocolate from the kitchens, which he presents with the gravity of an ambassador delivering terms.)*
> "The charter's flower." He hands her a cup. The English, now, entirely — no accent worn like a mask, no polish laid on like varnish. "You speak of it like a person, I know. It is more reliable than most persons."
> "You speak English like you mean it, these days."
> "I do mean it." He drinks. "The garden is the one place in England where I do not have to be French or English. I can just be —" he searches — "the man who brings the chocolate."
> *(She laughs, and he looks pleased in the unguarded way that still surprises them both. Ten seasons of the polished Frenchman, and underneath it all along was this: a man who notices buds, and brings chocolate, and speaks English like he means it.)*
> "I have decided —" he stops, because Laurent never announces decisions; he arrives at them — "that the garden is my favorite room in your house. Do not tell the ballroom. It would be wounded."
> *(He looks at the buds for a long moment, and then he says, in French so perfect it hurts, "Elle sera magnifique" — and then, catching himself, he grins.)*
> "She will be magnificent. In English." He bows to the rose, solemn as a courtier. "Even my French has stopped performing, these days."
> "Your French never performed, Laurent. Only you did."
> "Ah." He considers this. "You are right, and I am annoyed, which means you are very right." The direct look. "The Assembly's garden party — I shall stand by this row and tell the ton about the grafting. In English. Badly. They will be charmed."
> "They will be terrified."
> "Also good." He takes her hand, and his is warm from the chocolate cup, and the morning is simple and complete. The mask is off — permanently, this time. She holds him to it with a look, and the chocolate is finished, and the morning does what mornings do at the Park now: it behaves.)*

scenes.synopsis: Octavia, the rose — the painter, the flower's; the precise, the blooming. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Octavia comes to the rose garden with her sketchbook, which she does the way other people come with a parasol — as a matter of course — and she stands before the Hartwell rose's row for a long time without opening it.)*
> "I have painted you angry, afraid, triumphant, exhausted, laughing —" a look — "but I have never painted the thing you made. The rose." The precise voice, quiet. "I mean to try."
> *(She sketches with quick, sure strokes, and Rose watches the rose become lines — the canes, the buds, the architecture of the thing — and it strikes her that Octavia is the only person she knows who looks at the world the way she looks at ledgers: exactly, and without flinching.)*
> "The bud there." Octavia nods at it, not looking up. "The one about to open. That is the one the portrait wants."
> "The portrait gets what it wants, does it?"
> "Always." The precise voice, warm. "Two houses, one shared life, Rose. That was the arrangement. The rose is my half of it too, now."
> *(She closes the book and they walk the row together, and the painter sees the garden the way the gardener sees it: as a work in progress that is already perfect.)*
> *(Octavia turns the sketchbook so Rose can see — the rose in quick, sure lines, the bud about to open caught at the exact moment before — and it is so true that Rose laughs aloud.)*
> "The color." Octavia frowns at the bud. "I cannot get it in the book. It will need the oils. The bud there — the one about to open — that is the one."
> "And the portrait gets what it wants."
> "Always." She closes the book. "It is hung in the gallery, Rose. The laugh. And the flower before it." The precise smile. "I see what is there, Rose. That is the whole of painting."
> *(They stand together in the morning garden — the painter, the mistress — and the bud waits, and the portrait waits, and Octavia has already seen what the rest of them will have to wait for. The sketchbook closes with a small, definite snap, and the garden gets on with its business around them.)*

scenes.synopsis: Henry, the rose — the soldier, the flower's; the devotion, the blooming. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Henry rides over with the morning post, as he does most mornings, and today the post bag is not the excuse — he says so himself, which is new.)*
> "I came to see it." He dismounts at the garden gate, and the smallest smile is already there. "The Hartwell rose. The post —" he holds up the bag — "the post is the excuse today. Usually it's the other way around."
> *(She laughs, and he looks pleased, and they walk the row together with the horses cropping the grass beyond the wall.)*
> "The small things continue." He straightens — the soldier's habit, even in a garden. "The watering, the watching, the waiting. The head gardener says I have the hands for it. High praise. From a gardener, that is —" he considers — "the equivalent of a commendation."
> *(They stop before the best bud, and he looks at it with the attention he gives to everything: complete, and without hurry. The devotion in him is the quietest thing in the Park — the daily riding over, the sorted post, the small things practiced on purpose.)*
> "It'll open soon," he says.
> "Days."
> "Then I'll ride over." He mounts, and the post bag goes over the saddle. "I mean to be here when it does. Some things —" he looks at her, and the smallest smile does the rest — "some things you don't read about in a letter."
> *(She watches him ride down the drive — the straight back, the easy seat — and the morning does what mornings do at the Park now: it behaves. She unfolds the top letter from the bag and reads it standing on the path.)*
> "'The Hartwell rose,'" she reads aloud to no one. "'We have heard of the bud. The ton awaits the blooming.' London, Henry's sorting — the interesting at the top."
> *(She folds the letter and keeps it. The horses crop beyond the wall. The rose is returning, and the soldier is returning, and the small things continue, and the continuing is the whole of it.)*
> *(And it is enough. She has learned, these ten seasons, to let enough be enough — a harder lesson than any of the garden's, and one the head gardener could never have taught her.)*

scenes.synopsis: the second summer — the blooming, the returning; the lesson, the bloomed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The second summer comes in hot, and the Hartwell rose does not disappoint. The buds open — one, then three, then a dozen — and the row is suddenly a corridor of color, and the garden smells of the rose the way the kitchens smell of bread: essentially, and from a distance.)*
> *(She walks it at dawn, before the heat, and the blooms are heavy with dew, and the petals hold the light. The lesson she named in the winter sits in her like a kept promise — she does not say its name; the garden is the proof of it, written in flowers — and the year begins its middle, and the middle is holding.)*
> *(The head gardener is already there, of course. He is standing in the middle of the row with his hands behind his back, looking at the blooms the way a father looks at a christening.)*
> "The second summer, miss." He does not turn. "It knows what it's doing. You can see it. Kept roses —" he stops, because gardeners do not make speeches — "they remember, miss. That's all."
> "It's beautiful."
> "It is." He allows himself the admission.
> *(She cuts nothing. She only looks — the blooms, the bees working them, the way the color deepens at the petal's edge. She walks back to the house through the heat, and the scent follows her.)*
> *(She cuts for the house at noon — the head gardener nodding permission — and the blooms go into vases in the saloon, the morning room, the gallery. Mrs. Quick inspects each one with the air of a general reviewing troops.)*
> "The house, miss." The immovable mouth does something nearly warm.
> *(The servants' hall gets its own bloom, on the dresser, and the footmen pretend not to notice it, and notice it all the same. The scent comes through the open windows on the heat, and the whole house smells of the rose. She walks back through the heat with the empty basket, and the garden hums behind her, and the middle of the year is holding, and holding, and holding.)*

scenes.synopsis: the cutting — the flower's; the house, the flowered. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She comes to the rose bed at dusk with the secateurs, and the head gardener sees what she means to do and steps back, and the boy holds the basket.)*
> *(She chooses the best bloom — the one Octavia sketched, the one Henry rode over to see open — and she cuts it clean, low on the stem, the way she was taught. The bloom comes away in her hand, and it is heavier than she expected, and the scent rises off it like something released.)*
> "The house, miss?" The boy holds the basket.
> "Not yet." She holds the bloom up to the dusk light. "First I want to look at it."
> *(She looks. The Hartwell rose, open: the petals layered the way Élise layers silk, the color deep at the heart and pale at the edge, the whole flower a small, perfect argument for the charter. She has grown this — her hands, her gardeners, her year — and the pride of it is clean and uncomplicated, which is rare in her life.)*
> *(She lays it in the basket with the care of a woman laying a child in a cradle. The garden holds the dusk. The cut stem weeps a single drop. She walks back to the house with the basket, and the bloom rides in it like a passenger.)*
> *(The still-room, and she sets the basket down, and the bloom lies among the cut stems like a queen among courtiers. Letitia appears in the doorway, drawn by the scent.)*
> "Darling." The hawk's eyes widen. She bends to the bloom. "Oh. Oh, that's —" she stops, because even Letitia is sometimes without words.
> *(Together they put it in water — the small Sèvres, the cool still-room — and the bloom stands in it like a small sun. The boy hovers in the doorway, proud as a father.)*
> "You've done well, boy." Letitia pats his shoulder. "The quartermaster has noted it."
> *(He goes red to the ears and flees, grinning. The still-room smells of roses and oranges. The cut stem weeps its single drop into the water, and the evening holds its light, and the light holds the bloom.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Dowager, the cut flower — Augusta, the bloomed; the line, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta is in her morning room with her letters, and Rose comes in with the basket, and the Dowager looks up over her spectacles and sees the bloom, and something in her face changes before she can stop it.)*
> *(Rose lays the cut bloom before her, and Augusta takes it — the old, ringed hand, careful — and holds it up to the light.)*
> "The charter's flower —" the voice does something extraordinary, something soft at the edges — "the line's flower, child."
> "It's for you, Grandmama."
> "I know it is, child. I am not stupid." But she holds the rose a moment longer than ceremony requires, and she bends to it — seventy-two years bending — and breathes it in, and Rose sees what she is not supposed to see: the Dowager, moved, in her own morning room, in daylight.
> *(Augusta rings for a vase, and the maid brings the small Sèvres, and the rose goes into water on the desk among the letters. The Dowager looks at it for a long moment, and then she looks at Rose.)*
> "Your grandfather planted the first Hartwell bed," she says quietly. "He would have —" she stops, because Augusta never finishes sentences about the dead when she can let the living do it. But her hand rests near the vase, and that is the whole of it.
> "Your grandfather," the Dowager says, not looking up from her letter, "cut one for me every June, without fail, for forty years. I have told you this."
> "You have, Grandmama."
> "I am telling you again." She dips the pen. "See that Honoria sees it, when she comes. The dragon's daughter should know what the line grows."
> *(Rose laughs — she cannot help it — and Augusta's mouth does the extraordinary thing, and the rose blooms between them on the desk like a small, pink treaty.)*
> *(She leaves the Dowager with her letters and her rose, and the morning room holds its light, and the line keeps the flower, and Rose carries the Dowager's pleasure down the corridor with her like a warm coin.)*
> *(In the gallery she stops at the window and looks out at the walled garden, and the thought comes to her whole and uninvited: the grandfather planted, the father let go to briar, Rackham would have sold the soil. And the granddaughter — the granddaughter grew something new, and cut it, and brought it indoors, and the Dowager held it like a treaty. Forty years of June roses, and now this one. The line, it turns out, can learn a new flower.)*

scenes.synopsis: Letitia, the cut flower — the quartermaster, the bloomed; the strategy, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Letitia is in the still-room, decanting something that smells of oranges, when Rose comes in with the second bloom. The aunt looks up, sees the rose, and puts down the decanter with the air of a woman abandoning strategy for joy.)*
> "Darling." The hawk's eyes, the house's light on them. She takes the bloom. "Oh." She breathes it in. "The charter's flower — darling."
> "It's for the household book," Rose says solemnly. "I thought it should be pressed between the pages. For the accounts."
> "For the —" Letitia stares, and then she laughs — the real laugh, the one that shakes the still-room shelves. "Darling! You know what this costs? Nothing. This one is free. The garden gives it, and the giving is the whole of the accounts."
> *(She finds the household book, and together they lay the rose between blotting paper — the year's accounts, the flower pressed flat among the figures. Letitia writes in the margin, in her best hand: the first bloom. The ink is barely dry before she has drawn a small, perfect rose beside it.)*
> *(The pressing takes the afternoon — the rose between the blotting paper, the household book weighted with the estate ledger — and Letitia supervises like a general.)*
> "And the cost, darling —" she taps the page — "nothing. This one is free. The garden gives it."
> "The quartermaster approves of free?"
> "The quartermaster, darling, approves of value." She touches the pressed petals, gently. "And this is beyond value. Which is why it goes in the book. So the accounts remember what the money can't buy."
> *(They close the book together, and the rose is pressed flat among the figures. The still-room smells of oranges and roses.)*
> *(Letitia runs a finger down the page's columns — the manure, the straw, the boy's wages, all the honest costs of the year — and shakes her head at the arithmetic of it.)*
> "Do you know, darling, I have kept this book for ten years, and it has never once balanced on the side of joy." She looks at the pressed rose in the margin. "It balances today. The quartermaster will allow herself the observation, and then she will never make it again."
> "Darling." Letitia at the door. "You did that."
> "We did that, Aunt."
> "We." The hawk's eyes, warm. "The quartermaster accepts the correction."
> *(The door closes. The book holds the rose. The still-room smells of oranges, and the afternoon is entirely theirs.)*

scenes.synopsis: the portrait's flower — the hung, the bloomed; the painted, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The portrait hangs in the west gallery now — Octavia's picnic portrait, finished at last: Rose, laughing, the Park behind her, the paint dry and the laugh caught forever. And before it, in the small Sèvres vase, the third bloom.)*
> *(She stands before it alone, and the bloom is a small, deliberate offering — the painter's flower before the laugh's portrait. Octavia's precise eye has done what it always does: seen truly. The woman in the painting is laughing the way she laughed at the picnic, the way she has not laughed in years, the way the rose blooms: without permission.)*
> *(A housemaid passes with a duster and bobs at the portrait, unselfconscious. The gallery holds its beeswax smell. The laugh holds its light. The flower holds its color. She stands a long time, and the portrait looks back at her — the almost-laugh, the caught joy — and she understands that the legacy is not the stone or the charter. It is this: the laugh, the rose, remembered.)*
> *(Octavia comes to the gallery at noon, and sees the bloom before the portrait, and stops dead — the precise woman, arrested.)*
> "The portrait's flower." She goes to it. She looks from the rose to the painting — the laugh, the caught joy — and back. "It is right. The flower belongs to the laugh."
> "You approve?"
> "I approve." She adjusts the vase by a quarter inch. The precise voice, warm. "The truest thing."
> *(They stand together before the portrait — the painter, the mistress — and the gallery holds its beeswax smell, and the laugh holds its light, and the flower holds its color.)*
> *(A housemaid passes with a duster and bobs at them both, unselfconscious. Octavia nods back, grave as a duchess. Rose bites her lip to keep from laughing, and the portrait laughs for all of them, caught forever in oils.)*
> *(They walk the gallery's length together, and Octavia stops at the empty place where the next portrait will hang — there is always a next portrait with Octavia, the way there is always a next season with the garden — and looks at the wall the way she looked at the row: measuring, exact, already painting it in her head.)*
> "Not yet," Octavia says, seeing the question. "The rose first. The laugh first. Everything in its season, Rose. You taught the garden that. The garden taught it back to me."

scenes.synopsis: the ballroom's flower — the forty paces', the bloomed; the danced, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The ballroom at noon: forty paces of polished floor, the chandeliers dressed, the windows giving onto the terrace. And on the windowsill, in a plain glass, the fourth bloom.)*
> *(She stands in the room's center and looks at it, and the flower is absurdly small against the grandeur, and absurdly right. She walks the floor's length, counting her steps the way she counts everything. Forty paces. The room is forty paces of polished possibility, and the rose on the sill is the promise of it: the ball will come, the Assembly will dance here, and the flower will be the witness.)*
> *(The image comes uninvited: the ballroom full, the candles lit, the Hartwell rose on every table — her flower, her house, her people. She does not smile — she is alone, and there is no one to perform for — but something in her eases.)*
> *(She leaves the bloom on the sill and goes to dress for dinner, because even houses with roses in the ballroom keep dinner hours. Mrs. Quick finds her there, and the housekeeper looks at the bloom on the sill, and then at the forty paces, and then at Rose.)*
> "The ballroom's flower, miss." The immovable voice, nearly warm.
> "The charter's dance's rose, Mrs. Quick."
> "When the Assembly dances here, miss —" she stops, because housekeepers do not dream aloud — "the flower will be the witness, miss."
> *(They stand together in the noon light — the mistress, the keeper — and the ballroom holds its forty paces, and the sill holds the rose.)*
> "The silver's polished, miss. The linen's pressed twice. The house is ready."
> "The house is always ready, Mrs. Quick. That's the whole of it."
> *(The immovable mouth does the extraordinary thing. The chandelier holds the light. The flower holds the room. The dance's rose, forever.)*
> *(Alone again, she walks the forty paces one more time, slower now, and stops at the windowsill, and looks at the small pink bloom against the great polished emptiness. Somewhere in London, Lavinia is telling everyone who matters that the Hartwell rose is the only flower worth seeing this year. Somewhere at the Park, the gardeners are mulching and waiting and trusting, which is the whole of gardening. She touches the petal's edge with one fingertip — cool, exact, alive — and goes to dress for dinner, because even houses with roses in the ballroom keep dinner hours.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE BLOOM'S GIFT (where the first bloom goes: the Dowager, the house, or the portrait). The summer deepens; decide the giving. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The summer deepens, and the bloom asks its gift in the plain fact of its abundance. The row is full of open roses, and Rose walks it with the basket, and the season asks its plain question: where does the first bloom go?)*
> *(To the Dowager — seventy-two, who watched her grandfather plant the first Hartwell bed and her father let it go to briar, who holds her cut rose on the morning-room desk like a treaty. To the house — the stone, the whole, the rooms that held the blooming's promise all year, the ballroom's sill still holding the fourth bloom's plain glass. Or to the portrait — Octavia's laugh, caught in paint, waiting in the west gallery for its flower, the vase already standing empty before it.)*
> *(She holds the secateurs, and the garden holds its breath. The Dowager is the past. The house is the present. The portrait is the forever. She looks down the row — the blooms, the light, the kept year standing in flowers — and the gift will shape how the bloom is remembered, and the remembering will outlast them all.)*
> *(The head gardener watches from the gate, and he does not advise, because some decisions are the mistress's alone. The boy holds the basket, and he does not fidget, because even the boy understands the weight of it.)*
> *(The secateurs are cool in her hand. The best bloom waits on the cane like a held breath — the one the light loves, the one Octavia would have chosen. She cuts — clean, low on the stem — and the summer deepens around her, and she decides the way she decides everything now: firmly, and for good.)*
> *(The bloom comes away in her hand, heavier than she expected, the scent rising off it like something released. She looks at it for a long moment — the petals, the light in them, the whole argument of the charter written in pink — and then she turns for the house, and the giving begins. The Dowager's desk, the house's rooms, the portrait's wall: one of them is about to receive the first bloom, and whichever it is, the rose will not mind. Roses are like the ton. They bloom on their own terms, and they give on hers.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The bloom's gift:*
- **The Dowager** — *the line, flowered.* The first bloom goes to Augusta — the line's, the kept. (Consequence: the gift is the line's — but lines are past's, and the bloom is the year's.)
- **The house** — *the Park, flowered.* The first bloom goes to the house — the Park's, the flowered. (Consequence: the gift is the Park's — but Parks are vast's, and the bloom is the one.)
- **The portrait** — *the hung, flowered.* The first bloom goes to the portrait — the hung's, the forever. (Consequence: the gift is the hung's — but hungs are wall's, and the bloom is the living.)

scenes.synopsis: the giving — the gift, the given; the bloom, the placed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She gives it as she chose, and the placing is a small ceremony. The rose goes where she decided — the bloom, carried herself, because she will not trust it to a tray — and the garden watches her go.)*
> *(The head gardener sees the empty space on the row where the best bloom was, and he nods — once — the way he nods at everything she does now. The rose was cut for a purpose. The purpose was kept. The garden understands.)*
> *(She walks back through the beds with the empty basket, and the giving sits in her the way the dusk sits on the lawn: complete, and not to be hurried. The evening comes on, and the remaining blooms hold the light, and the row is still beautiful — the giving did not diminish it. That is the lesson of the gift, and it is a good one: a kept rose gives, and the giving does not cost it anything.)*
> *(The head gardener meets her at the gate as she comes back, and he looks at the space on the row where the best bloom was.)*
> "It was the right one, miss. The best of the row."
> "You don't know where it went."
> "Doesn't matter, miss." He touches his hat. "The row's still beautiful. That's the thing about a rose that's kept. It gives, and the giving's no loss to it."
> *(She leaves him to the watering, and walks back through the beds, and the placed bloom keeps its color wherever she put it — the Dowager's desk, the house's rooms, the portrait's vase, as she chose. She goes in to dress for dinner, and the garden keeps the dusk, and the dusk keeps the garden.)*
> *(At the terrace steps she stops and looks back at the row, and the empty space where the best bloom was is already invisible — the other blooms have shifted into it, the way water closes over a stone. That is the lesson of the gift, and she carries it up the steps with her: the giving cost nothing, and the garden is already whole again, already humming in the dusk.)*

scenes.synopsis: the second autumn — the cutting, the returning; the lesson, the rested. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The second autumn comes, and the garden turns gold again, and the head gardener is waiting with the pruning knife, and the Hartwell rose's canes — spent, glorious, done — stand ready for their rest.)*
> *(She works beside him this time, and her cuts are cleaner than last year, and he says so, which is the highest praise in the garden's language.)*
> "You've learned the whole of it, miss. There's gardeners of forty years as haven't."
> "Mulch, wait, trust."
> "Mulch, wait, trust." He almost smiles. "Aye."
> *(They mulch the bed together, and the straw goes down in neat handfuls, and the garden smells of leaf-mold and coming rain. The rose is asleep again. The year has been kept again. The returning is not a surprise anymore — it is a promise, and promises are meant to be kept, and this one has been kept twice.)*
> *(The hips go to the gardener's wife for syrup — the basket over Rose's arm, the dusk coming on — and the boy walks with her to the still-room door, carrying the straw.)*
> "Miss." He hesitates at the door. "Next year — the fourth year. Will I —" he stops — "will I still do the watering, miss?"
> "The rose row is yours, boy. Till you leave it."
> "I won't leave it, miss." He stands very straight. "It's the charter's, miss."
> *(She looks at him — fourteen, solemn, straw-dusted — and the image comes uninvited: the boy grown, the head gardener old, the rose still blooming. She nods, and he grins, and flees with the straw.)*
> *(The bonfire is lit behind the potting shed, and the year's cuttings go on it, and the smoke rises straight in the still air. She stays till it burns low — the sharp, sweet smell of burning rosewood, the garden folding itself for winter around her. Two autumns she has watched this fire. The first one she was still learning the garden's grammar. This one she could light herself.)*
> *(She walks back through the falling leaves, and the lesson she named is in her bones now, and the second autumn is the first autumn's echo, and the echo is sweeter than the sound, and the bones are content.)*

scenes.synopsis: the second winter — the sleeping, the returning; the garden, the dreamed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The second winter, and the snow comes early. The walled garden is white again, and the Hartwell rose sleeps under the straw, and Rose walks the bed's length in the still air with her breath making brief clouds.)*
> *(She has stopped worrying about the frost. The straw does its work. The rose does its. The garden keeps its counsel, and she has learned to keep hers. The robin is back on the north wall — the same robin, she likes to think, though she knows better. She has nothing for it. The garden in winter gives nothing away, and she has stopped asking it to.)*
> *(The image comes uninvited, as her real thoughts do: the rose dreaming under the snow, the roots doing the winter's slow work, the whole kept year folded into the dark like a letter. She stands at the row's end, and the cold gets into her boots, and she does not mind.)*
> *(The frost comes hard in the night, and she wakes to white, and the first thing she does — before the letters, before the household book — is walk to the walled garden.)*
> *(The head gardener is already there, laying the extra straw, and he looks up, and touches his hat, and neither of them is surprised to see the other. The rose is the household's first business in hard weather.)*
> "The extra layer'll see it through." He pats the straw. "You can feel it, if you put your hand down. Warm. Like a sleeping dog."
> *(She puts her hand down into the straw, and it is warm — impossibly, against all the cold — and she looks up at him, and he nods, and neither of them says anything, because some things are too true for talking.)*
> *(She leaves a crust of bread on the wall for the robin — the gardener pretends not to see — and walks back through the snow. The warmth stays in her palm all the way to the house, like a kept secret.)*
> *(In the hall she stops at the window and looks out at the white garden, and the lesson she named in the late light is still sitting in her, quiet and certain. Two winters the rose has slept under the straw, and twice she has stood here with the cold in her boots and the warmth in her palm. The drawer she cannot force, the ledger she cannot close, the ton she cannot command — none of them matter against this. The rose sleeps. The straw is warm. The year will come back, because that is what it does.)*

scenes.synopsis: the third spring — the buds, the returning; the rose, the eternal. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The third spring — and the garden does not bother with ceremony, because the garden never does. The straw is raked back, and the buds are there, and the Hartwell rose begins its year as if the winter had been a rumor and the autumn a dream.)*
> *(She walks the row with the head gardener, and he is not trying to hide his pride anymore, and she is not trying to hide hers.)*
> "Three years." He touches a bud. "It'll outlive us all, miss." He says it the way other men say grace. "That's the thing about a rose that's kept. It stops being a planting and starts being a fixture. Like the house. Like the stone."
> "Three years."
> *(She bends to the buds, and they are green and tight and absolutely certain, and the third spring has become the sound itself, not the echo. She straightens, and the spring air is full of the garden's business, and the year begins, and she is ready — she has always been ready; that was never the question.)*
> *(The new labels are tied — boxwood, the year's date burned in — and the cuttings along the terrace are putting out their first leaves, and the garden is all ambition.)*
> "The third spring." The old man looks down the row. "The charter's flower."
> *(The boy — not a boy anymore, quite; taller, surer — waters the terrace cuttings with the ceremony of a priest, and the head gardener watches him, and nods.)*
> "He's learned, miss."
> "He has."
> "It passes down." The old man looks at his own hands — knotted, scarred, forty years in the soil. "The tending. Like the house. Like the stone."
> *(She walks the row once more — the buds, the labels, the whole kept year standing green and certain — and the question was never whether she was ready. The question was whether the garden was, and the garden has answered.)*
> *(At the gate she looks back, and the boy is already arguing with the watering can, and the old man is already finding fault with a label, and the row stands behind them green and certain and entirely uninterested in ceremony. Three years. The charter's flower. She carries the spring into the house on her boots, and this time Mrs. Quick only sighs, which for the housekeeper is practically a welcome.)*

scenes.synopsis: the gardeners, the third year — the tending, the eternal; the hands, the year's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The head gardener finds her at the row's end with his hat in his hands, which he only does for serious business.)*
> "The third year, Miss Hartwell." He touches his hat, though it is already in his hands, which tells her how serious the business is. "The charter's flower —" he looks at the beds — "it's the whole Park's flower now, miss. And it's been kept. Properly kept."
> "You've kept it beautifully."
> "We've kept it, miss." He corrects her gently. He looks at her hands — the plain leather gloves, the soil under the nails that no amount of washing quite removes. "Your hands too, miss. Don't think we haven't noticed."
> *(It is the highest praise in the garden's language, and they both know it. The old gardener, the young mistress, the boy with the watering can hovering at a respectful distance — the Hartwell rose blooms behind them in the morning light, and nobody says anything for a while, because there is nothing to add.)*
> *(She walks back toward the house, and stops, and turns, because the business is not quite concluded — she can tell by the way he is still holding the hat.)*
> "Miss." The boy hesitates, and the old man nods him on. "The charter's flower — will it always be here? When I'm old?"
> "If it's tended, boy. That's the whole of it. Tended."
> "Then it'll always be here, miss." He stands very straight. "I'll see to it."
> *(He puts his hat on — the business is concluded — and he touches it to her, and goes back to the beds. The boy stays a moment, then follows, the watering can swinging.)*
> *(She watches them go — the old back, the young back, the certainty of both — and the image comes uninvited: the boy old, the rose still blooming, the tending passed down like the house. She carries it back to the house with her, and the morning holds its promise.)*
> *(In the hall she stops at the window and looks out at the walled garden one more time, and the thought sits in her the way the morning sits on the lawn: the gardeners have noticed her hands. Forty years of soil under the old man's nails, fourteen years under the boy's, and now hers, which no amount of washing quite removes. She has joined the only order that matters at the Park — the order of the tending — and she did it the way she has done everything: by showing up, and staying, and learning the grammar.)*

scenes.synopsis: the first bloom, the ending's — the rose, the promised; the legacy, the flowered. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(It comes on a June morning, the way the best things come — without announcement. She walks into the walled garden before the household is up, and there it is: the first bloom. The Hartwell rose, open.)*
> *(The bud she watched all spring has opened in the night, and the petals are layered the way Élise layers silk, and the color is deep at the heart and pale at the edge, and the scent rises off it in the cool air like something the garden has been saving.)*
> *(She stands before it for a long time. Ten seasons of scaffolding, and now this: a rose, open, hers. The head gardener arrives, sees it, stops dead. He does not speak. There is nothing to say that the rose has not already said.)*
> *(She bends to it — close, but not touching — and the image comes uninvited: the whole decade folded into this flower, the ruin and the war and the claim and the building, all of it answered by a bloom. The rose does not know about the entail. The rose does not care about the ton. The rose only knows the tending, and the seasons, and the return. She straightens, and the June light does the rest, and the first bloom holds the morning.)*
> *(She sends the boy for the household — the head gardener, Letitia, Augusta — and they come, and they stand around the bloom in the morning garden, and nobody speaks.)*
> *(The head gardener takes off his hat. Letitia puts her hand to her mouth. Augusta looks at the rose through her spectacles for a long time, and then she looks at Rose, and the Dowager's face does the extraordinary thing.)*
> "The first bloom." Augusta's voice is quiet. "The promise kept."
> *(The boy breathes — "Cor" — and Letitia laughs through her hand, and the head gardener puts his hat back on, and the morning holds them all around the small, perfect flower.)*
> *(She bends to it once more — close, but not touching — and the June light does the rest, and the first bloom holds the morning, and the morning holds them all, and nobody is in any hurry to leave.)*

scenes.synopsis: the bloom, the held — the first, the ending's; the woman, the flowered. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She holds it — the first bloom, the ending's rose — and the head gardener cuts it for her, low on the stem, and lays it in her hands, and it is heavier than she expected, and the scent is the garden's whole year in a single breath.)*
> "The held." He steps back. "Yours, miss."
> *(She holds the rose up to the light, and the petals hold the June sun. She thinks of the drawer she cannot open by force — and understands, finally, that she never needed to force it. The tending was the opening. The waiting was the key.)*
> *(The boy brings water in the small Sèvres vase, unasked. She sets the bloom in it, and the three of them stand around it in the morning garden like courtiers around a throne.)*
> *(She carries it back to the house herself — she will not trust it to a tray — and the bloom rides in the vase like a passenger. The corridors turn to look. A housemaid stops with the duster. A footman straightens. Mrs. Quick appears at the stairhead, and looks, and nods — once.)*
> "The held, miss." The housekeeper's voice is nearly warm.
> *(The library door, and she sets the vase on the desk — among the estate books, the bound Gazettes, Quill's sealed paper — and the Hartwell rose blooms there like a full stop.)*
> *(The boy hovers in the doorway, unasked and unforbidden, and she lets him stay. They look at the rose together — the mistress, the boy — and the bloom holds the light, and the light holds the room.)*
> "The promise, boy."
> "Kept, miss."
> *(She sends him back to the garden with a nod, and the bloom stays, and the morning stays, and the rose holds the desk the way the charter holds the house: completely.)*
> *(Alone, she looks at the bloom beside Quill's sealed paper — the flower beside the law — and the image comes uninvited: the charter written in ink, and the charter written in petals, and both of them hers. She does not touch the bloom. The gardener was clear, years ago: it opens when it is ready, and not a day before. It has opened. It is ready. The library holds its light, and the rose holds its color, and the morning is entirely hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the legacy — the yearly, the flowered; the charter, the bloomed. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She sets the vase on the library desk, among the estate books and the bound Gazettes, and the Hartwell rose blooms there like a full stop.)*
> *(The library holds the afternoon the way it holds everything: patiently, and as a promise kept. Quill's final paper lies sealed on the desk beside it — the house, hers beyond challenge, forever. The rose beside the paper. The flower beside the law. She looks at them together, and the image comes uninvited: the charter written in ink, and the charter written in blooms, and both of them hers.)*
> *(She does not touch the bloom. The gardener was clear, years ago: it opens when it is ready, and not a day before. It has opened. It is ready.)*
> *(Harrow comes to the library at noon with a paper for the archive, and he stops at the desk, and looks at the rose.)*
> "The legacy, Miss Hartwell." The scarred gentleman, exact. "History doesn't flinch, miss. That's its job. And the history'll say —" he looks at the bloom — "the history'll say the rose was the charter's flower. And it'll say it was kept. That's the whole of it, miss. It was kept."
> *(He bows — to her, to the rose, she isn't sure which — and goes back to his papers. The library holds the afternoon. The rose holds its color.)*
> *(She looks at the bloom beside Quill's sealed paper — the flower beside the law — and the thought comes to her whole: the paper says the house is hers beyond challenge, forever, Quill's word charged at nothing. The rose says the same thing, in a language the paper can't speak. She leaves them together on the desk, the law and the flower, and goes to walk the Park, because some afternoons ask for walking.)*
> *(On the terrace she stops and looks back through the library window, and there it is: the small pink bloom beside the great sealed paper, the two of them keeping each other company on the desk. Ten seasons she has fought for what is written in ink. It took a rose to show her that the ink was never the whole of it. The walk does her good. The Park is blooming. The light does what light does in a finished garden: it stays.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Park, the blooming — the whole, the flowered; the light. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She walks the carriage sweep in the June morning, and the Park holds its light the way the rose holds its bloom: completely.)*
> *(The head gardener has planted the Hartwell rose's cuttings along the terrace — the legacy, spreading — and the young plants stand in their rows, green and eager. The Park is the rose's ground now, not just the walled garden. She walks to the lake, and the water holds the morning, and the pavilion gleams, and the grounds are dressed. The rose's year has turned, and the Park has turned with it.)*
> *(A moorhen crosses the water, leaving its exact line. The sun is warm on her shoulders. She walks back to the house through the light, and the blooming follows her.)*
> *(The cottages, and the widow's garden — the parish prize garden — and the widow is at her gate, and she sees Rose, and she bobs.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." She gestures at the terrace cuttings, visible from the lane. "The whole Park's gone pink, miss."
> "The rose's ground, Mrs. —" Rose stops, because she has never learned the widow's name, and the widow laughs.
> "The Park's the rose's ground, miss. And we're the Park's." She offers a posy — violets, faithfulness — from her own bed. "For the house, miss."
> *(Rose takes the violets — faithfulness, the edging of the paths — and the widow bobs again, and the lane holds the morning.)*
> *(She walks back to the house with the violets in her hand and the Hartwell rose on the terrace, and the light does what light does in a finished garden: it stays.)*
> *(The widow's violets go into water in the morning room, beside the Hartwell rose. Faithfulness and the charter's flower — the edging and the bed — and the house holds them both in the morning light.)*
> *(She stands at the window and looks down the lane toward the cottages, and the posy is small and plain beside the Hartwell rose, and somehow it is the posy she keeps looking at. The widow has never learned the Latin names and never needed to. Faithfulness, in violets, from a parish prize garden, offered at a gate. She makes a note in her head — the agent's book, the rents, the schoolroom's slates — and then she puts the note aside, because this morning is not for arithmetic. This morning is for the light, and the violets, and the rose's ground.)*

scenes.synopsis: the house, the blooming — the stone, the flowered; the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She walks the west gallery, and the portraits hang straight, and in every room the Hartwell rose blooms in vases — the saloon, the drawing room, the morning room, the charter's flower in the charter's house.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick passes in the hall and nods at the vases — the immovable mouth doing something nearly warm. The servants' hall has its own bloom, on the dresser. She stops in the great hall beneath the chandelier and looks at the rose on the table below it. Ten seasons ago she stood in a ruined house and priced what it would cost to save. Tonight the house blooms. The arithmetic is done.)*
> *(The strong room, and Augusta is there with the plate — the silver, the gilt, the pieces that survived — and Rose comes in with the Hartwell rose for the great epergne.)*
> "The house, blooming." The Dowager watches her set the bloom among the silver. "The stone, flowered."
> "Kept, Grandmama."
> "Kept." Augusta touches the epergne — the piece that survived her hiding it from them all. "The plate is the family's memory, child. It remembers what the people tried to forget. And now —" the rarest smile — "now it holds the flower too."
> *(The silver and the rose — the memory and the blooming — and the strong room holds its candlelight.)*
> *(She leaves the Dowager with her plate and her flower, and walks the gallery — the portraits, the vases, the whole house flowered — and the stone holds its bloom the way the charter holds its terms: completely.)*
> *(The epergne holds the rose like it was made for it — the silver, the bloom, the kept. Augusta's hand rests near it a moment. The plate remembers. The flower blooms. The strong room's candlelight keeps them both, and Rose carries the image upstairs with her, and it stays.)*
> *(In her bedroom she stops at the window and looks out at the Park — the lake, the woods, the walled garden dark now — and the whole house is behind her, flowered and silvered and kept, and the thought comes uninvited: the grandfather planted, the father let go to briar, Rackham sold the soil stone by stone. And the granddaughter put a rose in the epergne. The plate remembers what the people tried to forget. Tonight it will have to remember this too.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE YEAR'S MEANING (what the rose's year means: the patience, the legacy, or the returning). The year deepens; decide the meaning. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year deepens, and the rose's year asks its meaning in the plain evidence of the turning seasons, and the turning will not be hurried. Rose sits in the library with the Hartwell rose blooming on the desk beside Quill's sealed paper, and the dusk comes on, and the question sits in her the way the dusk sits on the lawn.)*
> *(Patience — the waiting, the season kept. The straw raked back, the buds, the bloom; the mulch, the wait, the trust. Legacy — the charter's flower, the year's flower. The bloom that exists nowhere else, the line's flower, the Assembly's flower. Returning — the year come round again. The second spring, the third spring; the rose that will outlive them all.)*
> *(She thinks of the strongbox drawer. She thinks of the ledger. She thinks of the gardeners, and the boy with the watering can, and the robin on the north wall. The meaning will shape how the year is remembered — and the remembering will outlast the year, the way the pressed rose outlasts the summer in Letitia's book.)*
> *(The lamp is lit. The rose blooms on the desk. Quill's paper lies sealed beside it. The dusk comes on, and the library holds it.)*
> *(She thinks of the boy's "Cor," and Letitia's laugh through her hand, and Augusta's face, and the head gardener's hat in his hands. The year has taught her all three meanings, and the rose has kept them all, and it does not care which she names first — but the naming matters, because the name is the one she will keep.)*
> *(The lamp gutters. The rose holds its color in the lamplight. She decides the way she decides everything now: firmly, and for good — and the year's meaning settles into her like the last page of a ledger, and the ledger balances.)*
> *(She puts out the lamp, and the rose blooms in the dark — she can smell it, though she cannot see it — and the corridor is dark, and the stairs are dark, and her bedroom holds the day's warmth. She stands at the window, and the garden is dark beyond, and the year turns in her like a page. Whatever name she gave it, it is kept: not in the garden, but in the book, and in the memory, which is the garden's real bed.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The year's meaning:*
- **The patience** — *the waited, meant.* The year means patience — the season, the waited. (Consequence: the meaning is the waited's — but waiteds are endured, and the year was the tended.)
- **The legacy** — *the charter, meant.* The year means legacy — the charter's, the yearly. (Consequence: the meaning is the charter's — but charters are ink's, and the year was the bloomed.)
- **The returning** — *the again, meant.* The year means returning — the year, the again. (Consequence: the meaning is the again's — but agains are future's, and the year was the now.)
