scenes.synopsis: the year, the kept — the rose's, the lesson's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She writes it in the household book, in her own hand: the rose's year — the lesson, the meaning, the bloom. The ink is barely dry before Letitia has drawn a small, perfect rose in the margin.)*
> *(The head gardener comes to the library door with his hat in his hands, and she shows him the entry, and he reads it slowly, moving his lips. He nods — once — and goes back to the garden.)*
> *(The dusk deepens. The rose on the desk holds its color. She closes the book and sets it on the shelf among the estate books, and the lamp gutters, and the library holds the dusk.)*
> *(The head gardener's nod. The boy's "Cor." Letitia's rose in the margin. Augusta's hand on the cane. She puts out the lamp, and the rose blooms in the dark — she can smell it, though she cannot see it.)*
> *(The corridor, the stairs, her bedroom. The day is done. She stands at the window, and the garden is dark beyond, and the kept year turns in her like a page, and the page is turned, and the turning is finished.)*
> *(She does not say the lesson's name aloud. She does not say the meaning's name. The names were for the choosing; the keeping is for the book. The garden is dark, and the straw is warm under the snow that has not yet come, and the rose is dreaming, and she has done what she set out to do.)*
> *(And it is this, she thinks, standing at the window with the day's warmth still in the room: the household book has held ten years of accounts — the manure and the straw and the wages, the settlements and the charters and the invitations — and tonight it holds a rose, pressed flat, with Letitia's small perfect drawing in the margin. The ledger balances. It has never balanced on the side of joy before. Tonight it does, and she lets it stand, and lets it be.)*

scenes.synopsis: the letters — the year, reported; London writes. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The evening post, and the letters. London writes: the company, the ton, the young. She reads them in the library with the Hartwell rose blooming on the desk, and the witnessing is in writing.)*
> *(Lavinia's letter is all angles and velocity: the rose, darling, the ton must see it. Honoria's is quiet: the dragon asks after the bloom. The young write in a round hand: the advance guard salutes the flower.)*
> *(She answers them all — personally, every one — because that is the Assembly's way. London writes, and the Park answers, and the correspondence is the year's record, fair-copied in ink.)*
> *(She writes the replies at the desk — the rose blooming beside her — and the sealing wax is the color of the rose's heart, and the post bag fills. Lavinia: the ton must see it. Honoria: the dragon asks after the bloom. The young: the advance guard salutes the flower. She seals the last letter, and the wax cools, and the evening holds its light.)*
> *(Henry rides over at noon for the bag, and he sees the rose on the desk, and the smallest smile appears.)*
> "The year, reported."
> "Tell London the rose is real."
> "London already knows." He takes the bag. "Bell told them."
> *(He rides down the drive with the post, and the rose blooms on the desk, and the letters wait for the morning post, and the year's report is written, sealed, and sent.)*
> *(Alone, she picks up Honoria's letter and reads it once more — the quiet hand, the measured sentences: the dragon asks after the bloom, and asks it, Honoria writes, with something very like interest, which in their family passes for warmth. She folds it carefully. Drummond's daughter, sponsored and grown, writing about roses. Ten seasons ago that sentence would have been a contradiction. Tonight it is only a letter, and the letter is only true, and the truth is only pleasant, which is the strangest victory of all. She sets it with the others and goes to the window, and the Park is dark beyond the glass, and somewhere in London the ton is writing about her rose, and the rose is blooming on the desk behind her, and the whole of it — the letters, the wax, the quiet hand of Drummond's daughter — is more than she ever expected the evening post to bring.)*

scenes.synopsis: the ton, the year's — the blooming, awaited; the convened, the flowered. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The London letters say it plainly: the town is waiting for the bloom. The Assembly's flower. The charter's rose.)*
> *(The Almerias write: we shall come for the rose. The Craykes write twice, to be sure. The milliners are in despair — Lavinia's doing, no doubt.)*
> *(She reads the letters with the rose blooming on the desk. The town will come, and the garden will be ready, and the bloom will be the witness.)*
> *(Lavinia's letter, read twice — the angles, the velocity: "Darling — the rose! The ton is beside itself. I have told everyone who matters that the Hartwell rose is the only flower worth seeing this year, which means everyone who matters will see it, because no one can bear to miss what I have seen.")*
> *(Rose laughs aloud, alone in the library, which is the correct response to Lavinia and has been for years.)*
> *(The Craykes have written twice, to be sure — enthusiasm, or insurance. The Almerias: we shall come for the rose. The milliners are in despair; the rose has started a fashion for pink, and the ton is scrambling, and Lavinia is taking full credit, which is only fair, because it is mostly her doing.)*
> *(She sets the letters down, and the rose blooms on the desk. The town will come — the Craykes, the Almerias, all of them — and the garden will be ready, and the rose will be waiting.)*
> *(She folds Lavinia's letter and sets it with the others. The evening deepens. The rose holds its color. The ton waits, and the waiting is the whole of it, and the whole of it is hers.)*
> *(Letitia comes in with the household book and reads the Craykes' double letter over Rose's shoulder, and snorts.)*
> "Twice, darling. To be sure. The Craykes would RSVP to their own funeral twice, to be sure."
> "They're coming for the rose."
> "Everyone's coming for the rose, darling. That's the point of a rose." The aunt taps the Almerias' letter. "And these two will bring the milliner, and the milliner will bring the fashion, and the fashion will bring everyone else. The quartermaster calls it a sound investment." She pats Rose's cheek. "I told you, darling. Less than the kitchens spend on ices."

scenes.synopsis: the woman, the gardener's — Rose, the evening's; the mistress, the tended. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her evening. She sits at the window with the garden beyond, the rose beds dark now, the bloom on the desk behind her.)*
> *(The Park beyond, bloomed. She thinks in ledgers, as she always does — planted, tended, wintered, bloomed — and the arithmetic is the simplest she has ever kept.)*
> *(The image comes uninvited, as her real thoughts do: her hands in the soil, the head gardener's nod, the boy with the watering can, Julian's finger on the bud, Laurent's chocolate, Henry's smallest smile, Octavia's sketchbook, Augusta's ringed hand, Letitia's laugh in the still-room. The year was hers. The tending was hers. She does not need to name it to keep it.)*
> *(The lamp is lit. The gardening gloves lie by the door — the plain leather pair, ruined and beloved. She sits at the window, and the garden is dark beyond, and the bloom is on the desk behind her.)*
> *(She thinks — the image she would never say aloud — of the drawer she cannot open by force, and understands that she never needed to. The tending was the opening. The waiting was the key. The rose was the answer.)*
> *(The light goes. The garden holds the dark. The rose holds the desk. The gloves wait by the door for the morning.)*
> *(The gloves wait by the door. The garden waits beyond the glass. She waits in her chair, and the waiting is hers, and the morning will come, and the garden will be there, and the rose will be blooming, and that is the whole of it, and the whole of it is enough.)*
> *(And it is enough. She has spent ten seasons refusing to let enough be enough — the house unfinished, the claim unanswered, the war unfought — and tonight, for the first time, the ledger in her head closes on a balance she does not want to argue with. The gloves are ruined. The nails are dirty. The bloom is on the desk. The woman in the chair is the gardener, and the gardener is the mistress, and the mistress is whole, and the evening asks for nothing more, and she gives it nothing.)*

scenes.synopsis: the rose, the charter's — the flower, the legacy's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She walks the walled garden at dawn, and the Hartwell rose blooms in its row.)*
> *(The head gardener is already at work, and the boy is raking back the mulch on the new cuttings, and the garden does not bother with ceremony. She touches a bloom — just the edge of a petal, the lightest touch — and the rose is cool with the dawn, and the charter is kept.)*
> *(She walks the row with them — the boy with the watering can, the head gardener with the knife, the labels tied square — and the Hartwell rose blooms, and the morning belongs to the year, and the year belongs to her.)*
> *(The boy looks up, and grins — the watering, the tending, the boy grown taller since spring — and the head gardener touches his hat, and the garden gets on with the morning, because the garden always does.)*
> "The charter's, miss." The old man gestures at the row.
> "The year's, and the year's again."
> "Aye, miss." The rarest smile. "That's the whole of it."
> *(She closes the gate behind her — the latch clicks — and walks back to the house through the morning. The garden holds its light. The rose holds its color.)*
> *(The morning holds its light a moment longer, as if the garden were seeing her off.)*
> *(In the hall Mrs. Quick is already at her lists, and the house smells of bread and beeswax, and the day is beginning the way days begin at the Park now: exactly on time. She takes the stairs two at a time, which the Dowager would disapprove of and Letitia would applaud, and goes to dress for the morning, because even houses with roses in every room keep morning hours. The garden holds its light behind her. The rose holds its color. The charter is kept, and the keeping is the whole of it, and the whole of it is morning.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's bloom report — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"This year the Hartwell rose has turned through its seasons — budded, bloomed, rested, returned — and the Gazette — having watched the blooming from the first — finds it the charter's true flower. The legacy, yearly. The Gazette will watch, annually."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (annually! watching!), then the reckoning: the year is pronounced true in print as well as in the garden's soil, and Bell has made the blooming permanent, which is Bell's way of making it forever. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the blooming the Gazette watches annually is the blooming that's real.* — remembered: *the lesson: the blooming the Gazette watches annually is the blooming that's real.*
scenes.sting: This year the Hartwell rose has turned through its seasons — budded, bloomed, rested, returned — and the Gazette — having watched the blooming from the first — finds it the charter's true flower. The legacy, yearly. The Gazette will watch, annually.

scenes.synopsis: the household's year — the keepers, the turned; the charter's, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and she walks the house — the household's year, coming — and the keepers turn through their year.)*
> *(She watches — the keepers, the year's — the household's year, the turning: the charter's, the kept.)*
> "The household's year." She looks at the house — the whole, the kept. "The keepers —" she stops — "through their year." She breathes. "The charter's —" another stop — "the kept, the yearly."
> *(The chapter closes on the turning — the keepers, the year's — and the Season turns toward the household: the keepers' year — and the Season holds its breath.)*

scenes.synopsis: the year's turning — the household's year; the keepers, the seasons. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She wakes before the house, which is her habit now — the mistress's hour, the one hour nobody else claims. The bedroom is dark and the corridor darker, and she walks them without a candle, the way she has learned to walk everything here: by memory, and by trust.)*
> *(The house at dawn is a held breath. The gallery sleeps under its dust sheets, the saloon's shutters are closed, and the morning room's desk sits clean — Harrow's doing, the steward's nightly round, the inkwell capped, the blotting paper squared. She puts her hand on the newel post at the stairhead, and the wood is cold, and the cold is honest, the way oak is.)*
> *(Below stairs the first sounds: the kitchen range being coaxed awake, the clink of the cook's pans, Mrs. Quick's keys turning in the still-room lock — the immovable's morning, exact to the minute. Rose stands at the top of the servants' stair and listens, and the listening is a kind of ledger. Every sound is an entry.)*
> *(At the east window she stops, and the Park lies below in the first light — the lake, the woods, the rose garden's dark line — and the year's turning is visible from here if you know how to look. She knows how to look. Ten seasons have taught her.)*
> *(The kitchen girl comes up the back stairs with the first tray, and she stops dead when she sees the mistress at the east window — the chocolate slopping in its cup — and bobs so low the tray tilts.)*
> "Miss! I didn't — shall I bring it here, miss? To the window?"
> "Here is perfect." Rose takes the cup before it can spill. "What's your name?"
> "Nell, miss. New from the village, miss."
> "Nell." She drinks — the chocolate scalding, sweet, perfect. "How long have you been up?"
> "Since five, miss. The range, miss — it won't coax itself."
> *(The chocolate warms her hands through the cup. Outside, a thrush starts up on the north wall, arguing with the morning as it does every year, and the lake shows its first silver seam. She drinks slowly. Nobody hurries the mistress at her window. That is the entire point of the hour.)*
> *(The girl hovers, and Rose dismisses her with a nod, and the tray goes back down, and the east window holds the Park's first light. Five o'clock. The keepers' day starts in the dark, and the mistress's starts at the window. Between them, the house.)*
> *(She finishes the chocolate and sets the cup on the sill for Nell to find. The cup cools there. The light moves an inch up the glass.)*

scenes.synopsis: the keeper, the year's — Mrs. Quick, the household's; the immovable, the turned. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Mrs. Quick does her morning round at seven, whatever the weather, whatever the company, whatever the year. Rose falls in beside her at the still-room door, and the housekeeper accepts the company the way she accepts everything: without comment, and without slowing.)*
> *(They walk the corridor together — the mistress, the keeper — and Mrs. Quick opens doors, checks sills for dust with one gloved finger, straightens a picture that has hung straight for forty years. The finger comes away clean. The picture stays straight. The round continues.)*
> "The west wing, miss." The immovable voice, nearly warm. "The winter's damp got into the sheets. I've had them aired twice."
> "Twice?"
> "Twice, miss." The keys turn in the linen press. "The Assembly's year, miss — the ton will sleep in those beds. They'll not sleep damp."
> *(The linen press opens on its aired ranks — the sheets folded the exact way Mrs. Quick demands, the lavender between them, the whole press smelling of soap and cold air. Rose runs a hand along a folded stack, and it is cool, and dry, and immaculate.)*
> "Has the silver been done?"
> "The silver's done, miss. Twice." The immovable mouth does the extraordinary thing. "The plate that survived — it's polished, miss. For the year."
> *(They reach the morning room — the round's end — and Mrs. Quick stops with her keys in her hand, and does something Rose has never seen: she hesitates.)*
> "Miss." The immovable voice. "The mattresses, miss. I've had the sheets aired twice, miss, but the mattress —" she stops — "the mattress wants turning, miss. It's the damp, miss. It gets in."
> "Then we'll turn the mattresses, Mrs. Quick. All of them."
> "All of them, miss." The keys turn in her hand — the thought being turned over. "The Assembly's year, miss. The ton'll not sleep damp."
> *(It is the longest speech Rose has ever heard from her, and it is entirely about mattresses, and she finds it the most eloquent thing said in the house all year.)*
> *(She goes — the keys, the corridors — and Rose stands in the morning room's light, and the mattresses will be turned, and the ton will sleep dry, and nobody will ever know. That, Rose thinks, is the whole arrangement: the ton sleeps dry, and never knows why.)*

scenes.synopsis: the steward, the year's — Harrow, the household's; the book, the turned. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Harrow waits in the estate office with the year's book open on the desk — the steward's morning, the honest figures. He rises when she comes in, and the scarred gentleman's bow is exact, and the office smells of ink and beeswax and the year's business.)*
> *(She sits, and he stands at her shoulder, and they go through it together — the figures, the names, the year's honest arithmetic. The maids' wages. The grooms'. The cook's. The gardeners'. Every name a line, every line a keeper.)*
> "The wages, Miss Hartwell." He lays the book open. "The tending." He turns a page with the care of a man handling something alive. "The Assembly's year, miss — the ton'll eat, and sleep, and be kept. It costs." He names no figure she hasn't approved.
> "And the honest?"
> "The honest, miss." He closes the book. "Every penny accounted. That's the charter's house."
> *(She looks at him — the scarred face, the exact hands, the forty years of service in the set of his shoulders — and the image comes uninvited: Harrow young, new to the house, learning the books the way she learned them. The house kept him, and now he keeps the house. It is not a thought she says aloud. Harrow would pretend he hadn't heard it.)*
> *(He turns to the last page — the year's totals — and his pen stops, and the dry face does something complicated.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." A pause. "The —" another pause — "the boy, miss. The gardener's boy. His wages, miss —" the dryest — "he's due the man's rate, miss. He's doing a man's work."
> *(The recommendation sits between them like something alive. Rose thinks of the boy with the watering can, the way he touches his cap the way the old man touches his hat, the charter rose watered first. She does not make him wait for it.)*
> "The man's rate, Harrow. From this quarter."
> "From this quarter, miss." He writes it in — the pen scratching. "The honest, miss. Every penny."
> *(It is a small figure in a big book, and the pen makes its little mark, and the boy will get the man's rate, and the book will balance, and nobody will make a speech about it. Which is, Rose thinks, the whole difference between a house and a sermon.)*
> "The Assembly's year, Harrow."
> "The year's, Miss Hartwell." He blots the page. "Accounted."
> *(She leaves him with his pen and his honest figures, and the boy will get the man's rate, and the book will balance, and the blotting paper takes the last of the ink like a full stop.)*

scenes.synopsis: the cook, the year's — the kitchen's; the serene, the turned. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The kitchen at eight is the warmest room in the house, and the cook reigns in it the way Augusta reigns in the morning room: absolutely, and without raising her voice. Rose comes down the back stairs, and the cook looks up from the pastry board, and the serene face does the welcoming thing.)*
> "What are we feeding them, Cook? The Assembly's year — the ton'll sup here."
> "The honest, miss." The serene smile. She goes back to her rolling — the pin moving like a metronome. "The home farm's, the garden's, the dairy's. Nothing bought that can be grown, miss. That's the rule, miss. Your rule, miss."
> "My rule." Rose breathes in — the yeast, the butter, the year's first baking. "They'll sup well."
> *(She shapes a roll with one practiced turn of the wrist, and the dough takes the shape the way it has taken it ten thousand times, and Rose finds herself watching it the way other people watch concerts.)*
> "The keepers eat first, miss." The cook looks up. "The kitchen's rule. A hungry keeper's a careless keeper."
> "The hungry keeper, miss —" the serene smile — "is a keeper who leaves, miss."
> *(It is the plainest economics Rose has heard all year, and it comes from the cook, and it is why the kitchen never loses a girl to London. She makes a note of it for the household book, in the margin, where the best things go.)*
> *(The spit-boy eats his roll standing by the range — the keepers first — and the cook watches him with her whole serene attention, and he is trying, very hard, not to look as though the roll is the best thing that has happened to him all week. It probably is.)*
> "The Assembly's year, miss." The cook wipes her hands on her apron. "The ton'll sup. But the keepers, miss —" she stops — "the keepers sup first, miss. That's the rule, miss. Your rule, miss."
> "My rule." Rose takes another half-roll, warm from the board. "The hungry keeper's a careless keeper."
> "And the fed one, miss —" the serene smile — "is yours."
> *(She goes up the back stairs with the bread warm in her hand, and the kitchen hums below her — the range ticking, the pin turning, the boy at the spit — and the whole warm machine of it turns, and nobody is hungry in it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the gardeners, the year's — the Park's; the tending, the turned. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The head gardener is waiting by the rose bed with the year's plan in his head, and the morning is fine and clear. He touches his hat when she comes down the path, and the boy is already at the watering, and the can glints.)*
> "The Park at its best this year, Miss Hartwell." The old man touches his hat again. He looks along the beds — the rose row, the kept rows beyond. "The Assembly year — the ton will walk this ground, miss. They'll walk it bloomed."
> "The Hartwell rose, and the rest?"
> "The rest, miss." The rarest smile cracks the weathered face. "The rose belongs to the charter, miss — but the lawns, the woods, the lake edge." He gestures with the pruning knife. "The Park'll do the rest itself, miss. It knows the way."
> *(They walk the beds together, and he talks — the year's plan, the tending calendar, which bed gets the manure and which the bone — and the boy waters, and the bees work the blossoms, and the Park does what the Park does in a fine morning: it grows.)*
> "The boy's learning, miss." The old man watches him. "The watering, the watching. He'll be a gardener, miss."
> "Then the Park's future is in the boy's hands."
> "Aye, miss." He touches his hat. "Safe hands, miss."
> *(The boy comes up the path with the watering can, and he stops when he sees the mistress, and touches his cap the way the old man touches his hat — the gesture copied so faithfully it is almost a quotation.)*
> "Miss." He stands very straight. "The charter rose, miss. I watered it first, miss. Before the rest."
> "Before the rest?"
> "The charter rose first, miss." He looks at the old man, then at her. "That's the —" he stops — "that's the rule, miss. The head gardener's rule."
> *(The head gardener says nothing, and the nothing is his whole approval, and the boy glows with it, and Rose has to look at the rose bed for a moment because the glow is too bright to look at directly.)*
> "The charter rose first." Rose nods. "The Park rule."
> "The Park rule, miss." The boy goes back to his can, and the old man watches him go, and the rarest smile cracks the weathered face again, and the bees work on, indifferent to everything but the blossoms.
> *(She leaves them — the rule, the tending — and walks back through the Park's morning, and the charter's flower got the first water, as is the rule, and the old man's silence follows her down the path like approval made audible.)*

scenes.synopsis: the maids — the year's; the house's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The maids are at the west wing by nine — Rose finds them on the landing with the dust sheets half off and the windows open to the morning, and the work goes the way it always goes: fast, thorough, and cheerful.)*
> *(She stops to watch — the mistress, unobserved a moment — and the maids move through the rooms like a tide: the sheets off, the shutters open, the dust chased from the cornices. One girl hums. Another laughs at something the third says. The house wakes under their hands.)*
> "Miss!" The eldest spots her, and they all bob at once, a small flurry of curtsies. "The west wing, miss. For the Assembly."
> *(They show her — the aired sheets, Mrs. Quick's twice-aired, the sills dusted, the grates blacked — and the pride in it is plain. This is their keeping. The house is theirs as much as hers, and they know it.)*
> "The Assembly's year," the eldest says, straightening a curtain. "The ton'll see it, miss. They'll see the kept."
> "They'll see your work, and they'll not know it's work. That's the whole of keeping."
> *(The girl goes pink with pleasure, and the others grin, and the landing hums again as Rose goes on, and the west wing stands aired and ready, and the dust hangs gold in the light, and nobody hurries, because nobody needs to.)*
> *(The eldest maid shows her the linen press, and the sheets are folded in the exact way Mrs. Quick demands, and the girl's hands move with the pride of the well-taught, and the press smells of soap and lavender and cold air.)*
> "Miss." She hesitates. "The —" she stops — "the Assembly's year, miss. The ton'll sleep in these, miss. I want —" another stop — "I want them to know, miss. That they're kept."
> *(Rose looks at her — the girl, the sheets, the wanting — and there is no grander ambition in the house this morning than a folded sheet.)*
> "They'll know." She touches a folded sheet — the linen cool, the fold exact. "It tells, even when no one speaks."
> "Mrs. Quick says —"
> "Mrs. Quick is always right."
> *(They laugh — the mistress, the maid — and the landing holds the laugh with the aired-linen smell, and the west wing stands ready, and the girl goes back to her folding, and the folding is perfect.)*

scenes.synopsis: the grooms — the year's; the stables', the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The stables at ten — the head groom's lad runs ahead to announce her, and the yard opens around her: the horses, the tack, the smell of hay and leather and the morning's work.)*
> *(The grooms are at the stalls — the mucking, the grooming, the feeding — and the work has the rhythm of music. A horse blows through its nose. A boy laughs. The head groom touches his cap and comes over, and his hands are full of bridle.)*
> "The Assembly's year, miss. The ton'll ride, miss. They'll ride kept horses."
> "Then we'd better have kept horses." She puts her hand on a hunter's neck — the warmth, the power, the trust. "This one's fit."
> "Fit as a fiddle, miss. They all are."
> *(They walk the stalls together, and he talks — the feeding, the shoeing, the year's tending — and the horses watch them go with the calm of well-kept animals, and the straw is fresh, and the water buckets are full, and the whole yard says the same thing the linen press said: this is done properly, and nobody is told about it.)*
> "The lads are learning, miss." He nods at the boys. "The grooming, the handling. They'll be grooms, miss."
> "Then the stables' future is the lads'."
> "Aye, miss." He touches his cap again. "Safe hands, miss."
> *(The head groom shows her the new foal, and the foal stands on unsteady legs in the straw, and the mare watches with the calm of the well-kept, and the lads hover at the box door with the particular pride of boys who have done a man's thing.)*
> "Miss." He touches his cap. "Born in the night, miss. The lads sat up with her."
> *(Rose bends to the foal — the soft nose, the new smell — and the lads hover, and the pride is plain, and she lets them have it, because there is nothing in the world like having sat up all night with a foaling mare and being thanked for it by the mistress.)*
> "All night?"
> "All night, miss." He looks at the boys. "They'll be grooms, miss."
> "They already are." She straightens. "Feed them first at supper. The keepers eat first — that's the rule."
> *(She leaves them — the foal, the mare, the watching — and walks back through the yard's morning, and the year's first foal stands in the straw on its wobbling legs, and the straw is fresh, and the boys are grinning, and the yard gets on with its day.)*

scenes.synopsis: the spring — the household's; the waking, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The spring comes to the household the way it comes to the garden: all at once, and everywhere. She stands at the morning room window and watches it arrive — the light changing, the Park greening, the shutters opening wider to the morning.)*
> *(Below stairs, the spring work goes on: the winter stores inventoried and found sufficient, the spring cleaning begun in earnest, the maids airing rooms that have slept since autumn. The housekeeper's keys turn more often. The steward's book gains pages. The cook plans the first suppers of the year with new lamb from the home farm.)*
> *(She walks the house, and the household wakes around her: the footmen polishing the brasses, the maids dusting the portrait frames, the garden boy bringing the first cut flowers for the saloon. The keepers are awake, and the year is awake with them.)*
> *(The thrush is back on the north wall, arguing with the morning as it does every year. She listens, and counts the notes the way Augusta taught her to count everything that matters — every note an entry.)*
> *(In the rose garden, the canes of the Hartwell rose are greening — the charter flower. She stops at the end of the row and looks at it: the spring's beginning, green on the cane.)*
> *(She turns for the house as the breakfast bell rings, and the spring does what spring does at the Park now: it behaves. The morning goes on, and the house goes on with it, and there is something deeply satisfactory about a season that knows its business.)*
> *(After breakfast she goes down to the rose garden, and the head gardener is there with his knife, and the boy with the watering can.)*
> "Miss." He touches his hat. "The grafts, miss. The new ones."
> *(He shows her the buds, and she bends a cane the way he taught her, and the green shows through the bark — the year's first green, under the old wood.)*
> "They'll take."
> "Aye, miss." He watches the boy water. "The tending, miss. The year's own work."
> *(She walks the row — the greening canes, the waking buds — and the thrush argues on the north wall, and the boy whistles at his watering, and the morning belongs to the keeping, and the keeping, for once, is entirely pleasant.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE KEEPING'S LESSON (what the keeping teaches: the steadiness, the care, or the returning). The year deepens; decide the lesson. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year deepens, and the keeping asks its lesson. Rose walks the house in the evening's light — the tended rooms, the kept corridors — and the question sits in her the way the dusk sits on the lawn: early, and not to be hurried.)*
> *(Steadiness, the immovable says — Mrs. Quick's keys, the twice-done silver, the house kept whatever the weather. Rose has watched the housekeeper keep this house through ten seasons of war and wedding and Assembly, and the keeping never wavered. There is something to be said for a woman who does not waver.)*
> *(Care, the servants say — the cook's first bread broken for the mistress, the maids' aired sheets, the grooms' kept horses. She has the year's evidence in her hands and her mouth and her mornings. There is something to be said for feeding people well.)*
> *(Returning, the year itself says — the spring come again, the rose greening, the household turning through its seasons. It has come back from winter, and will come back again, because that is what years do when they are kept. There is something to be said for coming back.)*
> *(She thinks of the household book — the names, the wages, the honest figures — and the lesson will shape the keeping's memory. She stands at the stairhead, and the dusk deepens through the east windows, and she decides the way she decides everything now: firmly, and for good.)*
> *(She goes to the estate office, and Harrow lays the book open without being asked, and the honest figures stand in his exact hand.)*
> *(She reads the names — the maids, the grooms, the cook, the gardeners, the boy — and the wages beside them, and the quarters, and the honest.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." He waits — the steward, the exact. "The —" the dryest — "the lesson, miss?"
> *(She looks at the book — the year's record — and the lesson sits in her the way the dusk sat on the lawn: early, and not to be hurried. She will write it in the margin in her best hand, whatever it is.)*
> *(Steadiness is the keys turning. Care is the bread broken. Returning is the spring come again. She stands in the office's ink-and-beeswax smell, and the book holds the year, and the deciding is hers.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: steadiness, care, or returning. The keeping's lesson is hers.)*

> *(The summer comes to the household with the hayfields gold and the kitchens at full stretch — the year's middle, the working. > *(She takes her luncheon in the garden — the shade, the roses, the Hartwell rose blooming — and the working goes on around her: the boy with the watering can, the maids with the linen, the footmen with the silver for the evening.)*
> *(A maid brings the cold chicken and the bread, and Rose eats in the shade with the garden humming, and the charter flower blooms beside the empty plate, and the afternoon is entirely unremarkable, and that is the remark.)*
> "Miss." The maid hesitates. "The —" she stops — "the heat, miss. Mrs. Quick says the shutters, miss. Against the afternoon."
> "The shutters, and the cool rooms." Rose nods. "The keepers know."
> "The keepers know, miss." The girl grins and goes.
> *(In the afternoon she rides the Park's boundary with the head groom — the whole of it — and the estate lies in the heat like something held: the lake, the woods, the home farm's fields. The middle of the year. The working.)*
> *(The evening brings the cool, and the household eases — the supper served, the shutters opened, the garden holding the dusk. She walks the terrace as the light fails, and the keepers' day is done.)*
> *(She stands at the terrace's edge, and the Park holds the dusk, and the swallows work the eaves, and the day has been exactly what a summer day at the Park should be: long, hot, and well managed.)*
> *(She goes in as the light fails, and the cool rooms receive her, and the house hums its evening note, and the note says the same thing the whole day has said: it is going well.)*

> *(The ledger in her head turns its own page: figures beside the names, and names first. Every wage is a keeper kept. Every keeper is a name. She knows every name.)*
> "The year's, miss." Harrow closes the book when the last one goes. "The honest, the paid." The dry smile. "The keepers, miss."
> "The kept," she agrees. "And the honest?"
> "The honest, Miss Hartwell." He sets down his pen. "Every penny. That's the charter's house."
> *(At the stairhead she stops, and the house hums below her, and the wages sit honest in the book, and the book sits honest on the desk, and the whole arrangement is so plain and so decent that she wonders why anyone ever does it any other way.)*
> *(She follows the boy from the garden with her eyes — the last paid — and he goes down the corridor with the wages in his pocket, and he walks like a man. The pocket is not deep, and the wages are not grand, but the walk is.)*
> *(Harrow comes up behind her — the steward, the exact — and he follows her looking, and the dry face does the satisfied thing.)*
> "The man's rate, Miss Hartwell." The dryest. "From this quarter."
> "The man's work, the man's rate."

> *(They stand together at the stairhead — the mistress, the steward — and the house hums below, and the boy walks like a man down the corridor, and the wages are in his pocket, and the pocket is buttoned.)*
> *(She thinks of the ledger in her head — figures beside the names, names first — and every name a line, and every line a keeper, and every keeper paid, and every penny honest.)*

> *(Mrs. Quick's round goes on — the keys, the corridors — whatever the weather. The cook's dark loaves come out of the range.)*
> *(At the east window she stops, and the white holds the light, and the keepers move through it, and the winter's business goes on: the coal, the feed, the straw.)*
> *(The light is short. The quiet is long. The house is warm. It is enough, and the enough is the whole point of winter.)*

scenes.synopsis: the third spring — the household's; the waking, the eternal. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The third spring comes to the household, and Rose stands at the morning room window and watches it arrive for the third time: the light, the greening, the shutters opening to the year again.)*
> *(Below stairs, the spring of the third year: the stores inventoried, the cleaning begun, the maids airing. The steward opens a new book for the year, the third one. The cook plans with the spring lamb.)*
> *(She walks the house — the waking rooms, the kept corridors — and the household wakes for the third spring, and the waking is familiar the way a well-worn glove is familiar.)*
> *(In the rose garden, the Hartwell rose greens for the third spring — the charter flower. She stops at the row, and the green is the same green, and the row is the same row, and the satisfaction of it is entirely unreasonable.)*
> *(The thrush, the bell, the breakfast. She turns for the house, and the spring behaves. The kept are waking.)*
> *(At breakfast Letitia is already there, and the hawk's eyes are bright.)*
> "Darling." She pours. "The third spring, darling."
> "The kept are eternal, Aunt."
> "The kept, darling." The warm look. "The quartermaster approves, darling."
> *(They eat, and the thrush argues, and the bell's echo hangs, and the morning does what mornings do at the Park now: it behaves.)*
> "The Assembly's year, darling." Letitia sets down her cup. "The ton, darling. They'll come, darling."
> "They'll find the kept."
> "The kept, darling." She rises. "The year's."
> *(The head gardener is at the rose garden — the charter flower — and he touches his hat, and the greening goes on.)*
> *(The boy waters, and the bees work, and the Park wakes, and the kept are waking, and the watering can glints in the morning light the way it glinted the first spring, and the second.)*
> *(She stands in the morning light, and the third spring goes on, and the household goes on with it, and the bees work the blossoms, and the Park goes about its year.)*
> *(At the stairhead she stops, and the house hums its morning note, and the note is the same note, and the sameness is the whole pleasure of it.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE HOUSEHOLD'S GIFT (how the year is marked for the keepers: the wages, the feast, or the rest). The year deepens; decide the marking. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year deepens, and the household asks its marking. Rose walks the house in the evening's light — the tended rooms, the kept corridors — and the question sits in her the way the dusk sits on the lawn: early, and not to be hurried.)*
> *(The wages, the honest says — Harrow's book, the paid, the keepers kept. She has watched them come to the office door, quarter by quarter, and take the honest wages, and the paying never wavered. There is something to be said for marking the year as it was kept: in coin.)*
> *(The feast, the kitchen says — the cook's serene, the served, the year's suppers. She has eaten the year's first bread standing in the kitchen, and the serving never faltered. There is something to be said for sitting them all down at one table.)*
> *(The rest, the winter says — the snow, the fires, the keepers resting. She has watched the house rest completely, and without guilt, and the resting never needed permission. There is something to be said for giving them the one thing the year never gave: time.)*
> *(She thinks of the keepers — the names, the faces, the year's honest — and the marking will shape the household's memory. She stands at the stairhead, and the dusk deepens, and she decides the way she decides everything now: firmly, and for good.)*
> *(She goes down to the kitchens, and the cook looks up from the range, and the serene face does the questioning thing.)*
> "Miss." She wipes her hands. "The marking, miss?"
> *(Rose asks her — the keepers, the year's — what the marking should be, and the cook considers the way she considers everything: completely.)*
> "The keepers, miss." The serene smile. "The —" she stops — "they'd not ask, miss. But they'd —" another stop — "they'd remember, miss."
> *(She climbs back to the stairhead — the dusk, the kept — and the marking waits in her the way the winter waits in the ground: patient, and certain.)*
> *(The wages, the feast, the rest. She stands in the evening's light, and the cook's words stand with her: they'd not ask. They'd remember. The deciding is hers.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick passes with the keys — the evening's round — and the housekeeper nods, and the nod says the house is ready, whatever she chooses.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: wages, feast, or rest. The household's gift is hers.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The household's gift:*
- **The wages** — *the honest, marked.* The year is marked with wages — the honest, the paid. (Consequence: the marking is the paid's — but paids are due, and the year was the given.)
- **The feast** — *the kitchen, marked.* The year is marked with a feast — the kitchen's, the served. (Consequence: the marking is the served's — but serveds are meals', and the year was the kept.)
- **The rest** — *the winter, marked.* The year is marked with rest — the winter's, the given. (Consequence: the marking is the given's — but givens are mistress's, and the year was the keepers'.)

scenes.synopsis: the marking — the gift, the given; the keepers, the marked. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The marking is given — the gift, as she chose — and Rose walks the house in the morning and watches it land: the keepers told, the household marked, the year's gift going out like light.)*
> *(She marks it the way the keeping asks: personally, and completely. The wages, the feast, the rest — whichever she chose, the choosing was hers, and the giving is done in person, room by room.)*
> *(She tells them herself, going room by room through the morning: the kitchen first, where the cook receives it with the serene's nod, and the nod says she knew, and she is glad.)*
> *(The stables next — the grooms — and the head groom touches his cap, and the horses stamp, and the lads grin, and the marking lands in the yard the way good news always lands in a yard: loudly.)*
> *(The garden — the head gardener, the boy — and the old man touches his hat, and the boy stands very straight, and the boy's grin is so wide it nearly unseats his cap.)*
> *(The still-room last — Mrs. Quick, the keys — and the housekeeper receives it with the immovable's nod, and the nod is the deepest thing Rose has seen from her in a year of deep things.)*
> "Miss." The boy stops her on the path. "The marked, miss? The year's?"
> "The marked, boy. The year's."
> "The year's, miss." He grins — the watering can, the pride. "The kept."
> *(Harrow enters it in the book — the year's record — and the pen scratches, and the honest holds the marking, and the margin takes the ink the way it takes everything: exactly.)*
> *(The maids bob on the landing, and the footmen stand a fraction taller, and the keeping goes about the year's business with a spring in it that was not there yesterday.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick receives it with the immovable's nod. Harrow enters it in the book. The cook serves it, or rests in it. The keepers are marked.)*
> *(She walks back through the house, and the marking sits on the household like light, and the light is warm, and the house hums, and the hum is glad.)*
> *(At the stairhead she stops, and the house hums below her, and the gift is given, and the giving was hers, and the house hums on.)*

scenes.synopsis: the keeper, the marking — Mrs. Quick, the year's; the immovable, the moved. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Mrs. Quick comes to the morning room, and she stands before Rose with something in the immovable face that has never been there before.)*
> "Miss." The immovable voice, nearly breaking. "The —" a pause — "the year's, miss."
> *(Rose waits, and the housekeeper gathers herself the way she gathers everything: exactly.)*
> "The keepers —" she looks at Rose — "the keepers are —" she stops — "marked, miss." The rarest — "The keeper —" another stop — "the keeper is —" she stops — "moved, miss."
> *(Rose puts her hand over the housekeeper's. The hand is cold from the morning round. Rose holds it anyway.)*
> "Then the marking did its work, Mrs. Quick."
> *(The extraordinary mouth does the extraordinary thing: it trembles, and steadies, and does not pretend it hasn't.)*
> "The Assembly's year, miss." Nearly warm. "The kept."
> *(She goes back to her round — the keys, the corridors — and Rose watches her go. Nobody thanks Mrs. Quick. That is understood. But Rose follows her, and Mrs. Quick accepts the company the way she accepts everything: without comment, and without slowing.)*
> *(They walk — the mistress, the keeper — and the keys turn in the linen press, and the still-room, and the silver closet. The round is the house at its work, and Rose walks it beside her.)*
> "Miss." Mrs. Quick stops at the stairhead. "The —" a pause — "the keepers, miss. They're —" she stops — "glad, miss."
> "I'm glad they're glad."
> "They are, miss." The extraordinary mouth. "The year's."
> *(They part at the morning room, at the round's end — and the housekeeper goes on with her keys, and Rose stands in the light.)*
> *(She thinks of the thirty years — the housekeeper's own — and the immovable moved, and the moved showing plain on the immovable face, and the face going back to its round.)*
> *(The corridors hold the afternoon, and the house hums, and the humming is the keeper at her round, and the round goes on, and the keys turn, exact to the minute.)*
> *(At the window she stops — the Park, the light — and the marking sits on the household like good tailoring, and the house wears it well.)*
> *(The afternoon goes on, and the house goes on with it, and Mrs. Quick's keys turn in the far corridor, exact to the minute, as they have turned for thirty years.)*

scenes.synopsis: the household, the marked — the keepers, the year's; the kept, the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The household is marked, and Rose walks the Park in the morning and watches the keepers go about the year's business: the gardeners tending, the grooms riding, the maids airing.)*
> *(She sees it in the way they move: a fraction taller, a fraction surer. The marking sits on them like good tailoring, and the house wears it well.)*
> *(Harrow comes out to the Park, and he carries the book, and the marking sits in the margin in his exact hand — a line of ink, no longer than a thumb.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The dry smile. "The —" the dryest — "the marked, miss."
> "How do they wear it, Harrow?"
> "Well, miss." He closes the book. "The footmen stand taller. The maids sing louder. The boy waters straighter." A pause. "It is a small marking, miss. It lands large."
> *(They walk the gallery — the portraits, the vases — and the afternoon light moves along the wall, and the light does what light does in a kept house: it stays.)*
> *(The gardeners are at the beds, and the grooms are at the stables, and the Park works its afternoon, and the working has a spring in it that was not there last week, and Rose notes it the way she notes everything: silently, and for the record.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick's keys turn below, and the cook's range ticks, and the house hums, and the hum is glad.)*
> *(She thinks of the charter — the written, the permanent — and the marking walks the charter's terms about the house: breathing, working, keeping.)*
> *(She stops at the window — the Park, the light — and the keepers go about the year's business, and the business is the keeping, and the keeping is the day, and the day is enough.)*
> *(At the stairhead she stops, and the hum rises — the marked household at its work.)*
> *(The evening comes on, and the household holds its marking the way a well-dressed woman holds her posture: without thinking about it.)*
> *(She stands at the window — the Park, the light, the dusk — and the day has been exactly what a marked day should be: ordinary, and glad, and well kept.)*

scenes.synopsis: the house, the year's — the stone, the kept; the whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The house in the light of the year, and Rose walks it room by room, the way she walked it at dawn when the year began: the gallery, the saloon, the morning room, the whole of it.)*
> *(The walls are clean. The windows are clean. The floors are waxed and hold the light. She walks slowly, the way you walk a thing you have paid for in full.)*
> *(Below stairs the housekeeper's keys turn. The steward's pen scratches. The cook's range ticks. The house hums, and the hum is the sound of everything being done on time.)*
> *(She stops in the gallery — the portraits watching, the vases holding the last roses — and the gallery holds its beeswax smell, and the portraits watch, and the whole arrangement is so settled it is almost smug.)*
> *(She puts her hand on the newel post — the cold, the honest — and the oak is the same oak, and the hand is the same hand, and the house is the same house, and all of it is hers.)*
> *(She stops before the Dowager's portrait — Augusta, the painted — and the keeping of the line looks back at her: the spectacles, the set of the mouth, the seventy-two years of it.)*
> "The kept, Grandmama." She says it aloud, and the gallery holds the words. "The whole."
> *(The painted spectacles do not move. The painted mouth does not smile. But Rose has known Augusta for twenty-five years, and she knows what the Dowager would say, and what she would say is: good.)*
> *(She thinks of the Dowager's keeping — the seventy-two years, the line — and the vases hold the last roses, and the charter flower keeps the gallery, and the keeping goes on.)*
> *(Below, the keys turn and the pen scratches and the range ticks — the afternoon of the house, and the house is keeping it the way the house keeps everything: exactly.)*
> *(The afternoon light moves along the wall, and the portraits watch it go, and the light makes itself at home the way it always does in a finished room.)*
> *(She walks on — the gallery, the portraits — and at the gallery's end she stops, and the Park lies in the light, and the light lies on the Park, and the Park is hers.)*
> *(The house in the light of the year, and she stands in it the way she stands in everything now: as the mistress, and the mistress is where she belongs.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Park, the year's — the whole, the kept; the light. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The Park in the year's light, and Rose rides its boundary in the morning: the lake, the woods, the home farm's fields, the light.)*
> *(The mare is fresh and wants her head, and Rose gives it to her along the lake path, and the hoofbeats come back off the water.)*
> *(She stops at the lake's edge, and the water holds the sky, and the held sky trembles a little where the swan disturbs it, and then settles.)*
> *(She turns for home, and the Park lies in its light, and the light lies on the Park, and the morning is going well.)*
> *(She rides back through the Park, and the home farm's men are at the harvest, and the fields lie gathered, and the wagons stand loaded on the drive.)*
> *(The head groom rides past on a young hunter, and he touches his cap, and the horses move easy, and the young one is learning his manners.)*
> "Miss." He reins in. "The Park, miss. The year's."
> "The year's, and the kept's." She nods at the hunter. "He's coming on."
> "He's coming, miss." He rides on, and the young horse goes kindly.
> *(The lake holds the sky behind her — the water, the light — and the light lies flat on the water, and the morning is going well.)*
> *(She comes up through the garden — the beds, the year's — and the gardeners nod, and the keepers are at the year's business, and the business is the tending.)*
> *(The swan moves on the lake — the ripples spread, and settle, and the water holds the sky, and the whole lake is doing the one thing lakes do well: reflecting.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick meets her at the door — the keys — and the housekeeper nods, and the round goes on, and the keys turn, exact to the minute.)*
> *(The house rises before her — the stone — and she stands in the doorway with the Park behind and the house before, and the doorway is exactly where the mistress belongs: between them.)*
> *(She dismounts, and the lad takes the mare, and the yard takes the morning in its capable hands, and the mare blows warm into the lad's palm the way she blew warm into hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the keepers, the eternal — the household's; the charter, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Rose stands on the terrace in the evening light and watches the keepers at their work: the gardeners, the grooms, the maids, the footmen, the cook, the steward, the housekeeper.)*
> *(She knows every name. The ledger in her head holds them all — figures beside the names, but names first. Mrs. Quick with her keys. Harrow with his book. The cook with her range. The head gardener with his knife. The boy with his can. The maids, the grooms, the footmen. Every name a line, every line a keeper.)*
> *(She thinks of the charter — the sealed line, the permanent — and here are its living terms, walking about in aprons and caps, watering and polishing and baking.)*
> *(She raises her hand — the smallest gesture — and the head gardener touches his hat, and the groom touches his cap, and the maids bob from the landing, and the whole terrace answers her like a well-drilled regiment that has never been drilled.)*
> *(The housekeeper nods from the door. The steward bows from the office. The cook waves from the kitchen stair. The boy grins from the garden, and the watering can glints in the evening light.)*
> *(She stands a moment longer, and the keepers go back to their work, and the work goes on the way it always goes: thoroughly, cheerfully, and without being watched.)*
> *(The ledger in her head turns its page. The evening deepens. The terrace holds the last of the light.)*
> *(She thinks of the girl who came here ten seasons ago, who knew none of these names, and the woman on the terrace now, who knows them all, and the distance between them is the whole education of the keeping.)*
> *(She goes in as the light fails, and the house receives her, and the corridors hold the evening's quiet, and the quiet is the sound of the keepers at their rest.)*
> *(The night comes on, and the Park darkens beyond the glass, and the house hums its night note, and the note is low, and content, and entirely unhurried.)*
> *(At the stairhead she stops, and the house sounds below her — the full house, humming, and the humming going on.)*

scenes.synopsis: the year, the kept — the household's, the lesson's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year in the evening light, and Rose sits in the morning room with the household book open: the year's record.)*
> *(The pages turn under her hand: the wages, the tending, the marking. She reads them the way other people read letters — slowly, and with attention, and with a pencil for the margins.)*
> *(The lesson she chose sits in the margin in her best hand. Whichever she decided, the ink is dry and the deciding is done.)*
> *(She closes the book, and the record of the year sits honest on the desk, and the desk sits in the morning room, and the morning room holds the dusk.)*
> *(She thinks of the lesson — steadiness, care, or returning — and the margin holds it in her best hand, and the whole of it is accounted for: the wages paid, the tending done, the marking given.)*
> *(She dips the pen and enters the day's account — the marking, given room by room — and the ink takes the page, and the page takes its place among the year's pages.)*
> *(The book is heavy in her hands. The leather is worn smooth at the corners where ten seasons of mistresses have held it. She runs a thumb along the binding. Now it is her turn to wear it.)*
> *(Letitia looks in, and the hawk's eyes soften, and she nods, and goes — the aunt of the night, making her own round.)*
> *(The housekeeper passes in the corridor — the night round — and the keys turn in the far door, exact to the minute.)*
> *(She rises at last. The dusk is complete, the book is closed, and the year is kept.)*
> *(She puts out the lamp with the little brass snuffer, and the wick smokes once, and the smoke rises straight in the still air.)*
> *(She thinks of the wages — the honest, the paid — and the tending — the garden's work through the year — and the marking — the gift, and the gladness it landed in — and the ledger of her head turns its page.)*
> *(The night holds the house, and the house settles into it, and the settling is quiet, and the quiet is complete.)*
> *(The lamp is out. The dusk is complete. The year is kept.)*

scenes.synopsis: the lesson — the steadiness, the care, the returning; the kept's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The lesson in the morning light, and Rose walks the house and sees it taught — not in words, but in the doing.)*
> *(Steadiness: the housekeeper's keys turning in the linen press, exact to the minute, whatever the weather. Rose watches from the corridor, and Mrs. Quick does not hurry, and does not falter, and does not need to be watched.)*
> *(Care: the cook's bread cooling on the board, the dark loaves scored with the cross, the kitchen warm with the morning's baking. The cook breaks one and hands Rose the heel, and the heel is hot, and the giving is the lesson.)*
> *(Returning: the garden greening beyond the glass, the Hartwell rose putting out its leaves for another year, the thrush on the north wall arguing with the morning. It came back. It always comes back.)*
> *(She stops in the gallery — the portraits, the vases — and the morning light lies along the wall, and the light teaches nothing and demonstrates everything.)*
> *(At the stairhead she stops, and the house hums below her, and the hum is the sound of the lesson being lived: the keys, the bread, the green.)*
> *(The steward comes up with the book, and the pen scratches, and the honest figures take the page.)*
> *(Harrow catches her eye over the book, and the dry face says what it always says: accounted for.)*
> *(The boy waters the terrace pots, and the old gardener watches, and nods, and the nod is his whole approval, and the boy glows with it.)*
> *(She thinks of the girl who came here ten seasons ago — who knew nothing of keys or bread or green — and the woman who keeps now, who knows them all, and the distance between them is the education.)*
> *(The house teaches the way it keeps — exactly, and without announcing it. Nobody gives a speech. The keys turn. The bread cools. The rose greens.)*
> *(She passes through the gallery — the portraits, the vases — and the morning goes about its business.)*
> *(At the stairhead she stops again, and the house sounds below her — the keys, the bread, the green — and the lesson is everywhere she looks, and she looks, and the looking is enough.)*

scenes.synopsis: the mistress, the kept — Rose, the year's; the woman, the keeping's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her evening, and Rose sits at the window with the house beyond: the corridors quiet, the rooms tended, the day done.)*
> *(The lamp is lit. The household book is closed. The keys are turned. She sits, and the quiet sits in her like a well-earned rest.)*
> *(She thinks — the image she would never say aloud — of the girl who came here ten seasons ago, with her ledgers and her nerve, and the woman at the window now, with her household and her year, and the distance between them is the whole education.)*
> *(Letitia comes in, and she looks at Rose, and the hawk's eyes are soft.)*
> "Darling." She sits. "The year. The keepers. Tell me everything, and do be quick about it — I have a prior engagement with the decanter."
> "The marking's given. The keepers are glad. Mrs. Quick was nearly moved."
> "Nearly moved." The hawk's eyes gleam. "Darling, that is the highest praise the immovable has ever bestowed. The quartermaster approves."
> *(They sit together — the aunt, the niece — and the evening holds the window, and the house holds the evening.)*
> *(She tells Letitia of the day — the kitchen first, the stables, the garden, the still-room last — and the aunt listens the way she listens to everything: completely, and with editorial opinions.)*
> "The woman at the window." Letitia rises. "Dressed for the evening, sitting at the window, surveying her year." The warm look. "You look, darling, precisely like the mistress of a kept house."
> "I am the mistress of a kept house."
> "Yes, darling." She pats Rose's shoulder. "That is the joke."
> *(The lamp is lit. The book is closed. The keys are turned. The house hums its night's note, and the note is low, and content.)*
> *(She thinks of the charter — the written, the permanent — and the woman at the window, and the window holds them both: the written and the woman.)*
> *(The night holds the Park beyond the glass, and the Park is dark, and the house is warm, and the woman at the window is exactly where she means to be.)*
> *(Letitia's step sounds in the corridor, unhurried, and the decanter waits, and the night goes on, and the house hums its note.)*

scenes.synopsis: the household, the charter's — the kept, the legacy's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The household in the light of the year, and Rose walks the gallery with the charter's terms in her head: the written, the permanent.)*
> *(The charter wrote the house. The keepers keep it. She keeps the keepers. The arithmetic is simple, and she likes simple arithmetic.)*
> *(She stops before the framed copy of the charter — the sealed line, the permanent — and the ink sits in the glass like something alive, and the wax seal hangs from its ribbon, and the whole document has the quiet confidence of a thing that cannot be argued with.)*
> *(She touches the frame — the glass cool under her fingers — and the sealed line sits beneath, and the permanent is permanent, and the permanent has her name on it.)*
> *(She thinks of Quill — the solicitor, the sealed paper — and the ten seasons it took to make the terms true. Ten seasons of paper, of strongboxes, of the Network's war. And now: a frame, a wall, a seal.)*
> "The kept, Quill." She says it to the empty gallery. "The forever."
> *(The gallery holds the words — the beeswax, the portraits — and the portraits do not answer, because portraits never do, and the silence is the answer.)*
> *(The Dowager's portrait watches — Augusta, the painted — and the keeping of the line looks back: the spectacles, the set of the mouth, the seventy-two years.)*
> *(The vases hold the roses — the Hartwell roses — and the charter flower keeps the gallery the way it keeps everything: by being exactly itself.)*
> *(The charter wrote the terms. The keepers live them. She keeps the keepers. The living goes on, term by term, keeper by keeper.)*
> *(She walks the length of the gallery, and the afternoon light moves along the wall, and the light has earned its place there, the way the charter earned its frame.)*
> *(The house hums below — the keys, the pen, the range — and the humming rises through the floorboards, and the floorboards hold it, and the gallery holds the humming.)*
> *(She stands in the light of the gallery, and the charter hangs in its frame, and the house hums below, and the whole of it — the frame, the seal, the humming — is kept.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE KEEPERS' MEANING (what the keepers mean: the steadiness, the household, or the future). The year deepens; decide the meaning. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year deepens, and the keepers ask their meaning. Rose walks the house in the evening's light — the tended rooms, the kept corridors — and the question sits in her the way the dusk sits on the lawn: early, and not to be hurried.)*
> *(Steadiness, the immovable says — Mrs. Quick's keys turning whatever the weather, the house kept through ten seasons. Rose has watched it, and the watching never wavered, and the never-wavering is the whole recommendation.)*
> *(The household, the whole says — the stone, the Park, the keepers all one keeping. She has walked it room by room and acre by acre, and the walking never ended, and the never-ending is the point.)*
> *(The future, the year says — the spring come again, the keepers' children learning the tending, the charter's terms outliving them all. It has returned, and will return, because that is what kept things do.)*
> *(She thinks of the keepers — the names, the faces, the year's honest — and the meaning will shape the keepers' memory. She stands at the stairhead, and the dusk deepens, and she decides the way she decides everything now: firmly, and for good.)*
> *(She goes down to the still-room, and Mrs. Quick is there with the jars, and the keeper looks up.)*
> "Miss." The immovable voice. "The —" a pause — "the meaning, miss?"
> *(Rose asks her — the steadiness, the household, the future — and the housekeeper considers the way she considers everything: exactly.)*
> "The keepers, miss." Nearly warm. "The —" she stops — "they're kept, miss. And the kept —" another stop — "the kept keeps, miss."
> *(It is the most philosophical thing Mrs. Quick has ever said, and Rose commits it to memory verbatim, because the immovable does not philosophize twice.)*
> *(She climbs back to the morning room — the dusk — and the meaning settles in her the way the snow settles on the Park: quietly, and to stay.)*
> *(Steadiness is the keys. The household is the stone. The future is the spring. She stands in the evening's light, and the deciding is hers.)*
> *(Harrow passes with the book — the year's record — and the steward bows, and the bow says the book is ready for whatever she writes in it.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: steadiness, household, or future. The keepers' meaning is hers.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The keepers' meaning:*
- **The steadiness** — *the kept, meant.* The keepers mean steadiness — the immovable, the kept. (Consequence: the meaning is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the keepers were the giving.)
- **The household** — *the whole, meant.* The keepers mean the household — the house, the whole. (Consequence: the meaning is the whole's — but wholes are vast, and the keepers were the ones.)
- **The future** — *the returning, meant.* The keepers mean the future — the year, the returning. (Consequence: the meaning is the returning's — but returnings are future, and the keepers were the now.)
