scenes.synopsis: the meaning, the kept — the keepers', the lesson's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The meaning in the morning's light, and Rose sits in the morning room with the household book open: the year's meaning.)*
> *(The pages hold it — whichever she decided, the ink is dry, and the deciding is done, and the done is written in her best hand.)*
> *(She closes the book, and it sits honest on the desk, and the desk sits in the morning room, and the morning room holds the morning light the way it holds everything: patiently.)*
> *(At the window she stops, and the Park lies in the light, and the light lies on the Park, and the morning is going well.)*
> *(Harrow comes in with the morning's entries — the steward, the exact — and he sees the margin, and the dry face does the approving thing.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The dryest. "The —" he stops — "the meaning, miss? In the book, miss?"
> "In the book, Harrow. In my best hand."
> "Your best hand, miss." He bows. "The honest, miss."
> *(He goes — the entries, the morning — and she closes the book, and the pen is capped, and the blotting paper takes the last of the ink.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick looks in — the keys — and the housekeeper nods at the book, and the nod says the book is where it belongs.)*
> *(The house settles — the keys turned, the books closed — and the settling is quiet, and the quiet is complete.)*
> *(She thinks of the keepers — the names, the faces — and the meaning sits among them the way a flower sits among stones: unexpectedly, and exactly right.)*
> *(The steward's pen scratches in the office below. The housekeeper's keys turn in the far corridor. The cook's range ticks. The meaning is written, and the writing is done, and the house goes on.)*
> *(At the window she stops again — the Park, the light — and the year holds its meaning the way the charter holds its terms: completely, and in writing.)*
> *(She puts out the lamp, though the morning hardly needs it, and the wick smokes once, and the year is kept.)*

scenes.synopsis: the letters — the year, reported; London writes. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The evening: the letters, and Rose sits at the desk with the post. London writes.)*
> *(Lavinia's letter lies open, and Rose reads it a third time, and laughs, which is the correct response to Lavinia.)*
> "The Assembly's year is the year's event. The ton is beside itself. The keeping is the talk of London — I dined out on it twice this week, and both hostesses pretended they had thought of it first."
> *(She answers it personally — every line — because that is the Assembly's way, and Lavinia's velocity deserves steadiness in return.)*
> *(The Craykes write of the guest lists — three pages, both sides, the ink cramped with names — and she answers with the household's year, and the household's year takes two pages of its own.)*
> *(The Almerias write at length — the old friendship, the health of the children, the state of the roses at Almeria House — and she answers at length, and the length is a pleasure.)*
> *(The young write collectively — the advance guard, all exclamation and underlining — and she answers them all, and the answering takes the rest of the evening, and the evening is well spent.)*
> "Darling." She writes to Lavinia — the amusement, the reckoning. "The Assembly's year, darling. They will find it kept, darling. Do come early, and do bring your appetite."
> *(She seals them — the wax cooling on each in turn — and the post bag fills, and Henry will ride in the morning, and the morning will take the letters to London, and London will read them over breakfast.)*
> *(The sealing wax cools. The desk holds the dusk. The pen is capped. The blotting paper is full, and the evening is accounted for.)*
> *(She puts out the lamp, and the letters wait for the morning in the post bag, and the post bag waits by the door, and Henry's horse will be saddled at dawn.)*
> *(She thinks of the year reported — the keepers, the keeping, the marked — and the reporting is done, and the evening is done with it.)*
> *(The desk holds the dusk. The house holds the night. She caps the pen and puts it down.)*

scenes.synopsis: the ton, the year's — the keeping, awaited; the convened, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The ton in the light of the year, and Rose stands on the terrace and looks toward London. They will come — the letters say it plainly: the Assembly's year is the event of the year, and the ton will come.)*
> *(She thinks of the house ready — the aired sheets, the polished silver, the kept rooms — and the work is done.)*
> *(She walks the west wing with her inspection eye: the aired sheets, the kept rooms, and the coming of the ton sits in the house like a held breath.)*
> *(The maids finish the curtains — the last of the year's work — and the eldest looks down the landing, and the pride is plain.)*
> "Miss." She bobs. "The —" she stops — "the ton, miss. They'll see it, miss."
> "They'll see the kept."
> "The kept, miss." She grins. "The year's own."
> *(Rose checks the rooms — the sills, the grates, the linen — and the keeping passes muster. The sills are clean. The grates are blacked. The linen is folded the exact way Mrs. Quick demands.)*
> *(She opens a wardrobe — the spare blankets, the lavender between them — and closes it. She runs a finger along a picture frame and finds nothing. The west wing is ready for inspection by the ton, and the ton will not find a thing to criticize, which is the entire object of the exercise.)*
> *(The silver's done, twice. The mattresses turned. The shutters oiled. The west wing stands ready — the keepers' own work.)*
> *(The housekeeper comes up — the keys — and she surveys the wing, and the wing passes.)*
> "Miss." The immovable voice. "The west wing, miss. The ready."
> "The kept are ready."
> "The kept, miss." The extraordinary mouth. "The year's own."
> *(They walk the landing together — the mistress, the keeper — and the house is ready for them.)*
> *(The eldest maid curtseys them out — the landing, the curtains, the pride — and the afternoon light lies on the sills, and the sills are clean in it.)*
> *(She leaves them to the landing, and the light holds the afternoon, and the landing holds the light, and everything is where it should be.)*
> *(The ton will come, and the house will receive them, and the receiving will be worthy of the keeping: the aired sheets, the polished silver, the turned mattresses.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, the mistress's — Rose, the evening's; the kept, the keeping's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her evening, and Rose sits at the window with the Park beyond: the acres darkening, the grounds quiet, the day done.)*
> *(The lamp is lit. The book is closed. The keys are turned. She sits, and the quiet sits in her like a well-earned rest.)*
> *(She thinks of the charter — the written, the permanent — and the woman at the window, and the window holds them both.)*
> *(Augusta comes to the window, and she stands beside Rose, and the stick taps once on the floorboards.)*
> "Child." The spectacles lower. "The —" she stops — "the year, child. The keepers, child."
> "The keepers are marked, Grandmama. The year's gift, given."
> "Given." The rarest smile. "The line gives, child. It always has. Your grandfather gave the entail. Your father gave the house its ruin. You give the keepers their marking." A pause. "Yours is the better giving."
> *(They stand together — the Dowager, the mistress — and the evening holds the Park, and the Park holds the evening, and the seventy-two years stand beside the twenty-five, and the arithmetic of it is the whole lineage.)*
> "The Assembly's year, Grandmama."
> "The ton will come, child." She turns for the door. "Let them. The house is ready."
> *(Rose watches her go — the stick tapping, the back straight — and the tapping fades down the corridor, and the corridor holds it a moment longer than the ear does.)*
> *(Seventy-two years, and the back is still straight, and the spectacles still lower at exactly the right moment, and the Dowager is still the Dowager, and the house is still the house.)*
> *(She thinks of the seventy-two years — the keeping passed hand to hand, from the Dowager's hands into hers — and the hands are different, and the keeping is the same.)*
> *(The lamp burns low. The book is shut. The keys are turned. The house hums its night's note.)*
> *(The evening deepens, and the Park darkens beyond the glass, and she stays at the window, and the window holds the Park, and the Park holds the dark.)*
> *(The stick taps once more, faint, from the far corridor — the Dowager's goodnight, in her own language — and Rose smiles, and the night goes on.)*

scenes.synopsis: the charter, the kept — the household's, the legacy's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The charter in the evening light, and Rose stands in the gallery before the framed copy: the sealed line, the permanent, the written that outlives the writers.)*
> *(She thinks of the keepers — the names, the faces — and the household of the charter belongs to them as much as to her. That is what the charter is for.)*
> *(The portraits watch her think it: the Ravencrofts who built, the Hartwells who kept and broke and sold, and the empty frame at the end that is not empty anymore. They have heard it all before, and they approve, in the manner of portraits.)*
> *(She walks the length of the gallery, and beyond the windows the Park turns through its year — the lake, the woods, the fields — and the turning goes on whether she watches or not.)*
> *(She stops at the windows. The lake holds the last light. The woods hold the dusk. On the water the light thins to a seam and goes.)*
> *(Below stairs the keepers are at their evening rest. The keys are turned. The books are closed. The ranges are banked. The house is quiet in the particular way of a house that has done its day.)*
> *(She thinks of the year entire — the spring waking, the summer working, the autumn gathering, the winter resting — and the wages paid, and the tending done, and the marking given, and the meaning written in the margin in her best hand.)*
> *(The keepers moved through their seasons, and the seasons moved through the keepers, and the moving is done for this year, and the year is kept.)*
> *(The gallery holds its beeswax smell. The portraits watch. The Park turns.)*
> *(The vases hold the last roses — the Hartwell roses, the charter's flower — and the charter flower keeps the gallery the way it keeps everything: by being exactly itself.)*
> *(The house hums its night note. The humming rises through the floorboards. The floorboards hold it.)*
> *(She stands a long time, and the light fails, and the dusk completes itself, and the chapter closes on the turning.)*
> *(She goes in as the light fails, and the house receives her, and the corridors hold the evening's quiet, and the quiet is the sound of everything kept.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's keeping report — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"This year the Hartwell household has turned through its seasons — kept, keeping, kept — and the Gazette — having watched the keeping from the first — finds it the charter's true household. The keepers, yearly. The Gazette will watch, annually."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (annually! watching!), then the reckoning: the year is pronounced true in print as well as in the house's corridors, and Bell has made the keeping permanent, which is Bell's way of making it forever. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the keeping the Gazette watches annually is the keeping that's real.* — remembered: *the lesson: the keeping the Gazette watches annually is the keeping that's real.*
scenes.sting: This year the Hartwell household has turned through its seasons — kept, keeping, kept — and the Gazette — having watched the keeping from the first — finds it the charter's true household. The keepers, yearly. The Gazette will watch, annually.

scenes.synopsis: the Park's year — the estate, the turned; the whole, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and she walks the Park — the Park's year, coming — and the estate turns through its year.)*
> *(She watches — the estate, the year's — the Park's year, the turning: the whole, the kept.)*
> "The Park's year." She looks at the whole — the estate, the turned. "The —" she stops — "through its year." She breathes. "The whole —" another stop — "the kept, the yearly."
> *(The chapter closes on the turning — the estate, the year's — and the Season turns toward the Park: the estate's year — and the Season holds its breath.)*

scenes.synopsis: the year's turning — the Park's year; the estate, the seasons. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She wakes before the house does, and the year's first decision is a small one: the boots. They wait by the garden door where she left them, mud caked on the left toe from yesterday's boundary walk. The leather is cold when she pulls them on. It always is. She has stopped expecting otherwise.)*
> *(The house is still behind her — the lamps out, the stairs creaking under her feet, the hall dark as a held breath. She opens the garden door, and the Park is out there in the half-light, dew silvering the grass, the mist sitting low over the lake. She steps into it, and the air is cold enough to wake her properly.)*
> *(She takes the canal first, the way she always takes it first. The towpath is damp under her boots, and the water lies between the reeds without a ripple, holding what is left of the stars. A moorhen is out early, fussing in the rushes with business it will not explain.)*
> *(She walks the canal's whole length. The straightness of it pleases her — the engineer's pleasure, paid for by men long dead who dug it out with spades. She counts her strides without meaning to. It is the ledger's habit, and she lets the numbers run.)*
> *(The lake next, and the swans are on the water with this year's cygnets trailing behind in a line, grey and earnest. The boathouse door stands open and the covers are half off the boats. The season is getting under way, watched or not.)*
> *(The meadows after, and the grass is high and wet against her skirts, and the field waits for the scythe. She stops at the edge and looks across it — green to the hedgerows, the wind moving through it in long waves, the whole field breathing in its sleep.)*
> *(The woods last, before the climb, and the shade takes her, and the leaf-mould is soft under the boots. The old oaks stand in their ranks. A jay screams in the canopy and nothing answers, which is the woods' entire opinion of morning visitors.)*
> *(She comes back by the boundary's height, and the estate lies below in the first light — the lake, the canal, the meadows, the woods — and her head opens its ledger unasked.)*
> *(Letitia is at the garden door when she comes in, the household book under her arm. The hawk's eyes take in the boots, the mud, the hour. She says nothing, which is the quartermaster's form of approval.)*
> "You're up early, darling." Letitia looks at the boots. "The year's walking?"
> "The year's walking." Rose sits on the step to unlace them. "Every mile of it."

scenes.synopsis: the spring — the estate's; the waking, the whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The rose garden lies in the morning sun, and the head gardener is already among the canes. He has been at work since before she woke — he is always at work before she wakes — and the beds are weeded, the paths swept, and the whole garden wears the order of a man who has been keeping it for forty years and means to keep it for forty more.)*
> *(She walks the paths between the beds. The Hartwell rose is greening on its canes, and the buds are coming fat, and she takes the particular pleasure in them that she takes in a balanced column: completely, and without reservation.)*
> *(The old man straightens when he sees her and touches his hat.)*
> "Miss." He gestures at the canes with his knife. "The greening, miss. You'll see it properly by June."
> "And the buds, gardener?"
> "Fat as plums, miss." He bends a cane down for her to look. "This one's been tended. You'll know the color when it comes."
> *(She bends to look. The buds are green and tight and absolutely certain of themselves. She does not touch them. That is the gardener's rule, and she respects it the way she respects all rules made by men who know more than she does.)*
> *(The boy is at the far bed with the watering can, and he is watering with particular care — slow, deliberate, the can tilted just so — and there is something new in the care. Pride, perhaps. He sees her, and stands straight, and nearly drops the can recovering.)*
> "Miss." He touches his cap. "The watering, miss. The beds, miss."
> "Steady with it, boy. The roots, not the leaves."
> "Aye, miss." He grins. "The roots, miss. I know the roots."
> *(She walks on through the garden, and the bees are working the early flowers, loud in the still air. The head gardener follows her to the gate — he always follows her to the gate — and he is not a man of many words, and he does not waste the few he has.)*
> "Miss." He touches his hat again. "The rose'll bloom, miss. Tended things bloom."
> "Tended things bloom, gardener."
> "Aye, miss." The rarest smile. "That's the way of it."
> *(She walks back through the Park with the garden behind her, and the greening walks with her, and her head does its ledger-work unasked: the acres, the buds, the year's first entries. The figures sit beside the greening the way the ink sits beside the margin. The account is open, and the year has begun to fill it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the lake — the spring's; the water, the whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The canal runs straight through the Park like a ruled line, and she walks its length in the morning with the sun low over the water. The towpath is damp under her boots. The reeds stand at the edges, and a moorhen nests in the rushes, and the water is so still it holds the sky without a ripple.)*
> *(She walks it the way she always walks it: exactly, and without hurrying. The straightness pleases her — the surveyor's pleasure — and she thinks of the men who dug it, and the years it took them, and the water that has lain in it ever since, patient and level. Men dug, and women walk what they dug, and the world turns on the two of them.)*
> *(Her boots beat the towpath, and she counts the beats without meaning to — the ledger's habit — and she lets the numbers run the way she lets the water run: steadily, and without interference.)*
> *(The head groom rides the far bank on his morning round. The horse's hooves thud soft on the turf. He touches his cap when he sees her and reins in.)*
> "Miss." He looks at the water. "The canal, miss. Walked it all, miss?"
> "Walking it now, groom. The far bank's firm?"
> "Firm as Sunday, miss." He glances down at the lock. "The lock's holding, miss. No leakage."
> "Good. The year's water in the year's canal."
> "Aye, miss." He rides on. "The whole, miss."
> *(She watches him go — the horse, the rider, the far bank holding them both — and the clouds move in the canal's sky, and the clouds do not hurry, and neither does she.)*
> *(Beyond the second bend a heron stands in the shallows, motionless as a held breath. She stands motionless too, out of respect for the profession. The heron does not catch anything while she watches. It does not seem to mind.)*
> *(At the canal's end she stops at the lock. The water waits at the gates, dark and patient. She puts her hand on the lock timber, and the wood is wet and cold, and the cold runs straight up her arm like a report. She turns for home along the far bank, and the towpath carries her, and the morning goes with her.)*

scenes.synopsis: the canal — the spring's; the walked, the whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The summer comes to the Park with the light, and she walks it early, before the heat settles. The light lies on the lake in a broad band, and the meadows shine, and the woods stand dark against the brightness, and the year's middle holds the way a held breath holds.)*
> *(The path is dusty under her boots, and the dust rises and settles on her skirts, and she does not brush it off. The dust is what the summer charges, and everyone who walks pays it, and she pays it willingly.)*
> *(The hay is high in the meadows, and the men will cut it this week. She stops at the field's edge, and the hay moves in the wind in long waves, and the whole field breathes in its sleep, and she stands a while and watches it breathe.)*
> *(She thinks of the winter's hay — the cut, the stored, the barn full to the rafters — and the summer's cutting feeding the winter's keeping, and the arithmetic sits in her head like a balanced column, and the column balances.)*
> *(She seeks the woods' edge, and the shade takes her the way the Park takes everything: completely, and without asking. The birdsong hangs in the cool air. She stands in it a moment, and the cool is a mercy, and she takes it.)*
> *(The boy brings the water to the beds with his shirt sticking to his back, and the old gardener nods from the shade of his hat.)*
> "Miss." The boy stops by the path, breathless. "The beds, miss. Watered, miss."
> "I can see the watering, boy. The beds look pleased with you."
> "Aye, miss." He grins, and the grin is all summer. "They drink it up, miss."
> *(She walks on through the heat. She thinks of the first summer she walked here — the stranger's summer, everything new and everything watched — and the Park was a stranger then, and now it is not, and the difference is in her legs, and her legs know it.)*
> *(The afternoon comes on, and the heat thickens, and she turns for the shade of the woods. At the edge she looks back across the shining meadows, and the light lies on the lake in its broad band, and the year's middle holds, and holds, and she walks into the shade.)*

scenes.synopsis: the summer — the estate's; the light, the whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The autumn comes to the Park with the gold, and she walks it in the morning with the light slanting through the trees. The leaves are turning — the beech first, then the oak — and the Park puts on its gold the way a woman puts on her best dress: deliberately, and for the season, and with no apology.)*
> *(She walks the woods, and the leaf-fall has begun, and the paths are carpeted deep, and her boots sink in the leaves, and the sinking is soft. A jay screams in the canopy. The squirrels argue in the branches. The woods go about the autumn business with the particular energy of a household preparing for guests.)*
> *(The rookery is loud in the elms. The rooks argue the way rooks always argue — at length, at volume, about nothing she can discern — and she stands under the noise a moment and considers calling it a parliament, and decides the rooks would consider that flattery.)*
> *(She walks the boundary, and the hedgerows are heavy with berries, black and red among the leaves. She picks one and tastes it. The taste is sharp. The sharp tells her nothing she did not know, and she likes it anyway.)*
> *(The home farm's men are at the second cutting, and the scythes go through the morning in long sweeps, and the hay falls in lines, and the smell rises — sweet, green, cut — and she breathes it in, and the breathing goes all the way down.)*
> *(The eldest of the men sees her and straightens, and touches his hat.)*
> "Miss." He tests the scythe's edge with his thumb. "Second cutting, miss. The field's kind this year."
> "Kind fields make kind winters."
> "Aye, miss." He grins, and the grin is weathered. "That's the way of it, miss."
> *(She walks on through the gold. She thinks of the first autumn she walked here — the stranger's autumn, all angles and uncertainty — and the gold was a stranger's gold then, and she did not trust it. Now it is hers, and she trusts it the way she trusts a column that has balanced three years running.)*
> *(The afternoon comes on, and the light goes amber, and she turns for home with the gold behind her and the rookery still arguing, and the arguing follows her down the path like an escort she did not ask for and does not dismiss.)*

scenes.synopsis: the meadows — the summer's; the green, the whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The winter comes to the Park with the white, and she walks it in the thin light of the morning. The frost is on the paths, and her boots crunch on the frozen gravel, and the crunching announces everything: the Park sleeps, and the sleep is deep.)*
> *(The lake is iron under the sky, and the meadows lie blank to the hedgerows, and the woods stand black against the white. Black against white, stark and exact, the winter making its whole argument without a word.)*
> *(Her breath clouds in front of her. The keepers move through the white on the winter business — the boy with coal for the bothy, shoulders hunched against the cold; the groom with feed for the stables; the head gardener with his barrow of straw. The work goes on. It does not stop for weather.)*
> *(She thinks of the summer hay — cut, stored, the barn full to the rafters — and the winter white against the summer's gold, and the year turning on the two of them, and she keeps the books, and the books are honest.)*
> *(The head gardener is at the rose garden with the straw, and he touches his hat, and the Hartwell rose sleeps under its blanket, and his breath clouds in the cold.)*
> "Miss." He pats the straw with a gloved hand. "The resting, miss. The year's."
> "The kept's resting."
> "Aye, miss." The rarest smile, and the frost in his beard. "The spring'll come, miss. It always comes."
> *(She looks at the straw, tucked close around the canes, and she thinks of the impossible warmth inside it — the green sleeping under the white — and the old man sees her thinking it, and nods, because he has thought it himself every winter for forty years.)*
> *(The boy comes up the path with the empty coal scuttle, red-nosed and bright-eyed.)*
> "Miss." He touches his cap. "The bothy's warm, miss. The fire's in, miss."
> "Good. Mind you bank it before dark."
> "Aye, miss." He grins. "I know the banking, miss."
> *(She walks on through the white, and the Park sleeps around her, and her boots crunch, and the crunching is the only sound, and she does not mind the sound, because the sound means she is the one walking.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woods — the summer's; the shade, the whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The spring comes again to the Park, and she walks it in the morning with the light coming up behind the elms. It wakes again — the buds, the birds, the green pushing up through the leaf-mould — and the year keeps its single promise: again. She believes it the way she believes in ledgers — because it has never once been wrong.)*
> *(She walks to the rose garden, and the Hartwell rose is greening on its canes, and the head gardener is there with his knife, and he touches his hat.)*
> "Miss." The rarest smile. "Second spring, miss. Same canes."
> "Same canes, gardener. And the buds?"
> "Coming, miss." He bends one down. "Not plums yet. Give them a fortnight."
> *(The boy is at the watering with his can, and the bees work the early flowers, and the Park wakes around them, and she leaves them to it, because some mornings the garden does not need her.)*
> *(She walks the boundary with the primroses out along the banks and the rookery arguing in the elms, and she knows every rut and stile now — the stile with the loose rail, the rut where the cart got stuck in March, the gap in the hedge where the fox goes through. Three springs of walking, and the ground has given up its secrets.)*
> *(The ledger in her head turns its pages, and the entries come round again: the greening, the buds, the tended. Familiar entries, and the familiar is a kind of wealth, and she is rich in it.)*
> *(She stops at the boundary's height and looks back over the Park — the lake, the canal, the meadows, the woods — and the whole lies in the morning light like something counted, and she is the one who counted it, and the counting was the pleasure.)*
> *(The head groom rides past on the far bank on his morning round, and the horse's hooves thud soft on the turf, and he touches his cap.)*

scenes.prose:
> *(The year deepens, and the lesson asks its form. She walks the Park in the morning — the whole of it, the estate entire — and the question walks with her, and sits in her stride, and will not be hurried.)*
> *(The wholeness walks first, the way it always walks first: the Park entire, every acre in a single keeping. She has walked every mile of it — the canal's length, the boundary's height, the lake's edge, the woods' shade — and the miles are in her legs, and the legs remember. She looks down from the boundary's height, and the Park lies below in the morning light like something counted, and she is the one who counted it, and the counting says: one thing, not many.)*
> *(The ground walks second: the soil under the boots, the mud worked into the leather. She stops and looks at her boots, and the towpath dirt and the meadow edge and the wood's leaf-mould are all there, ground in. She thinks of the men who dug the canal, and the years it took them, and the water that has lain in it ever since, patient and level. The ground holds everything, and everything she has learned started with looking down.)*
> *(The returning walks third: the year come round, the spring arrived again. She has watched it turn — the greening, the blooming, the cutting, the white — and the turning has never once been wrong. The head gardener said it in the winter, with the frost in his beard: the spring'll come. It always comes. The returning says the walking will be worth walking again.)*
> *(Three forms, and each of them true, and each of them argued by the ground itself. She walks the canal's length, and her boots beat the dirt, and the lesson's form will shape the year's memory — what the year taught, and what of it she keeps. The dusk will sit on the lawn early, and not to be hurried, and neither is she.)*

> *(The winter comes to the Park with the white, and she walks it in the thin light of the morning. The frost is on the paths, and her boots crunch on the frozen gravel, and the crunching announces everything: the Park sleeps, and the sleep is deep.)*
> *(The lake is iron under the sky — flat, grey, unmoving — and the meadows lie blank to the hedgerows, and the woods stand black against the white. She walks the lake's edge, and the ice has begun at the margins, thin as paper — a first draft of winter — and she crouches to look at it, and does not step on it.)*
> *(Her breath clouds in front of her, and the keepers move through the white on the winter business. The boy carries coal to the bothy, shoulders hunched, and the groom leads a blanketed horse to the stable, and the head gardener pushes his barrow of straw toward the rose garden. The work goes on. It does not stop for weather.)*
> *(She thinks of the summer hay — cut, stored, the barn full to the rafters — and the arithmetic of the seasons sits in her head like a balanced column: the summer fed the winter, the winter will feed the spring, the spring will feed the summer. The column balances, and the balancing steadies her.)*
> *(The head gardener is at the rose garden with the straw, and he touches his hat, and the Hartwell rose sleeps under its blanket, and his breath clouds in the cold air.)*
> "Miss." He pats the straw with a gloved hand. "The resting, miss. The year's."
> "The kept's resting."
> "Aye, miss." The rarest smile, and the frost in his beard. "The spring'll come, miss. It always comes."
> *(She looks at the straw, tucked close around the canes, and she thinks of the green sleeping under the white, and the thinking warms her, which is absurd, and she lets it be absurd.)*
> *(A robin watches from the garden wall with its head cocked, bright-eyed, unafraid. She watches it back. Neither of them blinks first, or perhaps both of them do, and it hardly matters.)*
> *(She walks on through the white, and the Park sleeps around her. At the garden door she stops and looks back — the white, the black woods, the iron lake — and the morning holds them all, and she turns for the house, and the house is warm, and the warm is waiting.)*

> *(The snow comes in the night, and she wakes to the Park transformed — a blanket laid over every acre while the house slept. She pulls on the boots and walks out into it, and her boots sink to the ankle, and the paths are gone, and the going is slow.)*
> *(The Park lies white to the horizon. The lake is lost in the white — no water, no margin, only the flat white going on until the woods stop it. The woods are black strokes on the white, and the strokes are spare, and the spare is beautiful, and she stands a moment just to look at it.)*
> *(She makes for the rose garden through the drifted paths, lifting her skirts, and the going is hard work, and the hard work warms her, and she is glad of the warming. The Hartwell rose sleeps under its straw, and the head gardener is there before her with the snow on his shoulders, and he shakes it off like a dog, and touches his hat.)*
> "Miss." He pats the straw. "The blanket, miss. The year's."
> "The kept's blanket."
> "Aye, miss." He tucks the straw closer around the canes, and his fingers are quick and sure. "The warm, miss. The impossible."
> *(She puts her bare hand into the straw, and the warmth comes up to meet her — impossible, green, alive under all that white — and the old man nods, and the nod says everything, and she does not need the everything said aloud.)*
> *(The robin watches from the wall with its head cocked, bright-eyed and unafraid. She thinks of the spring canes greening under the straw, and the snow above them, and the year turning on the two of them, and she takes her hand out before her fingers go numb.)*
> *(She walks back with her own prints trailing behind her, dark in the white, a single line of coming and going. The boy is at the bothy door with the coal scuttle, and he waves.)*
> "Miss." He grins. "The snow, miss. The whole, miss."
> "The whole, boy. Mind the drifts."
> "Aye, miss." He laughs. "I know the drifts, miss."
> *(At the garden door she stops, and the Park is white to the horizon, and her prints run back across it like a signature, and she stamps the snow off her boots, and goes in.)*

> "Tell the cook to save me one."

> "Aye, miss." He grins. "That's the way of it, miss."
> *(The afternoon comes on, and the light goes amber, and she turns for home with the gold behind her, and she throws the core into the hedge for the fox, and the day's work is done.)*

scenes.prose:
> *(She walks to the lake in the morning, and the water lies in the light, flat and bright. The swans move on it with their cygnets trailing behind in a line, grey and earnest, and the sight of them is so exactly right that she stops to watch.)*
> *(The cygnets trail the swans in a line, and the line holds, and the water takes them all without comment. The lake has lain here longer than any living memory, and it will lie here longer than hers. She does the arithmetic, and the arithmetic humbles her, and she does not mind the humbling.)*
> *(She stands at the edge, and the boathouse wakes behind her, and the covers come off the boats, and the water laps the pilings, steady and low, and the sound is the morning talking to itself.)*
> *(A fish rises out beyond the reeds, and the ripples spread and settle, and the mirror mends itself. She thinks of the first spring's lake, and the second, and the third, and the lake has been the same in all of them, and the sameness steadies her.)*
> *(The head groom rides down to the water with a string of horses, and the horses drink, heads down, serious as clerks, and the seriousness becomes them.)*
> "Miss." He touches his cap. "The lake, miss. The water's good, miss."
> "The water's always good, groom. That's the lake's whole point."
> "Aye, miss." He grins. "That's the point, miss."
> *(She walks the lake's edge with the reeds whispering, and the swans glide, and the cygnets trail, and the line holds, and the holding is the whole of the lesson, and the lesson needs no explaining.)*
> *(A moorhen fusses in the rushes, and a dragonfly hangs over the water, blue and still, and she stands and watches it hang, and the morning is in no hurry at all.)*
> *(She thinks of the years the lake has lain here — through whose keeping, through whose walking — and the lake keeps its counsel, and she keeps hers, and the counsel is the same: stay, and hold, and reflect, and do not hurry.)*
> *(The ledger in her head counts the acres, and the counting is exact, and the lake is entered, and she turns for home along the water, and the water lies in the light, and the light goes with her.)*

scenes.synopsis: the canal, the eternal — the walked, the whole; the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The canal runs straight through the Park like a ruled line, and she walks its length in the morning with the sun on the water. The water is still. A moorhen nests in the rushes. The reeds stand at the edges, and the edges hold the light.)*
> *(Her boots beat the towpath, and the straightness holds, and she thinks of the men who dug it, and the years it took them, and the water that has lain in it ever since, patient and level. Somewhere there are men who dig, and somewhere there are women who walk what they dug, and the world turns on the two of them, and she has never been more certain of anything.)*
> *(She counts the beats without meaning to — the ledger's habit — and she lets the numbers run the way she lets the water run: steadily, and without interference. The numbers do not need her. The water does not need her. She walks anyway.)*
> *(The head groom rides the far bank on his morning round, and the horse's hooves thud soft on the turf, and he touches his cap.)*
> "Miss." He reins in. "The canal, miss. The walked, miss."
> "The year's walked, groom."
> "Aye, miss." He rides on. "The whole, miss."
> *(She watches him go — the horse, the rider, the far bank — and the sky lies in the canal, and the clouds move in it, slow and unhurried as the morning itself.)*
> *(At the lock she stops, and the water waits at the gates, dark and patient. A kingfisher flashes along the water, blue as a kept promise, and she stands and watches it go, quick and blue, and the morning does not hurry it.)*
> *(She thinks of the canal's digging — the men, the years, the spades — and the water has lain here ever since, patient and level. The canal makes its whole argument by lying still.)*
> *(She puts her hand on the lock timber, and the wood is wet and cold, and the cold is clean, and she turns for home along the far bank, and the towpath is hers, and the walking is hers, and the morning is hers, and that is enough.)*

scenes.synopsis: the meadows, the eternal — the green, the whole; the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She walks the meadows in the morning, and the hay stands high, and the field waits for the scythe. The field makes its case without a word: green to the hedgerows, wind moving through in long waves, the whole meadow breathing.)*
> *(The meadows lie in the light, and the home farm's men are at the edge with their scythes over their shoulders, and they nod as she passes.)*
> "Miss." The eldest touches his hat. "Third cutting, miss. The field's kind this year."
> "Kind fields make kind winters."
> "Aye, miss." He tests the scythe's edge with his thumb. "That's the way of it, miss."
> *(The scythes begin, and the swish goes through the morning in long sweeps, and the hay falls in lines behind the men, and the smell rises — sweet, green, cut — and she breathes it in, and the breathing goes all the way down.)*
> *(She walks the field's edge, and the stalks catch at her skirts, and she does not mind the catching. The field has been generous — the first summer, the second, the third — and the generous is a thing she has learned to accept, the way the field has learned to give.)*
> *(The boy comes across the field with the water jar for the men, running, and he is quick and sure.)*
> "Miss." He grins, breathless. "The water, miss. For the cutting, miss."
> "Good boy. The men'll want it in this heat."
> "Aye, miss." He runs on. "The cutting, miss."
> *(She thinks of the barn — the rafters, the full — and the winter fed from the summer's work, and the arithmetic sits in her head like a balanced column, and the column balances, and she does the balancing without thinking.)*
> *(A lark goes up from the uncut grass, and she stands and watches it climb until it is a speck, and the speck sings, and she listens.)*
> *(She walks home through the falling hay, and the field is smaller behind her, and the barn will be fuller, and the circle turns, and she walks inside the turning, and the walking is the whole of it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woods, the eternal — the shade, the whole; the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She takes the woods in the afternoon, and the trees close over the path, and the shade takes her. The shade is complete — the year's shelter, the green roof — and the birdsong hangs in the cool air, and her boots sink in the leaf-mould.)*
> *(The mould is soft with the years, deep and dark, and she walks it the way she walks everything now: on foot, and exactly, and without hurrying. The years are under her feet, and the feet know it.)*
> *(The old oaks stand in their ranks, and they were old when Augusta was young, and a jay screams in the canopy, and the squirrels argue in the branches, and the woods go about the year's business with no regard for hers, and the no-regard is the woods' whole charm.)*
> *(She puts her hand to the greatest oak, and the bark is rough under her palm, and she thinks of the charter — the written, the permanent, the sealed paper — and the woods are the charter made visible: kept, and keeping, and kept again. Quill would approve of the phrasing. She almost smiles.)*
> *(The path winds through the trees, and she follows it, and the following needs no reason beyond the afternoon.)*
> *(A deer starts from the bracken ahead of her, sudden as a dropped plate, and she stands still and watches it go — quick, clean, all woods.)*
> *(She thinks of the girl who came here — all angles and uncertainty — and the woman who walks now, and the between is the years, and the years are hers, earned step by step, mile by mile.)*
> *(At the woods' edge she stops, and the meadows shine beyond, and the light lies on the hayfields, and the fields are gold-green, and she stands at the boundary between the shade and the light, and the standing is her own.)*
> *(She steps out of the shade into the light, and the heat takes her shoulders, and the shelter is behind her, and the light is ahead, and the woods keep their counsel, and she keeps hers, and the counsel is the same.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE PARK'S GIFT (how the estate's year is marked: the walk, the planting, or the keeping). The year deepens; decide the marking. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year deepens, and the Park asks its marking. She walks the whole — the estate entire, the boundary's length — and the question walks with her, and sits in her stride, and will not be hurried.)*
> *(The walk speaks first, the way it always speaks first: the paths under her boots, the miles in her legs. She has walked every path — the towpath, the lake's edge, the boundary, the woods — and the paths are hers now, entered in her legs the way figures are entered in Harrow's book: exactly, and without apology. The walk says the keeping is in the going, and the estate is known by the feet, and the miles are the measure.)*
> *(The planting speaks second: the beds, the green in the gardeners' hands. She has watched every planting — the rose greening through three springs, the buds fat as plums, the boy learning the watering — and the head gardener is at the beds as she passes, and he touches his hat, and the boy stands straight by the watering can. The planting says the keeping is in the tending, and the tended will bloom, and the spring'll come. It always comes.)*
> "Miss." The old man straightens from the bed. "Thinking, miss?"
> "Deciding, gardener."
> "Aye, miss." He nods, and goes back to the beds.
> *(The keeping speaks third: the estate entire, the whole held. She has kept every mile — the walked, the tended, the turned — and the keeping says the whole is one keeping, and the charter's terms are living terms, and the Park is hers the way the ledger is hers. She stands on the boundary's height with the Park below in the light — the lake, the canal, the meadows, the woods — and the whole lies like something counted, and she is the one who counted it.)*
> *(Three forms, and the marking will shape the year's memory — what the year was marked by, and what of it endures. She walks home, and the marking sits in her the way the dusk sits on the lawn: early, and not to be hurried. She decides the way she decides everything now: firmly, and for good.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: walk, planting, or keeping. The Park's gift is hers to give.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The Park's gift:*
- **The walk** — *the paths, marked.* The year is marked with a walk — the paths, the taken. (Consequence: the marking is the taken's — but takens are feet's, and the year was the whole's.)
- **The planting** — *the gardeners, marked.* The year is marked with a planting — the gardeners', the planted. (Consequence: the marking is the planted's — but planteds are hands', and the year was the estate's.)
- **The keeping** — *the estate, marked.* The year is marked with keeping — the estate's, the kept. (Consequence: the marking is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the year was the walking's.)

scenes.synopsis: the marking — the gift, the given; the Park, the marked. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The marking is given — the gift, as she chose — and she walks the Park in the morning to watch it land. She does it the way the walking asks: on foot, personally, without ceremony.)*
> *(She walks the canal's length first. The towpath is damp under her boots, and the water lies still between the reeds, and a moorhen fusses in the rushes, and none of it knows it has been marked, and all of it has.)*
> *(She walks to the rose garden next. The head gardener touches his hat, and the boy stands straight by the watering can, and the beds are green and ordered, and she has only named what the gardeners made.)*
> *(She walks to the lake last. The swans glide, and the cygnets trail in their line, and the surface holds the sky without comment, and she has only witnessed it.)*
> *(She walks the whole circuit — the lake, the canal, the meadows, the woods — and her boots beat the dirt, and the dirt takes the print, and the print stays a while before the wind takes it.)*
> *(The head groom rides the far bank on his morning round, and he touches his cap, and the horse's hooves thud soft on the turf.)*
> "Miss." He reins in. "The marking, miss. The Park wears it, miss."
> "The Park wears it well, groom."
> "Aye, miss." He rides on. "Well, miss."
> *(The boy stops her on the path, bright-eyed.)*
> "Miss." He stops, and starts again. "Is it done, miss? The marking?"
> "It's done, boy. Walk it and see."
> *(He grins — the watering can, the pride — and goes back to the beds at a run.)*
> *(In the library Harrow enters it in the book in his exact hand. The pen scratches. The ink dries. He blots it with the particular care of a man who has blotted ten thousand pages, and the page holds the marking the way the Park holds it: exactly.)*
> *(She walks back through the Park, and the swans go about the year's business, and the reeds go about it, and the green goes about it, and the business does not pause for the marking, and the not-pausing is the whole point.)*

scenes.synopsis: the estate, the marked — the whole, the year's; the kept, the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The estate is marked, and she walks the Park in the morning and sees it worn. The paths, the beds, the water — and the Park holds itself a fraction prouder, a fraction surer, the way a man stands straighter in a new coat. The difference is small. The small is the whole point.)*
> *(She walks the canal first. The towpath is firm under her boots, and the water lies still between the reeds, and a moorhen fusses in the rushes with its morning business, and the business is brisk.)*
> *(She walks to the rose garden. The head gardener touches his hat as she passes, and the boy is watering with particular ceremony — slower than usual, more deliberate — and the ceremony makes her smile, and she does not hide the smiling.)*
> *(She walks to the lake. The swans glide in their lines with the cygnets trailing, unhurried, and the unhurried suits the day, and the day suits the lake.)*
> *(She walks the meadows. The hay stands high, and the field waits for the scythe, and the waiting is nearly over, and the nearly-over has a smell: sweet, green, cut.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick meets her at the garden door with the keys at her waist, and the housekeeper looks out over the Park, and nods.)*
> "Miss." The immovable look. "The estate, miss. Marked, miss."
> "Marked, Mrs. Quick. The whole of it."
> "Aye, miss." The nod again. "The whole, miss."
> *(She walks the boundary from end to end, and the miles go into her legs the way figures go into Harrow's book: exactly, and without apology.)*
> *(The head groom rides past on his round, and he touches his cap, and the horse's hooves thud soft on the turf. He does not speak — there is nothing to say — and she nods back, and the nodding is enough.)*
> *(At the boundary's height she stops and looks back — the lake, the canal, the meadows, the woods — and the morning light lies across them all, gold on the water and green on the fields, and she turns for home with the marked Park at her back.)*

scenes.synopsis: the whole, the eternal — the Park's; the charter, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The whole in the year's light, and she walks the boundary's length, and the charter walks with her. She has walked every mile — the canal, the lake, the meadows, the woods — and the miles are the charter made visible, kept and keeping.)*
> *(She thinks of Quill, the solicitor with the exact hand, and the sealed paper, and the ten seasons it took to make the terms true. Ten seasons of walking, and the walking made them true, and she does not apologize for the arithmetic.)*
> *(The boundary's height, and the estate below. The Park lies in the light like the charter's own map: the lake, the canal, the meadows, the woods, the whole, every acre a term, every term kept.)*
> *(She walks down the slope with her boots beating the dirt, and the head groom rides past on his round, and touches his cap.)*
> "Miss." He reins in. "The boundary, miss. The whole, miss."
> "The whole, groom. Every mile of it."
> "Aye, miss." He rides on. "Every mile, miss."
> *(She stops at the lake and looks across the water. The water holds the sky. She stands a while and lets it.)*
> *(She walks the towpath a way, and the reeds stand at the edges, and a fish rises beyond them, and the ripples spread and settle, and the water mends itself the way it always mends itself.)*
> *(She walks the woods, and the old oaks stand in their ranks, and they were old when Augusta was young, and the standing of them steadies her.)*
> *(She thinks of the girl who came here, all angles and uncertainty, and the woman who walks now, and the years between them, and the years are hers.)*
> *(The boy is at the beds with the watering can, and he waves.)*
> "Miss." He grins. "The whole, miss. The charter's, miss."
> "The charter's, boy. And the year's."
> "Aye, miss." He laughs. "The year's, miss."
> *(She walks the meadows, and the hay stands high, and the field waits for the scythe, and the waiting is nearly over, and the nearly-over smells of sweet cut grass.)*
> *(At the garden door she stops, and the Park lies in the light, and the charter holds, and she holds with it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the lesson — the wholeness, the ground, the returning; the kept's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The lesson sits in the morning light, and she walks the Park, and the Park teaches. It teaches the way it keeps — exactly, and without announcing it, and without asking for thanks. It is not a schoolmaster. It does not lecture. It goes on being kept, and she goes on watching, and the watching teaches her.)*
> *(She walks the canal from end to end. The towpath dirt holds the teaching: the whole mile walked, every path known, every beat counted without meaning to. The dirt is honest under her boots, and the honest needs no defending.)*
> *(She stops at the lake. The surface shows her the returning: the spring come again, the water holding the sky the way it held it last year and the year before. The water does not explain itself. It holds. The holding is the lesson, and the lesson needs no explaining either.)*
> *(The boy waters the beds, and the old gardener watches from the path, and nods. The boy has learned the watering — the roots, not the leaves — and the learning took a year, and the year was the teacher.)*
> *(She thinks of the girl who came here, all angles and uncertainty, and the woman who walks now, and the years have taught the difference, and the difference walks in her stride.)*
> *(The head groom rides past on his round, and he touches his cap.)*
> "Miss." He reins in. "The lesson, miss. Learned it, miss?"
> "Learning it still, groom. Every day."
> "Aye, miss." He rides on. "Every day, miss."
> *(She walks the woods, and the old oaks stand in their ranks. The terms, and the living of them: the charter kept by walking it, mile by mile.)*
> *(She walks the meadows, and the hay stands high. The cut, the stored, the barn full to the rafters: the field's generous arithmetic, worked out in public.)*
> *(At the garden door she stops with the Park in the light. The lesson is in her legs, and her legs carry it home, and the carrying is the whole of it, and the whole of it walks home with her through the dusk.)*

scenes.synopsis: the walker, the kept — Rose, the year's; the woman, the walking's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her evening, and she sits at the window with the Park beyond, and the boots stand by the door with the mud on them. The mud is honest — towpath dirt, meadow edge, wood leaf-mould, all of it ground into the leather — and the honest needs no explaining, and she does not explain it.)*
> *(She sits, and the year settles into the woman's quiet: the estate turned, the lesson decided, the Park marked. Her legs ache, and the aching is the miles, and she earned every one.)*
> *(She thinks of the morning's walk — the canal, the lake, the boundary, the woods — and the miles sit in her legs the way figures sit in Harrow's book: exactly, and without apology. Harrow would approve of the exactness. Harrow approves of very little else, and she counts the approval.)*
> *(She thinks of the decisions — the lesson, the marking, the meaning — and the deciding was done on the walking, and the work was hers. She decides the way she decides everything now: firmly, and for good, and then she stops deciding and sits still.)*
> *(The lamp is lit, and the light is warm, and the warm fills the room, and the room holds it.)*
> *(Letitia is across the room in her chair with the household book closed for once, and she hums an old tune, off-key in the pleasant way, and the humming fills the quiet, and the quiet holds the humming.)*
> "Darling." Letitia looks up, and the hawk's eyes are fond. "The year's walking. Done?"
> "The walking's done. The keeping goes on."
> "Aye, darling." The fond look. "It goes on."
> *(The boots stand by the door, and the mud dries on the leather, and neither of them hurries.)*
> *(She thinks of the year's walking — the miles, the paths, the seasons turning — and the thinking is quiet, and the quiet belongs to the evening, and the evening keeps it.)*
> *(The Park holds the dusk beyond the glass, and she watches, and the watching is enough.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick comes in with the evening tray, and the tray is set down without a sound, and the soundless is the housekeeper's art, and the art is practiced.)*
> "Miss." The immovable look. "The supper, miss. When you're ready, miss."
> "Soon, Mrs. Quick. The dusk first."
> "Aye, miss." She goes, and the going is silent.
> *(She sits a little longer with the dusk, and the dusk sits with her, and the day ends gently.)*

scenes.synopsis: the estate, the charter's — the kept, the legacy's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The estate in the year's light, and she walks the Park in the morning, and the legacy walks with her. The charter's ground is under her boots, and the ground is hers to walk, and the walking shows the legacy the way a window shows a room.)*
> *(She walks the meadows in the morning light, and the hay stands high, and the green is deep summer green, given freely, and the giving asks nothing back.)*
> *(She walks the woods in the afternoon shade, and the old oaks stand in their ranks, and they were old when Augusta was young. She thinks of Augusta — the Dowager, the seventy years — and the keeping passed hand to hand down the line, and the hand is hers now, and the hand is steady.)*
> *(The charter wrote the terms, and the Park lives them, and she walks the terms, and the walking keeps them living.)*
> *(At the lake she stops, and the water holds the sky, and the holding asks nothing, and she asks nothing, and the nothing is complete.)*
> *(She walks the canal, and the water holds the sky there too, and the holding is the same, and the sameness steadies her.)*
> *(The head gardener touches his hat as she passes the rose garden, and the boy waves from the beds.)*
> "Miss." The old man straightens from the canes. "The legacy, miss. The Park, miss."
> "The Park, gardener. The whole of it."
> "Aye, miss." The rarest smile. "The whole, miss."
> *(She walks the boundary's height, and the estate lies below in the light — the lake, the canal, the meadows, the woods — and the whole of it is the legacy, and the legacy is in her keeping.)*
> *(The head groom rides past on his evening round, and he touches his cap, and the horse's hooves thud soft on the turf.)*
> "Miss." He reins in. "The estate, miss. The legacy, miss."
> "The legacy, groom. Kept and keeping."
> "Aye, miss." He rides on. "Kept, miss."
> *(She walks home through the dusk, and the Park holds the last of the light, and she walks inside the holding, and the dusk goes with her.)*

scenes.synopsis: the year, the kept — the Park's, the lesson's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year in the evening's light, and she sits in the morning room with the estate's book open on the desk. She keeps it — the year, the Park — and the pages turn under her hand: the miles, the plantings, the marking, all entered in Harrow's exact hand, the ink still dark.)*
> *(Harrow stands at her shoulder in his exact way, and the pen scratches, and the ink is dark, and the dark holds the year without flinching.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The dry smile. "The walked, miss? In the book, miss?"
> "Put it in, Harrow. The miles, the marking, the whole of it."
> "Aye, miss." He writes it in with the exact hand. "The honest, miss. The walked, honest."
> *(The miles sit among the figures — the canal's length, the boundary's height, the lake's edge, the woods' shade — and the figures do not mind the miles, and the miles do not mind the figures, and the book holds them both the way the Park holds the year: without comment.)*
> *(She looks at the pages. The keeping was the lesson, and the lesson is entered, and the entering is exact.)*
> *(She thinks of the miles entered — the walked, the kept — and she did the entering herself, and the work was hers, and the book holds it now.)*
> *(Harrow blots the page with the particular care of a man who has blotted ten thousand pages. The blotter comes away clean, and the clean is a small satisfaction, and the satisfaction is his.)*
> *(She runs her finger down the column of figures, and the figures are exact, and the miles are there among the pounds and the acres, and the miles belong there, and the belonging needs no defending.)*
> "Miss." He closes the book. "The year, miss. Kept, miss."
> "Kept, Harrow. The whole of it."
> "Aye, miss." The dryest nod. "The whole, miss."
> *(The book sits closed on the desk. The lamp gutters. The morning room holds the dusk, and the holding asks nothing, and she gives it nothing, and the evening asks nothing either.)*
> *(She sits a moment longer with the closed book under her hand. The year is kept — the miles, the marking, the meaning — and the kept sits under her palm, and the palm keeps it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the whole, the walked — the estate's; the woman, the keeping's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her evening, and she walks it still, in the dusk, after the day's business is done. The dusk sits on the Park, and the paths go soft under her boots, and the going is soft and unhurried, and the unhurried suits her.)*
> *(She walks the canal's length in the failing light, and the water darkens between the reeds. The moorhen has gone in for the night, and the rushes are still, and the still asks nothing, and she gives it nothing.)*
> *(She walks the lake's edge, and the swans are settling on the water, and the cygnets tuck in close against the grey backs. The water darkens by degrees, and the degrees are the night coming on, and the coming-on is gradual.)*
> *(She walks the boundary's height, and the Park spreads below — the lake, the canal, the meadows, the woods — wide in the dusk, and the wideness needs no audience.)*
> *(The morning miles and the evening miles join in her legs, and the joining is the day entire, and the entire walks with her.)*
> *(The lamp is lit in the window, and the light reaches out through the dusk, and the reaching is the house calling her home, and she hears it, and she does not hurry.)*
> *(The head groom rides in from the far bank, dark against the dusk, and he touches his cap.)*
> "Miss." He reins in. "The evening walk, miss?"
> "The evening walk, groom. The dusk miles."
> "Aye, miss." He rides on toward the stables. "Good dusk for it, miss."
> *(She thinks of the day entire — the morning's walking, the evening's — and the thinking is quiet, and the quiet walks with her.)*
> *(She walks the meadow edge, and the cut hay smells sweet in the dusk, and the sweet is the summer lingering, and the lingering is welcome.)*
> *(She walks the wood edge, and the trees stand black against the dusk — the night advancing, slow and certain.)*
> *(At the garden door she stops with the Park in the dusk, and the walked miles are hers, and the dusk keeps them.)*
> *(Letitia is at the door with the lamp behind her, and the hawk's eyes take in the dusk on the boots, and she nods.)*
> "Darling." The fond look. "The dusk miles."
> "The dusk miles, and the day with them."
> *(She unlaces the boots, and the day is done, and the done sits easy.)*

scenes.synopsis: the mistress, the whole — Rose, the year's; the walked, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Her evening, and she sits at the window with the Park beyond in the dusk. The year has settled into a quiet she recognizes: the estate turned, the lesson kept, the marking given. The quiet is the reward of the walked miles, and she has walked them.)*
> *(The boots stand by the door with the mud on them — towpath, meadow, wood — and she does not clean them yet, and the not-yet is deliberate.)*
> *(She thinks of the first time she sat at this window, all angles and uncertainty, and the Park was a stranger then. Now it is hers, earned mile by mile, and the miles are in her legs, and her legs are tired, and the tired is honest.)*
> *(The Park holds the dusk beyond the glass. She watches it hold, and the watching steadies her.)*
> *(Letitia is across the room in her chair, and she hums an old tune, off-key in the pleasant way, and the humming fills the quiet.)*
> "Darling." Letitia looks up. "The year's quiet. Earned?"
> "Earned, darling. Every mile of it."
> "Aye." The hawk's eyes, fond. "I watched the earning."
> *(The dusk settles on the Park, gradual as a held breath let out, and the night comes on at its own pace, and the pace suits her.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick comes in with the candles, and the candles are lit one by one, silent, and the silence is the housekeeper's particular art.)*
> "Miss." The immovable nod. "The candles, miss."
> "Thank you, Mrs. Quick."
> "Aye, miss." She goes, and the going is silent.
> *(She turns from the window. The candles burn steady on the table. She sits with the quiet a while longer, and the sitting is rest, and the rest is earned.)*
> *(She thinks of the morning to come — the boots, the paths, the Park waiting in the half-light — and the thinking carries her toward sleep, and the carrying is gentle.)*
> *(Letitia's humming fades into the quiet, and the room holds them both.)*
> *(The night comes on outside the glass. She rises at last, and the rising ends the evening, and the evening was hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: the charter, the kept — the Park's, the legacy's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The charter in the year's light, and she walks the Park in the morning, and the charter walks with her. The charter's ground lies under her boots — every acre a term, every term kept — and the ground is hers to walk.)*
> *(She walks the boundary with her boots beating the dirt, and the lake wears the morning light fully, and without reservation.)*
> *(The boy touches his cap as she passes, and the head gardener nods from the beds, and the morning gets its courtesies, and the courtesies are freely given.)*
> "Miss." The boy grins, bright in the light. "The charter, miss. The year's, miss."
> "The year's, boy. Walked and kept."
> "Aye, miss." He laughs. "Walked, miss."
> *(She thinks of the sealed paper in Quill's exact hand, and the red tape, and the boxes in the solicitor's office, and the ten seasons it took to make the written true. Ten seasons of walking, and the walking made it true, and she never wavered.)*
> *(She walks the meadows, and the green is deep summer green, and the summer and the charter and she herself are in it together, and the together is the point.)*
> *(The morning light lies on the Park — the lake, the canal, the meadows, the woods — and the light does its work well, and the work belongs to the day.)*
> *(She walks the canal, and the water holds the sky between the reeds, and the holding keeps the charter's promise, and the promise holds.)*
> *(She walks the woods, and the old oaks stand in their ranks, and the standing of them steadies her the way it always steadies her.)*
> *(She thinks of Augusta, seventy-two, and the seventy years, and the keeping passed hand to hand, and the hand is hers now.)*
> *(The head groom rides past on his morning round, and he touches his cap.)*
> "Miss." He reins in. "The charter's ground, miss. Walked it, miss?"
> "Walking it now, groom. Every acre."
> "Aye, miss." He rides on. "Every acre, miss."
> *(At the garden door she stops. The charter is hers, and the kept is in her keeping, and the keeping walks with her.)*
> *(The Park lies in the morning light beyond the door, and she stands a moment with the charter in her head like a map, and the map shows the walked miles, and the miles are hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE WHOLE'S MEANING (what the whole means: the wholeness, the estate, or the future). The year deepens; decide the meaning. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year deepens, and the whole asks its meaning. She stands on the boundary's height with the Park below, and the question stands with her, and will not be hurried, and will not be answered lightly.)*
> *(The wholeness speaks first: the Park entire, every acre in a single keeping. She has walked every mile of it — the canal's length, the boundary's height, the lake's edge, the woods' shade — and the miles are in her legs, and the legs remember. She looks down, and the Park lies in the light like something counted, and she is the one who counted it. The wholeness says the estate is one thing, not many, and the keeping is entire or it is nothing. She thinks of the first spring's walking, and the stranger she was, and the woman she is, and the distance between them is the wholeness learned.)*
> *(The estate speaks second: the stone, the charter's ground, the kept terms. She has kept every term — the written, the sealed, the exact — and the keeping took a year's work. She thinks of Quill, and the solicitor's office, and the red tape, and the ten seasons it took to make the written true. The estate says the ground holds the terms and the terms hold the ground, and the stone and the soil are one keeping. She thinks of Augusta, seventy-two, and the seventy years, and the hand is hers now.)*
> *(The future speaks third: the year come round, the spring arrived again. She has watched it turn — the greening, the blooming, the cutting, the white — and the turning has never once been wrong. She thinks of the boy with the watering can, and the years he will walk, and the walking he will learn. The future says the keeping goes on, and the tended will bloom, and the spring'll come. It always comes.)*
> *(Three meanings, and each of them true, and each of them argued by the ground itself. The meaning will close the year's account — what the whole meant, and what of it endures. The ledger in her head closes, and the figures are exact, and the exactness steadies her.)*
> *(She walks home from the boundary's height, and the meaning sits in her the way the dusk sits on the lawn: early, and not to be hurried. She stands at the garden door, and she decides the way she decides everything now: firmly, and for good.)*
> *(The game remembers the choice — and the means: wholeness, estate, or future. The whole's meaning is hers to give.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The whole's meaning:*
- **The wholeness** — *the whole, meant.* The whole means wholeness — the Park, the whole. (Consequence: the meaning is the whole's — but wholes are said, and the whole was the walked.)
- **The estate** — *the kept, meant.* The whole means the estate — the stone, the kept. (Consequence: the meaning is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the whole was the living.)
- **The future** — *the returning, meant.* The whole means the future — the year, the returning. (Consequence: the meaning is the returning's — but returnings are future, and the whole was the now.)
