scenes.synopsis: the meaning, the kept — the whole's, the lesson's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The meaning in the evening's light, and she sits in the morning room with the estate's book open on the desk. She keeps it — the meaning is hers to keep — and the pages turn under her hand: wholeness, estate, future, whichever she chose. The choosing was hers, and she does not revisit it.)*
> *(Harrow stands at her shoulder in his exact way, and the pen scratches, and the ink is dark, and the dark holds the meaning without flinching.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The dry smile. "The meaning, miss? In the book, miss?"
> "In the book, Harrow. Write it plain, and write it true."
> "Aye, miss." He writes it in with the exact hand. "The honest, miss. The meaning, honest."
> *(The meaning sits among the figures — the acres, the pounds, the miles — and the figures do not mind the meaning, and the meaning does not mind the figures, and the book holds them both the way the Park holds the year: without comment.)*
> *(She looks at the page. The keeping was the lesson, and the lesson is entered, and the meaning is entered beside it.)*
> *(She thinks of the meaning kept — the chosen, the decided — and the evening holds the thought a while.)*
> *(Harrow blots the page with the particular care of a man who has blotted ten thousand pages, and the blotting is done with ceremony, and the ceremony is his.)*
> "Miss." He closes the book. "The meaning, miss. Kept, miss."
> "Kept, Harrow. The whole of it."
> "Aye, miss." The dryest nod. "The whole, miss."
> *(The evening light fades in the morning room, and the fading is gradual. The lamp is lit, and the light is warm, and the warm fills the room.)*
> *(The morning room holds the dusk. She sits a moment with the closed book under her hand. The year is kept — the miles, the marking, the meaning — and the book holds them, and her hand holds the book.)*
> *(Harrow goes out with the pen wiped and the ink stoppered, and the going is silent, and the silent is his particular courtesy. The room holds the dusk, and the dusk holds the year, and the year is entered.)*

scenes.synopsis: the letters — the year, reported; London writes. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The letters come with the morning post, and she answers them at the desk in the morning room. The season closes, and the world writes to say it noticed.)*
> *(Lavinia writes from town: The season was brilliant, and you were its sensation, and I knew it from the first. She writes of the town's talk — the walking, the marking, the meaning — and the talk is warm, and the warmth is all Lavinia. She ends with the old teasing: Darling, and the exclamation has not changed in ten seasons, and neither has she.)*
> "Lavinia." She folds the letter with affection. "Still brilliant, still darling. Some things the year leaves alone."
> *(Lavinia writes of the ball in particular — the dancing, the supper, the talk that went on till two — and the talk was of Rose, and the talk was kind, and the kind is rare enough in town to be remarked.)*
> *(She reads it twice, and smiles twice, and folds it with the others to keep.)*
> *(Quill writes in his exact hand: The year's account is closed, and the figures are exact, and the solicitor's office approves. She reads it through twice — the old habit — and the figures hold. She writes back her thanks in three lines, and the lines are plain, and the plain is the point.)*
> *(The Craykes write, and the letter is all politeness — the weather, the christening, the hope of seeing the Park in the spring, the compliments to the household — and she answers it in kind, briefly, and well.)*
> *(The pen runs dry at noon, and she shakes it, and it writes again, and the again is a small mercy.)*
> *(Other letters — the year's acknowledgments — and she answers them all before noon. The pen scratches in the morning room, steady as rain on a window, and she keeps at it till the pile is done.)*
> *(Letitia comes in with the seal and the wax, and the wax is red, and the red has been the year's color since the first spring.)*
> "Darling." The hawk's eyes, bright. "The year's letters, darling? Answered, darling?"
> "Answered, darling. Every one."
> "Aye." She seals the last with a flourish. "Sealed, darling."
> *(The sealed letters lie on the desk in a neat row. The morning's work, finished.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick comes for the post bag, and the bag is heavy with the year's correspondence closed. The immovable nod, and she goes, and the letters go out with her into the morning.)*
> *(She stands at the window with the morning beyond. The answering is done, and the done sits easy in her shoulders, earned and unhurried.)*

scenes.synopsis: the ton, the year's — the whole, awaited; the convened, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The year's close, and the ton awaited — the household, the staff, the estate's own — and she meets them all in the hall as the evening comes on.)*
> *(The gardeners come in from the grounds and stand in a row with their hands behind their backs. The head gardener steps forward with the year's last cutting — a single rose, late, perfect — and he bows with it.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." The deepest bow. "The year's keeping, miss. The kept, miss."
> "Kept, gardener. Every acre, and every season."
> "Aye, miss." He straightens, and the row straightens with him. "Every season, miss."
> *(The boy stands at the end of the row with the watering can, empty now, and the emptiness of it says the year is done better than any speech.)*
> *(The cook comes out from the kitchen, apron still on, and bobs a curtsy that has fed a household through ten seasons.)*
> *(The head groom comes in from the yard with the day's dust on his coat, and he touches his cap.)*
> "Miss." The level nod. "The year's riding, miss. The miles, miss."
> "The miles, groom. Kept and counted."
> "Aye, miss." The smallest smile. "Counted, miss."
> *(Harrow stands by the door with the book under his arm, exact as ever, and the hall fills the way a full glass fills — to the brim, and steady.)*
> *(Mrs. Quick comes down the stairs with the household behind her, and she curtsies, deep.)*
> "Miss." The immovable nod. "The year's housekeeping, miss. The kept, miss."
> "Kept, Mrs. Quick. Every room, and every season."
> "Aye, miss." The prim mouth, and the pleasure behind it. "Every season, miss."
> *(Letitia stands beside her, and the hawk's eyes are bright.)*
> "Darling." The warmest tone. "The year, darling. The whole of it, darling."
> "The whole of it, darling. And every season of it."
> "Aye, darling." The old hand finds hers. "Every season, darling."
> *(She looks at them all — the gardeners, the groom, the cook, Harrow, Mrs. Quick, Letitia — and takes her time about it, and the time is hers to take.)*
> *(The hall holds them all in the lamplight, and the looking is gratitude, and the gratitude needs no words.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, the walker's — Rose, the evening's; the whole, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The woman's evening, and she sits at the desk in the morning room with the year's book open before her. The year's end, and the ledger, and the kept — and she means to finish the sitting properly.)*
> *(The books close one by one — the acres, the pounds, the miles — and each closing is exact, and the exactness is hers.)*
> *(The ledger lies open at the year's last page, and the figures stand in their columns like soldiers on parade — the acres, the rents, the miles walked — and the parade pleases her.)*
> *(Harrow sands the last line with the particular care of a man who has sanded ten thousand lines, and the care is the steward's art.)*
> *(She writes the last line with Harrow's pen. The ink is dark, the line is plain, and the plain is the point.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." Harrow stands at her shoulder. "The last, miss? Written, miss?"
> "Written, Harrow. The whole of it."
> "Aye, miss." The dryest nod. "The whole, miss."
> *(The candle burns low on the desk. The flame gutters once, steadies, and goes on burning, patient as the night coming on.)*
> *(She shields it with her hand till it steadies, and the steadiness comes back the way it always comes back.)*
> *(Letitia comes to the door, and the hawk's eyes are soft in the candlelight, and she comes in and pours the tea, and the tea is strong, and the strong is what the evening requires.)*
> "Darling." The warmest tone. "The year, darling. The end of it, darling."
> "The end of it, darling. And the kept of it."
> "Aye, darling." She comes in and stands beside the desk. "The kept, darling."
> *(She sits a moment with the closed books under her hands — the walking, the marking, the meaning, all entered — and the entered stays entered, and that is the point of a ledger.)*
> *(Letitia takes the pen from her hand, gently, and sets it down.)*
> "Enough, darling." The old hand on her shoulder. "The year is kept. Enough."
> "Enough, darling." She rises. "The year is kept."
> *(The morning room holds the dusk. The dusk holds the year. The year is closed, and the closing holds.)*

scenes.synopsis: the legacy, the whole — the Park's, the charter's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The legacy, and she walks the boundary one last time in the year's last light. The ground holds her boots the way it has held them all year — towpath, meadow, wood — and the holding has never once failed her.)*
> *(The towpath runs beside her, and the water holds the last light between the reeds, and gives it back doubled.)*
> *(The rooks go over to the wood in a long black line, arguing all the way, and the arguing is the sound of the day ending.)*
> *(The boundary's height, and the Park below, and the walk is the last of the year, and she takes it slow.)*
> *(The old gardener waits at the gate. He touches his cap.)*
> "Miss." The deepest bow. "Closing, miss."
> "Closing, gardener. The year's last walk."
> "Aye, miss." He opens the gate. "The last, miss."
> *(The head groom rides up on his evening round. He reins in and touches his cap.)*
> "Miss." The level nod. "Kept, miss."
> "Kept, groom. Every acre."
> "Aye, miss." He rides on. "Every acre, miss."
> *(The light goes down behind the oaks, gradual, and the gradual suits her, and she does not hurry it.)*
> *(The boy runs past with the empty watering can and waves, and she waves back, and the waving is the last business of the day.)*
> *(The bell rings from the house, and the ringing carries across the Park, and the Park carries it on, and the carrying goes on after she has stopped listening.)*
> *(She walks on through the last light with the year beside her — the greening, the blooming, the cutting, the white — and the year walks the way it always walks: without hurrying, and without stopping.)*
> *(She walks the last of the towpath, and her boots beat the dirt the way they have beaten it all year, steady and unhurried, and the steadiness is her signature now.)*
> *(At the garden door she stops and looks back once — the Park in the last light, the whole of it, hers — and the looking-back is enough.)*
> *(She goes in, and the door closes behind her, quiet, and the quiet of it is the whole year in a single sound.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's estate report — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"This year the Hartwell estate has turned through its seasons — waked, shone, turned, slept — and the Gazette — having walked the whole from the first — finds it the charter's true ground. The estate, yearly. The Gazette will walk, annually."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first (annually! walking!), then the reckoning: the year is pronounced true in print as well as in the Park's paths, and Bell has made the estate permanent, which is Bell's way of making it forever. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the whole the Gazette walks annually is the whole that's real.* — remembered: *the lesson: the whole the Gazette walks annually is the whole that's real.*
scenes.sting: This year the Hartwell estate has turned through its seasons — waked, shone, turned, slept — and the Gazette — having walked the whole from the first — finds it the charter's true ground. The estate, yearly. The Gazette will walk, annually.

scenes.synopsis: the atelier's year — Élise's, the turned; the gowns, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and she thinks of the atelier — the atelier's year, coming — and Élise turns through her year.)*
> *(She imagines — the atelier, the year's — the atelier's year, the turning: the gowns, the kept.)*
> "The atelier's year." She looks toward London — the shop, the turned. "Élise —" she stops — "through her year." She breathes. "The gowns —" another stop — "the kept, the yearly."
> *(The chapter closes on the turning — the atelier, the year's — and the Season turns toward the atelier: Élise's year — and the Season holds its breath.)*

scenes.synopsis: the year's turning — the atelier's year; Élise, the seasons. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She wakes before the house, and the year's first decision is the boots: town boots, not walking boots. The carriage is ordered for eight, the case packed the night before, and Mrs. Quick is at the hall door with the keys at her waist when she comes down the stairs, exactly as if she had been informed, which she has been.)*
> "London, miss." The immovable look. "The atelier, miss."
> "London, Mrs. Quick. Élise has the year's silks waiting, and I mean to see them before noon."
> "Aye, miss." The nod, economical as ever. "The year's making."
> *(The road runs through the morning — hedgerows, wet fields, villages opening their shutters — and the estate falls behind the way a finished sentence falls behind the next: done, and not to be revisited. The Park will keep. The Park has learned to keep.)*
> *(She does the year's arithmetic on the way up, the way Augusta taught her: once for the sum, once for the nerve. Four seasons. Three gowns to begin — the dove, the leaf, the cream — every bolt an entry in the ledger she keeps in her head. The miles are not the journey this time. The silks are.)*
> *(The atelier in the afternoon: the shop below, the workrooms above, the good smell of pressed silk and tailor's chalk rising up the stairwell. The bell rings at the door, and Élise comes down the stairs with chalk on her fingers and the direct look that has not altered since she was a modiste's girl.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." Élise wipes her hands on her apron and leaves a white streak. "The year. It begins."
> "It begins, Élise." She steps inside, and the street noise follows her in — carts, hawkers, London getting on with it — and dies against the closed shop door. "Show me the silks."
> *(At the foot of the stairs she pauses, because the long table is already laid with the year's silks — the dove, the leaf, the cream — and the sight of them in the workroom light is the whole of the year's promise in one table's length.)*
> "The dove first," Élise says, following her look. "You always begin with the stone."
> "The stone," Rose agrees. "The Park. The argument."
> *(The workroom hums above — the apprentices, the basting, the morning's work already under way — and Élise leads her up the stairs, twenty-two, direct, chalk on her fingers, the atelier ordered behind her like a regiment behind its colonel: ready, and entirely hers.)*

scenes.synopsis: Élise, the year's — the couturière, the atelier's; the twenty-two, the turned. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Élise stands at the long table, and the year's silks run its length: the dove, the leaf, the cream, each bolt smooth and waiting. She speaks the way she sews — directly, and without waste, and without asking permission.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." She lays a hand on the dove. "The dove is the Park stone. The leaf is the garden. The cream is the house." The true look. "Tell me which is the year's."
> *(The workroom is warm, and the light falls on the silks, and the apprentices are at the far table, basting. Rose touches the dove. It is the color of the west front at noon — grey, with something warm underneath.)*
> "You've decided already, haven't you?" Rose says. "I can see it in your face."
> "I have opinions, Miss Hartwell." The rarest smile. "You taught me that opinions are allowed."
> "I teach a great many dangerous things."
> "The most dangerous." Élise picks up the shears, and the steel catches the light. "The year's cutting begins when you say."
> *(Rose runs a finger over the leaf — cool, heavy, honest silk — and the cream, which is warmer, the house color, generous. Three silks. Three seasons of weather in one table's length.)*
> "Begin with the dove," Rose says. "The stone."
> "The stone." Élise nods, and the shears come down, and the silk gives under the blades with a sound like a long sigh. "The year begins here."
> *(She stands at the table's end, and the silk is cool under her palm, and the cool is a fact, and the year's whole geography is in three bolts: the stone, the garden, the house.)*
> "The leaf next," she says. "The garden. Then the cream."
> "The leaf," Élise says, "and the cream. The dove to begin, the garden to follow, the house to keep."
> *(The shears come down again, and the dove gives with the long sigh, and the apprentices have stopped their basting entirely, and the workroom listens to the year's first cutting the way a theatre listens to the overture.)*
> *(The light falls on the silks — the dove, the leaf, the cream — and the silks take the light, and the morning is kind.)*
> *(She watches the cutting — the hands sure, the chalk marks quick on the grey — and the apprentices look up from the basting. The dove falls in clean lengths. The year has begun, and it began with the stone.)*

scenes.synopsis: the spring — the atelier's; the silks, the year's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The spring comes to the atelier with the materials. She walks the workroom in the morning, and the bolts lie on the tables, and Élise is at the long table with her shears, and the dove silk gives under the blades with a sound like a long sigh. Measure twice, cut once — Élise's whole religion.)*
> *(The apprentices baste at the far table. White cotton runs through dove silk in long loose stitches, temporary as a promise, holding the shape until the needle proper can set it. The workroom hums — needles, scissors, the low talk of girls who know their trade.)*
> *(She watches the cutting, and Élise's hands make the whole argument: the shears, the measuring tape looped round her neck, the chalk quick and sure on the silk. The hands know. They have always known.)*
> *(The Park's spring is waking outside London — buds, green pushing up through last year's leaf-litter — and here the green is silk, and the blooming is cut and basted. Two springs, and she has a stake in both.)*
> "Miss Hartwell." Élise looks up, and the chalk is on her cheek where she pushed her hair back. "The basting. Come and see."
> "Show me."
> "Here." She holds the seam to the light. "Straight and true. The year's first."
> "Straight and true." Rose takes it, and the white stitches stand up against the grey like a line of small honest intentions. "Begin as we mean to go on."
> *(She walks the workroom from end to end — past the tables, past the basting girls, past the bolts waiting their turn — and the spring settles into its rhythm. Cutting, basting, humming. The year has its first seam, and the seam holds.)*
> *(She studies the seam a moment longer, and the studying is satisfied.)*
> "The first of many," Élise says.
> "The first," Rose agrees. "And the truest."
> *(The spring settles into its rhythm — cutting, basting, humming — and the year has its first seam, and the seam holds.)*
> *(At the door she looks back. Élise is already chalking the next mark, quick as a signature. The workroom hums on without her, and the humming is the sound of the year being made.)*

scenes.synopsis: the spring gowns — the made; the client, the choosing. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The spring gowns wait on the rail, and the morning comes in through the workroom windows, and she stands before them the way a general surveys a map. Three gowns. Three springs. One choosing.)*
> *(The dove first. She lifts it off the rail — the bodice cut close, the skirt falling in the year's new line — and holds it against herself in the tall glass. The silk takes the light, and the glass gives her back a woman she almost recognizes.)*
> "The dove." Élise nods from the cutting table. "The stone color. The year begins here."
> "The year begins." Rose steps behind the screen. "Begin there."
> *(The leaf second. Garden green, the sash tied at the waist, the sleeves cut full to the season. The apprentice's fingers fly at the hooks — quick, practiced — and Rose steps out.)*
> "The leaf." Élise walks round her with the professional eye. "Yours entirely."
> "Mine entirely," Rose says, and turns, and the skirt swings out, and one of the apprentices laughs before she can stop herself.
> *(The cream third. The house color, the neckline modest, the skirt generous enough for a long evening. She stands in it, and the atelier's mirror stands in its corner, and the two of them consider each other at length.)*
> "The cream." Élise's voice is softer. "For the house. For the keeping."
> "All three," Rose says. "The year's, all three."
> *(The three gowns hang on the rail — the dove, the leaf, the cream — and the morning light finds them, and the light is kind.)*
> "The year's keeping color," Élise says of the cream. "For the house."
> "For the house," Rose agrees. "And for the year."
> *(The choosing is done, and the afternoon wears on.)*

> *(Dawn comes up the east windows of the corridor in long clean bars, and the Park at this hour belongs to nobody — not the servants, not the ton, not even quite to her. > *(Seventy-two. The number has been sitting in Rose's head all week the way a new coin sits in the palm — unfamiliar, worth turning over. Augusta at seventy-two takes the stairs a fraction slower and will not be hurried about it. She has opinions about the new footman's cuffs. She beat Letitia at piquet on Tuesday wearing a look of such complete serenity that Letitia accused her of witchcraft, and Augusta said, "My dear, I am far too old for witchcraft," which only made it worse.)*
> *(At the stairhead Rose stops and looks down into the dim gallery, the portraits hooded in shadow, and the whole long project of the place rises up in her — not the money, never the money first, just the sheer daily fact of it kept. The fires lit. The linen aired. The old woman's spectacles waiting on the side table for hands that have earned their slowness.)*
> *(She thinks of the years as Augusta's own private architecture: not built, exactly, but settled into, the way a river settles into its course. There is a peace in the house this morning that has nothing to do with victories. It is the peace of things done properly for a very long time.)*
> *(A maid comes up the back stairs with a can of hot water, sees her, and drops a curtsy so quick it is almost a stumble. Rose nods her on. The chocolate will be ordered, the letters will come, the day will arrange itself. She goes down, slippers silent on the waxed boards, to begin it.)*

scenes.synopsis: Augusta, the peace's — the Dowager, the years; the spectacles, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room smells of toast and the particular sharp green of the tea Augusta insists on, which Letitia claims could strip varnish. Augusta is already at the table when Rose comes in, spectacles on, the Gazette folded to the correspondence column, a pencil moving down the margin in small exact ticks.)*
> "Child." Augusta does not look up. "Sit. You are doing arithmetic in the doorway again. I can hear it."
> *(Rose sits. The toast rack is silver, old, dented on one corner from the year Letitia dropped it demonstrating a reel step, and nobody has ever let her forget it.)*
> "I wasn't doing arithmetic," Rose says.
> "You were." Augusta turns a page. "It is your face. You have your mother's forehead when you count things, which is to say you have mine. Eat."
> *(Rose eats. The tea is, as advertised, ferocious. Across the table Augusta reads on, pencil ticking, and there is something in the set of her shoulders this morning that Rose has been watching for weeks without naming: an ease. Not rest, exactly. Augusta does not rest. But the particular vigilance of the last years — the woman who held a house together by force of spectacles — has gone out of her like a tide.)*
> "The line is kept, child." Augusta says it suddenly, to the Gazette, without looking up. "I thought you should hear it said plainly, since you are always waiting for the other shoe. There is no other shoe. The line is kept."
> *(Rose looks at her — the white hair dressed close, the hands steady on the pencil — and feels something turn over in her chest, once, like the new coin.)*
> "Then I shall stop listening for it," she says.
> "You won't," says Augusta, turning another page. "But you may stop admitting it." The rarest smile. "More toast."
> *(The toast arrives, brown and buttered to the exact gold Augusta considers morally acceptable. Rose takes it, and the morning settles around them into its familiar shape — the pencil ticking, the tea steaming, the rain of small decisions falling exactly where they should. She thinks, not for the first time, that peace is not the absence of noise. It is noise in its right place.)*

scenes.synopsis: the mornings — Augusta's; the spectacles', the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta's mornings have a liturgy, and the house knows it by heart. Half past seven: the chocolate, black, in the Sèvres cup with the hairline crack she refuses to retire. Eight: the Gazette, correspondence column first, then the leaders, then — if Bell has been particularly waspish — read aloud to whoever is nearest with enormous satisfaction.)*
> *(Rose has taken to joining her uninvited, bringing the household book and her own correspondence, and Augusta has taken to pretending this is an imposition. "You rustle," she said on the first morning. "I do not rustle," Rose said. "You rustle with intent." It is now the established joke of the east wing.)*
> *(This morning the liturgy proceeds: the cup, the crack, the pencil. A letter from the Almerias about the autumn music. A bill from the ironmonger, ticked twice. Augusta holds each paper up to the light as though the paper might be lying, which — Rose reflects, watching the spectacles catch the sun — it occasionally is, and Augusta has caught more lying paper than any woman in England.)*
> *(What Rose notices, this particular morning, is the pace. There is no hurry in it. The old Augusta read the post like dispatches from a siege. This Augusta reads it like weather — worth knowing, not worth fearing. She sets the ironmonger's bill aside for Hodges with a small satisfied nod, as one might set aside a well-behaved dog.)*
> "Anything on fire?" Rose asks, not looking up from her own letters.
> "Nothing that won't keep till Thursday." Augusta folds the Gazette with precision. "Child — when you have a moment that is not rustling. Walk with me in the garden before the heat."
> *(It is barely eight. The garden will be all dew and blackbirds. Rose closes the household book.)*
> "I am entirely at your disposal," she says, "and entirely unrustled."
> "We shall see," says Augusta.
> *(The garden at eight is Augusta's private hour, and Rose knows better than to be late for it. The dew will be on the box hedges, the blackbirds performing their territorial operas, the gardener's boy pretending not to watch the Dowager pass. Some liturgies are worth keeping exactly as they are.)*

scenes.synopsis: the letters — Augusta's; the line's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The writing desk in the morning room is Augusta's true throne — rosewood, scarred along one edge where a toy phaeton was once driven across it at speed, decades ago. The scar has been polished by seventy years of sleeves into something almost decorative. Augusta writes her letters there every morning at nine, whatever the weather, whatever the house, whatever the century is doing.)*
> *(Rose, sorting the estate post at the smaller table, watches the ritual the way one watches weather: the spectacles lowered, the pen tried twice on the blotter, the first line always begun without hesitation. Augusta does not draft. She decides.)*
> *(The correspondence of the Dowager is a small empire. Cousins in Northumberland. A widowed cousin of the Almerias, whose letters are three pages of health and one of malice. The vicar, about the church roof. A former servant's children, educated at Augusta's expense for thirty years, without ever being mentioned where it could be overheard.)*
> *"The line," Augusta said once, sealing a letter with a decisive thumb, "is not kept by sentiment, child. It is kept by postage." Rose wrote that down in the household book under Tuesday, where it remains the finest thing in it.)*
> *(This morning there are eleven letters. Rose counts without meaning to — old habits — and Augusta catches her at it over the spectacles.)*
> "You may stop counting my letters," Augusta says. "They are not going anywhere."
> "I wasn't—"
> "You were." The pen scratches on. "It is your face." A pause, the pen lifted. "Though if you want something to count, one of them is ordained and preaching. Thirty years of postage, and the interest is sound. There. Count that."
> *(Eleven letters. Rose watches the pen move — tried twice on the blotter, never hurried, never hesitant — and thinks about the arithmetic of a life: thirty years of postage, and a boy gets a living, and nobody ever hears about it unless they happen to be sorting the estate post at the smaller table. The line, kept by postage. She writes that down too.)*
> *(Rose writes it in the margin of the household book — the boy, thirty years — where the fine things live. Augusta's pen goes on scratching, unhurried, and the morning room holds its particular quiet: the sound of a line being kept, one letter at a time.)*

scenes.synopsis: Augusta, the line's — the Dowager, the kept; the seventy-two, the peace. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(They are in the long gallery after luncheon, the light coming sideways through the tall windows in slabs, dust turning in it like slow snow. Augusta walks the length of it with her stick — she has finally, this spring, consented to the stick, a handsome malacca thing she pretends to despise — and stops before the Ravencroft portraits, the whole long argument of blood in oils.)*
> "The line." Augusta taps the stick once against the floorboards. "Everyone talks about the line as though it were a rope, child. Something you grip." She looks up at her great-grandfather, who glowers down with the confidence of a man who never once doubted his wig. "It isn't. It's a road. You don't grip a road. You keep it passable."
> *(Rose walks beside her, matching the slower pace without seeming to. This is new, this lecturing in galleries; the old Augusta gave orders, not discourses. Rose is not sure which she prefers. She is sure she prefers the woman giving them.)*
> "Passable for whom?" she asks.
> "For whoever comes next." Augusta moves on, stick ticking. "Your mother understood that. She kept the road for you before you knew you needed one." A glance, sideways, over the spectacles. "You are keeping it for someone you haven't met. That is the whole of it. There is no more."
> *(They reach the window at the gallery's end. Below, the drive curves away between the limes, empty and pale in the afternoon.)*
> "It sounds very simple when you say it," Rose says.
> "It is very simple." Augusta pats her hand once, decisively. "It is only difficult. There is a difference, and the difference is the whole of a life. Shall we go in? The tea will be getting ideas."
> *(They walk back along the gallery the way they came, the stick ticking a steady time between the portraits. The great-grandfather glowers after them. Rose finds she is smiling, and does not examine why, and Augusta — who misses nothing — pretends not to notice, which is her form of tenderness.)*
> *(At the gallery's end they turn toward the stairs, and the light has shifted while they walked, the slabs of sun gone amber at the edges. Augusta's pace is unhurried, and Rose matches it without thinking — the way you match your step to someone you intend to walk beside for a long time. The tea, she reflects, can get all the ideas it likes. It will wait.)*

scenes.synopsis: the evenings — Augusta's; the peace's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evenings at the Park have settled into a pattern as fixed as the mornings, and Rose finds she loves it with a fierceness that surprises her. Dinner at seven, never late. The drawing room after, the lamps lit in the particular order Hodges prefers. Augusta with her embroidery — she has taken it up again after twenty years, small furious roses on absurdly fine linen — Letitia with the piquet cards, Rose with whatever book is currently losing the argument for her attention.)*
> *(Tonight it is raining, a soft persistent rain that makes the windows into dark mirrors, and the room has the particular snugness of a house that is entirely sure of its roof. The fire ticks. Augusta's needle flashes. Somewhere in the house a clock strikes nine, and nobody looks up, because nine is when the clock strikes and that is all it is.)*
> *(Rose watches her grandmother's hands — spotted now, the knuckles swollen, moving with the same precision they brought to everything for seventy years — and thinks about what the day has actually contained. Nothing. Letters, a walk, luncheon, the gallery. Nothing that would fill a paragraph of the Gazette. And yet the day sits in her like a good meal.)*
> "You are staring, child," Augusta says without looking up.
> "I am admiring your roses. They are coming out remarkably martial."
> "They are roses. They are not required to be peaceful." The needle pauses. "Though I take your point." She holds the linen up to the lamplight, considers it the way she considers everything — as evidence — and nods once. "It will do. Everything, eventually, does. That is the great secret, and you may have it for nothing: it all does, if you keep at it long enough."
> *(The rain goes on. Letitia deals. The fire ticks. Rose turns her page, and does not read it, and is entirely content.)*
> *(Later, much later, Rose will try to describe this evening and fail, because there is nothing to describe. The rain. The fire. The roses, martial on their linen. It was the kind of evening the house had been building toward for ten years without knowing it — and the knowing, when it came, was as quiet as everything else.)*

scenes.synopsis: the portrait — Augusta's; the Dowager's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The portrait hangs in the small drawing room, where the afternoon light finds it — Augusta at sixty, painted the year before Rose came to the Park, in the grey silk she still calls her good dress. The painter caught her between expressions: not smiling, not severe, the spectacles in her hand, looking at the viewer the way she looks at the household book — as though deciding whether it will do.)*
> *(Rose stands before it with her hands clasped behind her back, the way Augusta stands before things, and considers the woman in oils. Sixty. A widow eleven years. The Park half-ruined and the money gone and the ton circling like weather. And the woman in the portrait looks out with absolute composure, as though ruin were merely a particularly tedious guest.)*
> *"She hated sitting for it," Letitia says from the doorway, making Rose jump. "Three sittings, and she told the fellow his shadows were impertinent. He painted them in anyway. She never forgave him, and she hung it where the light hits it, which tells you everything about my sister."*
> *(Letitia comes to stand beside her, and for a moment neither speaks. The sisters, Rose thinks — the Dowager and the quartermaster, the line and the laughter. Between them they held this house together through years that would have finished most families.)*
> "Did she know?" Rose asks. "At sixty — did she know it would come right?"
> "Good God, no." Letitia is brisk. "Nobody knows, darling. That's the entire trick of it. She behaved as though she knew, which is better, and cheaper, and frightens the creditors more." She tilts her head at the portrait. "Though between you and me, I think the spectacles knew. They've always known."
> *(Rose laughs, and the portrait looks on, composed, spectacles in hand, keeping its counsel the way its subject keeps everything — exactly, and without fuss.)*
> *(She stays a little longer after Letitia goes, studying the grey silk, the set of the shoulders. Sixty. Eleven years a widow. The line, kept, before there was any reason to believe it could be. She straightens her own shoulders without thinking, and goes to dress for dinner.)*

scenes.synopsis: the years — Augusta's; the peace's, the turned. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The years turn the way the Park's great beech turns its leaves — not all at once, but with a daily, almost insulting gradualness. Rose notices it in the small treacheries: Augusta reaching for the stair rail she once scorned, the spectacles coming off more often to be polished, the afternoon nap that is never called a nap but is taken, daily, at half past three, in the chair by the library fire.)*
> *(She notices it, and says nothing, because there is nothing to say that Augusta does not already know. The Dowager has been counting her own years far longer than Rose has been counting anything. Instead Rose rearranges the house around the fact the way one rearranges furniture around a draft — quietly, without announcement. The stair rail gets a fresh coat of paint. The library chair acquires a footstool. The afternoon's engagements begin, mysteriously, to end by three.)*
> *(Hodges, who has served the house for thirty years and understands everything, understands this too. "The Dowager's chair, miss," he says, appearing with the footstool as though it had always existed. "Thought it wanted company." It is the most words he has volunteered in thirty years.)*
> *(And Augusta — Augusta accepts the footstool, the rail, the mysteriously shortened afternoons, with the air of a general accepting reinforcements she had already requisitioned. She naps at half past three with her embroidery folded in her lap and her spectacles on her nose, and wakes at four precisely, and is never, ever to be told she was asleep.)*
> "I was resting my eyes," she tells Rose, daring her.
> "Of course," Rose says. "Your eyes have earned it."
> "Hmph." But she is pleased. The years turn, and the house turns with them, and nobody — least of all the Dowager — is so vulgar as to comment.
> *(What Rose understands, watching all this quiet rearrangement, is that the house has learned something she is still learning: that love, at a certain point, stops being grand and becomes administrative. The footstool. The rail. The engagements ending by three. Nobody makes a speech about it. The beech turns its leaves, the years turn, and the Park — which has survived everything — survives this too, by the simple expedient of paying attention.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE PEACE'S LESSON (what the peace teaches: the line, the keeping, or the returning). The years deepen; decide the lesson. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The years deepen — Rose feels it the way you feel a season change: not in any single day, but in the accumulation. The mornings a fraction slower. The opinions a fraction sharper. The peace, settling over the Park like afternoon light over the gallery. And with the deepening comes the question she has been carrying for weeks without quite asking it: what does the peace teach?)*
> *(She takes it to the walled garden in the late morning, the question, and walks it past the white rose — twenty-five years from a twig — and past the rosemary, the garden that remembers. The peace has been Augusta's great demonstration: seventy-two years of Tuesdays, and one morning the house is quiet and the letters are answered and there is nothing left to fight.)*
> *(But what is the lesson, exactly? She turns it the way Augusta turns paper to the light. Is it the line — the blood, the road, kept passable for whoever comes next? Augusta at sixty, a widow eleven years, behaving as though she knew it would come right. The line, kept, before there was reason.)*
> *(Or is it the keeping — the behavior, not the blood? The chocolate at half past seven. The eleven letters. The peas, unmangled. Show up, write the letters, keep the roof on. The tedious, where the line actually lives. The Dowager's peace, practiced daily until it looked like ease.)*
> *(Or is it the returning — the yearly, the cycle? The white rose, flushing again. The Assembly, convened annually. The road, walked in both directions — the dead, the living, the unborn, in conversation through furniture and bindings. The years, returning, and the peace with them.)*
> *(Three shapes, and all of them true, and all of them Augusta. Rose stands before the white rose with the question, and the garden keeps its counsel, and the years deepen around her like tea in the pot. The peace asks its lesson. The lesson will shape the peace's memory.)*
> *(She thinks of Letitia's fourth shape — the enjoying, unwritten, the most important — and smiles, and holds the three shapes up one last time: the line, the keeping, the returning. The peace asks its lesson. The lesson is hers to decide — and whatever she decides, she will have to live inside it, the way you live inside a house: daily, and without fuss.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — The peace's lesson:*
- **The line** — *the kept, taught.* The lesson is the line — Augusta's, the kept. (Consequence: the lesson is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the peace was the given.)
- **The keeping** — *the peace, taught.* The lesson is keeping — the Dowager's, the peace. (Consequence: the lesson is the peace's — but peaces are kept, and the line was the year's.)
- **The returning** — *the yearly, taught.* The lesson is returning — the years, the yearly. (Consequence: the lesson is the yearly's — but yearly's are time's, and the peace was the now.)
> *(The choice is made — line, keeping, or returning, as she decides. The peace's lesson is hers, and the keeping of it starts now.)*

scenes.synopsis: Augusta, the lesson's — the Dowager, the taught; the spectacles, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(They are in the stillroom after luncheon, Augusta decanting the last of the lavender water with the care of a woman handling explosives, when Rose brings her the household book — open, pencil ready — and says, "Tell me what the lesson was." Augusta does not look up from the lavender.)*
> "The lesson," she repeats. "Child, I am seventy-two. There have been several."
> "The peace's lesson. The one you'd want kept."
> *(The lavender drips, slow and fragrant. Augusta sets the decanter down with precision and looks at Rose over the spectacles, and something in her face does the extraordinary thing it does — softens without weakening, the way good steel takes an edge.)*
> "Very well." She folds her hands. "The lesson is this: the line is not the blood, though the blood helps. The line is the behavior. Show up. Write the letters. Keep the roof on. Do it when it is tedious, which is most of the time, because the tedious is where the line actually lives. Anyone can be magnificent in a crisis. It is the Tuesdays that finish people."
> *(Rose writes it down — the Tuesdays — underlining it twice.)*
> "And the peace?" she asks. "Where does the peace come in?"
> "The peace is what the Tuesdays buy you." Augusta picks up the decanter again. "Thirty years of Tuesdays, and one morning you wake up and the house is quiet and the letters are answered and there is nothing left to fight. That is the peace. It is not given. It is accumulated." She holds the lavender to the light. "Like interest. Only reliable."
> *(Rose closes the book on that — like interest, only reliable — and helps her grandmother carry the lavender upstairs, and neither of them mentions that they are both a little moved, because some things are better carried than said.)*
> *(Upstairs, the lavender water is shelved in the stillroom cupboard in its ranked blue bottles, each labeled in Augusta's hand — the same hand that writes eleven letters before nine, that beat Letitia at piquet, that held a ruined house together by force of will. Rose looks at the labels a moment before she closes the cupboard. Like interest. Only reliable.)*

scenes.synopsis: the garden — Augusta's; the peace's, the walked. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The walled garden is at its best in the late morning, the walls holding the warmth like cupped hands, and Augusta walks it daily whatever the season — slower now, the stick finding the gravel path with a steady tick, but walking it. Rose goes with her when the household book allows, which is most days, because the garden walk has become one of the liturgies.)*
> *(Today the roses are out in force, the late ones, heavy-headed and impossibly pink against the old brick. Augusta stops before the white rose she planted the year Rose was born — twenty-five years, and the bush is taller than either of them now — and touches a bloom with one finger, the way she touches everything she values: briefly, and as though it might burn her.)*
> "The rosemary," Augusta says, "over there, by the gate. For remembrance — a garden should remember things, even if people won't." She moves on, stick ticking. "Though nobody has ever kept the aphids off the standards. Some battles are not worth the winning."
> *(They walk in companionable silence past the herb beds, the bees loud in the lavender. Rose finds herself watching her grandmother's profile — the nose, the chin, the absolute refusal to hurry — and understands, suddenly and completely, that she is walking with the future. Not her own future. The family's. The road, kept passable.)*
> "The Assembly will want the garden open for the supper interval," Rose says. "The ton will trample the box."
> "The box will recover." Augusta does not break stride. "The ton, regrettably, will too. Open the garden, child. A house that won't show its garden has something wrong with its house."
> *(At the garden gate Augusta stops, and looks back along the path they have walked — the box hedges, the roses, the white rose nodding — with the expression she wears for things she has decided to keep. Twenty-five years, of the rose: a twig. She says it the way other women say grace.)*
> *(The white rose nods behind them in the light wind. The walls hold the warmth. They walk on together, unhurried.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Assembly — Augusta's; the convened, the Dowager's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The Hartwell Assembly has settled into its annual rhythm now — the house party, the ball, the morning after with its glorious wreckage of supper rooms — and Augusta attends it the way a monarch attends a coronation: as the source of its legitimacy. She holds court in the small drawing room during the ball itself, receiving the ton in relays, and the ton comes, because to be received by the Dowager at the Assembly is to be stamped genuine.)*
> *(Rose, circulating with the perpetual half-smile of the hostess, keeps finding her way back to that doorway to check. Each time: Augusta enthroned, spectacles gleaming, some terrified debutante being told — kindly, devastatingly — exactly what is wrong with her curtsey. Each time Rose's chest does the small warm thing.)*
> *"One of the Almeria girls," Augusta reports during a lull, accepting a glass of negus. "Curtseys like a closing fan. I told her so. Her mother thanked me." She sips. "The Assembly suits me, child. I am too old for balls and exactly the right age for courts."*
> *(And it is true — the Assembly is Augusta's element in a way the old London seasons never were. There she was a soldier. Here she is an institution. The difference, Rose reflects, watching the next debutante approach with visible trepidation, is that institutions get to enjoy themselves.)*
> *(Later, when the dancing is at its height and the ballroom glows like a held breath, Rose slips away to the small drawing room and finds Augusta holding forth to a circle of dowagers on the subject of the church roof — still, after all these years, the church roof — and she stands in the doorway a moment, unseen, and simply looks: the white hair, the grey silk, the absolute command. The line, convened. The Dowager, in her kingdom.)*
> *(She goes back to the ballroom before she is missed, but the image stays with her all evening, lit from within like the ballroom itself.)*
> *(Near two in the morning, when the last carriage has gone and the candles are being snuffed in their hundreds, Rose finds Augusta in the small drawing room alone, spectacles off, looking — for once, and only for a moment — her full seventy-two years. "Well," the Dowager says, putting the spectacles on. "That was satisfactory." It is the highest praise she has.)*

scenes.synopsis: the toasts — Augusta's; the line's, the raised. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The toasts come at midnight, as they always do at the Assembly — the company gathered, the glasses charged, and Augusta rising with the particular deliberateness that means she has something to say and intends to be heard. The room quiets the way rooms do for her now: completely, and at once.)*
> *"The line," Augusta says, lifting her glass. She looks around the supper room — the candles, the faces, the whole glittering apparatus of the ton at its best behavior. "People ask me what it means. It means this." She pauses, and the pause is a professional instrument. "It means we show up."*
> *(A small ripple — laughter, recognition. The Tuesdays, Rose thinks, translated for company.)*
> *"To the Park," Augusta says. "To the Assembly. To showing up." She drinks, and the room drinks, and the applause starts somewhere near the Almerias and rolls forward like weather.)*
> *(Rose, applauding with the rest, catches Letitia's eye across the room. Letitia mimes wiping away a tear with enormous theatricality, then mouths, "She's magnificent," and Rose has to look at the ceiling to keep her composure, because her aunt is right and it is suddenly, absurdly moving.)*
> *(Afterward there are a dozen people wanting Augusta's ear, and she gives it to each in turn — the exact attention, the pencil-sharp question — and Rose watches the line being kept in real time, one conversation at a time, and thinks that this, this ridiculous glittering midnight, is what all the Tuesdays were for.)*
> *(Much later, unpinning her hair, she finds she is still smiling. The toast. The line. Showing up. She writes it in the household book under the date, in the margin, where the fine things live: "To showing up.")*
> *(The drive at one in the morning is a river of carriage lamps, and Rose watches it from the stair window with her hair coming down — the Assembly dispersing, the ton carrying the night home like a purchase. Somewhere in that river is one of the Almeria girls, practicing her curtsey in the carriage. Rose hopes Augusta's instruction takes.)*
> *(The household book, the next morning, gets its marginal note — "To showing up." — and Rose sits with the pen for a moment afterward, thinking about midnight toasts and martial roses and the particular sound of a room going quiet for Augusta. Then she blots it, closes the book, and goes down to breakfast, because the Tuesdays continue.)*

scenes.synopsis: the night — Augusta's; the peace's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The Park at night is a different house — the same rooms, but holding their breath. Rose walks the corridor in her wrapper long after the lamps are lit, past the doors behind which the household sleeps in its various dignities, and thinks about how strange it is that a place so loud by day can be so completely, so competently silent.)*
> *(In the small drawing room the portrait of Augusta at sixty catches the lamplight as she passes — the grey silk, the spectacles in hand, the look that decides whether things will do. Rose stops, as she always stops, and the painted eyes meet hers with the composure of a woman who has already survived everything worth surviving.)*
> *"Still here," Rose says to it, quietly, so as not to wake the house. The portrait says nothing, which is its prerogative. But there is something steadying in the silence — the knowledge that the line was kept before her, and will be kept after, and her part is only the keeping of her own years.)*
> *(She thinks of Augusta asleep upstairs — the embroidery folded, the spectacles on the night table, the white hair in its night plait — and of the mornings to come: the chocolate, the Gazette, the eleven letters. The liturgy. The peace.)*
> *(A clock strikes eleven somewhere deep in the house, and the sound goes through the rooms like a stone through water. Rose turns from the portrait and walks on, slippers silent, and the night settles back around her — competent, complete, kept.)*
> *(The other portraits watch her pass — the Ravencrofts, the Hartwells, the whole long argument of blood — and she nods to them the way you nod to fellow travelers. They kept their years. She is keeping hers. The arrangement, she reflects, is satisfactory to all parties.)*
> *(At her own door she pauses and looks back along the corridor, the lamps burning in their order, the portraits hooded in shadow. Nothing is on fire. Nothing is unfinished. The thought arrives uninvited and she lets it stay: this is what winning looks like, when nobody is watching. She goes in, and sleeps.)*

scenes.synopsis: the later years — Augusta's; the peace's, the deepened. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The later years deepen the way tea deepens in the pot — gradually, then all at once, and then it is simply the color of things. Augusta at seventy-two and some months has settled into a new exactitude: the mornings a fraction slower, the opinions a fraction sharper, the tenderness — which was always there, buried like a foundation stone — a fraction closer to the surface.)*
> *(Rose watches it happen with the particular attention of someone who knows she is witnessing something unrepeatable. The Dowager explaining to the new footman, at length, why the claret glasses go on the left. The Dowager writing about a first sermon, underlining "first" twice. The Dowager, caught — actually caught — humming in the walled garden, who then claimed it was the bees.)*
> *"It was not the bees," Rose says, over breakfast. "I know your humming. It was the bit from the Assembly."*
> *"The bees hum in G major," Augusta says with dignity. "I hum in nothing. There is a difference."*
> *(Letitia, pouring the tea, has to leave the room.)*
> *(And yet — and yet — beneath the comedy of it, Rose feels the deepening like a tide coming in. The years are doing their work, patiently, the way they do. Augusta's hands on the spectacles. The stair rail, freshly painted. The footstool, now so established that Hodges polishes it without being asked. The house, rearranging itself around its Dowager with love disguised as administration.)*
> *(At breakfast the sisters perform their ancient comedy — Letitia accusing Augusta of moving the marmalade on purpose, Augusta denying it with the serenity of the innocent, both of them perfectly aware that the other knows. Rose butters her toast and watches, and thinks that seventy-two looks a great deal like every other age, only better informed.)*
> *(Hodges polishes the footstool without being asked, and catches Rose watching, and they share the look of co-conspirators. The house runs on such looks. It always has.)*
> *(She finds herself, some evenings, simply watching — the embroidery, the lamplight, the white head bent — and memorizing. Not morbidly. Practically. The way you memorize a road you intend to travel later. The later years, deepening. The line, kept. The peace, accumulated like interest — only reliable.)*

scenes.synopsis: Augusta, the later's — the Dowager, the deepened; the spectacles, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(They are shelling peas in the stillroom — Augusta insisted; "the kitchen girls mangle them," she said, which is both true and beside the point — and the work has the particular companionableness of tasks that require the hands but not the head. The peas tick into the bowl. The afternoon light comes through the small window in a comfortable slant.)*
> "Child." Augusta does not look up from the peas. "You have been watching me."
> *(Rose considers denying it. Discards the idea. Augusta can smell evasion at twenty paces.)*
> "I have," she says. "I'm memorizing."
> "Memorizing what, exactly?"
> "The way you do things. The Tuesdays." The peas tick. "The peace. I want to get it right."
> *(Augusta's hands pause — just for a breath — on the pea pods. Then go on, steady as ever.)*
> "There is no getting it right, child. There is only getting it done." She tips her bowl into the larger one with precision. "You will do it differently. You do everything differently — louder, faster, with more people watching. It worried me, once." A glance, over the spectacles, and the rarest smile. "It no longer worries me. The road stays passable. That is the whole of the requirement."
> *(The peas tick. The light slants. Rose feels something loosen in her chest — a knot she did not know she was carrying, the fear of doing it wrong, of not being enough like the woman across the table.)*
> *(The peas, shelled, go into the bowl — a small green mountain, absurdly satisfying. Augusta surveys it the way she surveys everything: as evidence. Supper will have peas. The kitchen girls will be instructed. The line, in its way, is kept one pea at a time, and Rose finds she does not mind the metaphor.)*
> *(Rose eats the peas at supper with particular attention, and they are excellent — sweet, exact, the reward of unmangled labor. Augusta accepts the compliment on behalf of the stillroom with a nod of absolute monarchy.)*
> "The peas are for supper," Augusta says, standing, brushing her skirts. "And Rose —" at the door, turning back — "you are doing it right. I thought you should hear that said plainly, since you are always waiting for the other shoe."*

scenes.synopsis: the spectacles — Augusta's; the seventy-two, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The spectacles are the true Dowager — more than the stick, more than the grey silk, more than the voice that does the extraordinary thing. Rose has watched those spectacles conduct the business of the house for years: lowered for scrutiny, raised for pronouncement, removed and polished when something requires the full, unmediated attention of Augusta Hartwell.)*
> *(This morning, in the morning room, Rose watches the full sequence. The Gazette arrives. The spectacles come down. The correspondence column is read with the pencil ticking. Then — a letter, the boy ordained and preaching his first sermons — and the spectacles come off, are polished on the handkerchief Augusta keeps for the purpose, and are set down with the particular care of a woman laying down arms after a victory.)*
> *"Good news?" Rose asks.*
> *"The boy preached on the loaves and fishes." Augusta folds the letter with precision. "His mother says the congregation wept. Thirty years of postage, and the interest is sound." She looks at the spectacles on the table, and something in her face does the softening thing. "They have seen a great deal, these. Ruin, and recovery, and your mother's wedding, and you —" she stops, polishes them again unnecessarily — "and you, child, arriving like a small determined storm."*
> *(Rose laughs, and her throat does something complicated.)*
> *"They'll see more," she says. "They're good spectacles."*
> *"They are." Augusta puts them on, and the Dowager is fully present again, armed and exact. "They intend to see the Assembly through several more years, and they will thank you not to make them weep. Pass the toast."*
> *(The spectacles case is tortoiseshell, worn smooth at the corners by decades of handling. Rose has seen it on every table in the house, in every decade she has known — the small deliberate flag of the Dowager's presence. She understands, suddenly, that she has been navigating by it for years.)*
> *(But later, tidying the morning room, Rose finds the letter left open on the table — deliberately, she is certain — where she can read the mother's grateful postscript. She reads it twice, and folds it as carefully as Augusta had, and understands that some victories are meant to be shared sideways.)*

scenes.synopsis: the hands — Augusta's; the line's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta's hands are seventy-two years old, and they show it — spotted, the knuckles swollen, the veins like small blue rivers under thin skin. Rose finds herself watching them the way she once watched the money: with attention, and with the knowledge that the numbers tell a story.)*
> *(The story this morning is the embroidery — the martial roses on absurdly fine linen, the needle flashing in and out with the same precision the hands brought to everything: to letters, to accounts, to the hair of grandchildren, to the throat of more than one crisis. Seventy-two years of exactitude, written in the fingers.)*
> *"You are staring at my hands, child," Augusta says, without looking up.*
> *"I am admiring your roses. They remain remarkably martial."*
> *"They are coming along." The needle pauses. Augusta holds up the linen, studies it, and — to Rose's astonishment — holds it out. "Here. You try a leaf. Your stitches were always too impatient."*
> *(Rose takes the frame with the care of someone accepting a commission. The linen is impossibly fine. The needle is impossibly small. Her first stitch is, as predicted, impatient — too long, pulling the fabric.)*
> *"Again," Augusta says. "Smaller. The thread goes where you tell it, not where it wants."*
> *(They work in silence for a time, the two heads bent — white and dark — over the martial roses. Rose's leaves improve. Augusta's mouth does the thing it does when she is pleased and has decided not to say so.)*
> *(The linen is French, impossibly fine, older than Rose — part of Augusta's trousseau, never used for its intended grandeur, repurposed at last for martial roses. There is something in that which pleases Rose enormously: the best linen, saved for decades, finally given over to flowers with opinions.)*
> *"Better," she allows, finally. "You will never be neat, but you will be effective. It is the Hartwell way." She takes the frame back and sets three perfect stitches in succession, quick as breathing. "The hands remember, child. Long after the head has opinions about it. That is the mercy, and the warning."*
> *(Rose looks at her own hands — young, ink-stained, hasty — beside her grandmother's, and thinks about seventy years of Tuesdays, and picks up the needle again.)*

scenes.synopsis: the voice — Augusta's; the extraordinary, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The voice does the extraordinary thing — that is what the household calls it, in the servants' hall and the stillroom and everywhere Augusta is loved, which is everywhere. The voice that can strip varnish off a footman at twenty paces can also, without warning, do the extraordinary thing: soften, drop half a register, and say something that rearranges the furniture of your heart.)*
> *(It does it this afternoon in the library, where Rose is hunting a misfiled estate account and Augusta is supposedly reading — actually, Rose suspects, napping behind the Gazette. The account is found. The silence stretches. And then, from behind the paper: "You have your mother's laugh, child. I heard it just now, at something in that ledger."*
> *(Rose stops, the ledger half-shut. "I wasn't laughing.")*
> *"You were smiling at the figures. It is the same thing, in this family." The Gazette lowers. Augusta's eyes are bright over the spectacles — not with tears; Augusta does not do tears; with something older and more durable. "She did the accounts the same way. Pen between her teeth, muttering. Drove the steward mad."*
> *(This is new. Augusta speaks of Rose's mother rarely, and never lightly, and Rose has learned not to chase the subject when it surfaces — to sit still, the way you sit still for a shy animal.)*
> *"Tell me," Rose says, carefully, "about the muttering."*
> *"It was mostly arithmetic, with occasional French." The extraordinary thing is fully present now, the voice low and warm. "She said the numbers behaved better if you scolded them. I told her that was superstition. She said all accounting is superstition with better stationery." A pause. "She was right, of course. She usually was. It was extremely irritating."*
> *(Rose laughs — and hears it, the laugh, her mother's laugh, in her own throat — and Augusta smiles the rarest smile, and the library holds them both in its dusty golden quiet, and the misfiled account lies forgotten on the desk, because some audits matter less than others.)*
> *(The misfiled account, when Rose finally looks at it properly, turns out to be nothing — a timber receipt from March, filed under February by a clerk with more haste than method. She corrects it, blots it, and writes the clerk a note so gentle it will frighten him more than a scolding. Augusta's influence. It spreads.)*

scenes.synopsis: the lesson — the line, the keeping, the returning; the kept's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The lesson, Rose decides, needs writing down properly — straight, in ink, in the household book's fair pages, where she can find it when the years get loud. She takes a fresh sheet after breakfast and writes at the top, in her best hand: "The peace's lesson, as taught by Augusta Hartwell, aged seventy-two." Then she sits with the pen for some time, because the lesson keeps resolving into three different shapes.)*
> *(The line: show up, write the letters, keep the roof on. The keeping: the behavior, not the blood — the Tuesdays. The returning: the road, kept passable for whoever comes next. Three shapes, and all of them true, and all of them Augusta, and none of them quite the whole of her.)*
> *(She writes all three. The line, the keeping, the returning — each with its evidence: the living, the martial roses, the white rose planted the year she was born. The sheet fills. The ink dries. It is, she reflects, the least orderly lesson she has ever taken down, and the truest.)*
> *(Letitia finds her at it and reads over her shoulder, uninvited, the way aunts do.)*
> "The peace's lesson," Letitia reads. "Good God. She's been lecturing again."
> "She has been teaching," Rose says. "There is a difference, and the difference is the whole of a life."
> "She said that to you." Letitia sits, uninvited, the way aunts do. "She's been saying it for fifty years. I used to think it was pompous. Then I turned forty and it started making sense, which was extremely irritating." She taps the sheet. "You've missed one, darling."
> "Have I?"
> "The fourth shape." Letitia's voice does something unusual — drops the comedy, just for a breath. "The enjoying. Augusta never says it, because she thinks it sounds frivolous, but the lesson isn't complete without it. The white rose. The humming that wasn't the bees. She enjoys it, darling — the keeping, the line, all of it. That's the part nobody writes down."
> *(Rose picks up the pen and writes, at the bottom of the sheet: "The enjoying. (Letitia.)" Then, after a moment: "The most important. (Also Letitia.)")*
> *(Letitia reads it, and laughs until the tea comes, and the lesson — four shapes now, and true — goes into the household book under the date, where the fine things live.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE DOWAGER'S GIFT (how the peace is marked: the portrait, the letters, or the keeping). The years deepen; decide the marking. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The years deepen, and the Dowager asks her marking — not in words; Augusta has never asked for anything in words when a look will do. But the look has been there for days: over the spectacles, at breakfast, at the portrait, in the garden. The peace has been kept. Now it wants marking. The marking will shape the Dowager's memory.)*
> *(Rose considers it the way she considers everything now — by asking what Augusta would inspect. The portrait at sixty hangs in the small drawing room, in the afternoon light, the grey silk, the spectacles in hand. It could be cleaned, rehung where the morning finds it, given the place of honor the years have earned it. The hung, the forever — the Dowager, visible, for whoever comes next.)*
> *(Or the letters — the correspondence, thirty years of postage, the boy's sermons. They could be bound in morocco, the dates gilt on the spine, shelved beside the estate ledgers where the house can hold them. The written, the line's — the Dowager, in her own hand, eleven letters before nine.)*
> *(Or the keeping itself — the practice, not the monument. A new article for the charter, written in Rose's own hand and witnessed: the peace's requirements, set down. The chocolate, the letters, the garden walk. The Tuesdays, legislated. The kept, the peace's — the Dowager, honored in the only currency she respects: continuation.)*
> *(Three markings, and each of them true. The portrait: visible, forever, the line's image. The letters: written, exact, the line's hand. The keeping: practiced, daily, the line's behavior. Rose walks the gallery past them all — the portrait, the strongbox, the morning room where the eleven letters wait — and feels the weight of the choosing.)*
> *(Augusta, in the morning room, is writing. The pen scratches — tried twice on the blotter, never hurried. She looks up as Rose passes, and the spectacles do the bright thing, and Rose understands that the Dowager knows exactly what is being decided, and is saying nothing, which is her form of trust.)*
> *(The choice is hers to make — portrait, letters, or keeping. The marking, once decided, wants doing: promptly, exactly, without fuss. The Dowager's gift is hers to decide.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The Dowager's gift:*
- **The portrait** — *the hung, marked.* The peace is marked with a portrait — the hung's, the forever. (Consequence: the marking is the hung's — but hungs are wall's, and the peace was the living.)
- **The letters** — *the written, marked.* The peace is marked with letters — the line's, the written. (Consequence: the marking is the written's — but writtens are ink's, and the peace was the kept.)
- **The keeping** — *the peace, marked.* The peace is marked with keeping — the peace's, the kept. (Consequence: the marking is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the peace was the given.)
> *(The choice is made — portrait, letters, or keeping, as she decides. The Dowager's gift is hers, and the doing starts now.)*
