scenes.synopsis: the later years — Letitia's; the rest's, the deepened. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Time is doing its quiet work on the quartermaster — not diminishing her, exactly; concentrating her. The mornings have gone a fraction slower, the comedy a fraction sharper, and the warmth that was always the whole engine of her sits a fraction closer to the surface, like cream rising.)*
> *(Rose watches it happen with the particular attention of someone who knows she is witnessing something unrepeatable. The quartermaster explaining to the new footman, at length, why the chocolate requires the absurd sugar ("it is medicinal"). The quartermaster writing to the Trelawneys about the seating, underlining "two" three times. The quartermaster, caught — actually caught — napping over her novel at half past three, who then claimed she was "strategizing horizontally.")*
> *"You were asleep," Rose says, over breakfast. "I saw the dribble."*
> *"I was strategizing," Letitia says with dignity. "Horizontally. There is a difference."*
> *(Augusta, pouring the tea, has to leave the room.)*
> *(And yet — and yet — beneath the comedy of it, Rose feels the deepening like a tide coming in. The years are doing their work, patiently, the way they do. Her eyes, warm, watching the house run itself. The ledger, closed. The novel, open. The Park, rearranging itself around its quartermaster with love disguised as administration.)*
> *(At breakfast the sisters perform their ancient comedy — the war over the Gazette, which arrives in a single copy and is wanted by both of them at once. Augusta claims seniority. Letitia claims she reads faster. They have divided it by column, by treaty, and the treaty is violated daily. Rose butters her toast and watches, and thinks that forty-some looks a great deal like every other age, only funnier.)*
> *"The correspondence column is mine," Augusta says, "by right of years."*
> *"The correspondence column is yours," Letitia agrees, "and I have already read it."*
> *(Hodges brings the post without being asked, and catches Rose watching, and they share the look of co-conspirators. The house runs on such looks. It always has.)*
> *(The dribble, for the record, was imaginary — Rose invented it for the joke, and Letitia knows it, and the comedy of the accusation will sustain them both through the week. Some lies are load-bearing. This is one of them.)*
> *(She finds herself, some evenings, simply watching — the novel, the lamplight, the laugh lines deepening — and memorizing. Not morbidly. Practically. The way you memorize a road you intend to travel later. The later years, deepening. The strategy kept. The rest, accumulated like interest — only warmer.)*

scenes.synopsis: Letitia, the later's — the quartermaster, the deepened; the hawk's, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The attic, and dust in the afternoon light, and Letitia on her knees before an old trunk with the air of a woman excavating a civilization — which, Rose reflects, is exactly what she is doing.)*
> *"Darling." Letitia does not look up from the trunk. "You have been watching me."*
> *(Rose considers denying it. Discards the idea. Letitia can smell evasion at twenty paces, and finds it hilarious.)*
> *"I have," she says, sitting on a hatbox. "I'm memorizing."*
> *"Memorizing what, exactly?"*
> *"The way you do things. The showing-up." The dust turns in the light. "The rest. I want to get it right."*
> *(Letitia's hands pause — just for a breath — on the trunk's contents. Then go on, steady as ever, lifting out a riding habit twenty years out of fashion.)*
> *"There is no getting it right, darling. There is only getting it done, and laughing when it goes wrong." She holds the habit against herself, critically. "I was magnificent in this. The skirts were absurd and the elbows wore through and I rode like a sack of grain. Magnificent." She folds it away. "You will do it differently. You do everything differently — faster, with more arithmetic, with fewer jokes. It worried me, once." A glance, warm as ever. "It no longer worries me. The army marches. That is the whole of the requirement."*
> *(Rose feels something loosen in her chest — a knot she did not know she was carrying, the fear of doing it without the laughter, of not being enough like the woman across the trunk.)*
> *(Under the habit: dance cards, tied with ribbon, twenty years of Assemblies. Letitia unties them with reverence, and they both dissolve, there among the trunks, laughing at the young quartermaster's handwriting.)*
> *(They close the trunk on the habit and the dance cards, and the dust settles, and going down the attic stairs Rose carries the smell of camphor and old ribbon with her like a kept thing.)*
> *"The dance cards are for the museum," Letitia says at the stair foot, brushing her skirts. "And Rose —" turning back, the comedy dropped just for a breath — "you are doing it right. I thought you should hear that said plainly, since you are always waiting for the other shoe."*

scenes.synopsis: the hawk's eyes — Letitia's; the warm, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(This week the quartermaster has a new campaign, and it is being fought with a spyglass on the roof leads: the estate's hawks. Letitia has taken to tracking them the way she once tracked seating plans — and Rose, summoned upward, understands she is about to be educated.)*
> *"Darling." Letitia does not lower the spyglass. "Come up. The tiercel is hunting over the lower field and you are missing the entire campaign."*
> *(Rose climbs to the leads — the wind, the whole Park spread below like a map — and takes the spyglass. The hawk hangs over the field, motionless, the way Letitia used to hang over a seating plan.)*
> *"There," Letitia breathes. "Watch. He'll stoop in three — two —"*
> *(The hawk folds and falls like a thrown knife, and comes up with something small and furious, and Letitia makes a sound of pure triumph.)*
> *"Magnificent. Did you see the commitment? No hesitation. That is how you take a mouse, darling. That is how you take anything." She takes the glass back. "They have the right idea, hawks. Warm eyes, sharp eyes, and absolutely no opinions about the seating."*
> *(Rose watches her aunt track the hawk across the sky — the warm eyes narrowed now, the strategist's eyes, reading the air the way she once read a room — and understands what the eyes have always been for. Not just seeing. Choosing. The seating, the suppliers, the moment to laugh. Forty-some years of choosing, daily.)*
> *"They'll see more," Rose says. "The eyes."*
> *"They intend to." The spyglass comes down. "The Assembly through several more years. The pigeons, repelled at last —" she glances at Rose — "your wedding, eventually, though I shall have opinions about the seating."*
> *"My seating," Rose says faintly.*
> *"Eventually. Not imminently. I am forty-some, not morbid." Her eyes gleam. "But they will see it, these eyes, and they will approve of the seating or they will not, and either way the strategy continues. That is what they are for. Seeing things continue — preferably with laughter."*
> *(The tiercel circles once more, high and unhurried, and settles to its meal on the old oak. Letitia hands back the spyglass, satisfied, and they go down the ladder with the wind in their hair, and Rose thinks about eyes that choose — warmly, sharply, daily — and finds it the finest job description she has ever heard.)*

scenes.synopsis: the hands — Letitia's; the strategy's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(October, and the new border by the south wall wants its bulbs — a hundred of them, in a sack like a giant's marbles — and Letitia has claimed the planting as her own. "The gardeners do them too deep," she says, which may or may not be true, and Rose finds her there at noon with the trowel and the sack, up to her wrists in earth.)*
> *"Darling. Kneel. You're no use standing."*
> *(Rose kneels. The bulbs are cool and papery in her hands — tulips, narcissi, the small wild things — and Letitia shows her the depth: three times the bulb, no more, no less, the way her mother showed her, the way she will show whoever comes next.)*
> *"You are staring at my hands, darling," Letitia says, without looking up.*
> *"I am admiring your strategy. It remains remarkably mobile."*
> *"It is coming along." She sets a bulb with finality. "Here. You do the narcissi. Yours are always too shallow."*
> *(They plant in silence for a time, the two heads bent — dark and laughing — over the dark earth. The hands that held the house together for a decade move with the same precision they brought to everything: to ledgers, to piquet, to the hair of nieces, to the defusing of more than one crisis with a joke. Now they press bulbs into the soil like small promises.)*
> *"They won't flower till spring," Rose says.*
> *"I know. That's the point." Letitia wipes her forehead with an earthy wrist, leaving a smudge. "The strategy, darling, was always about spring. You do the work in October and trust April. Ten years of Octobers, and look —" she gestures at the Park — "April kept coming."*
> *(Rose looks at her own hands — young, ink-stained, hasty — beside her aunt's, and thinks about ten years of showing-up, and presses another bulb into the earth.)*
> *"Deeper," Letitia says. "Trust April."*
> *(The last bulb goes in as the light goes gold, and Letitia pats the earth flat with the tenderness of a woman tucking in a child. The hands remember, darling. Long after the head has opinions about it. That is the mercy, and the warning — and the spring.)*

scenes.synopsis: the laugh — Letitia's; the warm, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The apple loft, late afternoon — the rafters low, the stored apples breathing out their sweet cidery smell in their ranked trays — and Rose comes up the ladder with the last basket of windfalls, and stops, because Letitia is singing.)*
> *(Not humming. Singing — an old song, half-remembered, the words mostly wrong, in a voice that is nothing like the warm laugh and everything like a girl again. She is checking the trays as she sings, turning the apples that have spotted, entirely unaware she has an audience.)*
> *(Rose stands on the ladder, the basket on her hip, and does not move. Letitia speaks of her girlhood rarely, and never sings where anyone can hear, and Rose has learned that some doors open only if you don't touch them.)*
> *(The song ends. The last apple is turned. Letitia straightens — and sees her.)*
> *"Darling." The extraordinary thing happens: the quartermaster blushes. Actually blushes. "How long have you been on that ladder?"*
> *"Long enough to learn the chorus is wrong."*
> *"The chorus is traditional." But she is laughing, embarrassed, delighted — a combination Rose has never seen on that face. "It was my — oh, it was a song we sang at — never mind where. I am forty-some and I still get the words wrong. It is my only consistent failure."*
> *"Sing it again. The right words this time."*
> *"Absolutely not. The wrong words are the tradition." Letitia takes the basket, brisk again, but the blush lingers. "Not a word to Augusta. She thinks I have no music in me, and I intend to keep it that way. It is my only mystery."*
> *(They go down the ladder with the empty basket, and Rose thinks about the girl — the one before the quartermaster, before the wars — who sang with the wrong words and kept it secret for years. Not wisdom. Not a lesson. Just a girl, singing, in an apple loft. The extraordinary thing, it turns out, was shyness.)*
> *(That evening Rose hears it again, very faintly, through the floor — the wrong chorus, the girl's voice — and smiles into her book, and keeps the mystery exactly as instructed.)*

scenes.synopsis: the lesson — the strategy, the warmth, the returning; the kept's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The lesson, Rose discovers, is not hers to keep. It leaks.)*
> *(It happens in the church porch after Sunday service — the vicar's wife in a state about the Almerias' music, the seating, Mrs. Fane's girl, the whole apparatus — and Rose hears herself say, without thinking, in exactly Letitia's cadence: "Move the Trelawneys down two. Put Mrs. Fane's girl where they were. And stop worrying — the plan is what you tell people. The strategy is what you actually do when the plan meets the vicar's wife."*
> *(The vicar's wife stares. Then laughs. Then does exactly as told.)*
> *(Behind them, in the porch's shadow, somebody makes a sound — a warm laugh, stifled. Letitia, who came out by the side door and heard everything.)*
> *"Darling," her aunt says, falling into step on the church path, "that was my voice coming out of your mouth. It was extremely alarming. I am so proud I could burst."*
> *"It just came out. She was in a state, and the seating was wrong, and —" Rose stops. "Is this what it feels like? The knowing?"*
> *"This is what it feels like. It feels like theft, and then it feels like inheritance, and then one day you catch yourself saying something appalling in someone else's voice and realize the army marches." Letitia links arms. "The lesson, darling, was never the words. It was the doing. You did it. In a church porch. Your grandmother would have done it in the vestry. I did it in worse places. The tradition continues."*
> *(They walk home through the churchyard with the bells still ringing, and Rose thinks about leaking — the lesson, seeping out of her into the world without permission, the way water finds the cracks. Not written on a sheet. Not filed. Just said, in a porch, to a worried woman, in a borrowed voice that is becoming her own.)*
> *(At the lychgate Letitia stops, and looks back at the church, and says, very quietly, for no audience at all: "Well done, darling." And the lesson — four shapes now, and true — goes on leaking, exactly as it should: out of the porch, down the church path, and into the world.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE QUARTERMASTER'S GIFT (how the rest is marked: the strategy, the laughter, or the keeping). The years deepen; decide the marking. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The look has been there for days — over the chocolate, warm; on the terrace at dusk, among the rooks — and Rose finally names it for what it is: the quartermaster, asking. Not in words; Letitia has never asked for anything in words when a laugh will do. The rest has been kept. Now it wants marking, and the marking will shape how the quartermaster is remembered.)*
> *(Rose walks the terrace as the rooks go over, and considers it the way she considers everything now — by asking what Letitia would find funny. The private ledger, ten years of strategy in a hand that gets illegible when pleased. It could be bound in morocco, her maps gilt on the spine, shelved beside the estate ledgers where the house can hold it. The mind, the kept — the quartermaster, visible, for whoever comes next.)*
> *(Or the laughter — the small portrait at thirty, the hawk's eyes already warm, the laugh already lines. It could be cleaned, hung where the morning finds it, given the place of honor the years have earned it. The warm, the sounded — the quartermaster, laughing, forever, for whoever needs it.)*
> *(Or the keeping itself — the practice, not the monument. A new article for the charter, written in Rose's own hand and witnessed: the rest's requirements, set down. The chocolate, the novel, the shrubbery or nowhere in particular. The showing-up, legislated. The laughing, protected. The rest, the kept — the quartermaster, honored in the only currency she respects: continuation with comedy.)*
> *(Three markings, and each of them true. The strategy: bound, exact, the mind's map. The laughter: hung, warm, the heart's portrait. The keeping: practiced, daily, the life's behavior. Rose walks the terrace past them all — the rooks, the dusk, the lit windows — and feels the weight of the choosing, and the lightness.)*
> *(Letitia, in the billiard room below, is practicing cannons. The click of the balls comes up through the dusk. She looks up as Rose passes the window, and her eyes do the warm thing, and Rose understands that the quartermaster knows exactly what is being decided, and is saying nothing, which is her form of trust — and her form of comedy.)*
> *(The choice is hers to make — strategy, laughter, or keeping — and then comes the doing: promptly, warmly, with a joke. The quartermaster's gift is hers to decide.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The quartermaster's gift:*
- **The strategy** — *the mind, marked.* The rest is marked with strategy — the mind's, the kept. (Consequence: the marking is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the rest was the given.)
- **The laughter** — *the warm, marked.* The rest is marked with laughter — the warm's, the sounded. (Consequence: the marking is the sounded's — but soundeds are heard, and the rest was the strategy's.)
- **The keeping** — *the rest, marked.* The rest is marked with keeping — the rest's, the kept. (Consequence: the marking is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the rest was the mind's.)

scenes.synopsis: the marking — the gift, the given; Letitia, the marked. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Decisions, in this house, are only the overture; the performance is the doing. So Rose sets about the marking the way Letitia taught her — promptly, warmly, and with a joke. The ledger, if strategy was chosen, goes to the binder in morocco with her maps gilt on the spine; the portrait, if laughter, is cleaned and hung where the morning finds it; the charter article, if keeping, is written fair in her own hand and witnessed. Once done, the choice stops being a choice and becomes a fact — and the house, more importantly, can hear it laughing.)*
> *(She chooses the doing the way she chooses everything now — by asking what Letitia would find funny. The ledger's new binding: would those eyes crinkle? The portrait's new position: would the laugh go off? The charter's article: would the quartermaster approve, or would she say it needs more goats?)*
> *(It is, she realizes halfway through the morning, an odd kind of comedy — the dead and living and unborn, conducted through bindings and pictures and the placement of jokes. The strategy, kept laughable. The road, walked in both directions, with excellent company.)*
> *(Hodges is summoned, and instructed, and, to his visible satisfaction, finds the instructions exact but funny. "Very good, miss," he says, which from Hodges is a speech. The marking is carried out to the quartermaster's standard — completely, and with a joke.)*
> *(By luncheon it is done — the marking, marked, in whatever shape the choice gave it. Rose stands back and looks at the morning's work and feels the particular satisfaction of a task completed exactly as Letitia taught her: promptly, warmly, and with a joke.)*
> *(The house absorbs the marking the way it absorbs everything: without comment, and completely. By the time the luncheon bell goes, the morning's work is simply part of the rooms — the way the seating plans are part of the estate office, the way the rooks are part of the dusk. Done, and therefore invisible, and therefore perfect.)*
> *(Letitia, told at luncheon, listens with warm eyes, and laughs once, low. "Satisfactory," she says, stealing Augusta's word with complete shamelessness. And then, the extraordinary thing: "Though the joke was unnecessary." Augusta, across the table, looks decorated.)*

scenes.synopsis: Letitia, the marking — the quartermaster, the years'; the hawk's, the moved. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(She is among the runner beans, tying off stems with twine, when Letitia appears — the kitchen garden, the late afternoon, the poles standing like a small green army — and her aunt stands beside her in silence for some time, tying off a stem here and there with the expertise of long practice.)*
> *"Darling." Her eyes, warm, the marking's. "You have marked it."*
> *"I have." Rose does not look up from the twine. "The marking is done. The strategy, kept."*
> *(Letitia ties another stem — the real her, not the portrait, with bean dust on her cuffs — and considers her niece with the attention she gives to seating plans.)*
> *"You know what it is," her aunt says slowly, "to be looked at by your own young face and found satisfactory? No. You are twenty-five. You will learn." She takes Rose's hand — the gesture, familiar now as breathing — and her fingers are warm and quick, bean-stained. "The quartermaster in that frame was thirty. The Park half-ruined. And she is —" the voice does the extraordinary thing, dropping half a register — "she is proud of you, darling. The frame doesn't show it. Frames never show the important things. But I am telling you, so that it is said."*
> *(Rose's throat does the complicated thing. She looks at the painted face in her memory — laughing, warm, keeping its counsel — and then at the living one beside her, and understands that they are the same woman, and that the woman is telling the truth.)*
> *"The eyes knew," Rose manages. "Augusta said so."*
> *"Augusta says a great deal." But Letitia is smiling the rarest smile. "In this instance, she is right. They knew." She pats Rose's hand once, decisively, and turns toward the house. "Now. The novel is getting ideas, and I intend to have beans again. One does not mark a quartermaster every day."*
> *(They have tea in the kitchen garden, on the bench by the poles, and the beans appear at supper — a triumph repeated, which Letitia accepts as her due. The conversation is ordinary: the goat, the Trelawneys, the new footman's cuffs. But Rose keeps glancing at her aunt, and the thing keeps happening in her chest.)*

scenes.synopsis: Letitia, the marked — the quartermaster's, the years'; the kept, the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(In the weeks after the marking, Rose notices the change the way you notice a room has been repainted — not all at once, but in the small things. The billiard room holds the marking the way it holds everything: as part of the furniture of days, settled in, intending to stay, and to be laughed about.)*
> *(And Letitia — Letitia wears the marking the way she wears everything: lightly, and as the setup for a joke. She does not refer to it. She does not need to. But Rose catches her, twice in one week, practicing cannons with a particular flourish that means those eyes are satisfied.)*
> *(There is a lesson in that, Rose thinks, about how honors work when they are real: they are not announced, they are absorbed — usually with laughter. The house does not celebrate the marking. The house simply continues, a fraction warmer, the way a room warms when someone funny walks in.)*
> *(Augusta, of course, celebrates it — Augusta celebrates nothing, which makes it momentous — with a supper she calls "the Marking Dinner," which consists of the beans again (a triumph, they agree), a syllabub, and a toast she has clearly rehearsed: "To Letitia — marked, and marking us!" The table applauds. Letitia accepts it with the dignity of a monarch and the pleasure of an aunt, which is to say: completely, and while laughing.)*
> *(The syllabub, Rose reflects, scraping the last of it from her glass, was the true flourish — the cook makes it with sherry and smugness in equal measure. The Marking Dinner will be remembered, she suspects, longer than the marking itself, which is exactly as it should be. Dinners are for remembering. Markings are for continuing.)*
> *(Letitia retires early, pleading the novel — which everyone accepts and nobody believes — and the supper party lingers without her, toasting the marking in progressively warmer language. Rose lets it run. Some celebrations need the quartermaster present. This one, she judges, needed her absent, so the love could be loud.)*
> *"The joke," Augusta says afterward, to Rose alone, "was unnecessary."*
> *"It was essential," Rose says, "and you loved it."*
> *"Hmph." The spectacles gleam. "It was satisfactory." Which, from the Dowager, about a joke, is a fireworks display.)*

scenes.synopsis: the strategy, the eternal — Letitia's; the kept, the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Eternal is a large word, and Rose distrusts large words — but walking the yew walk at dawn, she lets herself test it against the strategy, checking for lies. The Park is not eternal; the Park is maintained. The strategy is not eternal; the strategy is rested. But there is something in the resting that points the way a fallow field points toward harvest: not there yet, but certain of the direction.)*
> *(She walks the yew walk at dawn, before the household book — the ancient yews, clipped for a century, dark and patient on either side — and thinks about keeping. The yews were planted by hands long dust. They are kept by hands she pays by the quarter. The eternal, it turns out, is just keeping, with a longer view.)*
> *(The comfort in that is unexpected: the strategy does not require her to be eternal. It requires her to be next. To keep the army marching for whoever comes after, the way Letitia kept it for her. The eternal takes care of itself, or doesn't. The next is the assignment — and the laughter comes with it.)*
> *(She stops where the walk opens to the Park — the mist, the rooks, the whole kept expanse — and thinks about the quartermaster's version of forever. Not a memorial. Perhaps a funnier household book, in time. Perhaps nothing for a while, the plans holding their breath the way the house holds its breath at dawn. The strategy does not require the future to be planned. It requires the road to be passable — and enjoyable.)*
> *(A blackbird performs its territorial opera from the top of a yew, indifferent to eternity. Rose walks on between the dark green walls, and the strategy walks with her as easy company, never a weight. The showing-up, kept. The rest, practiced. The niece, keeping.)*
> *(She reaches the walk's end as the clock strikes seven, and goes in to order the chocolate — both cups — because the strategy, like everything else in this house, begins with breakfast.)*
> *(Behind her the yews stand in their century-long patience, and the blackbird finishes its opera, and the eternal — whatever it is — keeps its own counsel, dark and green and entirely unhurried.)*

scenes.synopsis: the rest, the kept — the quartermaster's, the lesson's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Half past four, whatever the weather: the walk. Down the yew walk, along the water, past the moorhens, and back by the shrubbery — the quartermaster's newest campaign, practiced daily until it has become law. The rest, Rose is learning, is not a retirement, signed and filed. It is a practice.)*
> *(The walk is the quartermaster's newest campaign — the constitutional, retired. Half past four, every day, rain or shine: down the yew walk, along the water, past the reeds where the moorhens argue, and back by the shrubbery. Letitia does it in all weathers with the grim cheer of a woman who has decided that fresh air is a moral requirement.)*
> *"You don't have to come," she told Rose the first day.*
> *"I'm coming. Somebody has to witness the moral requirement."*
> *(She watches Letitia practice it — the pace, the swing of the arms, the pause at the water to check the moorhens' dispositions — and understands at last what the quartermaster has been demonstrating for weeks without ever quite saying it: rest is not the absence of effort. It is effort so complete it can be laid down, and then picked up again, daily, for the pleasure of it.)*
> *(The household has learned the practice too. Hodges has the boots by the door at half past four without being asked. The maids know not to schedule anything across it. The gardener's boy times his pretending-not-to-watch to the yew walk. The whole Park moves through its afternoons with the competence of a body that has learned its own rhythms.)*
> *(And the lesson, underneath the practice: that the rest was never the prize. The prize was the showing-up. The coal order. The seating slips. The beans, tied. Letitia at forty-some, striding to the lake in the rain, having earned every step of it the hard way — one showing-up at a time.)*
> *(That evening Rose adds a line to the margin, under the first: the practice is the prize. She looks at the two lines together, and laughs at her own circularity — Letitia's influence — and leaves them both, because they are true even if they are round.)*
> *(Half past four comes daily, whatever the weather. The boots are by the door. The walk is kept.)*

scenes.synopsis: the rest, the charter's — the kept, the legacy's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The fair copy book lives in the morning room — the big one, mostly in Augusta's hand, the articles of the house set down fair — and Rose goes to it after breakfast with the practices on her mind. The rest has been kept daily until it became law; law, in this house, gets written down. She opens the book to see how the charter actually reads.)*
> *(The articles lie in their order: the Assembly's founding, the household's liturgies, the kept record of the years. She reads them over as though the names might be lying — and finds them sound, which is to say: exact, and a little funny.)*
> *(And there, at the foot of the household liturgies, in Augusta's precise hand: a codicil, added years ago and never quite explained. "No quartermaster, present or future, shall pretend she is strategizing horizontally when she is plainly asleep." Rose stares at it. She reads it twice. Then she starts laughing, there in the morning room's quiet, because she knows exactly when Augusta wrote it, and why.)*
> *"She will notice," Augusta says — appearing in the doorway with her morning tea, as grandmothers do. "She notices everything. She will pretend not to notice, which is her way of approving."*
> *"How long has that been there?"*
> *"Years. Since the first time she napped through the seating. I witnessed it myself." Augusta settles into the chair opposite, uninvited and entirely welcome. "Charters are living things, child. They grow codicils the way gardens grow weeds. The trick is to weed them into topiary."*
> *(Rose takes up the pen, and writes the new article fair — the rest's requirements, in her own hand: the chocolate, the novel, the walk or nowhere in particular, the showing-up legislated, the laughing protected — and Augusta witnesses it with her spectacles on, and Letitia, summoned from the billiard room, reads it over Rose's shoulder and signs it with a flourish.)*
> *"The rest will do," her aunt says. "The last clause will be reviewed."*
> *(It is never reviewed. The article goes into the fair copy with the others, the last clause intact, and Rose understands that this — the pretense of review, the reality of acceptance — is itself one of the practices. Augusta taught them both.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, the strategist's — Rose, the evening's; the strategy's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and the morning room belongs to Rose and the household book, which lies open under the lamp like a patient waiting to be discharged. She writes up the day — the charter, the beans, the chimney that smoked and was coaxed — in the fair hand she has practiced for ten years, and the pen moves without her thinking about it, which is new, and which she notices the way you notice a tooth has stopped aching: with suspicion, then relief.)*
> *(The door opens without a knock. Letitia, in her wrapper, the novel under one arm, with the air of a woman who has been reading and found a sentence too good to keep to herself.)*
> *"Darling. Listen." She finds the page. "'The heroine,'" she reads, "'had opinions about the seating, and was not afraid to state them.' Well? Is that not us? Is that not this house, in a sentence?"*
> *(Rose laughs, and the book is pushed aside while the sentence is properly appreciated, which takes some time, because Letitia reads it three times with different emphases.)*
> *(They sit. The lamp burns low and steady. Outside, the Park goes dark the way it does in October — all at once, like a curtain dropped, the limes black against the last light.)*
> *"You write a good hand," Letitia says, looking at the book. "Better than mine. Mine looked like a battle plan. Yours looks like someone who expects to be read."*
> *"The book is for whoever comes next."*
> *"I know." Letitia pulls her shawl closer. "That's what pleases me. You'll do it differently, and it will be right, and I shall be insufferable about having taught you. It's the natural order."*
> *(Rose looks at her aunt — the wrapper, the novel, the absolute ease of a woman who has stopped performing — and understands, suddenly, that the evening is not a pause in the strategy. It is the strategy, at rest. The showing-up, done for the day. The book, waiting for tomorrow.)*
> *(Letitia reads another passage — a dinner party that goes wrong in the right way — and they laugh, and the lamp burns, and the house holds its evening around them. When it is done, Rose opens the book and writes one more line: "The strategy, at rest." She blots it, closes the cover, and the heir — for tonight — is done.)*

scenes.synopsis: the legacy, the strategy — Letitia's, the charter's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Before the household book, at first light, Rose goes out to the new bulb border — the earth flat and dark where they planted, nothing showing, a hundred promises underground waiting for April — and stands there doing the only arithmetic that matters this morning: once for the sum, once for the nerve.)*
> *(The ledger was the map, but the legacy is not the map. She has understood that for years; this morning she feels it the way you feel a change in the weather — not in the head, but in the bones. What the map was for: the practices, the novel, the walk or nowhere in particular. The showing-up. The rest, accumulated like interest, only warmer.)*
> *(She kneels and presses her palm to the cool earth, the way Letitia did, and thinks about October work and April trust. What will the strategy become, eventually? Not a memorial — it would bore the pigeons. Perhaps a funnier household book. Perhaps nothing for a while, the plans holding their breath. The legacy does not require the future to be planned. It requires the bulbs to be deep enough — and the spring to be trusted.)*
> *(A blackbird performs its territorial opera from the south wall, indifferent to legacies. Rose stands, brushes the earth from her skirts, and walks the border's length — a hundred small promises, underground, exact.)*
> *(In the billiard room Letitia is already practicing — the click of the balls, the morning's first cannon — the order of battle, retired, proceeding exactly as it should. She looks up as Rose passes the door, and her eyes do the warm thing, and Rose understands that the legacy is not a thing to be counted. It is a border, planted. It is this.)*
> *(Rose walks on toward the house, and the legacy walks with her the way the morning walks beside her — alongside, unhurried, familiar. The showing-up, kept. The rest, practiced. The niece, keeping. She reaches the stairhead as the clock strikes seven, and goes down to order the chocolate — both cups — because the legacy, like everything else in this house, begins with breakfast.)*
> *(Behind her the border lies dark and flat and full of spring, and the blackbird finishes its opera, and April — distant, certain — keeps its own counsel underground.)*

scenes.synopsis: the hawk's, the kept — Letitia's, the years'; the warm, the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The paddock, mid-morning — and the year's foal has opinions. Letitia is in there with her, her eyes doing their full work: warm for the foal's absurd ears, sharp for the fence that wants mending, and then — the decision — narrowed in the particular way that means the quartermaster is naming something.)*
> *"It needs a name," Letitia says. "Everything on this estate gets a name eventually, or it gets a number, and numbers are for the ironmonger's bills."*
> *(The foal — leggy, bright-eyed, already showing opinions — nuzzles at Letitia's sleeve. She considers it with the gravity of a woman christening a ship.)*
> *"But not yet. The thing about naming, darling, is that it has to last longer than the joke." She looks at the foal for a long moment, and her eyes do the softening thing. "We'll know her better by spring. For now she's the year's foal, and that's name enough."*
> *(Rose watches from the gate, uninvited, the way nieces do. The foal skitters sideways on her long legs and comes back for another look at the woman who declined to name her. This is how the quartermaster sees the world, she thinks: warmly, sharply, and with complete attention — examined first, named when the time is right.)*
> *"They are good eyes," Letitia says, catching her at it, with the familiar frankness. "They have seen ruin and recovery, and forty-some years of showing-up, and they intend to see a great deal more. The Assembly through several more years. The pigeons, repelled at last. The year's foal, here, grown."*
> *"And my wedding," Rose says, "eventually. With opinions about the seating."*
> *"In due course. I am forty-some, not morbid." Her eyes gleam. "But these eyes will see it, and they will approve of the seating or they will not, and either way the strategy continues. That is what they are for — seeing things continue, and laughing while they do."*
> *(The foal gallops the paddock's length on her ridiculous legs, triumphant, and comes back. The eyes gleam. The morning holds. Some inheritances are not announced. They are simply worn, daily, like laughter — or given, like names.)*

scenes.synopsis: the charter, the kept — Letitia's, the legacy's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Rain on the estate-office windows, and nothing requiring her anywhere — so Rose opens the map drawer just to look, the way you look at things you have built, to make sure they are still true and still funny. Hodges has oiled the drawer runners; it opens without a sound.)*
> *(The supper-room diagram lies in its creases, the arrows faded but legible. Beneath it, the new article — the rest's requirements, in Rose's hand, witnessed by Augusta, signed by Letitia with a flourish — sits in its folder like the youngest child at a family dinner: slightly out of place, entirely belonging.)*
> *(She reads it over as though the names might be lying — and finds it sound: the chocolate legislated, the laughing protected, the walk or nowhere in particular. It is a strange document, she reflects: half law, half love letter. The law part keeps the army marching. The love-letter part is why anyone laughs while marching.)*
> *(Hodges appears in the doorway with the timing of a man who has been listening for the exact moment the papers stop being useful — thirty years of service have made him a connoisseur of her moods.)*
> *"The office chimney smokes, miss," he says. Which means: the afternoon requires tending, and the papers will keep.)*
> *(The chimney is coaxed — Hodges on a chair with the damper, Rose holding the lamp, the two of them in silent alliance against the smoke — and the fire draws, and the office warms, and they stand a moment in the dusty quiet, listening to the rain and the house move through its afternoon around them. The smoke curls up the chimney, defeated, and Hodges steps down from the chair with the dignity of a man who has won a small war.)*
> *(Hodges brings cocoa — thick, dark, the way the kitchen makes it when it rains — and they drink it among the maps, and Rose understands that the charter is kept in the drawer, but the keeping is done everywhere else — out loud, and laughing.)*
> *(The charter, kept. The quartermaster, kept. The chimney, kept. She closes the drawer, and the rain goes on, and the house holds its afternoon the way the strategy holds its years: warmly, and exactly.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE STRATEGY'S MEANING (what the strategy means: the keeping, the quartermaster, or the future). The years deepen; decide the meaning. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(Beneath all the chapter's other questions runs the one Rose has been circling since the first dawn walk: what does the strategy mean? The rest has been taught. The gift has been marked. The meaning is the last of the three — and the one that will shape how the strategy is remembered.)*
> *(She takes the question to the orchard at dawn, where the mist hangs between the trees and the rooks go over like slow punctuation — and walks it down the rows, past each kept tree. Is the meaning the keeping — the behavior, the showing-up, the laughing when it goes wrong? The strategy as practice: pay attention, keep the army marching, protect the comedy. The rest's meaning, kept daily.)*
> *(Or is the meaning the quartermaster — Letitia herself, forty-some years, the hawk's eyes, the novel, the loose grace? The strategy as person: a woman, concretely, who held a house together for a decade with maps and laughter and taught a niece to do the same. The warm's meaning, living.)*
> *(Or is the meaning the future — the army, marching, for whoever comes next? The bulbs, a hundred promises underground. The strategy as direction: what continues — the ledger, waiting; the foal, growing; the returning's meaning, unfinished.)*
> *(Three meanings, and all of them true. The keeping: the rest's, the kept — true, she has seen it daily. The quartermaster: Letitia's, the warm's — true, she has laughed beside it. The future: the years', the returning — true, but unfinished, which is its nature and its mercy and its joke.)*
> *(Rose stops among the trees — the mist, the rooks, the windfalls waiting — and holds the three meanings up to the morning light, checking them for lies the way she was taught. None of them lie. That is the difficulty. The strategy asks its meaning, and the meaning is hers to decide.)*
> *(The choice is hers to make — keeping, quartermaster, or future. She thinks of the chocolate waiting below, the novel, the walk, and understands that the meaning, whatever she decides, will be kept the same way everything in this house is kept: daily, warmly, and with a joke.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The strategy's meaning:*
- **The keeping** — *the kept, meant.* The strategy means keeping — the rest's, the kept. (Consequence: the meaning is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the strategy was the giving.)
- **The quartermaster** — *the warm, meant.* The strategy means the quartermaster — Letitia's, the warm. (Consequence: the meaning is the warm's — but warms are felt, and the strategy was the mind's.)
- **The future** — *the returning, meant.* The strategy means the future — the years, the returning. (Consequence: the meaning is the returning's — but returnings are future, and the strategy was the now.)

scenes.synopsis: the meaning, the kept — the strategy's, the lesson's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The meanings go with her the way the household book goes with her: everywhere, and without thinking about it. Keeping. The quartermaster. The future. Three of them, all true, and the carrying of them is the work of days — preferably funny days.)*
> *(She tests the meanings the way she was taught — holding each arrangement up, checking for lies. The keeping: true. She has seen it — the book, the beans, the boots by the door at half past four. The quartermaster: true. Forty-some years, and those eyes still see things continue. The future: — she holds this one longest — true, but unfinished. The future is always unfinished. That is its nature, and its mercy, and its joke.)*
> *(In the herb garden at noon the thyme is at its most fragrant, and Rose cuts it for the kitchen with the meanings for company: the keeping, practiced daily; the quartermaster, reading her novel; the future, curving away down the drive like the road it is. The basket fills. The meanings hold — as directions, never answers.)*
> *(Augusta finds her there, with a letter in her hand and purpose in her step.)*
> *"The Trelawneys have written," Augusta announces. "They accept for the music. Mrs. Fane encloses — separately, at length — an account of her daughter's discards, which I am spared by the happy accident of having spectacles to polish."*
> *"Poor Mrs. Fane's girl."*
> *"She will survive. They all survive." Augusta turns to go, then stops. "The meanings, child — the keeping, the quartermaster, the future. You are allowed to find them funny. That is also part of it."*
> *(She sweeps on toward the house, leaving Rose among the herbs with the basket, the meanings, and the distinct feeling of having been inspected and found satisfactory.)*
> *(The gardener's boy, pretending not to watch, is actually watching — Rose catches his eye and winks, and he turns the color of the thyme flowers. The garden keeps its own counsel, but it is not above enjoying the comedy. Letitia's influence. It spreads.)*
> *(She stays a little longer, the basket full in her hands. The keeping. The quartermaster. The future. The road, passable. The march, laughable. She goes in to write the Trelawneys' visit into the book, because the future, like everything else, begins with being written down.)*
> *(She opens the household book at last, and writes in the Trelawneys' visit — the music, the discards, the expression — with the care of someone setting down history. The meanings hold. The road is passable. The book closes with a soft thump, like a door well shut — and somewhere in the billiard room, a laugh goes off like sun through a window.)*

scenes.synopsis: the letters — the years, reported; London writes. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The afternoon post brings the outside world's verdict on the years — three of them, by three different hands, all saying the same thing. A London friend writes that Letitia's piquet tournament was "the only thing worth attending this Assembly season, and the peppermints were magnificent." The ironmonger writes that the account is settled, and adds — in a postscript that has clearly cost him effort — that the Park's orders are "a pleasure, which is more than I say for most." And Bell — Bell writes in the Gazette's own postscript column that the quartermaster was seen at the Assembly "running the card room like a campaign headquarters, the strategy's living argument." Rose reads all three on the orchard grass and laughs aloud.)*
> *"A campaign headquarters," she reads to Letitia, who is sorting windfalls with the care of a woman handling explosives.*
> *"Bell exaggerates," Letitia says. "It was a tournament. There were peppermints."*
> *"There was some force. Augusta said so."*
> *"Augusta is not a reliable witness to force." The windfalls tick into the basket. "Though the Assembly went well. Mrs. Fane's girl has improved her discards by a full degree. I take the credit."*
> *(Rose sorts the rest of the post — a note from the Trelawneys, the music confirmed — and thinks about London writing. The ton, reporting the years the way the Gazette reports the weather: with interest, with opinion, and with the absolute conviction that it matters. And it does matter, she reflects. The witnessing is part of the keeping.)*
> *(She writes back to the London friend — the quartermaster is well, the peppermints are ordered by the pound — and to the ironmonger — the pleasure is mutual — and the letters go out with the morning post, the years reported back to London, the correspondence of the rest proceeding exactly as it should.)*
> *(Letitia, sorting her windfalls, watches Rose at the smaller basket, her eyes warm.)*
> *"You write a good letter, darling," her aunt says. "Prompt. Warm. No force."*
> *"High praise."*
> *"It is the highest." The windfalls tick. "London writes. We answer. That is the arrangement, and it has held for ten years. See that it holds for ten more."*
> *(Rose blots her letters on her knee, and stacks them, and thinks about ten years of postage — the strategy, kept by correspondence — and the arrangement holding. London writes. The Park answers. The years, reported, on both sides — with the jokes intact.)*

scenes.synopsis: the ton, the years' — the rest, awaited; the convened, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(London has decided that something is happening at Hartwell Park — Rose reads it in the letters, in the Gazette's arch postscripts, in the Assembly invitations now answered within the week instead of the month. The ton is assembling its attention, and the ton is never wrong about where to be, especially when there is laughter.)*
> *(She counts it with Hodges in the wine cellar, the way generals count battalions — the champagne, the claret, the negus, chalked on the slate in Hodges's immaculate hand.)*
> *"Sixty bottles of champagne, miss. For the Assembly week."*
> *"Sixty? Last year was forty."*
> *"The ton awaits, miss." Hodges chalks the number without expression. "The ton, historically, drinks."*
> *(Rose considers the slate — the bottles, the chalk, the force assembling — and feels the familiar pre-Assembly tightening in her shoulders, the hostess's arithmetic beginning its annual turn. Supper rooms. Candles. The shrubbery, lit for the interval. The squirrels, regrettably, too — but laughably.)*
> *(And beneath the arithmetic, something warmer: the rest, awaited, is the rest confirmed. London does not await things it doubts. The ton's anticipation is the outside world's version of Hodges bringing the post without being asked — love, disguised as administration.)*
> *(Letitia's voice comes down the cellar steps — "Darling, if you're counting champagne, count me twice" — and Rose laughs, and chalks a small extra mark that is either a joke or a necessity.)*
> *"We'll need the card room for Letitia's tournament," Rose says, making a note. "And the peppermints will want ordering by the pound."*
> *"The peppermints always want ordering. They are the most demanding members of this family." Hodges closes the slate with a snap. "Cheer up, miss. The ton awaits. It is the finest possible review — and her ladyship will be insufferable about it."*
> *(Rose climbs the cellar steps into the daylight, and looks out at the drive — empty, pale, curving away between the limes — and imagines it in Assembly week: the river of carriage lamps, the arrivals, the glorious wreckage. The ton, awaited. The rest, kept. She picks up the pen, and begins — laughing, a little, at the prospect. The drive is empty now, but she can already hear it: the wheels, the voices, the beautiful chaos of Assembly week, coming.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, the strategy's — Rose, the evening's; the kept, the rest's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Dusk, and the billiard room to herself — Rose takes up a cue and practices the cannon Letitia taught her: the angle, the pace, the follow-through. The household book lies closed on the chair beside her. Beyond the windows the Park arranges itself for night. The lamps are lit, the table brushed, the evening entirely hers.)*
> *(She thinks about the day — the letters, the book, the ton assembling itself in chalk on a slate — and about the chapter behind it: the rest's lesson, taught; the quartermaster's gift, marked; the strategy's meaning, decided. Three decisions, and all of them hers, and each of them standing. The strategy, the warmth, the returning. The strategy, the laughter, the keeping. The keeping, the quartermaster, the future. She turns them over, checking for lies the way she was taught, and finds them true.)*
> *(The kept is the rest's — she practices the phrase once more, silently, and finds it sits naturally now. Not a retirement. A practice. The chocolate with the absurd sugar. The novel at nine. The walk or nowhere in particular. The years, deepening like tea, with laughter.)*
> *(A soft step — Letitia in the doorway, decisive, cheerful — and her aunt appears with two glasses of negus and the air of a woman executing a long-planned maneuver.)*
> *"Darling," Letitia says. "I have interrogated the novel. It denies everything."*
> *(Rose laughs, and stands aside, and Letitia comes in and looks around the billiard room — the table, the lamps, the Park going dark beyond — and nods once.)*
> *"Sound," her aunt says. "The woman, the strategy's, keeps a sound billiard room." She sets down the negus, picks up a cue, and sights along it. "One frame. The young must be educated. It is practically charity."*
> *(They play till the lamplight burns low, and Rose loses — narrowly, this time, which is progress — and the woman, the strategy's, is entirely, completely at peace — and entirely, completely laughing, inside.)*
> *(The last ball drops. The cues are racked. Letitia chalks her cue with a flourish, as though she has won a tournament rather than a friendly frame. The evening holds like a well-aimed cannon — unexpected, exact, and entirely delightful.)*

scenes.synopsis: the legacy, the rest — Letitia's, the charter's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(She wakes before the house on the chapter's last morning — an old habit, back for the occasion — and goes down to the kitchen, where the cook is already shaping the loaves and the first smell of the day's bread is going into the oven.)*
> *"Miss Rose." The cook does not stop kneading. "You're early. The bread isn't."*
> *"The bread is never early. That's its whole philosophy." Rose takes the stool by the range, uninvited, the way she did as a child. "How many years have you been making this bread, before I ask?"*
> *"Longer than you've been asking, miss." The cook slaps a loaf into shape. "Bread doesn't care who's quartermaster. Bread just wants the oven hot and the hands sure."*
> *(Rose thinks about that — the bread's philosophy — and about what the chapter has actually been. Not a story, exactly. A season. The quartermaster through her years: the mornings, the strategy, the orchard, the Assembly, the toasts. The lesson taught. The gift marked. The meaning decided. The strategy kept, in all its ordinary glory.)*
> *(And the forever — Rose turns that word over carefully. Not eternal; maintained. Not forever; continued. The strategy does not promise forever. It promises next. The army, marching. The showing-up, kept. The laughing, protected. That is the forever on offer, and it is enough. It has always been enough.)*
> *(She hears the house waking above — the morning, beginning — and the small domestic thunder of the day starting without her permission. The chocolate will be ordered — both cups, the absurd sugar. The novel will be resumed. Her eyes will come up, warm, over the post.)*
> *(Rose goes up the stairs, slippers silent on the waxed boards, toward the morning room and the practice and the quartermaster — toward the rest, kept, and the legacy, continuing. The chapter closes behind her like a door well shut. The Season turns.)*
> *(And in the kitchen the bread rises — the oven hot, the hands sure — and the legacy, the rest, keeps its own counsel in yeast and heat. It looks, Rose thinks, going up, satisfied. The strategy kept. The rest, the charter's. The forever, the next. She goes in to breakfast with the smell of bread in her clothes and the day already underway without her.)*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's rest report — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"The quartermaster rests — or what passes for rest in a woman who annotated a piquet bracket like a battle plan and called a coal order her finest hour. The Gazette notes that the social general's rest is merely her strategy with the volume lowered, and pronounces it sufficient. The Season was won; the winning may now be filed."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first, then the reckoning: Letitia's rest pronounced sufficient in print, and Bell has made it permanent, which is Bell's way of making it forever. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the rest the Gazette allows is the rest Letitia takes — filed, annotated, and exactly on schedule.* — remembered: *the lesson: the rest the Gazette allows is the rest Letitia takes — filed, annotated, and exactly on schedule.*

scenes.synopsis: the Englishman's turning — Laurent's, the turned; the unmasked, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and the quartermaster's rest is filed — annotated, exactly on schedule — and Rose's thoughts turn to the Englishman.)*
> *(Laurent. The design, the honeyed loops, the years of masks — and now the unmasking, coming the way weather comes: not asked for, and arriving exactly on time.)*
> *(She has watched him perform for ten seasons. She wonders, standing in the gallery as the lamps are lit, what the man looks like when he stops — and whether the stopping is the whole of the next chapter.)*
> *(The Season turns toward the Englishman. The mask lifts, and the Season holds its breath with it.)*
