scenes.synopsis: the years' turning — the Englishman's years; Laurent, the unmasked. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The boots are the first thing Rose notices — Laurent's boots, by the boot-room door, muddied to the ankle at an hour when no French comte has any business being muddy. It is barely light. The house is still holding its breath. And the boots say, plain as print, that the Englishman has been out in the Park since dawn, doing whatever it is he does out there before the household book.*
> *(Hodges, passing with the lamps, follows her look. "The Comte walks, miss," he says, with the particular gravity of a man reporting a change in the weather. "The parkland. Every morning. He has taken to naming the trees." A pause. "In English."*
> *"Does he get them right?"*
> *"Increasingly, miss. The lime took some weeks." Hodges picks up a lamp, considers the boots, and adds — because Hodges, too, has been watching the years turn: "He cleans them himself, miss. Wouldn't let the boy do it. Said the mud was —" the butler searches for the word — "'earned.'"*
> *(Earned. Rose stands in the boot room with the lamps going out one by one, and thinks about the turning of Laurent's years — not as an event, with trumpets, but as a pair of boots. The Comte de Varenne, thirty-one, French to the bone, has chosen England: the Park, the rain, the mud. And the choosing, once done, turns out to be a daily practice — like the household book, like the chocolate, like the naming of trees in a language he is still learning.*
> *(It began without announcement, as the true things do. Not with the formal ask — that came at the masquerade, the mask off for good, the old world given one more night and then set aside — but with the small surrenders after: the polish laid down, then the management, then the beautiful survival itself. What was left was a man speaking directly, the way she does. It terrified them both, at first. Then it became the ground.*
> *(The ground: England. Not Paris, not the brilliant match his family had pressed for, not the de Varenne name restored the way they wanted it restored. England — the mud, the mist, the directness. She looks at the boots a moment longer, and understands that the unmasking was not an evening's work. It was an arrival. The mask, removed, has stayed off — and the face underneath keeps choosing, every morning, before breakfast.*
> *(She leaves the boots where they are — earned mud, not to be disturbed — and goes to order the chocolate, both cups, because some liturgies continue even when the Englishman is unmasked. Especially then.*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent, the years' — the Englishman, the unmasked; the direct, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room, mid-morning, and Laurent is at the writing desk with three letters spread before him like a losing hand — writing, crossing out, writing again. He looks up when Rose comes in, and does the thing the unmasked do now: he does not manage his expression. He lets her see the difficulty.*
> *"The letter to my family," he says. "I have written it in French four times. It is perfect, and it is a lie." He pushes the French drafts aside. "So I am writing it in English. It will be clumsy, and it will be true."*
> *(Rose sits. The household book stays closed. This is not a morning for arithmetic.*
> *"Read me the true one," she says.*
> *"'My dear mother —'" he begins, and stops. "No. In English it must be simpler. 'Mother. I have chosen England. I have chosen her. The de Varenne name will not be restored the way you hoped. It will be —'" he searches — "kept. Differently." He looks up. "Is 'differently' too cruel?"*
> *"It's honest. Cruel would be pretending."*
> *"The French instinct," he says, "is to survive beautifully and fight later. My family survived the ruin that way — the speculation took everything, and we survived it beautifully. It was magnificent. It was also exhausting." He meets her eyes. "I am tired of being magnificent, Rose. I would like to try being kept."*
> *(She comes around the desk, and reads over his shoulder, and corrects one word — not the grammar, the courage — and he takes the correction the way he takes all her corrections now: as a form of love.*
> *"'Kept, differently,'" he reads back, trying it. "Yes. That is the whole of it." He signs it — the careful English hand, still learning — and sands it, and folds it. "The brilliant match they wanted for me —" a small, unmasked smile — "will have to find another comte. This one is taken. In English."*
> *(He seals the letter, and the wax is the Park's own red, and Rose understands that the directness is not a talent. It is a discipline — practiced at a writing desk, in a morning room, one true sentence at a time. The letter goes out with the post. The family will read it in Paris and understand, or not. The choosing, freely made, by both, does not require their permission. That was the whole point.*
> *("Kept, differently," Rose says, trying it herself, and finds it will do. Some sentences are load-bearing. This is one of them.*

scenes.synopsis: the mornings — Laurent's; the unmasked's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The estate office, and Laurent is frowning at the home farm account book the way other men frown at battle maps — which, Rose reflects, is exactly what it is to him. A field of engagement. The enemy: English weights and measures.*
> *"Explain to me again," he says, without looking up, "the stone."*
> *"Fourteen pounds."*
> *"Fourteen pounds is a stone. Sixteen ounces is a pound. Eight stone is —" he counts on his fingers, in French, then catches himself — "a hundredweight, which is not a hundred of anything." He looks up, betrayed. "Your country measures things the way your aunt plays piquet. By private agreement."*
> *"The bushel?"*
> *"The bushel I have mastered. The bushel is honest. It is the hundredweight that is French in its deception." He returns to the book, brow furrowed, actually reading — not managing the reading, the way the mask used to manage everything, but doing it: the direct brow, the unperformed attention.*
> *(Rose, bringing the household book out of habit, watches him work through the column — the seed, the feed, the labor, all in stones and bushels and hundredweights — and understands what the morning actually contains. Not a lesson in arithmetic. A man, inhabiting the ground he chose, down to its absurd measurements. The mask would have had a steward for this. The face does it himself, badly at first, then all at once well.*
> *"The lower field," Laurent announces, triumphant, "requires —" he checks the figure twice — "requires drainage, and I can prove it in hundredweights." He sits back. "In Paris, I survived beautifully. In England, I do sums. It is less elegant." His look doesn't waver. "It is more true. I have decided to prefer it."*
> *"The drains?"*
> *"The drains are insufficient, and I can now prove it in two systems of measurement." He closes the book with satisfaction. "This is what choosing England means, Rose. Not the terrace. The hundredweight."*
> *(She laughs — and the estate office holds the sound, dust and sealing wax and all — and thinks about the small surrenders, one after another, that the unmasking was made of. The polish. The management. The beautiful survival. And now the hundredweight, surrendered to. The choosing, practiced daily, in stones and bushels.*
> *(At nine the papers are set aside, and the morning goes on around them both — the house, the Park, the absurd honest measures — and Rose writes nothing in the margin, because some mornings are the margin.*

scenes.synopsis: the mask — the removed; the years', the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Augusta finds it in the library — the library drawer, the one that sticks in damp weather — and brings it to the morning room at tea-time with the air of a woman producing evidence: a domino mask, black silk, the elastic gone slack with years. The masquerade's. His.*
> *"It was in with the estate papers," Augusta says. "Filed. Your Frenchman files his masks with the drainage reports. I thought you should see it before I burned it."*
> *(Rose takes it. The silk is soft, the shape still holding the curve of a face. She remembers the night — the last great masquerade, the old world given one more night — and the moment in it: the mask, taken off, for good. Not lifted for the evening. Removed. The choice, made freely, this time by both, with everyone watching.*
> *"Don't burn it," she says. "Not yet. Let him see it first."*
> *"Sentiment," Augusta says, "is the enemy of bonfires. But very well." She pours the tea. "The mask kept a ruined family elegant through the worst of it, child. It kept your Frenchman safe — or safe-looking — for years. It deserves better than my grate. It deserves —" the dry pause — "a ceremony."*
> *(That is how it is decided: the mask will be burned, but properly — in the kitchen garden, at dusk, with the household as witnesses. Augusta, who never does anything by halves, sends Hodges for the brazier. Letitia, hearing of it, declares it "the first sensible bonfire of the Season" and offers to bring the negus. The servants' hall is informed. The mask, filed for years with the drainage reports, is about to be retired with honors.*
> *(Rose carries it upstairs, and lays it on the desk beside the household book, and looks at it a long time — the silk, the slack elastic, the curve of the face it used to keep. The mask was never a lie, Laurent will tell her later. It was a postponement. Beautifully managed. She turns it over in her hands, and understands the scale of what he laid down. Not a habit. A heritage — the de Varenne survival, administered daily, in French.*
> *"Tonight," she tells it, "you retire." The mask says nothing, having said everything it had to say years ago. She sets it by the book, and goes down to tell Laurent that Augusta has planned his mask a funeral, and finds she is smiling — because only this house would give a retirement ceremony to a piece of silk, and only this man would deserve it.)*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent, the mask's — the Englishman, the removed; the truth, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The kitchen garden at dusk, and the brazier is lit — Augusta presiding with the gravity of a woman conducting a state funeral, Letitia with the negus, Hodges with the household assembled at a respectful distance, and Laurent holding the domino mask in both hands like a man holding a sleeping animal.*
> *"Say something," Augusta instructs. "One doesn't burn a career without remarks."*
> *(Laurent looks at the mask — the black silk, the slack elastic — and his look is there, unmasked, in the firelight.*
> *"It was never a lie," he says. "I want that kept. It was a postponement. The French instinct: survive beautifully, fight later. My family survived the ruin that way — the speculation took everything, and we survived it beautifully. It was magnificent. It was also exhausting." He looks at Rose. "The mask was for the things too dangerous for faces. There were more of them than you'd think. A ruined name. A family's expectations. Paris."*
> *(The garden holds its breath. The brazier ticks.*
> *"And the removal?" Augusta asks — dry, precise, entitled to ask. "The unmasking — what was it, if the mask wasn't a lie?"*
> *"Permission." His look does not waver. "She gave me permission, in English, to stop postponing. The masquerade — the mask off for good. England, chosen. The choosing, freely made, by both." A pause. "The face was always there. It merely lacked the English to express itself."*
> *(He lays the mask on the brazier. The silk catches — quickly, beautifully, the way it did everything — and the household watches it go, and Letitia, of all people, wipes her eyes and claims it is the smoke.*
> *"To the postponed," Augusta says, raising her negus, "arrived at last." They drink. The elastic curls in the heat. And Rose understands that the removed's truth is not dramatic. It is arithmetic, of a kind: years, postponed; now, kept. The mask, retired with honors. The face, resident.)*
> *(Afterward, walking back through the dark garden, Laurent takes her hand — the unperformed gesture — and says, very quietly: "It is less beautiful than the survival. It is more true. I have decided to prefer it." The brazier cools behind them. The ceremony is over. The retirement, unlike the postponement, is permanent.*

scenes.synopsis: the evenings — Laurent's; the unmasked's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *"The drains," Laurent intones, one hand raised like a man addressing the National Assembly, "are insufficient."*
> *(The drawing room after dinner. The rain doing its soft persistent work on the glass. Laurent with the steward's report, feet up, reading the lower field's drainage in the accents of French tragedy — which makes Augusta's needle pause, which makes Rose choke on her tea, which makes Letitia applaud from the card table.*
> *"Laurent," Augusta says, without looking up, "if you do the drains again I shall retire."*
> *"You love the drains. They are the highlight of your evening." He finds the page. "The culvert —" a significant pause — "the culvert is the tragedian's great soliloquy. 'O culvert, culvert —'"*
> *"No," says the whole room, variously.*
> *"'O culvert,'" Laurent continues, undeterred, "'thou obstructed artery of the lower field —'"*
> *(Rose watches him — the direct eyes bright over the papers, the absolute delight in the performance — and thinks about what the evening actually contains. Nothing that would fill a paragraph of the Gazette. A report, a tragedian, the drains. And yet the evening sits in her like a good meal. This is the unmasking, she understands: the charm transfigured. The man who survived beautifully now performs the drainage report with the same total commitment and twice the truth.*
> *"Read the bit about the sluice," Letitia calls. "The sluice is my favorite."*
> *"The sluice," Laurent agrees, "is underappreciated." He clears his throat. "'O sluice —'"*
> *(Augusta retires — not really, she only threatens it — and the evening goes on: the rain, the fire, the tragedian's voice doing culverts beautifully. Later Rose will try to describe it and fail, because there is nothing to describe. It was the kind of evening the house had been building toward without knowing it.*
> *(Upstairs, much later, she listens to the house settle — the particular quiet of an evening that asked nothing and gave everything — and laughs, quietly, into the dark. The mask would have been magnificent tonight. The face was better. The tragedian does culverts beautifully, and means it. The house, she thinks, has never once been better entertained in all its years.*

scenes.synopsis: England — the chosen; the years', the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Beating the bounds — the old English custom, the parish walking its boundaries once a year so nobody forgets where the ground ends — and this year the steward has invited the Comte, because the Comte asked. Laurent, at the churchyard gate with a willow wand like everyone else, looks entirely serious about the whole affair.*
> *"Explain to me again," he says to Rose, falling into step, "why we are hitting the boundary stones."*
> *"So the parish remembers them. The boys get bumped on the stones, traditionally, so they remember."*
> *"And the adults?"*
> *"The adults get luncheon."*
> *(He considers this fair. They walk — the whole parish strung out along the hedgerows, the boys already jostling for position at the first stone — and Laurent watches it all with the attention he once gave to Paris salons: the steward calling the marks, the old men arguing about a ditch, the willow wands tapping the stones.*
> *(At the third stone — the one by the lower field, the insufficiently drained one — the steward turns to him. "Your land now, in a manner of speaking, Comte. You do the honors." And Laurent steps forward, and taps the stone with his willow wand, and the boys cheer, and someone bumps young Pike's boy on it for tradition, and Laurent laughs — the unmasked laugh, entirely his.*
> *"The ground," he says to Rose, walking on, "has edges. In Paris, the ground was —" he searches — "negotiable. Here it is marked. With stones. That one can hit." He holds her gaze. "I have chosen a country that hits its boundaries with sticks so as not to forget them. It is absurd."*
> *"It is England."*
> *"It is England," he agrees, "and I am beating its bounds with a willow wand, and I have never been more serious about anything." He taps the next stone with particular ceremony. "This one is mine. I have decided."*
> *(They walk the whole parish — the stones, the ditches, the luncheon — and Rose watches him learn the ground the way other men learn a language: stone by stone, with ceremony. What England asks of him, daily: the directness. The drains. The English words for trees. What England gives him: the ground, the rain, the woman who corrects his pronunciation. It seems, suddenly, like the fairest trade anyone ever made.*
> *(At the last stone he stops, and looks back over the walked parish — and does something the masked man never did: nothing. Just the look, direct, taking it in. "It is absurd," he says, "how English it is." "It is England," Rose says. "Absurdity is included."*

scenes.synopsis: the years — Laurent's; the unmasked's, the turned. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The tailor has come up from the town — the morning room turned fitting-room, the light good, the mirror brought in — and Laurent is standing on the little dais in his shirtsleeves while the old French coats are held up one by one for judgment. Ten years of Paris tailoring. Beautiful. Managed. Doomed.*
> *"This one," the tailor says, holding up a coat of claret superfine, "can be altered. The shoulders, taken in. The skirts, shortened. It will be —" he considers — "English. Eventually."*
> *"And this one?" Laurent indicates a bottle-green masterpiece with too many buttons.*
> *"This one," the tailor says, "is French. It will always be French. I cannot unmake Paris." He lays it aside with respect. "For evenings. For memory."*
> *(Rose, from the window seat with the household book unopened on her lap, watches the years turn in cloth. Each coat, held up: the beautiful survival, examined. Some can be altered — taken in, shortened, made English eventually. Some cannot be unmade. The tailor, without knowing it, is conducting the unmasking's final audit.*
> *"The claret," Laurent decides. "Alter the claret. The green stays as it is." He looks at Rose in the mirror. "The face, English. The coat, on evenings, French. That is the settlement. The mask retired; the wardrobe, bilingual."*
> *(The tailor chalks, pins, mutters in the particular dialect of his trade. Augusta, passing the door, stops — watches a moment — and says, dry as dust: "The green was always too many buttons. Even Paris thought so." She goes on. Laurent, on the dais, meets Rose's eyes in the mirror, and she has to look at the ceiling to keep her composure.*
> *"The years," he says, as the tailor pins the claret's shoulder, "turn in cloth before they turn in men. I have been the performance for years. Now I am the practice." He considers the pinned shoulder. "It worried me, once — the unmasking. It no longer worries me. The truth is kept. The face speaks English. That is the requirement, and it is enough."*
> *(The fitting goes on — the chalk, the pins, the bilingual wardrobe — and Rose understands that the turning of the years is not a diminishment. It is a promotion. The masked, become something rarer: the man the truth was for. She writes nothing in the margin. The tailor's chalk is keeping the record.*
> *("English, eventually," the tailor says, standing back from the claret. Laurent looks at himself in the mirror — the pinned shoulder, his steady look — and nods. Eventually is the English word he has learned best. It suits him.*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — THE UNMASKED'S LESSON (what the unmasked teaches: the truth, the choosing, or the returning). The years deepen; decide the lesson. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The home farm, mid-morning — a fence down where the yearlings got ambitious in the night, the rails scattered like dropped stitches — and Laurent is already there, in his shirtsleeves, examining the damage with the steward. He looks up when Rose comes down the field, and does not manage his expression. He lets her see the satisfaction.*
> *"The fence," he announces, "is insufficient. Like the drains. I am becoming a connoisseur of English insufficiency."*
> *"The yearlings did it."*
> *"The yearlings are opportunists." He takes a rail. "We mend it. You and I. The steward supervises, which means he watches and criticizes. It is the natural order."*
> *(They mend it — the rails, the posts, the nails held in the mouth in the approved fashion — and somewhere between the third rail and the fourth, with the steward's criticisms going on like weather, the question surfaces. Not the events — the events are recorded: the masquerade, the refusal, the money offered, the choosing — but the meaning. What the unmasked teaches. The thing the years will keep.*
> *(Rose turns it over between rails: the truth — Laurent's, the direct: the face, unmasked, saying the insufficient thing aloud. The choosing — England's, the chosen: the ground, the Park, the rain, freely chosen by both, no staging, no management. The returning — the years', the yearly: the practice, daily, the mask staying off not as an event but as a habitation.*
> *"The lesson," Rose says at last, sitting back on her heels. "The unmasked teaches. I am deciding what."*
> *(Laurent, across the fence line, is watching her do the arithmetic — the household book look, he calls it — and he waits, because the unmasked have learned that some sums must be done without management.*
> *"Take your time," he says. "The face is patient. It waited years to be enough. It can wait through a fence."*
> *(She laughs — and the field goes about its green work, and the question sits between them like another rail to be set: the truth, the choosing, the returning. The unmasked's lesson, to be decided — and the deciding, like the choosing, freely done.*
> *(The fence stands. Rose wipes her hands on her skirts, and understands that the lesson will be decided here, among the rails — directly, in the field, the way the English decide everything: while mending something.*
*★ KEY DECISION 1/3 — The unmasked's lesson:*
- **The truth** — *the direct, taught.* The lesson is truth — Laurent's, the direct. (Consequence: the lesson is the direct's — but directs are said, and the unmasked was the lived.)
- **The choosing** — *the chosen, taught.* The lesson is choosing — England's, the chosen. (Consequence: the lesson is the chosen's — but chosens are decided, and the unmasked was the years'.)
- **The returning** — *the yearly, taught.* The lesson is returning — the years, the yearly. (Consequence: the lesson is the yearly's — but yearly's are time's, and the unmasked was the now.)
> *(The lesson, decided — and the deciding, like the choosing, freely done. The fence stands: the rails set, the nails driven, the yearlings thwarted. The years will keep the lesson. The face will practice it — daily, direct, still learning, still arriving.*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent, the lesson's — the Englishman, the taught; the direct, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The fence stands — the rails set, the nails driven — and the steward, having criticized everything, departs satisfied, which is his version of praise. Laurent and Rose stay: the field, the yearlings at a sulky distance, the midday sun doing its steady work.*
> *"The lesson," Laurent says, sitting on the top rail — a thing the masked man would never have done, splinters be damned. "The unmasked teaches, Rose. That is the arrangement. The question is only what."*
> *(She looks at him — his steady attention — and understands that he is not asking for the answer. He is asking for the teaching. The lesson, once chosen, must be spoken. That is the English way.*
> *"The truth," she says, "is the direct's. The choosing is the chosen's. The returning is the yearly's." She turns it over. "But the teaching — the teaching is yours, Laurent. What does the unmasked teach?"*
> *(He considers. The sun does its plain work. Below, the Park goes about its own affairs.*
> *"The unmasked teaches," he says slowly, in the English he has been practicing, "that the face had been there all along. The mask was not a lie. It was —" he finds it — "a postponement. The French instinct: survive beautifully, fight later. Very elegant. Very tiring." He doesn't look away. "The lesson is not that the mask was false. The lesson is that the face was always enough. The fence. The rails. The English." A pause. "You."*
> *(Rose takes his hand — splinters and all — and they sit on the top rail while the sun does its level work, and the lesson, decided, settles between them like the field below: green, English, kept.*
> *"The lesson's taught," Rose says.*
> *"The lesson's kept," Laurent corrects, gently. "That is the teaching."*
> *(They sit a while longer, and the yearlings edge closer, and his lesson — truth, choosing, returning, all three — holds the field the way the fence holds it: plainly, and without announcement.*
> *(They sit until the steward's boy comes with the news that the yearlings are planning something near the lower field, and Laurent rises with the air of a man called to a second front. "The teaching," he says, "continues." They walk down together, and Rose understands that the lesson's telling is in the speaking, not the choosing — aloud, in a field, on a fence rail. The face was always enough. It merely wanted saying.*

scenes.synopsis: the walks — Laurent's; the unmasked's, the walked. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Laurent has taken to riding out alone in the mornings — not the Park's showy circuit, but the farm tracks, the long way round by the lower field — and this morning Rose goes with him, on the cob, with the mist still in the hollows.*
> *(He rides like a Frenchman, which is to say beautifully and with opinions. The cob plods. The mist burns off. And Laurent, from the saddle, conducts his English lesson at the landscape.*
> *"Oak," he says, pointing. "Ash." A pause. "Lime."*
> *"The tree is a lime," Rose confirms. "You have it now."*
> *"I had it approximately on Tuesday. Today I have it precisely." He walks the horse on, satisfied. "The English words for trees. It is the first thing I have learned since the mask, and I intend to master it."*
> *(A pheasant explodes out of the hedge. The cob doesn't turn a hair. Laurent's horse shies sideways, and Laurent sits it the way he does everything now: directly, without performance, and with a certain amusement at himself.*
> *"You know what I noticed?" Rose says, falling in alongside.*
> *"That my 'lime' was excellent?"*
> *"That your 'lime' was excellent," she concedes, "and that you haven't managed a single person in days."*
> *(Laurent considers. "It is Thursday. That is two full days without management." His look, bright. "A personal best. The mask would be appalled. The face is" — he searches — "developing." They ride on, and the farm track holds them, and the walks — Laurent's, the ridden — keep their own hours, exactly.*
> *(At the track's far turn he stops, and looks back at the house — the Park, the terraces, the whole chosen ground — and does something the masked man never did: nothing. No assessment. Just the look, direct, taking it in.*
> *"It is absurd," he says, "how English it is."*
> *"It is England," Rose says. "Absurdity is included."*
> *(They ride back as the mist finishes burning off, and the "lime" — precisely had, at last — sits in Laurent's English like a small, perfect stone. At the stable yard he dismounts, and hands the reins to the boy, and thanks the horse — in English — which the horse accepts with the indifference of the truly English.*

scenes.synopsis: the Assembly — Laurent's; the convened, the Englishman's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The carriage to the Assembly, and Laurent is nervous — actually nervous, the unmasked kind, which is worse than the masked kind because there is nowhere to hide it. He keeps adjusting his cuffs. Augusta, opposite, watches with the needle-sharp attention she gives everything.*
> *"You will waltz," Augusta says. It is not a question.*
> *"I will waltz," Laurent agrees. "I am practicing England. The waltz is" — he searches — "the examination."*
> *"You waltzed in Paris."*
> *"In Paris, I performed. Here, I —" his look steady — "here, I attend. It is different. The ton will be watching."*
> *"The ton is always watching," Rose says. "That's its hobby."*
> *(Augusta reaches into her reticule and produces a favor — a knot of ribbon, the Park's colors — and pins it to his coat with the gravity of a woman decorating a soldier.*
> *"There," she says. "Now you are marked as ours. Waltz adequately."*
> *(The Assembly: the music, the county, the watching. And Laurent — catching Rose's eye across the room, his look finding hers and holding — crosses to her through the crowd without charm, without management, without the beautiful survival. Just the walk, and the face, and the favor in the Park's colors.*
> *"Dance with me," he says, in English.*
> *"It's a waltz."*
> *"I know. I am practicing England." He offers the hand — ink on the fingers, from the drains — and they take the floor, and the Assembly watches the unmasked Comte waltz his Englishwoman, and the watching, for once, is kind.*
> *(What the Assembly sees: the Comte de Varenne, thirty-one, French to the bone, standing unmasked among the English county and not flinching. The ton had watched the refusal — Cecilia's weapon, set down in public, in English, direct — and the ton, being the ton, had absorbed it: as information, then as gossip, then as fact. The fact, now, is Laurent. Unmasked. Chosen. Choosing.*
> *(Later, in the carriage home, Laurent is quiet — the good quiet, the unmasked kind. "The Assembly," he says at last. "It was" — he finds it — "adequate." Rose laughs until the carriage turns into the drive. In her buttonhole, Augusta's favor — no, his favor — no. She stops trying to sort it. The favor did its work.*
> *(What Rose carries home, besides the waltz: the ton's watching, and the watching was kind. Not the old watching — the assessment, the beautiful survival appraised — but something new. It occurs to her, in the carriage, that England has been practicing too.*

scenes.synopsis: the toasts — Laurent's; the unmasked's, the raised. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The seating for the toasts is a crisis — or what passes for one in this house, which means Augusta has rearranged the cards three times and Hodges is pretending not to have opinions. The question: where does the unmasked Comte sit, now that he is not performing? At the head? At Rose's right? The old placement assumed the mask. The new placement must assume the face.*
> *"He sits where he sits," Augusta decrees at last, putting the card down with finality. "At Rose's right. The face, not the performance, is the guest of honor."*
> *(The dining room. The long table. The candles. And the house has decided, without deciding, that the Englishman shall do the honors this year. Laurent, at Rose's right, glass raised, his look going round the table like a man taking inventory of everything he has chosen.*
> *"To the house," Laurent says, in English. "To the Park, the drains, the insufficient lower field." The table laughs — the drains are famous now, the tragedian's drains. "To Augusta, who taught me that a needle can be an argument. To Rose —" his look finds her — "who taught me that the truth, said directly, is the only beautiful survival." He raises the glass higher. "To the unmasked. May they stay off."*
> *(They drink. And Rose — watching him, the direct eyes bright, the accent wrapping itself around English words — understands that the toasts are not toasts. They are a ledger. Everything named, everything kept.*
> *"And to Laurent," Augusta says, rising — which she never does — glass high, voice dry as dust. "Who learned, at thirty-one, to say the thing. Better late, Frenchman, than beautifully never."*
> *(The table drinks to Laurent. Laurent drinks to the table. The toasts go round, and the dining room holds the whole unmasked company — and much later, the candles burned low, Rose finds Laurent at the window with the last of the wine, looking out at the dark parkland.*
> *"The toasts," he says. "They were" — he searches — "true." She takes his hand. True: it is the highest praise the Englishman has. He uses it sparingly, and means it entirely.*
> *(In the morning the glasses will be washed, the candles replaced, the dining room restored to order. But the seating card — "the face, not the performance, is the guest of honor" — stays in Rose's pocket, because some crises deserve keeping.*
> *(Augusta finds her in the hall and says, dry as dust: "He'll do, your Frenchman." It is, from Augusta, a benediction. Rose carries it upstairs like a toast in itself.*

scenes.synopsis: the night — Laurent's; the unmasked's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The terrace at night, and the stars are out in the particular profusion they manage when the air is cold and the county has gone to bed. Laurent is at the balustrade, coat collar up, doing something Rose has never seen him do: nothing, on purpose, in the dark.*
> *"Come and look," he says, without turning. "The sky is being philosophical, and I require a witness."*
> *(She comes. The sky does its cold work. And Rose — watching him, the direct profile against the stars, the thirty-one years sitting easy — understands that the night is the unmasking's proof. The masked man performed his evenings. The unmasked man simply has them. No audience. No management. Just the dark, and the witness.*
> *"Name them," Rose says. "In English."*
> *"The Plough," he says, pointing. "The —" he searches — "the one like a W."*
> *"Cassiopeia."*
> *"Cassiopeia," he repeats, carefully. "The English sky is better stocked than the French. More —" he finds it — "more furniture."*
> *(She laughs — and the terrace holds the sound, stone and dark and stars — and he goes on, naming them: the Plough, Cassiopeia, the North Star, which he gets right first time and is insufferably pleased about. The accent wraps itself around the constellations. The mask would have known them all in French and named none. The face names them in English, badly, and means it.*
> *"The years," Laurent says at last. "I have been counting them."*
> *"Don't."*
> *"Thirty-one." His look, banked for night. "And the count has changed. Not managed, now. Kept. The years, kept. The face, kept. The truth, kept." He takes her hand. "It is a better arithmetic."*
> *(The stars go on with their cold work. And Rose thinks about the Englishman's rest — his, the kept — and understands that the night is a practice, not an ending. The mask needed the light. The face keeps the night.*
> *"Sleep," Laurent says, offering the hand. "The drains will be insufficient in the morning, and they will require our direct attention."*
> *"The drains are always insufficient."*
> *"It is their charm." He kisses her forehead — his kiss, direct, unperformed. "Come. The night is kept. The morning will be English."*
> *(They go in together, and the house settles around them — the particular quiet of a day that has done its work — and the constellations, English-named and half-right, keep their own counsel overhead.*

scenes.synopsis: the later years — Laurent's; the unmasked's, the deepened. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning room, and Rose finds the evidence not in anything Laurent says but in the household book's margin — his hand, where he has taken to adding notes to her accounts. The English of it, three months ago: careful, cramped, every letter formed like a small apology. The English of it now: looser, faster, the ink confident.*
> *"You are inventorying my handwriting," Laurent says, catching her at it. He does not mind. The unmasked do not mind being studied; they merely require the studying to be direct.*
> *"The household book never closes."*
> *"Then record this." He comes to look over her shoulder — the direct look, warm. "The deepening is not dramatic. There is no second masquerade. There is only" — he counts on his fingers — "the terrace, the papers, his look, the chocolate. Repeated until they are not practice." He looks at her. "Until they are simply the man."*
> *(She writes it that evening in the margin, in her own hand, under his: "The deepening: practice, until it is the man." Two hands, one margin. She blots it.*
> *"And the man?" she asks, over the book.*
> *"The man is thirty-one, unmasked, and resident." His gaze is steady. "The later years, deepened. The Englishman, kept. The drains —" a pause — "the drains remain insufficient, but they are ours, and we say so. That is the deepening. Nothing managed. Everything kept."*
> *(What the deepening actually is, Rose understands, looking at the two hands in the margin: the unmasking, lived in. The mask off for good was the arrival. This — the daily English, the claimed drains, the practiced trees — is the residence. A man, inhabiting his face, in ink.*
> *(At noon the papers are set aside, and at noon Laurent comes to find her — not as the mask came to things, with an objective, but as the face comes: to be where she is. They take the terrace in the flat midday light, and the deepening goes on around them unremarked, the way weather goes on.*
> *"The later years," Rose says, "are quiet."*
> *"The later years are kept," Laurent corrects. "Quiet is incidental."*
> *(She writes that in the margin too, because precision matters: "Quiet, incidental. Kept, essential." The deepening, recorded in two hands. The house, surviving it directly — no beautiful management required.*

scenes.synopsis: Laurent, the later's — the Englishman, the deepened; the direct, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The library, and a decision has to be made: the French books. Three shelves of them — poetry, memoirs, the tragedians — that came with Laurent like luggage, and the question, never quite asked until today: do they stay?*
> *(Rose finds him before the shelves, a volume in each hand, doing the thing the unmasked do: not managing the moment. Considering it.*
> *"The French have a word," he says, "for the thing after the revolution —" He stops. Catches himself. His look, rueful. "No. No French words. That was the old instinct — to borrow the polish when the English fails. The English for it is: the settling. The keeping." He sets down both volumes. "We are in the keeping, Rose. The truth, kept. The face, kept. The years, kept."*
> *(She waits. The rain, outside, does its soft persistent work on the glass.*
> *"The later years are not the unmasking," he goes on. "The unmasking is done. The mask is retired — with honors, in the kitchen garden, as you know. The later years are the habitation. Living in the face. Speaking the English. Keeping the truth." He looks at the shelves. "The books stay. They are not the mask. They are the luggage. There is a difference, and I have finally learned it."*
> *"The tragedians stay?"*
> *"The tragedians stay. They do the drains beautifully." He reshelves Racine with ceremony. "It is less dramatic than the unmasking. It is more true."*
> *(Rose sets down the household book. And she understands, suddenly, what the deepening actually is: no new event — the old event, lived in. The mask off for good was the arrival. This — the shelves, the keeping, his look, daily — is the residence.*
> *"The face is improving," she says, for the dozenth time, because it remains true.*
> *"The face is thirty-one and resident." He takes her hand — ink on the fingers, from the reshelving. "The later years, deepened. The Englishman, kept. That is the whole of the report."*
> *(They leave the French books where they are — the luggage, not the mask — and the library holds its three shelves of poetry like a kept promise: the past, shelved; the face, resident; the keeping, daily.*

scenes.synopsis: the direct look — Laurent's; the truth's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The estate's spaniel has transferred its allegiance. This is the fact Rose keeps coming back to, because it is the only review that matters: the dog — a judicious animal, twelve years old, unimpressed by everyone — now follows Laurent from room to room, and obeys him.*
> *"Sit," Laurent says, in the hall. The spaniel sits.*
> *"In English," Rose says. "It obeys you in English."*
> *"I taught it 'sit' on Tuesday. It already knew 'sit.' It was merely waiting for someone to say it without management." His gaze is steady. "Dogs, Rose, are the great critics of the unmasking. They can smell postponement."*
> *(She laughs — and the hall holds the sound — and watches him with the dog: the hand, unperformed, on the grizzled head; the voice, direct, giving the simplest orders in English. The old Laurent charmed every room and was obeyed by no dog. This one is followed everywhere by a twelve-year-old spaniel, which is the higher honor.*
> *"The eyes," Laurent says, "were always the problem. The mask could manage the smile, the posture, the beautiful survival. The eyes kept telling. You taught me that the telling was allowed." He scratches the spaniel's ears. "The dog taught me that the telling was believed. That is the whole of your pedagogy, Rose. Permission. The dog concurs."*
> *(Rose looks back — his look, answering hers — and the hall, the dog, the afternoon, all of it sits in her like a good meal. Laurent's look: it tells. It has always told. Now it is allowed, and now it is believed — by the household, by the county, by a spaniel.*

> *(The letter from Paris arrives on a Tuesday — thick, sealed, the family crest — and Laurent reads it in the morning room with Rose beside him, his look doing its steady work across the page.*

> *(Rose takes his hand — the ink on the fingers, the unmasked's signature — and they walk on, and the evening does its evening work on the hedgerows.*

> *(They walk the whole circuit, and the Park holds them — the green, the kept, the chosen — and Rose understands that the walk is the engine's answer, made in feet. What Hartwell Park is for: the keeping. What the power is for: the keeping. What the years are for: the practice.*
> *"The keeping," Rose says, "is the work."*
> *"The keeping is the work," Laurent agrees. "The choosing was the arrival. The keeping is the residence." His look holds. "I am resident. It is" — he finds it — "sufficient."*
> *(At the lower field they stop — the drains, the insufficient drains — and Laurent surveys them with the proprietorial air of a man who has proved their insufficiency in two systems of measurement. "The drains," he says, "are ours." She laughs. The evening holds the sound.*
> *(They walk back as the light goes, and the Park — the kept, the chosen — keeps its green counsel around them, and the engine's question, answered in feet, holds: the Park is for the keeping. The truth is for the saying. The years are for the practice.*
> *(At the terrace steps he stops, and looks back over the walked ground — the whole kept expanse — and does something the masked man never did: nothing. No assessment. Just the look, direct, taking it in. "It is absurd," he says, "how English it is." "It is England," Rose says. "Absurdity is included."*

scenes.synopsis: the charter, the kept — Laurent's, the legacy's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The future is discussed the way the English discuss everything important: sideways, over something else. In this case, over the household book — the accounts, the margins, the year's sums — with the rain doing its soft persistent work on the glass.*
> *"The years," Rose says, "are deepening. The face is resident. The keeping is the work." She looks up. "What is the future, Laurent?"*
> *(He considers — his steady attention — and the morning room holds its quiet.*
> *"The future," he says slowly, "is the practice, continued. The terrace at dawn. The papers at nine. His look at breakfast. The English, practiced. The truth, said. The keeping, kept." He takes her hand. "It is not dramatic. The unmasking was the drama. The future is the" — he finds it — "the habitation."*
> *(Rose writes it in the margin: "The future: the habitation." She looks at the line, and adds: "The practice, continued." She blots it.*
> *"The brilliant match," Laurent says, "is refused. Paris is set aside. The ruin is acknowledged, and set between us, not hidden." His look does not waver. "The future is England. The future is the Park. The future is" — the rarest thing, certainty — "us. Kept."*
> *(The rain goes on. The book holds the future — the margin, the habitation — and Rose understands that the future is a practice, not a destination. The years, deepened. The face, resident. The keeping, continued.*
> *"The future," she says, "is sufficient."*
> *"The future is kept," Laurent corrects, gently. "That is the grammar."*
> *(They sit with the book between them — the accounts, the margins, the kept future — and the morning room holds the whole of it: the practice, continued; the habitation, kept; the years, pointed at the kept. The future, discussed sideways, decided directly.*
> *(At noon the book closes, and the future — the habitation, the practice continued — goes on around them unremarked, the way weather goes on. The future is kept. That is the grammar, and it is enough. Outside the rain has stopped, and the Park is doing its green work in the sudden light, and the future looks, Rose thinks, exactly like the present — only more so.*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — THE TRUTH'S MEANING (what the truth means: the keeping, the Englishman, or the future). The years deepen; decide the meaning. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The household book, late — the candle low, the house quiet — and Rose turns to the last clean margin with the pencil, and does the final reckoning. Not the events — the events are recorded: the masquerade, the refusal, the money offered, the choosing. The meaning. What the truth means.*
> *(She turns it over in the candlelight: the keeping — his, the kept: the truth means keeping — the mask retired, the practice daily, the years held. The Englishman — Laurent's, the direct: the truth means the Englishman — the face, unmasked, his look, the English practiced. The future — the years', the returning: the truth means the future — the habitation, the practice continued, the keeping kept.*
> *(Laurent, across the desk — he has come to find her, the way the face comes: to be where she is — watches her do the arithmetic, and waits. The unmasked do not manage the deciding. They witness it, directly.*
> *"The truth's meaning," Rose says at last. "I am deciding it."*
> *(The candle does its low work. The house holds its breath.*
> *"The truth," Laurent says quietly, "means the keeping. It means the Englishman. It means the future." His look, banked for night. "It means all three, Rose. That is the meaning. The truth, kept, by the Englishman, for the future." He takes her hand. "But the deciding is yours. The meaning, decided — and the deciding, like the truth, direct."*
> *(She looks at him — his look, answering — and the candle does its low work, and the meaning waits: the keeping, the Englishman, the future. The truth's meaning, to be decided — and the deciding, like the truth, direct.*
> *(The pencil hovers. The margin waits. And Rose understands that the meaning is not a decoration. It is a direction — the truth, pointed. The keeping, the Englishman, or the future: the truth's meaning, shaped by her hand. The candle burns lower. The deciding comes.*
*★ KEY DECISION 3/3 — The truth's meaning:*
- **The keeping** — *the kept, meant.* The truth means keeping — the unmasked's, the kept. (Consequence: the meaning is the kept's — but kepts are held, and the truth was the given.)
- **The Englishman** — *the direct, meant.* The truth means the Englishman — Laurent's, the direct. (Consequence: the meaning is the direct's — but directs are said, and the truth was the lived.)
- **The future** — *the returning, meant.* The truth means the future — the years, the returning. (Consequence: the meaning is the returning's — but returnings are future, and the truth was the now.)
> *(The meaning, decided — and the deciding, like the truth, direct. The candle does its low work on the margin. The truth receives its meaning the way the Park receives the dusk: completely, without announcement. The truth's meaning, hers. The memory, shaped. Meant, kept — that is the meaning done.*

scenes.synopsis: the meaning, the kept — the truth's, the lesson's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The meaning, once decided, must be given — not recorded, given. Rose finds Laurent in the morning room at dawn — the mist, the blackbird, the first light — and does the thing the English do with true things: says it directly, without management.*
> *(If the keeping was meant — his, the kept — then the meaning is the keeping: the truth means keeping — the mask retired, the practice daily, the years held. She says it: "The truth means the keeping." And Laurent — his look, receiving — nods. "The keeping," he agrees. "It is the grammar."*
> *(If the Englishman was meant — Laurent's, the direct — then the meaning is the Englishman: the truth means the Englishman — the face, unmasked, his look, the English practiced. She says it: "The truth means the Englishman." And Laurent — moved, unmasked — takes her hand. "The Englishman," he agrees. "It is" — he searches — "sufficient."*
> *(If the future was meant — the years', the returning — then the meaning is the future: the truth means the future — the habitation, the practice continued, the keeping kept. She says it: "The truth means the future." And Laurent — his look, the kept man's — smiles. "The future," he agrees. "It is kept. That is the grammar."*
> *(Whichever was meant — the keeping, the Englishman, or the future — the meaning is given the same way: directly, at dawn, without management. Laurent receives it — direct, unperformed — and the morning room holds the whole of it: the meaning, given; the given, kept.*
> *(She writes it in the margin when he isn't looking — "The meaning, given" — because some sayings deserve keeping even when the receiver would disapprove of the recording.*
> *(The meaning is given. And the truth — Laurent's, the decided — receives its meaning the way the Park receives the morning: completely, without announcement.*
> *(They take the terrace afterward — the meaning decided, the giving done — and the dawn does its pale work on the drive, and Laurent walks beside her with the meant's new quiet: not the masked quiet, which was management, but the meant's, which is keeping.*
> *"The meant," he says, "is ours." He holds her gaze. "The truth, meant. The meaning, kept."*
> *(Rose writes that in the margin that evening: "The meant, theirs." The meaning's grammar, kept. The terrace, the dawn, the hand she holds — all of it, meant, given, kept.*

scenes.synopsis: the letters — the years, reported; London writes. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The letters arrive with the morning post — London writes, and writes, and writes — and Rose reads them at the desk with Laurent beside her, doing the thing the county does: absorbing, assessing, repeating.*
> *(The first is from a London friend, all news and all confidence: the refusal, reported back to them as history now — Cecilia's weapon, declined in public, in English, direct — and the unmasking, which London has decided to admire, the way London decides things: suddenly, and as if it had thought of it itself.*
> *(Laurent reads it over her shoulder — the unmasked laugh, the real one.*
> *"They have made it a fashion," he says. "The unmasking. In London."*
> *"They will tire of it by spring."*
> *"They will not tire of it," Laurent corrects. "They will absorb it. That is London's talent. It absorbs everything — the refusal, the choosing, the years — and calls it fact. The fact, now, is Laurent. Unmasked. Chosen. Choosing."*
> *(The second letter is longer — a cousin's friend, the kind who writes everything down — and it reports the year the way London reports everything: as a series of evenings. The masquerade, which she remembers differently. The Assembly, which she remembers exactly. The lesson, read in English, which London has decided was "beautifully done." The year, reported back to them, slightly rearranged, entirely recognizable.*
> *(Rose reads the London version aloud, and Laurent corrects it — "the drains were insufficient, not merely damp" — and they laugh, and the morning room holds the whole of it: the year, reported; the reporting, corrected; the truth, kept, in two hands.*
> *(The third letter is the one that matters — short, from a woman London listens to, and it says the thing plainly, the way the truth likes to be said: that the Comte de Varenne is unmasked, and that London has decided to believe it, and that the believing is the point. The years, reported. The meaning, kept.*
> *(Laurent takes up the pen — the English hand, still learning, still arriving — and they answer together, the way they do everything now: the French for the courtesy, the English for the truth. The replies go out with the post. London will read them and repeat them, or not. The choosing, freely made, by both, never needed London's agreement. That was always the point.*
> *(That evening the margin: "London writes. The year, reported." She blots it. The letters, answered. The years, kept.*

scenes.synopsis: the ton, the years' — the unmasked, awaited; the convened, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The Assembly, and the ton is watching — the county, the music, the whole apparatus — and Rose watches Laurent among them with the attention she once gave to money: noting where his look lands, what it buys. It buys the truth, kept. Every time.*
> *(The marking — the choice, the truth, or the keeping, whichever was chosen — goes public tonight. Not announced. Worn. The Englishman, marked, among the county: his look, easy grace, the marking worn like his look, like the coat that finally fits.*
> *(Mrs. Fane's girl, all grown boldness, asks him outright: "Comte, is it true you read the lesson? In English?" The room holds its breath. Laurent sets down his glass.*
> *"It is true," he says, in English, direct. "The genealogies, beautifully done. Your grandmother called it the real miracle." The room laughs — the relieved laugh of people who have been given permission to admire.*
> *(And Rose — watching him, the direct eyes bright, the accent wrapping itself around English words — understands that the aftermath is not an aftermath. It is a continuation. The meaning, decided; the marking, worn; the years, deepened.*
> *"The meaning," Augusta murmurs, at her elbow. "The truth's. It holds."*
> *"It holds," Rose agrees. "The keeping. The Englishman. The future. All three."*
> *(The Assembly goes on — the music, the watching, the waltz — and the ton does its witnessing: the watching, the absorbing, the fact. The fact, now, is Laurent. Marked. Kept. The wearing, well.*
> *(Later, in the carriage home, Laurent is quiet — the good quiet, the unmasked kind. "The Assembly," he says at last. "It was" — he finds it — "it will do." The carriage turns into the drive with them still laughing. The meaning holds. The marking holds. The years, deepened.*
> *(What Rose carries home, besides the waltz: the ton's watching, and the watching was kind. Not the old watching — the assessment, the beautiful survival appraised — but something new. It occurs to her, in the carriage, that England has been practicing too.*
> *(In the margin that night: "The Assembly. The meaning, held." She blots it twice and smiles. The aftermath, continued. The years, deepened. The truth, kept.*

scenes.synopsis: the woman, the unmasked's — Rose, the evening's; the kept, the truth's. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The terrace at night again — a different night, colder, the county asleep — and Laurent is at the balustrade, his look on the dark, and Rose comes to stand beside him, and the night is the meaning's proof.*
> *(The masked man performed his evenings. The unmasked man simply has them. No audience. No management. Just the dark, and the witness, and the meaning — the keeping, the Englishman, the future, all three — held.*
> *"The meaning," Laurent says, without turning. "The truth's. It is kept."*
> *(She takes his hand — the ink on the fingers, washed out by now, the unmasked's signature faded to the skin — and the stars do their cold work, and the terrace holds the whole of it: the meaning, kept; the kept, the Englishman, the future.*
> *"The Plough," Laurent says, pointing. "Cassiopeia. The North Star." The accent wraps itself around the constellations. "The English sky is better stocked than the French. More furniture."*
> *(She laughs — and the terrace holds the sound, stone and dark and stars — and he goes on, naming them, and the mask would have known them all in French and named none, and the face names them in English, badly, and means it.*
> *"The years," Laurent says at last. "The meaning. The keeping." His look, banked for night. "It is kept, Rose. All of it. The truth, meant. The meaning, kept. The years, deepened."*
> *"Sleep," Rose says, offering the hand. "The drains will be insufficient in the morning."*
> *"The drains are always insufficient." His eyes don't leave hers. "It is their charm." He kisses her forehead — his kiss. "Come. The night is kept, and the morning will be English."*
> *(They go in together, and the house settles around them — the particular quiet of a night that has been sufficient — and the constellations, English-named and half-right, keep their own counsel overhead. The stairs creak in the old place. The candles are out. The night is kept.*
> *(In the margin, by candlelight, the last line of the day: "The night, kept." She blots it. The meaning, held fast and certain and complete. The years, deepened. The truth, kept.*

scenes.synopsis: the legacy, the truth — Laurent's, the charter's; the forever. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The dawn walk — the last scene, the first light — and Rose goes alone to the terrace, and the Park is there: the mist, the oaks, the whole chosen ground. And then — footsteps, on the stone — and Laurent is there, in his shirtsleeves, his dawn look.*
> *"The Englishman," he says, "walks at dawn. It is the practice."*
> *(They walk the terrace's length — the mist, the blackbird, the first light — and the Park goes about its green work, and the years — Laurent's, the kept — do their deepening work around them, unremarked.*
> *"The lesson," Rose says. "The marking. The meaning."*
> *"The truth," Laurent says. "The choosing. The returning." He meets her eyes. "The keeping. The Englishman. The future." He takes her hand. "It is all three, Rose. The meaning does not narrow. It deepens."*
> *(They walk on — the terrace, the stone, their clasped hands — and the dawn does its pale work on the drive, and the unmasking — the mask off for good, England chosen, the choice freely made by both — holds as a habitation, not an event. The face, resident. The truth, kept. The years, deepened.*
> *"The Park," Laurent says, "is for the keeping."*
> *"The truth is for the saying."*
> *"The years are for the practice."*
> *(The three sentences — the engine's answer, the grammar — hold the dawn: the keeping, the saying, the practice. And Rose understands, finally, what the unmasked teaches: that the face was always sufficient. It merely lacked the English. Now it has the English. Now it is kept.*
> *(They walk the terrace's length again — the mist burning off, the blackbird, the first light strengthening — and the Park, the kept, the chosen, wakes around them: the tenants, the drains, the trees named in practicing English.*
> *"It is absurd," Laurent says, "how English it is."*
> *"It is England," Rose says. "Absurdity is included."*
> *(The dawn walk ends where it began — the terrace, the stone, the hand in hers — and the years, deepened, hold: the lesson, the marking, the meaning. The truth, kept. The Englishman, kept. The future, kept. The dawn does its pale work, and the Park receives the morning: completely, without announcement.*

scenes.synopsis: Bell's unmasked report — arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice:)*
> *"The Englishman, unmasked: what the design hid, the years revealed — and the Gazette finds the revelation satisfactory, which in this paper's experience is rarer than the unmasking. The charter's true choice was never the mask. It was the man underneath, once he stopped performing."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first, then the reckoning: the unmasking pronounced satisfactory in print, and Bell has made it permanent, which is Bell's way of making it forever. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the unmasked the Gazette prints is the unmasked the years proved — the man, not the mask.* — remembered: *the lesson: the unmasked the Gazette prints is the unmasked the years proved — the man, not the mask.*

scenes.synopsis: the free man's turning — Julian's, the turned; the terrace, the kept. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(Evening, and the Englishman stands unmasked — the man, not the mask, the years' proof of it — and Rose's thoughts turn to Julian.)*
> *(The terrace at dusk. The free life, coming: not the escape the Gazette spent ten seasons mistaking it for, but the staying. She has watched him learn the difference the slow way, the way everyone learns everything that matters.)*
> *(She goes down to the terrace, and the air is the evening's, and the free man's turning is the whole of the next chapter — and the chapter, she suspects, will be the keeping.)*
> *(The Season turns toward Julian. The terrace waits, and the Season — for once — says nothing.)*
