scenes.synopsis: the law — the legacy's; the Hartwell, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(In the estate office the second Assembly already has its own drawer — the acceptances a year early, the suggestions, the old countess's determined hand promising to come earlier and stay longer. Harrow has labeled the drawer in his exact hand. The future, filed.)*
> *(The law goes to work the way laws do: quietly, and everywhere, and without ever being spoken.)*
> *(In the household: the fires lit a fraction earlier, the shutters opened a fraction wider, the day's work taken up with a fraction more exactness. Harrow's ledgers balance straighter. Mrs. Quick's planning reaches further into the year. The maids' corners are sharper. Nobody has announced anything. The quiet ones shape everything.)*
> *(In the Park: the bailiff's rounds unhurried, the hedges' line true, the lake's clarity holding. In the post: the letters answered, the lists begun, the second Assembly's correspondence already a department with its own drawer. The law does not knock. It moves in.)*
> *(Rose feels it settle inside her like a compass needle finding north, and the years ahead arrange themselves around it without consulting her: the annual, the keeping, the practice. The choice was made at the lake's edge, in an instant, in the mist. The years will do the rest, and the rest will be the law, lived.)*
> *(The household feels it without knowing its name. That is the test of a law worth having — that it works in people who never heard it made. She watches Mrs. Quick measure the stillroom shelves for winter with a longer eye than last year, and says nothing, and the saying-nothing is the law, too.)*
> *(At noon she walks the Park with the law inside her, and the legacy — which has been approaching for ten seasons — points true north. The choice was made. The years will do the rest. She has done the choosing; the living is the easy part, and the hard part, and the whole of it.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Hartwell — the legacy's; the whole's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(In the attics the Assembly's borrowed finery is packed away — the extra chairs, the candelabra, the paper roses' wire frames saved for the village's next fete. The house's memory, in camphor and tissue. Hodges inventories it the way other men inventory silver.)*
> *(The house, a week after the Assembly, is itself again — and itself turns out to be the quiet, which ten seasons of labor bought.)*
> *(The state rooms stand in their ordinary order. The ballroom's floor is polished, the chandeliers bagged, the morning light doing what the candles did: filling the room, asking nothing. The dining room table is bare, the sideboards empty, the light lying on the wood like something put away carefully.)*
> *(The morning room: Letitia's desk, where the Assembly's lists are already becoming the second Assembly's — the social general cannot help herself, and has stopped apologizing for it. The library: the charter in the strongbox, the Gazette's run on the shelf. The west gallery: the Hartwell dead, watching, as they have watched everything, with the painted patience of people who have seen it all before and are prepared to see it again.)*
> *(The bedrooms: the guests' rooms aired and waiting — for next year, for the Assembly, for whoever the convening brings. The servants' quarters: the staff at the day's work, the talk of the Assembly still warm in the corridors. The house is the years' house, and the years' house is a household, not a monument.)*
> *(Rose walks the enfilade at midday, and the house receives her the way it receives everything: in order, without fuss. The ballroom, which held the Assembly, holds the morning now. The dining room, which held the supper, holds the light. The house does not commemorate. It continues.)*
> *(In the small drawing room she stops — the room where Augusta laid out the terms, where the marking was given — and lays her hand flat on the mantel for a moment, the way you touch a horse's neck to tell it the work is done. Monuments are visited. Households are lived in. She lives here.)*

scenes.synopsis: the house — the whole's; the Hartwell's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The slates were laid in the sixth season by a crew from the town, and the leadwork by a man who sang while he worked, and the maids complained they could hear him through the attics, and Mrs. Quick — who approved of the work and disapproved of the singing — compromised by having the attics aired at the hours he was on the far slope.)*
> *(The roof was re-laid in the sixth season — the slates true, the gutters clear before winter — and standing under it, Rose thinks that a roof is the most honest part of a house: it either holds or it doesn't, and this one holds.)*
> *(Under it, the household: the staff at the day's work, the kitchens at the day's bread, the servants' hall at the day's talk. The attics hold the Assembly's borrowed finery, packed away — the extra chairs, the candelabra, the paper roses' wire frames, saved for the village's next fete. The cellars hold the wine, accounted for to Harrow's particular satisfaction, the columns agreed.)*
> *(The shelter is not the slates, though the slates are true. The shelter is the order: everyone under the roof, everyone fed, everyone housed. The state rooms and the stillroom, the ballroom and the laundry, the guests and the staff — the house's roof holds them all, and the holding is the whole of the philosophy.)*
> *(Hodges is at the door as she comes down, presiding over the quiet with the gravity of a man who has seen the extraordinary and prefers the ordinary. "The house, miss," he says, "is itself." It is the butler's whole review of the week, and it is enough, and she tells him so.)*
> *("Quite itself, Hodges." "Quite, miss." He bows, and resumes being silent as weather, and she goes out to the terrace feeling that she has been given a benediction in four words, which is the butler's particular economy, and she would not trade it for a speech.)*
> *(Ten seasons ago the roof leaked and the house was a ruin. Now the roof holds, and the house holds. She stands on the terrace and looks up at the slates, true in their courses, and down at the Park, whole in its zones, and the simplest form of everything she has built is this: shelter, kept.)*

scenes.synopsis: the later years — the legacy's; the whole's, the deepened. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The post has tripled since the Assembly — the carrier brings it in a sack that was new at Christmas and is already shabby, and the estate office sorts it the way other houses sort laundry: the acceptances, the reconsiderations, the earl's bailiff instructed about the hedges. The future, arriving daily, in a shabby sack.)*
> *(The later years are already arriving, and they come by post.)*
> *(The old countess writes: "Next year we shall come earlier — the journey, at my age — and stay longer." The earl writes: "The hedges were much admired. My bailiff is instructed." The cautious ones write: "We have reconsidered." The former holdouts write: "We shall be honored — and earlier, if convenient." The later years, in their own hands, finishing their own sentences.)*
> *(Letitia has started the list — the social general at her happiest, a campaign with a year to plan it. The morning room's desk accumulates the future: acceptances a year early, suggestions, promises. "The second Assembly," she says over the chocolate, "will be — " and does not finish, because the possibilities are too many, and too delicious, and she is saving them.)*
> *(The village prepares a year ahead: the inn's best rooms held, the shops laying in stock, the carrier adding a cart. The Assembly's future is the village's future too, and the village knows it — the Park's own people, planning in ink.)*
> *(Harrow has opened a new ledger — the Assembly's own, separate from the household's — and the second year's columns wait, clean and expectant. Mrs. Quick is planning the kitchens a year ahead. The gardener's boy is propagating the Hartwell rose from cuttings. The household that carried the first Assembly on its back is already carrying the second, and the carrying is lighter this time, because the way is known.)*
> *(Rose reads the letters at the morning room desk, and the Hartwell's time stretches forward, administered: the dates, the lists, the ledgers. The future is not a dream. It is a department. Letitia said so a week ago, and Letitia — as usual, and as she will tell anyone who listens — was right.)*

scenes.synopsis: the proven — the legacy's; the kept, the shown. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(At the county's dinner tables the Assembly is the winter's standing dish — the ices described, the toasts repeated, the guest list recited like a litany. The neighboring houses have taken to timing their own evenings around Hartwell's date, the way towns time their fairs around the harvest. The evidence, traveling.)*
> *(The evidence is in, and it is all true, and it is all kept — which is the whole of what evidence is for.)*
> *(The charter: read aloud at the Assembly, drafted properly by Quill, witnessed by Augusta and Harrow and Letitia, sealed and kept in the strongbox. The Gazette: the Assembly reported, the verdict printed, the record made on the paper's own terms. The house: standing, whole, the Park working. Three evidences, and none of them argued — entered.)*
> *(The county's evidence: the neighboring houses talking — the Assembly, the verdict, the convening — over dinner tables for miles around. London's evidence: the clubs' arithmetic, the drawing rooms' verdict, the papers' notice. The proven travels, the way true things do, and arrives before you do.)*
> *(The ground's evidence: the hedges' line, the lake's clarity, the garden's order — the ten seasons written in earth and water, legible to anyone who walks it. The strongbox's order: the charter on top, the codicil beneath, the ledgers beside, filed by Harrow's exact hand. The paper, the book, the ground — witnesses, agreeing.)*
> *(Seven days since the Assembly, and the verdict has held — the arithmetic done aloud in every club, the invitation coveted in every drawing room. The shown, holding. The witnessed, standing.)*
> *(Rose files the last of the letters — the old countess's determined hand, a year early — and the filing is the point, she thinks, or near enough: the evidence kept, the keeping evidenced. The Assembly was the proof. The legacy is what the proof was for. She closes the drawer, and the drawer, being Hartwell's, closes exactly.)*

scenes.synopsis: the last word — the Gazette's; the woman's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The last word arrives on a Thursday, with the morning post — on top of the bundle, as it has been for ten seasons, as though the carrier knows.)*
> *(It is the final number of the Season: Bell's valedictory, the paper's last word on the ten years. Rose carries it to the morning room herself — the chocolate ordered, the window seat taken, the ritual observed — and opens it the way she has opened every Gazette for ten seasons: carefully, as though it might bite. The last word deserves its proper hour.)*
> *(The judgments, scored in Bell's arch precise hand: the ruin — survived, not prettified. The books — balanced, not cooked. The building — done in the open, not behind screens. The convening — earned, not bought. Bell scores each season and finds the accounts true. The verdict is not kind. It is just, and the just is the rarer thing, and the rarer thing is why the paper endures.)*
> *(She reads it twice — the amusement first, then the reckoning — and the paper does what the paper has always done: tells the truth slant, scores the game, refuses to flatter. Ten seasons of Rose Hartwell, and the woman in the paper is not quite her. She is the paper's her. Both are true, which is the familiar strangeness, and she knows the drill.)*
> *(Letitia reads over her shoulder, the social general reviewing the dispatches one last time. "The last word," she says. "On her terms, as always." "On her terms," Rose agrees, "which is why it's worth having." They stand at the window with the paper between them, and the Gazette's last word settles over the house like dust in sunlight.)*
> *(She folds the valedictory and lays it with the bound run in the library — the paper's memory, complete and consecutive. The last word is spoken. The woman continues. That is the whole of the arrangement, and it has worked for ten seasons, and she sees no reason it should stop working now.)*

scenes.synopsis: the woman — the changed's; the Season's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(Bell's pencil, Augusta says, has not lifted in ten seasons — the arrivals, the acknowledgment, the declaration, all of it scored in the proprietor's arch precise hand from the gallery's corner, where no one thought to look for a newspaperwoman. The watching, done properly, is invisible. The printing, done properly, is permanent.)*
> *(The paper describes her, and the description is Bell's: externals exact, internals slant, as papers do.)*
> *(Not the girl — the girl is gone, kept but gone. The woman: twenty-five, mistress of Hartwell Park, convener of the Assembly. Bell gets the shape true: the woman who kept the books and paid the debts and rebuilt the house in the open, where all could see. The figures are the argument — the debts paid, every creditor named; the building, the roof, the drainage, the garden's walls, costed to the penny; the Assembly, the guest list, the toasts, the ices, reported straight.)*
> *(Augusta takes the paper to the west gallery and reads it standing, among the Hartwell dead. "She has you," the dowager says at last, "to the life — the outside of it." The portrait, approved. The interior, as papers do, left blank — and the blank is honest, which is more than most portraits manage.)*
> *(Ten seasons of being Bell's subject: the arch phrasing, the precise scoring, the refusal to look away. She knows the drill the way she knows the morning room's light — the paper's her and the woman's her, both true, neither complete.)*
> *(What the paper got right: the books kept, the debts paid, the building done in the open. What the paper got slant: the motives, the meanings, the interior — papers do interiors badly, and Bell knows it, and does not try. The woman's record, in another's hand, on the paper's own terms.)*
> *(Rose folds the valedictory and stands a moment at the gallery's end, between the living house and the painted dead, and Augusta — still reading, spectacles at the exact angle of attention — does not look up, which is the dowager's way of saying the morning is satisfactory, and requires no further remark.)*

scenes.synopsis: the changed — the Season's; the kept, the proven. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The libel's number is the one the bound run opens to by itself — the paper's spine cracked there, the page thumbed thin by ten seasons of readers checking the exact wording. Bell keeps a framed copy in the office, the advertisers' fright and all. The peril, remembered. The survival, printed.)*
> *(Ten seasons, in ink — the Gazette watched them all, and the watching is the record.)*
> *(The libel, survived. The money, traced. The Network, closed. The house, rebuilt. The Assembly, convened. The paper scored it all and printed it all and refused to be bought by anyone, including the woman it favors — which is why the record counts. The record is not Rose's. It is Bell's.)*
> *(The paper's ten seasons had their own perils: the Gazette nearly folded in the fourth — the libel's costs, the advertisers' fright — and Bell kept it alive on stubbornness and subscriptions. The watching cost her, too. The record is Bell's the way the Park is Rose's: kept at a price, and the price is the proof.)*
> *(On the library's shelf the ten seasons stand in their row — the libel's number, the money's, the Assembly's — the paper's memory, complete and consecutive, shelved the way the Park holds the years: in order, under the Hartwell dead's gaze. The bundle tied. The ribbon on it.)*
> *(The Season changed because she did — the paper merely noticed, scored, and printed. The changed is not the paper's. The changed is the Season's. That is the whole of the philosophy, and it fits in a sentence, which is why Bell would approve of it, and would never say so.)*
> *(Rose ties the ribbon on the bound volume herself — the year's number, the last of the ten — and sets it in its place with the others. The record is complete. The paper's last word is spoken. And the changed, she understands, tying the knot, is not finished. It is only recorded. The woman continues past the recording, the way the Park continues past the map.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Season — the changed's; the whole's, the kept. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(One hostess's attempt at an annual evening foundered on the ices — hers arrived as soup, in March — and Letitia's report of it was so vivid that Rose laughed into her chocolate. "The convening," Letitia said, "is not the ices. Though the ices," she added fairly, "do not hurt.")*
> *(London is altered, and the alteration has settled into the ton's furniture — ten seasons ago the Season had no Hartwell evening, and now it has one, annual, and the having is the change.)*
> *(The drawing rooms do the arithmetic aloud, over morning calls and in the clubs: Hartwell convenes, the Assembly matters, the invitation is the one to have. The sums are done and done again, and they all come out the same. What is convened annually becomes custom; what becomes custom becomes London.)*
> *(The imitation has begun, which is the sincerest form of arithmetic: other hostesses attempting their own annual evenings now — the Assembly as the model, the convening as the fashion. London copies what it cannot resist. Letitia tracks the attempts the way a general tracks enemy movements, and reports them with relish, and is usually right about which ones will survive the winter.)*
> *(The cautious ones have learned, at last, that waiting is a choice with a cost. The change has its enthusiasts and its converts, which is how changes survive their first decade — not by being perfect, but by being repeated.)*
> *(She did not set out to change the Season. She set out to keep the house — the books balanced, the debts paid, the roof true, the Park working. The Season changed around the keeping the way the river changes around the stone: the water goes around, and the going-around becomes the course. She thinks of this standing at the lake, watching the water do exactly what it has always done, and finds the metaphor satisfactory, and tells no one.)*
> *(The next Season's anticipation: the invitations already coveted, the Assembly's date circled in every diary. The alteration holds. The holding is not dramatic. It is administrative — which, after ten seasons, she has learned is the more durable kind.)*

scenes.synopsis: the arc — the years'; the kept, the whole. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The office's morning light lies across the ten spines — the steward's exact hand, ten seasons lettered — and the row of them is the most honest portrait in the house. No painter could do what Harrow's columns do: show a woman's ten years, agreed to the penny.)*
> *(Harrow, asked for the years' names, declined — "The ledgers, miss, are the names" — and returned to his blotting. Rose named them herself, privately, in the order they came: the ruin, the money, the libel, the confrontation, the price, the fortune, the sins, the reckoning, the claimant, the legacy. The steward's columns. The woman's list.)*
> *(The measuring is done the way Rose does everything: in the morning, with the books open, the Park beyond the window giving its own account in hedges and water.)*
> *(Harrow closes the Season's ledger himself — the columns agreed, the measure complete — and blots the page with the care of a man signing a treaty. There is something in his manner, as he sets the pen down, that she has never seen in ten seasons of mornings. Satisfaction, unguarded. The books are not just balanced. They are beautiful, and the steward knows it, and will never say so.)*
> *(On his shelf the ten ledgers stand in their row — ten seasons, ten volumes, the spines lettered in the steward's exact hand. The physical measure of the span: the years, bound. Leather and ink, and every column agreed.)*
> *(The list is complete, and the completeness is the measure — or near enough; Harrow would want the figures, and the figures are in the ledgers, and the ledgers are beautiful.)*
> *(The mornings are the measure too, stacked like the years themselves, one upon another: the shutters opened, the fires lit, the chocolate at eight, ten seasons of ordinary days. The measure is the morning. The morning holds.)*
> *(She leaves Harrow with his beautiful books and goes out to the terrace, where the Park is doing its own accounting in light and water, and the two accounts — his and the ground's — agree, as they have agreed for ten seasons, to the penny and to the hedge.)*

scenes.synopsis: the span — the Hartwell's; the kept, the held. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The household book's cover is worn smooth where her palm rests — ten seasons of mornings, the leather polished by her own hand. Harrow offered to have it rebound. She refused. The wear is the record, too.)*
> *(The household book lies on the morning room desk — the cover worn, the pages full, the weight of ten seasons in her hands when she lifts it — and the future is the blank pages at the back.)*
> *(She does not total it. Totals are Harrow's department, and Harrow has totaled. She holds it: the second Assembly's lists begun, the years' entries waiting, the unwritten. The book is not closed. It is continued — the span kept, and the keeping continuing past the page.)*
> *(The ink is hers and Harrow's both: his pen, her hand, the columns entered daily for ten seasons, the way it has always been done. The measure entered by hand, in ink and habit. The book knows her the way the Park knows her boots.)*
> *(Everyone keeps the measure in their own way, which is the point of measures: the staff in the routine — the fires lit, the shutters opened, the bread baked; the village in the telling, growing truer; the ton in the verdict, settling into fact, keeping it by wanting. The kept, kept by wanting — London's own method, and not the worst one.)*
> *(She turns a blank page, and the page is clean, and the cleanness is not emptiness but readiness — the way a field is ready, the way the ballroom was ready. The years ahead will write themselves in the same hand, daily, exactly, for good.)*
> *(She closes the book and sets it square on the desk, and the squaring is the whole of the ceremony. The ten seasons, kept. The annual, begun. The forever, entered — in pencil, some of it, because even forever needs revising. She smiles at the thought, and tells no one, and goes down to the garden.)*

scenes.synopsis: ★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — THE WOMAN'S GIFT (how the legacy is marked: the last word, the changed, or the kept). The years deepen; decide the marking. (Turns: 3 — the decision)
scenes.prose:
> *(The years deepen, and the woman asks her marking. Rose stands in the walled garden — the Hartwell rose's first bush budding, the autumn beds in order — and understands that the legacy has three possible markings, and she must choose which one marks it.)*
> *(The last word: the Gazette's verdict, printed — Bell's valedictory, the Season pronounced, the paper's seal on the ten years. The changed: the Season's alteration — London different, the ton convened, the change made visible in drawing rooms and ballrooms. The kept: the house's promise — the Park, the practice, the annual, the keeping carried forward.)*
> *(The rose bush holds its buds — the breeding program's triumph, the thorns, the promise — and the gardener's boy tends it with the gravity of a boy promoted beyond his years, unaware that he tends the legacy's own flower. The autumn beds hold their order around it. The garden, reclaimed stone by stone across the seasons, waits.)*
> *(Three markings, and all of them true — that is the difficulty, again, and the pleasure. The last word is printed; it will outlast them all. The changed is real; London is different. The kept is hers; the house, the Park, the promise. None of them stain. A gift should be chosen, not settled for, and she holds the three the way she held the law: looking for the one that is most hers.)*
> *(The marking is a gift, and the giving wants its proper hour, and the hour is not yet — not standing in the garden with the gardener's boy watching. She will give it in the morning room, alone, the way the best things are done: quietly, and for good. The buds hold their promise. The woman holds her marking.)*
*★ KEY DECISION 2/3 — The woman's gift:*
- **The last word** — *the verdict, marked.* The mark is the Gazette's verdict: Bell's valedictory, the Season pronounced in print. (Consequence: the legacy will be sealed by the paper's word — the verdict outlasting them all, on the paper's own terms.)
- **The changed** — *the record, marked.* The mark is the altered Season: London different, the ton convened, the change made visible. (Consequence: the legacy will be sealed by the change itself — the Season different because she was in it.)
- **The kept** — *the held, marked.* The mark is the keeping: the house, the Park, the promise carried forward. (Consequence: the legacy will be sealed by the keeping — the practice, the annual, the promise renewed.)
> *(She leaves the garden with the marking ungiven, and the ungiven sits in her like a letter unsent — present, addressed, waiting for its hour. The gardener's boy goes about his work. The buds hold. The woman's gift is hers to give — the last word, the changed, or the kept — and whichever she gives, the giving is the point.)*

scenes.synopsis: the marking — the gift, the given; the legacy, the marked. (Turns: 7)
scenes.prose:
> *(The marking is given in the morning room, alone, without witnesses — no ceremony. The Assembly's marking was ceremony; this is the other kind.)*
> *(She lays three papers on the desk in a row: the Gazette's final number — Bell's valedictory, the verdict; the household book, open to the page — the record; the charter's draft — the promise. The three markings, in paper. She looks at them the way she looked at the hedges' line in the second season: checking for the true one. The light is the morning's. The chocolate cools. The gift wants daylight.)*
> *(The giving: a letter folded and sealed — Bell's direction, in Rose's hand — thanking the paper for the watching, and for the last word, on the paper's own terms. A page dated in the household book — the marking, entered. A word to Harrow in the office — the measure, the years. The gift is placed the way stones are placed: finally, and to stay.)*
> *(The quiet after: the room empty, the desk clear, the morning continuing — the post sorted, the day resumed. The marking is given, and the giving leaves no trace, which is the nature of the best gifts: they vanish into the ordinary and change it from inside.)*
> *(She feels it in her shoulders as she leaves the desk — the weight she felt ten seasons ago, holding the codicil for the first time. The same weight, the same shoulders, the woman grown to fit it. The morning continues. The gift sits on the day like light on water.)*
> *(Letitia finds her at the desk — the social general, reviewing the dispatches — and reads the room in a glance. "Given?" "Given." scenes.prose:
> *(The years deepen, and the woman asks her meaning. Rose stands in the west gallery at evening — the Hartwell dead on the walls, the house settling below — and understands that she has three possible meanings, and must choose which one she is.)*
> *(The whole: she means the Park — the ground, the hedges, the water, the whole she built, the ten seasons made visible in earth. The legacy: she means the keeping — the books, the debts, the practice, the ten seasons themselves, what she did and how. The future: she means the years ahead — the Assembly, the annual, the promise renewed, the forever begun.)*
> *(The painted dead watch with their painted patience — the Hartwell line, centuries of them, who kept the house in their own ways and their own weathers. She stands among them the way she stood among them ten seasons ago, a girl with a codicil, and the difference between then and now is the whole of the story, and the story asks its meaning.)*
> *(Three meanings, and all of them true — the difficulty, again, and the honor. The whole is hers; she built it. The legacy is hers; she kept it. The future is hers; she convened it. She holds the three the way she held the law and the marking: looking for the one that is most herself. The gallery is quiet. The house settles. The meaning waits, undecided, the way the best things wait: without hurry.)*

- **The whole** — *the Park, meant.* The woman means the Park: the ground, the hedges, the water — the whole she built. (Consequence: her meaning will be the ground itself — Hartwell Park, whole, as she made it.)
- **The legacy** — *the legacy, meant.* The woman means the legacy: the ten seasons, the keeping, the promise. (Consequence: her meaning will be the ten seasons themselves — what she kept, and how.)
- **The future** — *the future, meant.* The woman means the future: the annual, the years ahead, the promise renewed. (Consequence: her meaning will be the years to come — the Assembly, the keeping, the forever begun.)
> *(One of the painted dead — a Hartwell of the last century, by the north window — has the look of a woman who chose, and chose well, and never explained herself. Rose has always liked that portrait. She looks at it now, and the painted woman looks back, and neither of them says anything, which is the whole of the conversation.)*
> *(She does not decide it standing in the gallery — the meaning wants its proper hour, and the hour is not yet. The dead watch. The house settles. The lamps are lit below. Whichever she is, the being is the point, and the years will do the rest — the way they have done the rest for ten seasons, faithfully, in order, without fuss.)*

> *(The night staff move softly — the watchman on his rounds, the kitchen banked, the lamps turned low in the corridors. The house breathes in its sleep the way the Park breathes under the frost: steadily, and without being asked.)*
> *(The house at night is the legacy's own hour — the lamps lit, the shutters closed, the staff at the evening's service, the day's work put away.)*
> *(The legacy, the Hartwell: the charter in the strongbox, the codicil beneath, the ledgers on Harrow's shelf. The woman's — kept by her hand, in her ink, ten seasons of mornings. The charter's — sealed, witnessed, read aloud at the Assembly. The forever — the annual, the promise, the keeping kept forward.)*
> *(The west gallery sleeps under its painted dead. The ballroom sleeps under its bagged chandeliers. The library sleeps with the Gazette's run on its shelf. The house sleeps the way kept houses sleep: in order, without fuss.)*
> *(In the morning room the household book lies square on the desk — the second Assembly's lists begun, the years' entries waiting. The future, filed. The forever, entered — in pencil, some of it.)*
> *(Rose walks the night enfilade — the lamps, the quiet, the house's breathing — and the legacy is the Hartwell's the way the Park is the ground's: kept, and keeping.)*
> *(She stands at the stair's head, and the house is below her, whole, and the night is around it, whole, and the woman — the legacy's, the Hartwell's — goes up to bed, and the house keeps the night the way it keeps everything: without fuss, and for good.)*

scenes.synopsis: the Gazette's last word — Bell's final sting; arch, precise; reward-only, never mystery. (Turns: 1 — the reading)
scenes.prose:
> *(The morning Gazette, read over chocolate. Mrs. Nance Bell, proprietor, in her own dry voice — the last word:)*
> *"The Season being concluded, the Assembly convened, and the accounts balanced, this paper takes its leave of Hartwell Park with the following observations: that the ruin is gone, the debts are paid, the roof holds, and the rose is blooming. That the ton has given its verdict, the village has told its story, and the ground has kept its record — and that all three agree, which is rarer than it sounds. The rest is keeping."*
> (T1 · stance) *Rose reads it twice — the amusement first, then the reckoning: the years pronounced true in print as well as in the ground, and Bell has made the verdict permanent, which is Bell's way of making it forever. She files the sting under its lesson: in London, the Season the Gazette watched is the Season she changed — and the last word is the Park's, the rose's, the keeping's.* — remembered: *the lesson: the Season the Gazette watched is the Season she changed — and the last word is the Park's, the rose's, the keeping's.*

scenes.synopsis: the closing — no hook; the eight doors, open; the Season, whole. (Turns: 8)
scenes.prose:
> *(The Season's last light is on the garden, and the garden holds it the way the house holds everything: without fuss.)*
> *(The first rose is blooming — the Hartwell rose, the breeding program's triumph, open in the evening air, the shade exact, the thorns honest. The ten seasons, in one flower: the ruin, the labor, the finishing — the breeding, the failing, the blooming.)*
> *(Hartwell Park stands whole above the lawns — the roof true, the windows lit, the zones around it in their order: the hedges in their lines, the lake keeping the light, the garden in its autumn, the drive curving to the gates. The whole, in the last light.)*
> *(The eight doors stand open — the house's doors, open to the evening, the night air moving through the enfilade. The ballroom's floor holds the week's dancing in its polish. The library's shelf holds the Gazette's run. The strongbox holds the charter. The doors, open.)*
> *(Rose stands at the terrace's edge — the woman at the heart of it, the gown the evening's — and the Season's last light is on the changed Season, and the changed Season holds the light.)*
> *(No hook. The image holds: Hartwell Park whole, the first rose blooming, the eight doors open, the woman at its heart. The ten seasons, kept. The annual, begun. The forever, entered.)*
